#### “0.11” — Feynman simulation argument (line 289)

- **Positive note — excellent anti-parallelism correction:** The paragraph correctly rejects the misleading idea that a quantum computer simply evaluates all branches and reads them all out.
- **Strong dimensional defect:** An arbitrary `n-particle` system does not necessarily have $2^n$ amplitudes; $2^n$ applies to $n$ two-level systems. Use local dimension $d$ and $d^n$, then specialize to qubits.
- **Complexity precision:** Explicit full-state storage/update is exponential, but simulating selected observables/dynamics can be efficient for stabilizer, free, low-entanglement, sign-problem-free, tensor-network, Monte Carlo, perturbative, symmetry-reduced, and other structured regimes. The paragraph notes restrictions; avoid implying a proved generic lower bound over all classical algorithms/models.
- **Historical precision:** Feynman’s argument motivated quantum simulation but was not a modern formal complexity theorem. Distinguish heuristic/state-description pressure from unconditional hardness.
- **Physical-computation caveat:** A quantum system `enacts` dynamics without exposing all amplitudes; preparation, control, fault tolerance, runtime, precision, and extracting observables still consume resources. Nature’s evolution is not automatically a usable efficient algorithm.
- **Strong overclaim — exact dependency/source of power:** Exponential Hilbert-space dimension alone is neither sufficient for speedup nor an accessible memory. Classical stochastic systems also have exponentially large configuration spaces. Advantage comes from controllable dynamics, interference/entanglement, task structure, and measurement-accessible outputs under complexity assumptions.
- **Local-system nuance:** A local quantum simulator can evolve for physical time with polynomial gate cost under assumptions, but general state preparation and full-state output remain exponential. Connect to Lloyd accurately.
- **Formatting:** Replace code spans `$n,2^n$` with math. Split the very long paragraph into problem, caveats, and insight.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** The unnatural bookkeeping versus enacted dynamics contrast is among the prelude’s best, provided dimension is not made magical.

#### “0.11” — Deutsch universal quantum computation and first oracle problem (line 291)

- **Positive note — excellent scale contrast:** Tiny speedup, enormous conceptual move is a compelling and fair way to value the first result.
- **Universality precision:** Verify Deutsch’s exact Church–Turing principle and simulation theorem. A universal quantum machine simulates suitably encoded finite quantum systems/computations to specified accuracy; `any physical system ... including itself` may overstate scope, infinite dimensions, precision, and self-simulation.
- **Historical algorithm verification:** Check the original 1985 success/inconclusive probabilities and the attribution of the deterministic modern one-query circuit to Cleve–Ekert–Macchiavello–Mosca (1998), versus Deutsch–Jozsa (1992) and later textbook simplification.
- **Query-model precision:** The classical exact deterministic query complexity is two for deciding constant versus balanced on a one-bit Boolean oracle; randomized one-query success depends on prior/error criterion, and oracle construction cost is hidden. State the promise explicitly.
- **BQP/advantage caution:** An oracle query separation does not automatically yield an end-to-end runtime separation or physical advantage; the paragraph recognizes finer randomized comparison but should state this boundary.
- **Philosophical wording:** Physical law constrains efficiently realizable computation, while mathematical complexity models also depend on encoding/uniformity/error. `not mathematical convention` is a false dichotomy.
- **Formatting:** Probabilities and function/oracle notation should be LaTeX rather than code.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The historical precision about the original algorithm is exactly the kind of detail that makes this review-worthy history.

#### “0.11” — possibility/necessity/universality slogan (line 293)

- **Positive note — exceptionally memorable organization:** The sentence is an effective mnemonic and can serve as the episode’s spine.
- **Strong rhetoric qualification:** Feynman did not make quantum computers logically `necessary`; he made them compelling candidates for natural quantum simulation. Benioff/Deutsch contributions were not individually sufficient or literally indispensable in a counterfactual historical sense.
- **Internal inclusion defect:** The slogan says three contributions are `independent` while Manin has just been named an independent origin but omitted. Include Manin or explicitly call the slogan a pedagogical compression rather than complete priority map.
- **Complexity-history nuance:** Deutsch’s universal model did not by itself create a complete complexity theory; Bernstein–Vazirani, Yao, and many others formalized it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** Keep the cadence, soften historical absolutes in surrounding prose.

#### “0.11” — quantum circuits and QTM equivalence (line 295)

- **Positive note — model-choice explanation:** Readers learn why the book teaches circuits instead of merely encountering them as convention. The instruction-set analogy is useful for developers.
- **Turing-machine programming claim:** Turing machines are abstract models used for algorithms/proofs, not inherently `poor for programming`; circuit models expose parallel/local gate resources more naturally. Phrase as suitability for architecture/complexity, not quality.
- **Historical verification:** Verify Deutsch’s 1989 network result, gate-set/universality details, and Yao’s 1993 theorem assumptions (uniformity, approximation/error, overhead, input model). `Polynomially equivalent` needs the resource/error notion.
- **Strong overstatement:** The equivalence does not license the field to `forget ... entirely`; quantum Turing machines remain useful for uniform complexity definitions and foundational equivalence. Circuits dominate exposition/implementation.
- **Chapter consistency:** The preface assigns gates to Chapter 8 and circuits to Chapter 9, while this says `Chapter 8 onward actually uses` the circuit model. Verify the first formal circuit-model chapter/reference.
- **Analogy refinement:** A quantum circuit is closer to a program/IR or logical circuit than an instruction set alone; physical native gates and compiled instruction sets differ by platform.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The historical reason for the book’s visual/programming language is immediately relevant.

#### “0.11” — Lloyd universal simulation theorem (line 297)

- **Positive note — important constructive closure:** The paragraph correctly moves from Feynman’s motivation to a gate-model algorithm and previews later simulation methods.
- **Strong scope qualification:** Lloyd’s theorem addresses finite-dimensional/local Hamiltonians under efficient specification, bounded/local interactions, chosen norm/error, initial-state and observable assumptions. `Any local quantum system` and `essentially every physically realistic many-body system` are too broad for long-range interactions, fields/bosons, unbounded operators, continuum limits, and difficult encodings.
- **Complexity precision:** Product-formula gate complexity depends on number/norm/commutators of terms, time, error metric, and order; `polynomial in inverse error` may describe the original bound but not all modern methods. State the theorem’s actual scaling/assumptions, not only a high-level polynomial.
- **End-to-end caveat:** Efficient dynamical simulation does not guarantee efficient state preparation, observable estimation, or useful output extraction. These may dominate applications.
- **Historical wording:** `Deutsch had just defined` is odd a decade later and circuit models evolved through multiple contributors. Use `the emerging digital gate model`.
- **Priority/superlative:** `the moment quantum simulation entered the algorithmic catalog` and `completion` of Feynman are historiographic judgments requiring support; earlier specialized digital/analog simulation work may complicate them.
- **Method list:** Trotterization, LCU, qubitization, and qDRIFT belong to different eras/assumptions. Verify capitalization/coverage in Chapter 28 and avoid making the 1996 paper appear to contain later methods.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Turning intuition into constructive gates gives a satisfying technical endpoint, though the paragraph is overloaded.

#### “0.12 The Algorithmic Shock” — anti-hype checkpoint (lines 299–303)

- **Positive note — excellent early inoculation:** Measurement yields one sampled outcome; amplitudes must be shaped before measurement; problem structure matters. This is one of the manuscript’s clearest public-misconception corrections.
- **Qualification — “free” superposition:** Preparing a particular coherent superposition, loading data, maintaining it fault tolerantly, and implementing transformations are not free. A uniform Hadamard superposition is cheap in the gate model; arbitrary amplitude encoding can be expensive. Replace the slogan with this distinction.
- **Overunification:** Not every useful algorithm is best explained as amplitudes labeled `wrong` canceling and `right` reinforcing. Sampling, simulation, phase estimation, quantum walks, and state-generation tasks may have distributed outputs/no single right answer. `Interference engineering` is a powerful default lens, not a complete taxonomy.
- **Grover wording:** `geometric search space` suggests exploitable geometry, while basic Grover search is deliberately unstructured. Amplitude rotation occurs in a two-dimensional subspace, but that is algorithm geometry rather than input structure.
- **Resource nuance:** Superposition/interference also occur in classical waves; quantum advantage requires the whole state/control/measurement/computational model and favorable complexity, not interference alone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** The confident myth-busting voice and design-language framing are memorable.

#### “0.12” — oracle/query-complexity definitions and real-world bridge (line 305)

- **Positive note — unusually honest cost ledger:** Oracle construction, preparation, readout, and best classical algorithms are named explicitly, preventing query separation from being sold as an application speedup.
- **Oracle definition:** A quantum oracle is normally a coherent unitary such as $|x,y\rangle\mapsto|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle$ or a phase oracle, not merely an API returning $f(x)$. Reversibility/coherent superposition access is the resource and should be stated.
- **Overstatement:** Oracle problems can model concrete query-limited tasks; they do not `by themselves` prove no real-world speedup, but neither are they purely unreal. Phrase them as access-model results whose implementation relevance must be established.
- **Strong causal/historical concern:** Shor did not simply replace a Simon-style oracle with modular exponentiation, nor did `all` surrounding costs automatically survive. Simon inspired hidden-period methods; Shor supplied an efficient arithmetic function and end-to-end polynomial algorithm under standard models. State that specific bridge.
- **Complexity nuance:** Exponential query separation is neither necessary nor sufficient for practical advantage; oracle gates may hide exponential work/data access, and polynomial query improvements may still matter. `can later turn` is appropriately conditional but should not privilege one path.
- **Formatting:** Use mathematical notation rather than code spans and give both standard oracle forms.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The “asks fewer questions” paraphrase is intuitive and the honest ledger adds trust.

#### “0.12” — early-oracle-toolkit transition (line 307)

- **Positive note:** A brief chronological reset keeps a dense algorithm list navigable.
- **Scope:** Oracle research did more than expand a toolkit; it developed complexity classes/lower bounds and exposed limitations. `expanded the toolkit` is fine as narrative shorthand.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Functional pacing sentence.

#### “0.12” — Deutsch–Jozsa (line 309)

- **Correctness:** Under the constant-versus-balanced promise, the exact quantum algorithm uses one query and a deterministic exact classical algorithm needs $2^{n-1}+1$ worst-case queries.
- **Essential comparison caveat:** A bounded-error randomized classical algorithm distinguishes the cases with a constant number of random queries for fixed error, so the exponential separation is only against deterministic exact query complexity. The paragraph says this; make it visually inseparable from the milestone claim/table.
- **Mechanism nuance:** The final measurement is deterministic in the ideal algorithm because phase kickback and a Walsh–Hadamard transform encode a global parity-like signature; `answer concentrates` is accessible but should identify the oracle’s phase form.
- **Repetition:** `superposition is free...` repeats the checkpoint almost verbatim and retains the problematic `free` claim. Use this space for the randomized comparison or a one-line circuit intuition.
- **Formatting:** Convert $n$, $2^{n-1}+1$ to math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** One-versus-exponential is striking, but readers must not miss how restricted the comparison is.

#### “0.12” — Bernstein–Vazirani (line 311)

- **Correctness:** The standard noiseless linear inner-product oracle reveals an unknown $n$-bit string with one quantum query versus $n$ deterministic classical queries.
- **Model qualification:** Specify oracle $f_s(x)=s\cdot x\bmod2$, exact-query setting, and whether randomized bounded-error lower bounds are being claimed. End-to-end input/output already requires measuring $n$ bits, so query versus gate/readout complexity differs.
- **Historical verification:** `first paper to formulate BQP rigorously` should be tied to the Bernstein–Vazirani quantum complexity paper’s conference/journal chronology and exact definition; avoid assigning later polished terminology retroactively without citation.
- **Formatting:** Hidden string length belongs in math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The one-query recovery is clean but less dramatic after Deutsch–Jozsa without explaining phase kickback.

#### “0.12” — Simon algorithm and Shor connection (line 313)

- **Positive note — historically consequential bridge:** The hidden-symmetry formulation and connection to Shor accurately explain why Simon mattered beyond its oracle problem.
- **Definition precision:** State the promise $f(x)=f(y)$ iff $y=x$ or $x\oplus s$ for nonzero hidden $s$, and distinguish query count from total repetitions/classical linear algebra.
- **Lower-bound scope:** The $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ classical randomized query lower bound is under the promise and bounded error/average or worst-case distribution assumptions. `on average` needs a defined input/oracle distribution.
- **Historical anecdote verification:** STOC 1993 rejection, Shor’s program-committee role/advocacy, immediate recognition, and both papers’ FOCS 1994 appearance are specific claims requiring a reliable source or firsthand citation.
- **Group terminology:** $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n$ is fine; convert code to math and clarify the hidden subgroup is $\{0,s\}$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Rejection-to-breakthrough is compelling, though anecdotal details must be sourced.

#### “0.12” — Shor high-level explanation (line 315)

- **Positive note — layered-reader design:** A one-paragraph takeaway plus permission to defer machinery respects historical readers while preserving technical depth.
- **Algorithm description:** Factoring reduces probabilistically to order finding; period finding can be formulated via QFT sampling or phase estimation. `QFT applied via phase estimation` is a modern unification and should be labeled, not necessarily Shor’s original presentation.
- **Classical-hardness wording:** No efficient classical factoring/order-finding algorithm is known; it is not proved impossible. Replace `cannot do efficiently` with `is not known to do efficiently`.
- **Scope:** Shor’s algorithm is bounded-error/probabilistic with repetitions and classical checks. `find ... in polynomial time` should include success amplification.
- **Formatting:** $N$ belongs in math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The casual-reader handrail works extremely well.

#### “0.12” — Shor steps 1–3 (line 317)

- **Strong correctness qualification — reduction success:** The at-least-$1/2$ good-order probability requires conditions (typically odd composite $N$ that is not a prime power, with random $a\in\mathbb Z_N^*$); if $\gcd(a,N)>1$, a factor is already found. Handle even/prime-power cases and use both $\gcd(a^{r/2}\pm1,N)$.
- **Strong unitary-definition defect:** $U_a|x\rangle=|ax\bmod N\rangle$ is a permutation only on residues $0\le x<N$ when $\gcd(a,N)=1$. A $\lceil\log_2N\rceil$-qubit space also contains $x\ge N$; define a reversible extension (often identity there).
- **Strong eigenstate defect:** Standard phase-estimation order finding initializes $|1\rangle$, which is an equal superposition of eigenstates on its multiplicative orbit; it does not generally use `a uniform superposition over computational-basis inputs` as the target. Alternatively describe the two-register periodic-function/QFT version consistently. The current hybrid is wrong.
- **Eigenvalue precision:** On the cyclic subspace generated by $|1\rangle$, eigenphases are $k/r`; the entire permutation $U_a$ may contain other cycles/eigenvalues. `every eigenphase` is too broad.
- **Continued-fraction conditions:** The measured phase must be accurate enough, $k$ may share factors with $r$, and repeated samples/classical verification/lcm recovery may be needed. `smallest denominator` alone can return a divisor.
- **Notation/formatting:** Use $a^r\equiv1\pmod N$, $U_a$, ceilings, eigenvalues, and measured fractions as LaTeX, not code. This paragraph is too dense for prose; use four numbered blocks with assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High for prepared readers, low for cold readers.** The machinery is fascinating but current conflation can create a durable false model.

#### “0.12” — Shor step 4, resource cost, discrete log, and infrastructure impact (line 319)

- **Positive note — correctly deglamorizes QFT cost:** Modular arithmetic, not the QFT alone, dominates realistic logical resources.
- **Strong resource-scaling concern:** $O(n^2\operatorname{polylog}n)$ with Schönhage–Strassen-style multiplication depends on reversible arithmetic architecture, gate set, ancilla, depth versus count, and uniform construction. Traditional $O(n^3)$ is a common textbook count, but modern best bounds differ. Cite a resource model and do not present one asymptotic as implementation-neutral.
- **QFT nuance:** Exact QFT over a roughly $2n$-qubit control register uses $O(n^2)$ controlled rotations; approximate QFT can use fewer gates, while fault-tolerant synthesis costs/precision matter.
- **Discrete-log scope:** Shor-style algorithms solve discrete log in suitable finite cyclic/abelian groups with efficiently implementable group operations, including common finite-field and elliptic-curve groups. `Same construction` and `2D Fourier peak slope` are intuition, not a universal algorithm description.
- **Strong table consistency warning:** The QFT used for order finding acts over a power-of-two control register ($\mathbb Z_{2^t}$ in the standard circuit), not simply `over $\mathbb Z_N$` as the later table says. Correct the table.
- **Protocol impact:** RSA, finite-field DH, ECDH, DSA/ECDSA and related certificates/signatures/key exchange are affected; TLS/SSH/S/MIME/code signing also contain symmetric/hash components that are not wholly broken. Say vulnerable public-key components, not the infrastructures wholesale.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The industrial stakes land strongly; the single paragraph mixes too many abstraction levels.

#### “0.12” — symmetric cryptography and current NIST PQC status (line 321)

- **Positive note — valuable anti-apocalypse calibration:** Public-key migration is separated from symmetric/hash effects, and `doubling` is explicitly called a rule of thumb rather than theorem.
- **Cryptographic nuance:** Grover gives generic key/preimage search scaling, but circuit depth, parallelization, memory, multiple targets, security margins, and structured cryptanalysis matter. Quantum collision algorithms have different exponents/resources, so output-size recommendations cannot be summarized by universal doubling.
- **Overstatement:** `cryptographic apocalypse ... specifically a public-key event` understates authentication/signature ecosystems, harvest-now-decrypt-later, symmetric security reductions, and potential algorithm-specific attacks. `The most disruptive known generic impact is on current public-key cryptography` is safer.
- **Verified current fact:** NIST officially published FIPS 203/ML-KEM, FIPS 204/ML-DSA, and FIPS 205/SLH-DSA on 13 August 2024. Link the [official approval notice](https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2024/postquantum-cryptography-fips-approved) and individual standards/errata rather than embedding a long mutable catalog.
- **Clear current factual defect:** The manuscript says FN-DSA/FIPS 206 is `in draft as of 2026`. NIST’s current 2026 material says **Draft FIPS 206 is under development**, not that a public draft has been issued; the [NIST project page](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/Post-Quantum-Cryptography/Post-Quantum-Cryptography-Standardization?data1=v2) and [2026 NIST status slides](https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/presentations/2026/mpts2026-3b1/images-media/mpts2026-3b1-slides-nist-pqc-moody.pdf) support `in development`.
- **Verified HQC status:** NIST selected HQC on 11 March 2025 as a backup/complement to ML-KEM. Its [official announcement](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/03/nist-selects-hqc-fifth-algorithm-post-quantum-encryption) planned a draft about a year later and final standard in 2027. As of the current official project/publications pages, selection is confirmed; do not call it deployable/final.
- **Errata wording:** FIPS 203 has a current planning note about a future correction/update. `minor errata` should not characterize security/standards changes without quoting the official classification; link the live errata spreadsheet and date the snapshot.
- **Maintenance design:** Move volatile NIST pipeline details to Chapter 27/Appendix F or a generated `as of` table. The historical prelude should state durable 2024/2025 milestones and link current status.
- **Pacing:** This is an enormous sentence containing threat analysis plus six standards/status claims. Split into symmetric impact, finalized standards, and in-development algorithms.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High relevance, low readability.** Exact status is valuable, but catalog density derails the historical narrative.

#### “0.12” — Grover and amplitude amplification (line 323)

- **Correctness:** Unstructured marked-item search has quantum query complexity $\Theta(\sqrt N)$ for constant success and classical randomized query complexity $\Theta(N)$ under the black-box model; Grover achieves the upper bound and BBBV establishes optimality.
- **Problem scope:** `list` can imply physically stored random-access data. State oracle membership/search over $N$ candidates; loading/searching an ordinary database may dominate and requires a QRAM/oracle model.
- **Amplitude-amplification qualification:** Given coherent access to a unitary subroutine with success probability $p$, its inverse, and reflections/marking, amplification uses $O(1/\sqrt p)$ calls versus $O(1/p)$ independent classical repetitions. It does not boost literally `any` subroutine for free.
- **Practical-value rhetoric:** Quadratic speedups can be transformative at scale but may lose to fault-tolerance/oracle overhead; `not transformative` is context-dependent. The central square-root ceiling for unstructured black-box search is correct.
- **Formatting:** Use math for $N,O(\sqrt N),\Theta(N)$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The square-root-not-miracle framing is honest and memorable.

#### “0.12” — Shor/Grover public impact and harvest-now threat (line 325)

- **Positive note — strong structured-versus-unstructured contrast:** This is exactly the conceptual distinction readers should retain.
- **Time-sensitive certainty:** `will not be tomorrow either` is unnecessary and impossible to guarantee. State no publicly demonstrated machine currently approaches required fault-tolerant resources and date/source estimates.
- **Harvest-now precision:** Bulk data is typically symmetrically encrypted, while recorded quantum-vulnerable key exchange/wrapped keys/signatures can expose session keys later. Forward secrecy does not protect against future Shor recovery of recorded ephemeral classical DH. Scope protocols carefully.
- **Migration-timing defect:** Systems need migration when confidentiality lifetime plus migration time overlaps estimated cryptographically relevant quantum-computer arrival, not simply when secret lifetime exceeds the `lifetime of a Shor-scale machine`. Use the standard risk-timeline formulation.
- **Generic-Grover claim:** Grover/amplitude amplification applies where an efficiently realizable oracle/checker and coherent iterations exist; not `across the algorithmic landscape` without resource qualification.
- **Algorithm-power list:** Interference is overarching, period finding/amplification/simulation are task frameworks; this is a good nonuniversality slogan if `advantage` remains evidence/model-dependent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** The structure contrast and delayed-decryption scenario create urgency without claiming current breakage, apart from the needless tomorrow guarantee.

#### “0.12” — six-milestone mechanism table (lines 327–336)

- **Positive note — excellent table purpose:** Organizing by mechanism rather than inventor materially improves conceptual comparison and supports the anti-hype thesis.
- **Strong factual defect — Shor row:** `QFT over $\mathbb Z_N$` is misleading/wrong for standard order finding; the arithmetic function is modulo $N$, but the Fourier transform is over the power-of-two control domain (or another chosen sampling domain), while finite-group discrete-log variants differ. Correct the mechanism cell.
- **Deutsch row:** Original 1985 versus deterministic modern version is collapsed into `first strict separation`. Specify which algorithm/model/year establishes the exact separation.
- **BV row:** `first rigorous formulation of BQP` needs publication/source precision and may belong in historical-role footnote.
- **Simon year:** `1993 / 1994` should label submission versus publication explicitly, not present ambiguous alternatives.
- **Hamiltonian row:** Polynomial local-dynamics simulation requires efficient specification, bounded/local terms, state/observable and error assumptions; table brevity should link the qualified paragraph.
- **Formatting/accessibility:** Raw code group notation in table violates the book’s own warning about math in tables/rendering. Use renderer-tested math or a linear definition list. Provide accessible table headers/summary.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Mechanism scanning works; inaccuracies in compact tables propagate especially easily.

#### “0.12” — phase estimation as reusable primitive (line 338)

- **Positive note — excellent reuse insight:** Readers benefit from recognizing that a Shor subroutine reappears in chemistry, linear systems, and simulation.
- **Strong technical qualification:** QPE estimates an eigenphase when supplied coherent controlled powers of an efficiently implementable unitary and an eigenstate (or samples eigenphases according to overlap for a superposition), with precision/success costs. It does not generally `read the eigenvalues of any` unitary cheaply.
- **Historical attribution concern:** Standard quantum phase estimation is commonly associated with Kitaev and later circuit presentations; Shor used period/eigenphase structure but saying `the same gadget Shor built` may be anachronistic. Trace original versus modern formulations.
- **HHL/chemistry caveat:** State preparation, overlap, Hamiltonian simulation, controlled operations, precision, and observable extraction determine end-to-end cost.
- **Hyphenation:** `efficiently implementable` is not hyphenated after an adverb ending in `-ly`.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** A reusable “gadget” gives the algorithm catalog cohesion.

#### “0.12” — post-1996 transition (line 340)

- **Positive note — useful myth prevention:** Explicitly rejecting the hardware-waiting narrative prepares readers for modern algorithmic diversity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The rhetorical reversal creates curiosity about the next catalog.

#### “0.12” — quantum walks, amplitude estimation, HHL, modern simulation, variational algorithms (line 342)

- **Positive note — broad, caveat-aware expansion:** HHL’s fine print/dequantization and the connection back to Feynman prevent a triumphalist list.
- **Quantum-walk precision:** Name representative exponential/polynomial speedups and whether they are oracle, graph, or end-to-end results; `distinct from Fourier` is broadly useful but some spectral techniques overlap.
- **Amplitude-estimation wording:** Canonical QAE offers a quadratic query improvement in precision under coherent oracle/reflection assumptions. Finance/Monte Carlo end-to-end advantage depends on data loading, payoff oracle, fault tolerance, and comparison with advanced classical sampling.
- **HHL wording:** It prepares a state proportional to a linear-system solution and estimates properties; it does not output the full vector. The listed sparsity/conditioning/state preparation/output caveats are excellent and should add precision/error/readout.
- **Dequantization nuance:** Later classical algorithms often exploit matched data-access assumptions/low-rank structure rather than merely `attack` fine print. Use neutral wording and cite specific results.
- **Chapter-routing inconsistency:** Hamiltonian simulation is routed here to Chapter 16 but earlier to Chapter 28; explain frontier algorithms versus applications or correct the links.
- **Strong historical-intent defect — VQE/QAOA:** VQE used shallow variational circuits and early hardware, but QAOA was not necessarily `invented specifically` for noisy pre-fault-tolerant hardware, and `NISQ` was coined later. Present their later adoption as NISQ candidates rather than retroactive original intent.
- **Date/title verification:** QAOA’s 2014 preprint/publication chronology and VQE attribution should be specified; `Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann 2014` may refer to a preprint.
- **Pacing:** Five research programs in one sentence are cognitively overwhelming. Use a dated list/table with mechanism, claimed advantage, and principal caveat.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High for informed readers, moderate for newcomers.** Breadth is exciting, but acronym/concept compression limits retention.

#### “0.13 Quantum Error Correction” — decoherence mechanism (line 346)

- **Positive note — strong system/environment account:** Treating decoherence as entanglement plus loss of environmental access is much better than saying the wavefunction mysteriously disappears.
- **Strong scope correction:** Not every system–environment coupling produces entanglement/decoherence (eigenstates, classical correlations, decoupled/commuting cases), and not all errors arise from environmental information leakage. Coherent control errors, leakage, calibration drift, relaxation, crosstalk, and correlated events need distinct treatment.
- **Measurement analogy qualification:** Tracing out an environment can mathematically resemble an unobserved measurement channel in a selected basis/dilation, but not every channel is simply `someone measured and forgot`, and environment states need not encode a sharp classical outcome.
- **Strong conceptual defect — “collapses to a classical mixture”:** A reduced density matrix becomes partially/approximately diagonal in a pointer basis under decoherence; it is an improper mixture and may retain coherence. Decoherence alone does not solve the definite-outcome/measurement problem or make the system universally classical.
- **Phase wording:** Phases are not necessarily `randomized`; off-diagonal coherences are suppressed because environment branches become distinguishable. This distinction matters for non-Markovian recoherence and error models.
- **Examples:** Substrate vibrations, photons, fields, and thermal baths are useful, but `every nearby atom` is hyperbolic and platform dependent.
- **Cross-reference:** §0.5 introduced only high-level formalism, not open-system reduced states. Link Chapters 12/18 or locally define partial trace.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Privacy/leakage imagery makes open-system physics intuitive; the mixture language needs rigorous restraint.

#### “0.13” — classical emergence and engineering obstacle (line 348)

- **Strong foundational qualification:** Decoherence helps explain suppression of macroscopic interference and preferred stable states but does not alone explain unique outcomes or all classicality. `why the world looks classical` is acceptable only as `a major part of why`.
- **Superlative:** `single biggest engineering obstacle` is subjective; scalable control, fabrication/yield, decoding, cryogenics, interconnects, algorithm/resource overhead, and verification compete. Call noise/decoherence a central obstacle.
- **Privacy metaphor:** Keeping state `private` from the environment is memorable, but computation also requires controlled coupling for gates/readout. The real design tension is isolate from uncontrolled modes while coupling strongly to intended controls.
- **Logical contradiction:** `every isolated quantum system` cannot simultaneously leak information by definition. Use `every imperfectly isolated physical qubit`.
- **QEC role:** Error correction is one layer alongside suppression, materials/control, dynamical decoupling, error avoidance, and fault-tolerant architecture—not the sole answer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The privacy question creates a clean engineering mission.

#### “0.13” — physical/logical qubits and syndrome vocabulary (line 350)

- **Positive note — exceptionally important claim filter:** The warning that raw qubit count without logical status, code, errors, and operations says little is one of the book’s most valuable skeptical tools.
- **Logical-qubit scope:** Many stabilizer codes spread a logical qubit across many physical qubits, but bosonic codes can encode into one oscillator/mode and subsystem/topological encodings complicate `many physical qubits`. Say `redundantly across a larger physical system, often many qubits`.
- **Physical-qubit examples:** A transmon logical two-level subspace is embedded in a multilevel mode; an ion hyperfine qubit and defect spin are encoded level choices. This is a good place to reinforce physical qubit versus full physical Hilbert space.
- **Strong syndrome precision:** A syndrome generally identifies an error equivalence class/coset, not necessarily `which error occurred`; degenerate errors can share syndromes, and decoder inference uses a noise model/history. Replace exact-error language throughout.
- **Measurement type:** Stabilizer/check operators are more general than simple parity, though parity language is intuitive. Syndromes are measurement outcomes (often bits) processed by a classical decoder.
- **Rhetoric:** Calling syndrome existence a `miracle` is entertaining but conflicts with the book’s anti-magic stance. `key construction` preserves wonder without mystification.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Device-count skepticism plus protected-data/error-label separation gives immediate practical value.

#### “0.13” — historical skepticism and Unruh/Haroche–Raimond (line 352)

- **Positive note — takes skepticism seriously:** Naming technically credible critics instead of inventing a strawman makes QEC’s reversal more meaningful.
- **Sociological claim:** `dominant view among many` is internally awkward and needs surveys/citations. Describe documented influential skepticism without claiming field-wide dominance.
- **Bibliographic verification:** Check exact titles, dates, arguments, and publication venues of Unruh (1995) and Haroche–Raimond (1996). Nobel status does not validate every skepticism claim, though it usefully establishes expertise.
- **Noise overgeneralization:** `any uncontrolled interaction ... measurement` repeats the overly broad measurement-channel analogy; coherent unitary errors need not leak information or decohere.
- **Repetition:** This paragraph restates the preceding two decoherence explanations. Use the space for the critics’ actual quantitative/architectural objections.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Credible opposition raises stakes; repeated mechanism explanation slows pacing.

#### “0.13” — measurement/noise distinction and apparent impossibility (line 354)

- **Positive note — intended-versus-uncontrolled information flow:** This is a useful first operational contrast, and syndrome extraction as learning error information without logical information is the central insight.
- **Strong conceptual defect — intent is not the physical distinction:** Measurement is described by an instrument with classical outcomes; noise is a channel/process, which may be coherent and leak no information. An unrecorded measurement is noise, and an intended coherent control error can be noise. Categorize by mathematical information/output/control, not designer intention alone.
- **QEC wording:** Error correction does not literally turn noise into measurement; it couples ancillas to error syndromes, measures checks, decodes, and applies/tracks recovery while preserving logical information.
- **No-cloning nuance:** Classical repetition cannot copy an arbitrary unknown qubit, but quantum codes redundantly encode amplitudes/correlations through an isometry. If hypothetical independent copies existed, measuring one need not collapse another; that sentence relies on an impossible cloning setup and confuses entanglement with copies.
- **Error-correction history:** Classical majority vote is only one classical code; parity-check/syndrome ideas are precisely what quantum codes adapt. The narrative should emphasize constraints, not imply classical coding offered nothing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The apparent structural trap is compelling; precise channel language will make the reversal stronger.

#### “0.13” — reversal sentence (line 356)

- **Positive note:** Excellent dramatic pause and section pacing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** The short sentence earns the coming construction.

#### “0.13” — Shor nine-qubit code and stabilizer checks (lines 358–361)

- **Correctness:** The logical codewords and normalization $1/(2\sqrt2)$ are correct; the code combines repetition structures to correct arbitrary single-qubit errors.
- **Terminology nuance:** Describe precisely whether the outer code protects phase and inner blocks protect bit flips under the chosen encoding. `Concatenation` is intuitive but readers should see the block/factor grouping in semantic math.
- **Formatting defect:** Canonical codewords/check operators are raw Unicode/code blockquotes. Convert to display LaTeX with tensor/block separators and accessible labels.
- **Strong syndrome wording:** Checks such as $Z_1Z_2$ do not reveal a unique physical error in all cases; syndrome patterns locate/categorize correctable errors modulo stabilizers/degeneracy. `Which error occurred` is acceptable only within the single-error lookup table for this code.
- **Check completeness:** The examples $Z_1Z_2,Z_2Z_3,X_1\cdots X_6$ are only part of the eight-generator stabilizer set. Say `for example` is present, but link/display the full set later and verify indices.
- **Arbitrary-error explanation:** Any one-qubit operator expands in Pauli $I,X,Y,Z$; correcting that basis corrects linear combinations. State this rather than listing `bit, phase, or any linear combination` without why.
- **Historical verification:** Shor’s first QEC paper/date and whether this exact presentation was original should be sourced.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Concrete codewords make the “impossible” correction tangible, though cold readers may need block coloring/diagram.

#### “0.13” — no-cloning, syndrome projection, and error digitization (line 363)

- **Positive note — excellent three-stage explanation:** Distributed encoding, syndrome subspaces, and Pauli digitization communicate the core QEC mechanism unusually well.
- **Entanglement qualification:** Encoded arbitrary logical superpositions are distributed and commonly entangled, but entanglement alone is not the redundancy mechanism; code-subspace distance/error-correctability conditions are. Some codewords/subsystem encodings complicate the blanket claim.
- **Strong mathematical wording defect:** Syndrome operators’ eigenstates are not `errors`. Stabilizer/check eigenvalues label syndrome subspaces; error operators map code states into those subspaces. Correct this type error.
- **Degeneracy:** Syndrome measurement may not reveal which physical Pauli occurred, only sufficient equivalence information for recovery. Multiple errors differing by a stabilizer act identically on logical data.
- **Digitization qualification:** A coherent single-qubit rotation expands into Pauli components and ideal syndrome measurement can project onto syndrome sectors. Degenerate/coherent errors sharing a syndrome, multi-qubit errors, correlated noise, imperfect checks, leakage, and logical components may not become one uniquely correctable Pauli.
- **Probability wording:** `no error with probability close to 1` depends on a small rotation angle and code state; give the $\cos^2(\theta/2)$/$\sin^2(\theta/2)$ example if desired.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** `Continuous → discrete → correctable` is a powerful progression; its assumptions must be explicit.

#### “0.13” — Steane, CSS, and stabilizer formalism (line 365)

- **Positive note — strong classical-to-quantum coding bridge:** Generator/parity-check/dual-code inheritance gives developers and coding theorists a useful lineage.
- **Resource-efficiency qualification:** Seven data qubits versus nine is lower block length, but `better resource efficiency` can depend on ancillas, syndrome circuits, transversal gates, fault-tolerant gadgets, and target noise. Say smaller encoding block.
- **CSS convention risk:** CSS code notation varies. Under $C_2\subseteq C_1$, specify which code/dual controls $X$/$Z$ distance and required dual-containment/orthogonality precisely. The current one-sentence recipe may have swapped roles under other standard conventions and omits dimensions/distances.
- **Finite-field formatting:** Use $\mathbb F_2$ or define GF(2), with $C_2\subseteq C_1$ and $C_2^\perp$ in math rather than code.
- **Stabilizer precision:** A stabilizer group is an abelian Pauli subgroup not containing $-I$; its common $+1$ eigenspace is the code. Errors that anticommute with checks change syndromes, while normalizer elements can be undetectable logical operators.
- **Scope overclaim:** Stabilizer formalism covers many central codes (Shor, Steane, surface, color, many LDPC) but not all practical/interesting codes or bosonic/nonadditive structures. Replace `most other practical codes` with a scoped statement.
- **Historical attribution:** Calderbank–Shor, Steane, Gottesman, and stabilizer precursors/publication chronology should be checked; `roughly a year` may conflate thesis/preprints.
- **Pacing:** This paragraph contains three major abstractions. Split into Steane/CSS and stabilizers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High for mathematically prepared readers, moderate for newcomers.** The unification is exciting but notation arrives too fast.

#### “0.13” — threshold theorem statement (line 367)

- **Positive note — identifies the true scaling result:** Below-threshold recursive suppression with controlled overhead is exactly what turns code existence into architecture plausibility.
- **Strong theorem-statement defect:** Threshold theorems simulate an ideal circuit of size/depth $L$ with total failure target $\epsilon$ using overhead polylogarithmic in $L/\epsilon$ (details vary), not merely `poly(log(1/epsilon)) per logical operation` independent of circuit size. State the complete scaling target.
- **Noise-model qualification:** There is no one scalar operation error $p$ or universal $p_{\rm th}`; thresholds depend on stochastic/local/coherent/correlated noise norms, gate/measurement/preparation, geometry, decoder, leakage, and fault-tolerant gadgets.
- **Mechanism scope:** Early proofs used concatenation among other constructions, but threshold theorems are not synonymous with concatenated codes; topological and LDPC families use distance scaling instead.
- **Double-exponential claim:** For concatenated codes below threshold, logical error can decrease roughly doubly exponentially with concatenation level while qubit/gate overhead grows exponentially in level, yielding polylogarithmic target dependence. State recursion assumptions/constants.
- **Attribution verification:** Aharonov–Ben-Or, Knill–Laflamme–Zurek, Kitaev dates/preprints/publications and theorem variants need precise citations; avoid one `standard form` masking differences.
- **Formatting:** Convert $p,p_{th},\epsilon,\operatorname{polylog}$ to math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The theorem is the section’s genuine payoff; rigor increases rather than diminishes drama.

#### “0.13” — thresholds, surface code, and 2024 bivariate-bicycle codes (line 369)

- **Strong comparability warning:** Threshold percentages are meaningless without a noise model, circuit, decoder, logical task, and definition. Surface-code code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level thresholds differ by an order of magnitude; `around 1%` is a representative circuit-level depolarizing figure, not a platform guarantee.
- **Historical nuance:** Kitaev’s toric-code proposal, planar/surface variants, fault-tolerant operations, lattice surgery, decoders, and experimental architectures emerged across many papers. Attribute surface code development in a clearer mini-timeline.
- **Hardware mapping:** A 2D nearest-neighbor layout is attractive for superconducting arrays, but routing, boundaries, couplers, leakage removal, control wiring, and fabrication yield prevent a perfectly clean mapping. Ion traps may benefit from nonlocal connectivity but face other costs.
- **Verified BB-code claim with needed numbers:** The 2024 Bravyi et al. paper reports a 0.7% circuit-level threshold on par with its surface-code baseline and a $[[144,12,12]]$ code requiring 288 total physical qubits including ancillas for the cited memory protocol, degree-6 connectivity, and simulated performance under an independent circuit-noise model. Cite the [primary Nature paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07107-7), not only `IBM’s` branding.
- **`Gross` code nuance:** `144-qubit instance` refers to 144 data/code qubits encoding 12 logical qubits; the full syndrome protocol uses ancillas (288 total in the primary comparison). State $[[144,12,12]]$ and explain the nickname (gross = 144) rather than making it sound like a one-logical 144-device code.
- **Projection-versus-demonstration:** The BB results are code/protocol simulations/theory, not a hardware demonstration of the claimed million cycles. `Report thresholds` should say `estimate under the modeled noise/decoder`.
- **Connectivity/decoder state:** Long-range degree-6 connectivity and decoding are explicit design requirements; newer morphing circuits/decoders continue to change the comparison. Date the snapshot and avoid `still under evaluation` without sources.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High relevance, low readability.** This sentence is far too long; split historical surface-code facts from current LDPC research.

#### “0.13” — threshold assumptions and engineering question (line 371)

- **Positive note — assumptions are made visible:** Fresh ancillas, fault-tolerant syndrome/recovery, locality, and subthreshold operations prevent a magical theorem interpretation.
- **Noise-model overrestriction:** Threshold results can tolerate some spatial/temporal correlations if sufficiently local/decaying/bounded; `no correlated bursts` is not a universal theorem assumption. Conversely, cosmic-ray bursts/leakage can defeat simplified independent models. State the relevant theorem’s norm/correlation condition.
- **Missing assumptions:** Efficient classical decoding/feedforward, leakage handling, parallelism/local architecture, accurate preparation/measurement, and bounded coherent/non-Markovian effects matter.
- **Overhead:** Polylogarithmic inverse-error overhead does not mean practical overhead is small; constants, algorithm size, logical gate synthesis, magic states, connectivity, and decoder latency dominate.
- **Positive style:** Impossible → how much engineering is an excellent question shift and should be retained.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The theorem’s conditions turn abstract possibility into an engineering checklist.

#### “0.13” — surface codes, newer families, and current demonstrations (line 373)

- **Surface-code historical qualification:** Kitaev’s 1997 toric/topological code is not identical in every detail to the later planar surface-code architectures. Explain evolution and source `dominant since mid-2000s` rather than asserting it.
- **Category defect:** Lattice surgery is a logical-operation/patch-management technique, not a code family that inherently `compresses overhead`; color codes and quantum LDPC/bivariate-bicycle codes are separate families/tradeoffs, not surface-code variants.
- **Current Google claim — verified but scope it:** Google’s corrected/current [Nature paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y) reports below-threshold **surface-code memories** on Willow at distances 5 and 7, including a distance-7 101-qubit memory with $0.143\%\pm0.003\%$ error per cycle and real-time decoding for distance 5. It explicitly says logical computation still poses additional challenges. The paper has an author correction dated 28 April 2026; cite the corrected version.
- **Strong Quantinuum comparison concern:** Microsoft/Quantinuum reported logical-error/break-even/error-detection results on H-Series and marketed them as `far below the break-even point`; this is not automatically the same evidence as demonstrating asymptotic below-threshold scaling with increasing code distance. The [official announcement](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2024/04/03/advancing-science-microsoft-and-quantinuum-demonstrate-the-most-reliable-logical-qubits-on-record-with-an-error-rate-800x-better-than-physical-qubits/) is promotional and should be backed by the technical paper/protocol before the book calls it a `below-threshold demonstration`.
- **Platform comparison:** Google demonstrates memory, not a universal fault-tolerant processor; Quantinuum demonstrations use different codes/tasks/error metrics. Do not place them in one phrase as equivalent milestones without a comparison table.
- **Cross-reference:** Chapter 25 must carry exact dates, corrected citations, metrics, task scope, and distinction among break-even, error detection/postselection, correction, threshold scaling, logical gates, and fault-tolerant computation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Current milestones make history feel alive, but marketing vocabulary must not replace comparable metrics.

- **Positive note — excellent miniature engineering narrative:** Fatal objection → code → theorem → optimization is a powerful summary and mirrors the book’s broader model-replacement theme.
- **Qualification:** Error correction made scalable quantum computing possible under explicit models; practical system architecture also requires fault-tolerant logical gates, state preparation/distillation, decoding/control, and viable overhead. `Possible system architecture under noise` is appropriately cautious.
- **Historical wording:** `Three decades of resource reduction` includes theoretical estimates and early demonstrations, not a monotonic path to practicality; retain uncertainty about which architecture wins.

#### “0.14” — liquid-state NMR demonstrations (line 383)

State this so `proved abstract algorithms could be run` is not overread.

#### “0.14” — DiVincenzo checklist framing (lines 385–386)

- **Positive note — excellent vendor-evaluation bridge:** Treating the criteria like a deployment checklist directly serves the intended reader.
- **Strong scope defect:** The original five concern quantum computation; the two extra criteria concern communication. A standalone universal quantum computer need not satisfy stationary/flying conversion/transmission. Therefore a vendor failing communication criteria is not necessarily `selling something other than a universal quantum computer`.
- **Necessary/not-sufficient:** The paragraph later admits criteria do not suffice; likewise details such as fault tolerance, error rates, control bandwidth, manufacturability, verification, and economics are not captured. Label them enduring necessary design questions, not a complete vendor test.
- **Historical verification:** Cite the exact 2000 source/version and wording; DiVincenzo’s list circulated in earlier forms.
- **Tone:** `selling something other than` is punchy but accusatory and ignores special-purpose/annealing/simulation/sensing products. Say `making a different or narrower claim`.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The checklist framing makes hardware immediately inspectable.

#### DiVincenzo criterion 1 — scalable characterized qubits (line 387)

- **Qualification:** Logical qubits may be encoded in multilevel systems, oscillators, topological degrees, ensembles, or subsystems; individual addressability can be replaced by global/control schemes. Preserve the criterion’s intent without requiring literal enumerated two-level devices in every architecture.
- **Scaling nuance:** A scalable architecture may change modular hierarchy/interconnect as it grows; `without changing basic architecture` is too rigid. Require a credible scaling path and bounded/manageable overhead.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Concrete and useful.

#### DiVincenzo criterion 2 — initialization (line 388)

- **Positive note:** Initialization as computational boundary is a useful systems insight.
- **Formatting:** Write $|0\rangle^{\otimes n}$ in math, not Unicode/code.
- **Qualification:** Fault-tolerant computation also needs repeated reset/ancilla preparation during operation, not only initial global state. Initialization fidelity, leakage, correlation, speed, and verification matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The boundary analogy is effective.

#### DiVincenzo criterion 3 — coherence versus operation (line 389)

- **Strong metric concern:** $T_{\rm coh}/T_{\rm gate}$ is a crude budget, not a predictor of circuit fidelity. Gate errors, SPAM, crosstalk, leakage, idling, correlated/non-Markovian noise, parallelism, and error correction matter; coherence has $T_1,T_2,T_2^*$ variants.
- **Wording defect:** The state does not generically `randomize` after one coherence time; relaxation/dephasing are channel- and basis-specific exponentials.
- **Threshold perspective:** Useful depth need not fit inside one bare coherence time if active QEC operates below threshold. Criterion predates mature fault-tolerant framing; state that evolution.
- **Formatting:** Convert ratio to math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Gate-budget intuition is useful if clearly labeled rough.

#### DiVincenzo criterion 4 — universal gates (line 390)

- **Correctness qualification:** A universal gate set approximates any target unitary/circuit to chosen accuracy, with scalable uniform compilation; continuous native families may implement subsets exactly. Efficiency/overhead matters, not merely existence of a finite sequence.
- **Physical scope:** Universality at logical level can arise from native gates plus encoded operations, magic-state injection, measurement/feedforward—not necessarily native physical universality.
- **Cross-reference:** Link Chapter 8 and ensure Chapter 8 defines approximate universality, global phase, and gate synthesis.
- **Formatting:** $n$ belongs in math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Familiar software notion of expressive completeness transfers well.

#### DiVincenzo criterion 5 — measurement (line 391)

- **Positive note:** Fidelity, outcome discrimination, demolition/QND consequences, and replaceability turn `readout exists` into an engineering requirement.
- **Historical wording:** Check whether QND preservation/replacement are original criterion or modern elaboration; label additions.
- **Fault-tolerance nuance:** Mid-circuit measurement/reset latency, parallelism, crosstalk, leakage discrimination, classical feedforward, and correlated SPAM are critical beyond terminal readout.
- **Basis scope:** A fixed known basis plus premeasurement gates can realize other projective bases; generalized measurements may use ancillas. Avoid requiring direct arbitrary-basis hardware.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** Destructive versus nondemolition readout is a concrete hardware tradeoff.

#### DiVincenzo communication criteria and checklist limits (line 393)

- **Positive note — explicitly says not a theorem/sufficiency proof:** This is an important restraint.
- **Architecture nuance:** Stationary/flying conversion can be avoided in all-photonic or modular schemes with different encodings; `flying qubit` must include loss/transduction/fidelity/entanglement-generation rates.
- **Historical evidence:** `community converged on` and two decades of influence should be sourced, ideally with examples of platform roadmaps adopting the criteria.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Useful completion of the checklist.

#### “0.14” — diversification transition (line 395)

- **Causal oversimplification:** Platform programs grew from much broader atomic/condensed-matter/optics/control/fabrication lineages than four named precursors. Use these as conceptual influences, not direct roots.

#### Platform catalog — trapped ions (line 398)

- **Positive note — strong species/control specificity:** Hyperfine versus optical/Zeeman encodings and bus/connectivity scaling are accurately distinguished at a useful level.

- **Oversimplified challenges:** Defect centers’ principal challenge is not `not primarily a computing platform`; list physical scaling/entanglement-generation/fabrication/readout constraints. Silicon `small size` is not itself the challenge—variability/addressing/control density are.

- **Accessibility:** Dense six-column Markdown tables are difficult on mobile/screen readers. Provide a linearized definition list or smaller strength/tradeoff table with detailed source-linked snapshot elsewhere.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High scan value, moderate trust.** The bargains are memorable but current rankings look like marketing without evidence normalization.

#### “0.14” — bargains, no winner, and chapter routing (line 416)

- **Positive note — superb organizing metaphor:** `Different bargain with nature` captures multidimensional tradeoffs and discourages single-metric platform wars.
- **Judgmental wording:** Calling defect centers a `poor fit` for general-purpose computation and diversity a `sign of maturity` are plausible interpretations, not facts. Diversity can also indicate unsettled requirements/immaturity. Present both readings.
- **Metric consistency:** `None unambiguous winner` is sensible and should replace all preceding absolute highest/most rankings.
- **Cross-reference usability:** Link Chapters 20–22 and ensure their comparison criteria match this table exactly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** The repeated `buys ... at cost` cadence is engaging and genuinely explanatory.

#### “0.14” — qubit-count warning and hypothetical comparison (line 418)

- **Positive note — high-value skepticism:** Connectivity, gate/readout fidelity, coherence-to-gate time, native set, stability, code, and logical error are the right dimensions beyond raw count.
- **Missing metrics:** Add gate speed/parallelism, leakage/correlations, yield/availability, logical operations, decoder/control bandwidth, uptime/calibration overhead, and task-specific benchmark/resource estimates.
- **Strong unsupported conclusion:** A million nearest-neighbor qubits at $10^{-2}$ versus a thousand all-to-all at $10^{-4}$ cannot be totally ordered without code thresholds, noise bias/correlation, operation times, algorithm, yield, and logical architecture. One might support many logical qubits if 1% is below an appropriate threshold. Do not declare one universally `smaller`.
- **Threshold wording:** `demonstrated below-threshold logical operations` is stronger than below-threshold memory or break-even; use precise milestones.
- **Tone:** `advertising, not measurement` is memorable but too categorical—physical count is a valid measured resource, merely insufficient as performance. Say `a partial inventory metric, not computational capacity`.
- **Formatting:** Error rates belong in math.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The provocative comparison grabs attention; it must not substitute one simplistic ranking for another.

#### “0.14” — quantum system versus useful computer (line 420)

- **Positive note — excellent category boundary:** Quantum effects/control/reproducibility do not establish scalable programmable computation. This directly counters vendor and media conflation.
- **Wording:** `it almost always is` understates that all physical systems are quantum at foundation; the relevant question is accessible coherent degrees and computational control.
- **Scope:** Special-purpose quantum simulators, annealers, sensors, and networks can be valuable without universal gate-model status. The paragraph appropriately legitimizes this; keep that non-dismissive tone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** A clear evaluative principle with real-world use.

#### “0.14” — adiabatic quantum computation (line 422)

- **Category concern:** This is a computational model, while the preceding list is physical platforms. It does not sit `outside` the hardware list in the same taxonomy; adiabatic computation can run on multiple platforms. Separate model taxonomy from platform taxonomy.
- **Correctness qualification:** Ideal AQC follows a ground-state path slowly relative to spectral-gap/matrix-element conditions; degeneracy, endpoint preparation/readout, and runtime matter. `Kept in instantaneous ground state` is an ideal approximation.
- **Attribution:** Farhi et al. introduced algorithmic AQC around 2000, while polynomial equivalence to the circuit model was proved later (e.g. Aharonov et al.) under formal assumptions. Do not attach equivalence to the Farhi citation implicitly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** Ground-state computation offers a striking alternative mental model.

#### “0.14” — quantum annealing and D-Wave (line 424)

- **Positive note — important distinction:** Universal AQC versus heuristic annealing and gate-model milestones are often conflated; separating them is valuable.
- **Definition nuance:** Quantum annealing spans algorithms and hardware with varying coherence/temperature/control; `without strict adiabaticity guarantees` is useful but not a complete definition. Some theoretical annealing models overlap AQC.
- **Speedup wording:** Evidence depends on problem distribution, embedding, classical baselines, wall-clock/resource normalization, and quantum-versus-thermal dynamics. `Contested` is appropriate; cite representative matched studies.
- **Date concern:** D-Wave’s first commercial system is generally associated with 2011; `commercial from late 2000s` needs precise sale/announcement/availability evidence.
- **Universality wording:** D-Wave annealers implement restricted Ising/QUBO schedules; `not universal adiabatic devices` should be sourced and distinguished from theoretical universality with control extensions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Marketing clarification is directly useful and fairly worded.

#### “0.14” — measurement-based quantum computation (line 426)

- **Positive note — clear architectural inversion:** Resource state first, adaptive single-qubit measurement afterward is an excellent concise explanation.
- **Technical qualification:** Universality requires a suitable cluster/resource state, measurement bases/adaptivity, classical feedforward/Pauli-frame tracking, and initial/output handling; not every large entangled state suffices.
- **Model taxonomy:** MBQC is mathematically equivalent to circuit computation but can be compiled from/to gates; calling it `non-gate-model` is acceptable architecturally, not a separate computability class.
- **Photonic fit:** Photonic fusion/cluster architectures exploit measurement and resource-state generation, but measurement is not universally `cheap` once detector efficiency/loss/feedforward are included.
- **Cross-reference:** Link Chapter 32 and ensure it also covers adiabatic/annealing distinctions and universality proofs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Computing by consuming an entangled state is a memorable alternative.

#### “0.14” — engineering synthesis (line 428)

- **Positive note — excellent systems-level close:** Noise, electronics, fabrication, drift, bandwidth, and orchestration correctly widen hardware beyond qubit physics.
- **Optional refinement:** Add packaging/interconnects, cryogenics/vacuum/lasers, yield, verification, decoding, and reliability—but the sentence is already effective and should not become another catalog.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Crisp and concrete, with strong chapter-ending cadence.

#### “0.15 NISQ, Quantum Advantage, and the Present Reality” — heading and era frame (lines 430–432)

- **Positive note — useful consolidation:** The heading groups three concepts readers routinely conflate: a hardware era, computational-advantage experiments, and the state of fault tolerance.
- **Scope concern:** `roughly 2018 to the present` makes NISQ sound like a clean period boundary. Preskill coined the term for an anticipated regime, not a universally agreed era beginning in 2018; fault-tolerant prototypes now coexist with NISQ devices. Prefer “the term emerged in 2018 and still describes much present hardware.”
- **Durability:** `present` dates immediately. The explicit June 2026 timestamp later helps, but the heading would be more durable as “The NISQ era and early fault-tolerance demonstrations.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The promise of a candid present-day reckoning creates momentum.

#### “0.15” — Preskill and the NISQ framing (line 434)

- **Attribution check:** Preskill’s 2018 paper is the correct canonical source; cite the article directly ([Preskill’s publication record and paper](https://www.preskill.caltech.edu/pub.html)).
- **Historical precision:** Preskill described “intermediate scale” as roughly 50 to a few hundred qubits in the near-term devices he anticipated. `tens to thousands` is a useful 2026 extension, but it is not the original definition; distinguish original framing from contemporary usage.
- **Definition concern:** NISQ is not determined by qubit count plus a universal error-rate interval. Connectivity, circuit depth, crosstalk, leakage, measurement, calibration drift, and application-specific utility matter; some devices with thousands of atoms are not equivalent to thousands of programmable gate-model qubits.
- **Metric concern:** `gate error rates around 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴` mixes one- and two-qubit gates, native operations, average benchmarking metrics, and platforms. Some advertised one-qubit errors are below this range; some useful operations are above it. Label the range illustrative and identify the metric.
- **Overstatement:** `no error correction at scale` is ambiguous after the demonstrations described below. If “at scale” means algorithmically useful, sustained fault-tolerant computation, say so; otherwise small logical encodings already contradict the plain reading.
- **Causal overreach:** Variational algorithms, mitigation, hardware-efficient ansätze, and software stacks did not all develop *around the Preskill framing*. Several predate the paper or arose from broader hardware availability. The term organized and popularized an ecosystem; it did not cause the entire lineage.
- **List/date concern:** Qiskit, Cirq, t|ket⟩, and PennyLane are representative rather than exhaustive, and their inclusion will age. A category-first sentence followed by dated examples would be safer.
- **Typography:** Inline scientific values should use the manuscript’s mathematical convention rather than code spans: `$10^{-2}$` to `$10^{-4}$`.
- **Accessibility:** Briefly explain “ansatz” on first use (“parameterized trial circuit”) and why error mitigation differs from error correction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** “The name compressed the awkwardness into a category” is memorable and humane. Preserve it while loosening the causal claim.

- **Essential qualification:** Google did not run the corresponding classical computation for 10,000 years; it extrapolated a benchmark under the classical methods and machine assumptions used then. Write “Google estimated” directly in the headline sentence.

- **Positive note:** The heading promises payoff rather than more chronology, which is exactly what a long prelude needs here.
