## Chapter 13, §13.7 — Complexity-Theoretic Framing (lines 123–145)

### BQP definition, containments, and open separations (lines 123–131)

- **Correctness:** BQP is the class of decision languages decided with bounded error by polynomial-time uniform quantum computation; uniform polynomial-size circuit families are an equivalent standard formulation with gate-set/approximability conditions.
- **Uniformity detail:** Define classical polynomial-time uniform generation of circuits and a fixed finite universal gate set (or efficiently approximable gates). “Uniform family” is important enough not to leave as jargon.
- **Containments:** `$\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}` and `$\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{AWPP}` are known. Showing the sharper chain `$\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{AWPP}\subseteq\mathrm{PP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}` would explain why AWPP is mentioned.
- **Equality-belief nuance:** `$\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}` is a major derandomization belief supported by hardness-vs-randomness results, not a consensus theorem; the paragraph appropriately labels it expected. “Beliefs are not uniform” is a useful epistemic warning.
- **Strict-separation wording:** It is correct that no unconditional strict separation `$\mathrm{BPP}\ne\mathrm{BQP}` or `$\mathrm{BQP}\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}` is known. “No strict separation among BPP, BQP, and PSPACE” should not be read as no oracle/relativized separations; oracle results provide evidence but do not resolve the unrelativized classes.
- **“Only nearby” overclaim:** `$\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{EXP}` is a standard unconditional hierarchy separation, but “the only nearby” is undefined and ignores many hierarchy/space/nondeterministic separations. Use it as one contrast, not an exhaustive claim.
- **Simulation equivalence:** `$\mathrm{BQP}=\mathrm{BPP}` concerns efficient classical randomized simulation for **decision languages** at bounded error, not every notion of strong/weak sampling or full-state simulation. The prose’s general-simulation paraphrase needs this scope.
- **Candidate evidence:** “Candidate hard problems below” supports belief only conditionally/best-known-algorithmically. Oracle separations and complexity-theoretic evidence could also be mentioned; absence of proof is well emphasized.
- **Cross-reference audit:** Verify §17.1 states the deterministic time hierarchy and `$\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{EXP}` with matching definitions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The clean separation of theorem from belief is excellent and intellectually honest; the dense paragraph would benefit from a diagram/table.

### Claimed exponential-speedup region (line 135)

- **Correct epistemic core:** Factoring/discrete logarithm have polynomial-time quantum algorithms and no known polynomial-time classical algorithms, so exponential/superpolynomial speedup claims are conditional on current classical knowledge rather than proven separations.
- **Problem-type nuance:** Factoring, discrete logarithm, Pell’s equation, and period finding are function/search problems; relating them to BQP decision-language separations requires decision versions/reductions.
- **Family overcompression:** Factoring/discrete log/order finding fit finite abelian HSP/period-finding frameworks cleanly. Pell’s equation uses more specialized infrastructure/periodic real-valued structure and should not be casually reduced to the same finite `$\mathbb Z_N` QFT slogan without explanation.
- **QFT wording:** There is no finite-register literal “QFT over `$\mathbb Z`” as a unitary on a finite circuit. Algorithms approximate periodic Fourier analysis using finite registers; name the finite quotient/register and precision.
- **Nonabelian status:** Dihedral HSP has subexponential quantum algorithms and connections to lattice problems; symmetric-group HSP/graph-isomorphism remains resistant to standard Fourier sampling. “Sporadic and fragile” is evocative but not technical—state the known qualitative status with citations.
- **Attribution/evidence:** Current best-known classical/quantum complexities and “long resisting attack” are research-status claims requiring dated sources.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The boundary between spectacular algorithms and unproved class separation is compelling; finer family distinctions increase credibility.

### Claimed polynomial-speedup region and fault-tolerant crossover (line 137)

- **Overstatement:** Polynomial speedups are not all “based on amplitude amplification.” Element distinctness and many graph problems use quantum walks; collision algorithms combine sampling/storage/amplification ideas. Amplitude amplification is one major source, not the universal basis.
- **“Provable” scope:** Query-complexity separations can be proven relative to a matched oracle; end-to-end time speedups over all classical algorithms may remain conditional. Specify the model for Grover, element distinctness, collision, and graph claims.
- **Grover precision:** Unstructured search has optimal quantum query complexity `$\Theta(\sqrt{N/M})` versus classical randomized `$\Theta(N/M)` for constant success under standard promises/access, giving a quadratic query improvement.
- **Fault-tolerance reasoning:** Fixed constants and polylog overhead can erase advantage at finite sizes, while a genuine asymptotic polynomial exponent improvement eventually wins if both cost models and scaling remain valid. The parenthetical correctly acknowledges this distinction.
- **Instance-comparison strength:** Requiring fault-tolerant end-to-end quantum runtime versus the best practical classical method on the same task/accuracy/hardware assumptions is excellent claim-evaluation discipline.
- **Missing costs:** Include data loading, oracle synthesis, magic-state factories, routing, decoding latency, repetitions, classical coprocessors, and verification—not only “error-correction overhead.”
- **Temporal evidence:** “Every practically reachable size” is a strong hardware-era prediction and cannot be inferred from asymptotics; qualify as possible for specific resource estimates and cite them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The asymptotic-versus-crossover distinction is unusually mature and practical; removing universals would make it exemplary.

### Simulation-speedup region (line 139)

- **Correctness:** Sparse/local Hamiltonian simulation admits quantum algorithms polynomial in appropriate system/time/precision/access parameters, and classical simulation of generic quantum dynamics is believed hard.
- **Input/output qualification:** Complexity depends on Hamiltonian access/local description, evolution time, norm, precision, initial-state preparation, and requested observable. A quantum computer does not output the full wavefunction; comparison must match observable/sample tasks.
- **Evidence framing:** “Exponential for many natural physical problems” is a best-known-method gap, not an unconditional separation, as the paragraph commendably says. “Many” and “natural” still need representative problems and classical baselines.
- **Near-term speculation:** “Most likely to be of practical importance in the near term” is a recommendation/prediction requiring a dated evidence base and definition of near term. Fault-tolerant simulation may require substantial resources; near-term analog/digital claims differ.
- **Feynman history:** The motivation is standard, but cite the relevant primary historical source if the book uses named-origin claims elsewhere.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Returning to physics gives the speedup map historical and practical stakes; the final forecast should be marked as judgment.

### Cost-metric taxonomy and T-count claim (line 143)

- **Strong taxonomy defect:** “Time complexity counts gates” and then “gate complexity may distinguish…” does not define four distinct metrics. Total gate count measures circuit size/work; circuit depth (with connectivity/scheduling) approximates parallel time/latency; query count abstracts oracle uses; T-count/T-depth/factory volume are architecture-specific logical resources.
- **Gate weights:** A fixed universal gate-set count can weight all gates equally, while practical resource estimates separate one-/two-qubit gates, measurements, routing, and synthesized rotations. Call this weighted gate cost rather than a separate mathematical definition of time.
- **T-count overclaim:** T-count is often crucial in surface-code/Clifford+T designs because non-Clifford resources are expensive, but it is not universally dominant. T-depth, magic-state factory footprint/rate, spacetime volume, routing, measurements/feed-forward, and code cycles may dominate.
- **Architecture qualification:** “Every `$T` gate consumes a magic state” holds for common magic-state-injection implementations, not every fault-tolerance architecture or native logical gate scheme. State the assumed Clifford+T/surface-code model.
- **Cross-reference audit:** Verify §8.10 discusses T gates, magic-state distillation/injection, and architecture assumptions; the pointer may be misplaced given Chapter 8’s gate focus.
- **Practical rule:** Asking which metric a paper optimizes is excellent; also ask which costs are omitted and how logical resources map to physical qubits/time/error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The accounting warning is essential, but the definitions must themselves be trustworthy.

### Quantum-inspired/dequantization caution and Part 6 promise (line 145)

- **Correct core:** Tensor-network and sample/query dequantization methods can narrow or remove claimed quantum advantages for structured/low-entanglement or powerful-access settings.
- **“Realistic” overclaim:** Tang-style sample-and-query access is a strong data-structure assumption; whether it is realistic depends on preprocessing, updates, storage, and application. Say “comparable access models,” not categorically realistic ones.
- **Parameter specificity:** A claimed exponential dependence on ambient dimension may become polylogarithmic classically while gaps remain polynomial in rank, condition number, precision, sparsity, or error. “Deflate to polynomial” must name the parameter and comparison.
- **Vintage rhetoric:** “A 2018-vintage” is memorable but imprecise and will age. Name the recommendation-system result and dates/citations, then state the lesson generally.
- **Tensor-network distinction:** Tensor networks are broad classical simulation/representation methods, not all “dequantizations” of a named quantum algorithm. Keep the two examples conceptually separate.
- **Promise audit:** Later Chapters 14–16 must explicitly state input access and status of speedup for each algorithm; this line creates a concrete review invariant.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The willingness to revise speedup narratives is excellent and equips readers to resist hype.

- **Overall strengths:** The chapter has a confident, useful mission: replace “all answers in parallel” folklore with amplitude/interference analysis, teach oracle-model skepticism, emphasize transforms and coherent phase access, separate success-amplification modes, and distinguish proven from believed speedups.

- **Highest-priority period/QFT defect:** §13.4 describes exact multiples `$N/r` and a uniform “support” state as Shor-like period finding. Use coset states and distinguish `$r\mid Q` toy peaks from realistic near-`$kQ/r` samples and continued fractions.
- **Highest-priority cost-taxonomy defect:** Time, gate, depth, T-count, and architecture costs are conflated. Replace with a coherent resource table and qualify magic-state/T dominance by fault-tolerance architecture.
- **Highest-priority rhetoric repair:** Interference is a recurring mechanism, not a sufficient universal source of advantage; absence of a clean path-cancellation story is not an impossibility proof; not all abelian functions yield efficiently measurable features; amplitude amplification is not the sole non-Fourier alternative.

- **Grover repairs:** Generalize from one marked item to `$M`, use the two-dimensional rotation angle, distinguish reflection about the prepared state from “all-states average,” and discuss unknown `$M`.
- **Complexity/evidence repairs:** The containment/belief discussion is strong. Qualify decision-language simulation, oracle versus end-to-end separations, Pell/nonabelian-HSP grouping, near-term simulation forecasts, practical crossover claims, and Tang parameter/access details with dated sources.

- **Source-format/render queue:** Long display equations and dense one-line circuit schematics need renderer inspection for overflow and ket/arrow readability. Literal escape defects should be established from raw source/render evidence, not JSON-escaped tool output.
- **Pacing/structure:** At 161 lines the chapter is admirably compact, but several paragraphs carry five or more conceptual claims. Small “model assumptions” and “common template—not universal law” callouts would preserve pace while curbing absolutes.
- **Accessibility:** Metaphors are memorable and math prerequisites modest. Biggest accessibility danger is replacing one myth with another (“interference alone,” “all algorithms are phase sandwiches,” “QFT reads the whole transform”).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10 overall.** The voice is energetic, candid, and often witty. Its punchiest absolutes need narrowing so the fun feels earned rather than polemical.

## Chapter 14, §14.1 — Deutsch’s Algorithm (lines 11–23)

### Problem, promise, and query separation (lines 11–15)

### Circuit initialization and first Hadamards (lines 15–19)

- **Correctness:** `$|0\rangle|1\rangle` followed by `$H\otimes H` produces `$\frac12(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)=|+\rangle|-\rangle`.
- **Pedagogy:** Name `$|+\rangle|-\rangle` immediately and explain why the target begins in `$|1\rangle`: Hadamard turns it into the `-1` eigenstate of `$X`, enabling kickback.
- **Circuit completeness:** A small circuit diagram would be more readable than prose plus only the first-state equation, especially since the chapter already has SVG algorithm figures elsewhere in Part 6. If no diagram is used, display the post-oracle and post-final-H states too.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The deliberate `$|1\rangle` ancilla feels like a trick whose reason is satisfyingly revealed by kickback.

### Phase-kickback derivation and output rule (line 21)

- **Correctness:** `$|-\rangle` is an `$X` eigenstate with eigenvalue `-1`, so XOR by `$f(x)` contributes `$(-1)^{f(x)}` while returning the target unchanged. The first-register state becomes `$((-1)^{f(0)}|0\rangle+(-1)^{f(1)}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2`.
- **Output correctness:** If values agree, the first register is `$|+\rangle` up to global phase and final `$H` yields `$|0\rangle`; if values differ, it is `$|-\rangle` up to global phase and yields `$|1\rangle`. Thus the result is exact.
- **Conceptual precision:** The eigenvalue is not stored on a single basis-state data register observably; relative phases between the `$x=0,1` branches carry parity `$f(0)\oplus f(1)`. Say this explicitly.
- **“Kicked back” direction:** The target is an eigenstate and remains unchanged; the controlled choice produces branch-dependent phase on the control. This is the cleanest place to reconcile the definition pointers §9.3/§13.2/§14.1.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The entire function property emerging from one relative sign is an excellent payoff.

- **Strength:** As an exhibit for Boolean phase-kickback algorithms, Deutsch is genuinely canonical.
- **Major overclaim:** “Almost every speedup in this chapter and the next” does not use this exact primitive. Standard Simon uses coset entanglement/sampling; Grover/amplitude amplification uses reflections; amplitude estimation combines QPE with a Grover operator; other Chapter 15 methods may differ.
- **Template repair:** Restrict the four-step template to Deutsch, Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani, and phase-oracle formulations. Then explicitly introduce the separate coset, eigenphase, and reflection families.

## Chapter 14, §14.2 — Deutsch–Jozsa Algorithm (lines 25–58)

### Promise and exact query separation (line 27)

- **Correctness:** The promise is exact: `$f` is constant or maps exactly half of `$2^n` inputs to each Boolean value.
- **Classical exact bound:** A deterministic worst-case algorithm needs `$2^{n-1}+1` queries: after `$2^{n-1}` identical answers the function could still be balanced, while one more identical answer proves constant. The text explains the adversarial intuition correctly.
- **Quantum criterion:** The one-query quantum algorithm is exact in the ideal oracle model. State “exact quantum query complexity one versus exact deterministic classical `$2^{n-1}+1`” so readers do not compare unlike error models.
- **Edge case:** For `$n=0` the balanced promise is meaningless; assume `$n\ge1`. This is minor but easy to state.
- **Oracle cost:** As in Deutsch, oracle construction and all non-query gates are excluded from the headline separation.

## Chapter 14, §14.3 — Bernstein–Vazirani Algorithm (lines 59–73)

### Problem, oracle structure, and query comparison (line 61)

- **Correctness:** `$f_s(x)=s\cdot x\pmod2` with `$s,x\in\{0,1\}^n` defines a linear Boolean character over `$\mathbb F_2^n`; querying standard basis vectors classically reveals one secret bit per query, so `$n` exact deterministic queries suffice and are necessary.
- **Definition:** “Bitwise inner product” should explicitly mean `$s\cdot x=\bigoplus_i s_ix_i`; ordinary bitwise AND alone is not the scalar parity.
- **Comparison model:** State exact worst-case query complexities. For randomized bounded-error recovery of the entire uniformly/arbitrarily chosen secret, an information-theoretic success criterion is needed before asserting the same lower bound; the exact comparison is cleanest.
- **Oracle-access fairness:** Both algorithms receive the same Boolean oracle, but a quantum query acts coherently. The separation is a query-model result; implementing `$U_{f_s}` when `$s` is literally known to the implementer would trivialize the hidden-input story, so treat it as black-box access.
- **Information intuition:** One quantum query can reveal `$n` structured bits because the final `$n`-qubit measurement has `$2^n` possible outcomes and the promise family contains `$2^n` linear functions. This does not exceed the output register’s `$n` accessible bits.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Recovering an entire hidden string in one exact query is immediately striking and cleaner than a yes/no promise.

### State derivation and exact output (lines 63–69)

- **Correctness:** Kickback produces `$2^{-n/2}\sum_x(-1)^{s\cdot x}|x\rangle`, which equals `$H^{\otimes n}|s\rangle` under the chapter’s Walsh convention. Since `$H^{\otimes n}` is self-inverse, the final state is exactly `$|s\rangle`.
- **Ancilla omission:** As before, the unchanged `$|-\rangle` factor is omitted. Say the displayed equation is the reduced/factored data-register state.
- **Circuit identity:** The gate skeleton is identical to Deutsch–Jozsa, but the oracle promise changes the full Walsh spectrum from a decision feature (zero coefficient) to a delta at `$s`. This is the key lesson and deserves one sentence.
- **Bit order:** A future circuit/code example must reconcile mathematical string order with SDK little-endian output order; the SVG should be checked for wire-to-bit labeling when reviewed separately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The phase character turning back into its label through a self-inverse transform is exceptionally elegant.

### Figure reference and transform-then-read interpretation (lines 71–73)

- **Figure handling:** `figures/bernstein-vazirani.svg` is a separate tracked book file and remains deferred for structural/rendered review. Its alt text accurately states the intended oracle, structural similarity, one query, and output.
- **Subjective superlative:** “Cleanest example” is defensible instructional opinion, not a theorem. It works stylistically; avoid repeating “cleanest” twice in one paragraph or define what is clean (exact delta-spectrum decoding).
- **Amplitude wording:** “Uses `$2^n` amplitudes” describes coordinates of one `$n`-qubit state, not `$2^n` readable values or independent processors. Explicitly connect this to §13.1’s warning.
- **Correct structural explanation:** Linearity over `$\mathbb Z_2^n` makes `$(-1)^{s\cdot x}` a group character, and the Walsh–Hadamard transform maps characters to labels. This is the precise reason for the one-query decoding.

## Chapter 14, §14.4 — Simon’s Algorithm (lines 75–81)

### Promise, classical lower bound, and quantum/classical costs (line 77)

- **Correctness:** The iff promise `$f(x)=f(y)\iff x\oplus y\in\{0,s\}` with nonzero `$s` makes `$f` exactly two-to-one on pairs `$\{x,x\oplus s\}` and uniquely defines the hidden XOR mask.
- **Correct comparison:** Randomized bounded-error classical query complexity is `$\Omega(2^{n/2})` by collision/birthday reasoning, whereas Simon uses `$O(n)` quantum queries/samples and succeeds with high probability. The explicit warning that this is an oracle/query separation—not unconditional time separation—is excellent.
- **Historical priority:** “First instance” of exponential quantum speedup over randomized classical query algorithms is a specific historical/model claim. Cite Simon’s original paper and define whether exact/bounded-error/promise query separations are the comparison universe.
- **Sample bound:** Drawing from an `(n-1)`-dimensional subspace, `$n-1+t` samples span it except with probability at most on the order of `$2^{-t}`; thus `$O(n+\log(1/\delta))` runs is appropriate. State that samples may be linearly dependent, so exactly `$n-1` runs do not guarantee recovery.
- **Classical postprocessing:** Naive Gaussian elimination over `$\mathbb F_2` costs `$O(n^3)` bit operations; faster matrix methods exist, but cubic is a clear standard bound. Include oracle-output handling and sample storage if doing end-to-end accounting.
- **Birthday intuition:** Briefly explain that classical information about `$s` appears only after finding a collision pair, which random queries need about `$2^{n/2}` samples to produce. This makes the exponential gap intuitive.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** The jump from collision hunting to linear equations is one of the cleanest genuine exponential oracle separations.

### Circuit and orthogonality samples (line 79)

- **Correctness:** Preparing uniform inputs, computing vector-valued `$f`, ignoring or measuring the output register, applying `$H^{\otimes n}` to the input, and measuring yields uniform `$y\in s^\perp` satisfying `$y\cdot s=0\pmod2`.
- **Missing derivation:** After conditioning on output `$f(x_0)`, the input is `$(|x_0\rangle+|x_0\oplus s\rangle)/\sqrt2`; Hadamard amplitude contains `$(-1)^{x_0\cdot y}[1+(-1)^{s\cdot y}]`, which vanishes unless `$s\cdot y=0`. This two-line proof is the conceptual heart and should not be omitted.
- **Output-register nuance:** The algorithm need not physically measure the output; tracing/ignoring it yields a mixture of coset states with the same input measurement distribution. Say “measure or discard/ignore” to avoid making an unnecessary measurement part of the query count.
- **Uniformity:** Once restricted to `$s^\perp`, all allowed `$y` have equal probability. State this follows after averaging over cosets, not just the cancellation condition.
- **Linear solve:** `$n-1` independent equations make the orthogonal complement’s nullspace one-dimensional, leaving `$0` and the unique nonzero `$s`; choose the nonzero solution.
- **Critical consistency:** This mechanism confirms that Chapter 13’s Boolean `$(-1)^{f(x)}` phase-sandwich schematic does not literally cover Simon. Cross-reference the coset-state distinction in both files’ remediation queue.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10.** The coset pair annihilating exactly half the Fourier outcomes is highly satisfying and deserves the explicit derivation.

### Simon–Shor/HSP relationship (line 81)

- **Correct structural link:** Simon is an abelian HSP over `$\mathbb Z_2^n` with hidden subgroup `$\{0,s\}`. Period/order finding can be viewed as hiding `$r\mathbb Z` in `$\mathbb Z`, implemented through finite approximate Fourier sampling.
- **Excellent qualification:** The sentence explicitly warns that finite vector-space and approximate cyclic/integer cases require different output analysis and postprocessing. This directly repairs over-unified claims elsewhere.
- **Historical evidence:** “Acknowledged inspiration for Shor’s” is a causal/history claim; cite Shor’s account, original papers, or a reliable interview/history source. Structural kinship alone does not prove inspiration.
- **Terminology:** “HSP over the integers” is mathematically meaningful in generalized/infinite-group formulations but the finite quantum circuit uses a large power-of-two register. The parenthetical appropriately notes this; §14.9 should maintain the distinction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The lineage from XOR masks to integer periods gives the toy algorithm genuine historical and conceptual weight.

### Definition and sign convention (lines 83–89)

- **Correctness:** The displayed `$F_N|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_y e^{-2\pi ixy/N}|y\rangle` is a valid negative-exponent QFT convention for `$N=2^n`.

### Circuit factorization, complexity, and FFT comparison (line 91)

- **Correctness:** For `$N=2`, the negative/positive sign coincide and QFT equals Hadamard. The power-of-two QFT decomposes into `$n` Hadamards, `$n(n-1)/2` controlled phases, and optional/final swaps for natural output order, hence `$O(n^2)` idealized gates.
- **Gate definition:** `$R_k=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{-2\pi i/2^k})` is consistent with the negative convention, but controlled-phase notation and qubit/control ordering should be tied to the actual circuit. Include final bit reversal/swaps in prose rather than only figure alt text.

- **Excellent comparison caveat:** Contrasting `$O(n^2)` quantum gates with `$O(N\log N)` classical arithmetic is not an end-to-end speedup because the QFT inputs/outputs amplitudes rather than explicit coefficient arrays. Calling the caveat load-bearing is exactly right.
- **Further input caveat:** Efficiently preparing the amplitude-encoded input may itself cost `$O(N)` without structure. The useful algorithms generate the state coherently rather than load an arbitrary classical vector.
- **Resource model:** The `$O(n^2)` count assumes arbitrary precise controlled rotations are primitive. The later paragraph changes the gate model; make the assumption explicit here.

### Readout caveat and structural usefulness (line 95)

- **Correctness:** QFT maps amplitudes to Fourier-transformed amplitudes but measurement does not reveal the full coefficient vector; useful algorithms arrange distributions with decodable concentrated structure.
- **“Only sample” qualification:** Direct measurement samples the computational-basis probability distribution and loses phases; with repeated controlled procedures one may estimate selected amplitudes/properties. “Cannot extract them all efficiently from one/few copies” is more exact than absolute “only sample.”
- **Phase-estimation direction:** Depending on the convention, QPE uses the inverse QFT to decode kicked phases. Ensure “situation in phase estimation” does not blur forward versus inverse.

### Inverse QFT, finite-gate synthesis, and approximate QFT (line 97)

- **Correctness:** Inverting conjugates the exponent; reversing the circuit and adjointing phases implements `$F_N^{-1}`. Tiny controlled rotations motivate approximation in fault-tolerant settings.
- **Strong theorem/cost defect:** Original Solovay–Kitaev synthesis has sequence length `$O(\log^c(1/\delta))` for `$c>1` (classically around 3–4 in standard statements), not the asserted linear `$O(\log(n/\epsilon))`. - **Error allocation:** To approximate an `$O(n^2)` circuit within total error `$\epsilon`, per-rotation synthesis accuracy must be allocated (often `$\delta=O(\epsilon/n^2)` by a triangle bound), changing the logarithm to `$\log(n/\epsilon)` up to constants/powers. Derive the stated total rather than asserting it.
- **Resource mixing:** `$O(n^2\log(n/\epsilon))` counts synthesized elementary gates/T gates under a particular compiler, while `$O(n\log(n/\epsilon))` for banded QFT counts retained ideal controlled rotations. If those rotations also require discrete synthesis, an additional precision-dependent cost remains.
- **Approximation bound:** Dropping rotations below a threshold yields a circuit/operator/output-distribution error bound; “negligible fidelity cost” is undefined and input dependent. State the norm/error guarantee and how cutoff `$m=O(\log(n/\epsilon))` leads to `$O(nm)` rotations.

- **Alternative implementations:** Semiclassical QFT, measurement/feed-forward, phase-gradient states, and architecture-native rotations may change depth/ancilla/T tradeoffs. A short caveat would prevent one cost formula becoming universal.

## Chapter 14, §14.6 — Quantum Phase Estimation (lines 99–105)

### Task, circuit, QFT direction, and success probability (line 101)

- **Correct setup:** Given eigenstate `$|u\rangle` with `$U|u\rangle=e^{2\pi i\varphi}|u\rangle`, a `$t`-qubit estimation register, Hadamards, controlled powers, Fourier decoding, and measurement form standard QPE.
- **Sign-convention correctness:** Because the kickback state has positive phases `$e^{+2\pi i\varphi x}`, the book’s negative-exponent **forward** `$F_{2^t}` decodes it. This is consistent with §14.5; many positive-sign texts use inverse QFT.
- **Bit-order omission:** Specify which estimation qubit controls `$U^{2^k}` and whether QFT swaps/reverses output bits. SDK circuits commonly reverse control-power order or omit swaps.
- **Precision wording:** “`$t` bits of precision” should mean nearest-grid additive error at most `$2^{-(t+1)}` (or another stated convention). Exact first `$t` binary digits, rounding, and truncation are different at boundary cases.
- **Probability:** The nearest-integer outcome has probability at least `$4/\pi^2` in the basic `$t`-qubit scheme; exact grid phases succeed with probability one. To reach confidence `$1-\delta`, use extra bits/repetition/median methods and state the overhead.
- **Eigenstate assumption:** Supplying `$|u\rangle` can be as hard as the target problem. When the system input is `$\sum_jc_j|u_j\rangle`, QPE samples eigenphases with weights `$|c_j|^2` and projects the system accordingly; this important practical behavior is omitted.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The circuit compactly turns an invisible eigenvalue into bits; convention and confidence details make the magic reproducible.

### Fourier-state explanation and non-grid phases (line 103)

- **Correct derivation:** Controlled powers produce `$2^{-t/2}\sum_{x=0}^{2^t-1}e^{2\pi i\varphi x}|x\rangle` (up to qubit ordering), the discrete phase-gradient state.
- **Strong exactness defect:** It equals `$F_{2^t}^{-1}|j\rangle` only if `$j=2^t\varphi` is an integer modulo `$2^t`. For generic `$\varphi`, `$|2^t\varphi\rangle` is not a computational-basis ket. Applying QFT yields a Dirichlet-kernel distribution concentrated near `$2^t\varphi`.
- **Repair:** Split exact and approximate cases. Derive amplitude `$2^{-t}\sum_xe^{2\pi ix(\varphi-y/2^t)}` and then quote/bound the nearest-integer probability.
- **“Reads off” qualification:** The QFT does not deterministically read a generic phase; it reshapes the phase gradient into a sampleable peak. This reinforces §14.5’s readout caveat.
- **Convention warning strength:** The conjugation warning is valuable and should be backed by a small sign-direction table and tested SDK example.

## Chapter 14, §14.7 — Amplitude Amplification (lines 107–113)

### Grover search model and query scaling (line 109)

- **Correctness:** With `$M\ge1` marked items among `$N=2^n`, unstructured classical randomized search needs `$\Theta(N/M)` queries for constant success and Grover search needs `$\Theta(\sqrt{N/M})` quantum oracle queries under the standard phase/Boolean oracle model.
- **Criterion:** State expected versus worst-case/constant-success classical cost and assume `$M` is known or discuss unknown-`$M` algorithms. If `$M=0`, finding a marked item is impossible and the formula diverges appropriately but the promise must exclude it.
- **Oracle notation:** Define whether `$O_f` is an XOR oracle or the phase reflection `$I-2P_{\rm good}`. The next paragraph treats it as a phase flip, while earlier chapters use `$U_f` for XOR; show kickback conversion or use distinct symbols.
- **Output:** After amplification, computational-basis measurement returns a marked element with high probability; say this explicitly.
- **Optimality:** Grover’s quadratic scaling is query-optimal for unstructured search. Mentioning the lower bound would distinguish a convenient algorithm from the best possible black-box one.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The general `$M`-marked formula is clear and immediately reusable.

### Two-reflection rotation geometry (line 111)

- **Correctness:** Decomposing `$|\psi\rangle=\sin\theta|\psi_{\rm good}\rangle+\cos\theta|\psi_{\rm bad}\rangle` with `$\sin^2\theta=M/N`, the product of reflections rotates the invariant plane by `$2\theta`; after `$k` iterations the good amplitude is `$\sin((2k+1)\theta)`.
- **Iteration-count precision:** The peak is near `$k\approx\pi/(4\theta)-1/2`, rounded to a suitable integer, not simply `$\pi/(4\theta)`. The asymptotic scaling is unchanged, but the offset explains overshoot and exact small cases.
- **Reflection convention:** `$2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I` reflects about `$|\psi\rangle`; `$I-2P_{\rm good}` phase-flips good states. Reversing signs/order changes only global phase or rotation direction under some conventions; keep it consistent with the generalized formula.
- **Marked-state normalization:** Define `$|\psi_{\rm good}\rangle` and bad counterpart as normalized projections; otherwise the two-dimensional claim arrives without basis definitions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** Two reflections becoming a controlled planar rotation is one of quantum algorithms’ best geometric pictures.

### General amplitude-amplification construction (line 113)

- **Assumption/notation:** Assume `$A` is unitary and use `$A^\dagger`, not generic `$A^{-1}`. If state preparation is a nonunitary channel, coherent amplification requires a unitary dilation and access to its inverse.
- **Sign check:** With `$S_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I` and `$S_f=2P_{\rm good}-I`, the prefactor `-` makes `$-AS_0A^\dagger S_f` equivalent to the prior product convention. This is correct but sign-heavy; state that global phases/conventions vary.
- **Cost accounting:** One amplification iteration uses calls to `$A`, `$A^\dagger`, and the good-state phase oracle/reflection, not just “calls” generically. Query/resource counts should name which primitive is expensive.
- **Success guarantee:** If `$\theta` is known, an integer number of standard iterations gets near the optimum; exact unit success generally needs phase matching. If `$\theta` is merely bounded/unknown, fixed-point amplification or randomized schedules/counting give different `$\delta` and logarithmic overheads—ordinary tuning is not guaranteed.

## Chapter 14, §14.8 — Amplitude Estimation (lines 115–121)

### Canonical QPE-based amplitude estimation (line 117)

- **Correctness:** On the good/bad invariant subspace, the Grover iterate has conjugate eigenphases `$e^{\pm2i\theta}` (subject to sign/global-phase convention), and estimating them determines `$a=\sin^2\theta` despite the sign ambiguity.
- **Input-state detail:** QPE is not supplied a single known eigenstate; the prepared `$A|0\rangle` is a superposition of the two Grover eigenstates. Phase estimation samples either phase, both mapping to the same `$a`. Explain this to connect with §14.6’s omitted eigenstate-superposition behavior.
- **Error guarantee:** Canonical QAE with `$M` effective Grover-query scale yields a more detailed error such as `$O(\sqrt{a(1-a)}/M+1/M^2)` at constant success; worst-case additive `$\epsilon` uses `$O(1/\epsilon)` coherent queries. State success probability/confidence, not only precision.
- **Resource accounting:** Controlled powers of `$G` require repeated `$G` calls, and each `$G` uses `$A,A^\dagger`, and good-state reflections/oracles. “Grover iterations” should be translated into calls to the actual expensive primitives.
- **Phase convention:** Reconcile `$e^{\pm2i\theta}` with §14.7’s exact definition/sign of `$G` and the book’s negative QFT convention; global `-1` factors can shift phases by `$\pi`.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Turning a success probability into an eigenphase is a beautiful synthesis of the previous two sections.

### Quadratic Monte Carlo comparison and applications (line 119)

- **Classical baseline:** Independent Bernoulli sampling estimates `$a` to worst-case additive error `$\epsilon` with constant confidence using `$\Theta(1/\epsilon^2)` samples; confidence `$1-\delta` adds `$\log(1/\delta)` factors.
- **Quantum qualification:** The `$O(1/\epsilon)` advantage assumes coherent reversible access to state preparation and its inverse plus a good-state predicate. If classical data access is cheap but coherent loading/oracle synthesis is expensive, end-to-end advantage may shrink/disappear.
- **Lower-order/variance nuance:** Modern amplitude-estimation bounds can be variance/adaptive dependent; compare matched error and confidence, not just headline powers.
- **Application scope:** Quantum Monte Carlo/integration, derivative pricing, and partition-function methods use amplitude estimation under condition, loading, payoff-rotation, and error-budget assumptions. “Source of many advantages” should point to concrete later algorithms and distinguish proved query speedups from end-to-end claims.
- **Cross-reference audit:** Verify Chapter 29’s option-pricing caveats include state preparation, distribution loading, arithmetic, fault tolerance, and classical baselines.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Halving the precision exponent has immediate numerical significance; access-model honesty makes it credible.

### QFT-free/likelihood variants and hardware claims (line 121)

- **Terminology:** “Iteration-friendly” is unclear; perhaps “implementation-friendly,” “QFT-free,” or “shallow-circuit” variants is intended.
- **Variant specificity:** “Iterative amplitude estimation” names multiple algorithms with different interval updates and query/confidence bounds. Cite the exact method and state whether the extra logarithm is in `$1/\epsilon`, `$1/\delta`, or both.
- **Depth/query tradeoff:** QFT-free methods avoid a large coherent estimation register/controlled-QFT but can still require large Grover powers, many circuit executions, and adaptive classical processing. They are not automatically shallow in maximum oracle depth unless schedules cap power.
- **Maximum-likelihood caveat:** MLE amplitude estimation fits outcome probabilities from selected powers; finite-sample bias, phase aliasing, schedule choice, and confidence guarantees matter. Distinguish heuristic/practical estimators from rigorously quadratic-query variants.
- **Time-sensitive overclaim:** “Standard route on present-day devices” and “deep phase-estimation circuits are infeasible” require a dated platform/resource basis. Near-term demonstrations do not establish application advantage; fault-tolerant hardware changes the preference.
- **Noise:** Grover powers amplify coherent circuit depth and noise; likelihood models assuming ideal sinusoidal probabilities can be biased under device noise. This belongs in the practical caveat.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The algorithm-family view is useful and practical, though blanket near-term language will age quickly.

## Chapter 14, §14.9 — Hidden Subgroup Problem Framework (lines 123–134)

### HSP definition and Deutsch–Jozsa boundary (line 125)

- **Correctness:** The standard HSP promise is that `$f` is constant and distinct on cosets of an unknown subgroup, equivalently `$f(g)=f(g')` iff the relevant cosets agree; the goal is to identify/generate `$H`.
- **Nonabelian precision:** For nonabelian `$G`, specify left or right cosets (`$gH` versus `$Hg`) because they differ unless `$H` is normal. The displayed generic definition silently assumes a convention.
- **Representation/oracle:** State that group elements have an efficient encoding and coherent group/function operations are available. Without these, `$|G|` and QFT complexity claims are not algorithmic.
- **Deutsch–Jozsa qualification:** An arbitrary balanced Boolean function need not hide a subgroup, so the stated exclusion is correct. Some special DJ/BV-like functions do arise from subgroup characters/kernels; “sits just outside” is a heuristic taxonomy, not a hard boundary.
- **Scope:** For infinite/continuous groups, the finite uniform superposition and exact QFT template needs limiting/approximate treatment. The later `$\mathbb Z` Shor item is such a generalized case, not literally covered by finite `$|G|` notation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The coset promise provides an elegant umbrella, and explicitly identifying a near-miss (DJ) helps define its boundary.

### Simon and Bernstein–Vazirani as `$\mathbb Z_2^n` HSPs (lines 127–128)

- **Simon correctness:** `$H=\{0,s\}` is exactly the two-element hidden subgroup, and Fourier samples lie in `$H^\perp=s^\perp`, matching §14.4.
- **BV correctness with algorithm caveat:** `$f_s(x)=s\cdot x` has kernel `$H=s^\perp` and distinguishes its two cosets, so it is an HSP instance. However, standard coset Fourier sampling returns a uniform element of `$H^\perp=\{0,s\}`, giving `$s` only with probability `$1/2`; the phase-kickback BV algorithm deterministically returns `$s` in one query. Do not imply the generic HSP procedure reproduces identical performance.
- **Degenerate secret:** For `$s=0`, BV’s kernel is all of `$G`; ensure the HSP statement allows this while Simon explicitly excludes nonzero `$s` only.
- **Notation:** Define orthogonal complement with the mod-two character pairing to link kernels and Fourier outcomes.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Seeing two algorithms as hiding subgroups of the same vector space is illuminating, especially when their oracle/readout differences are retained.

### Shor/order finding as an integer-period HSP (line 129)

- **Structural correctness:** `$x\mapsto a^x\bmod N` has period equal to the multiplicative order `$r` when `$\gcd(a,N)=1`, and its level sets are cosets of `$r\mathbb Z` in `$\mathbb Z`; factoring probabilistically reduces to order finding.
- **Missing condition:** State `$a` is invertible modulo `$N`; otherwise the gcd may already reveal a factor and the periodic-group formulation changes.
- **Finite implementation:** A finite power-of-two control register approximates Fourier sampling over the integer period; it is not simply a finite cyclic group in which `$r` necessarily divides the register size. Retain §13.4’s near-peak analysis.
- **Reduction qualification:** Factoring reduction has random-choice, even-order, nontrivial-square-root, and repetition conditions; “reduces” is correct but not deterministic one-shot.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The XOR-period-to-integer-period progression makes Shor feel like a conceptual culmination rather than a bolt from nowhere.

### Dihedral HSP and lattice connection (line 130)

- **Grammar/definition:** “`$G = $ a semidirect product” is malformed and too vague. Define the dihedral group `$D_N\cong\mathbb Z_N\rtimes\mathbb Z_2` (with the book’s order convention) and the hidden reflection subgroup/coset problem.
- **Reduction precision:** Regev’s connection is parameter- and direction-sensitive: sufficiently efficient solutions to appropriate dihedral coset/HSP variants imply algorithms for specified unique shortest-vector regimes. Do not loosely say “unique- and gap-shortest-vector cases” without the exact approximation factors, dimensions, and reduction type.
- **Cryptography relevance:** Lattice-based cryptography uses several problems/parameter regimes; a reduction connection does not mean solving generic dihedral HSP immediately breaks deployed schemes. State scope carefully.
- **Current status:** No polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for general dihedral HSP; Kuperberg-type algorithms are subexponential with time/space tradeoffs. Cite current primary/improved results and date the status.
- **Duplication:** The dihedral/lattice status is repeated again in line 132. Consolidate into one coherent example.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The bridge to lattice cryptography is compelling but high stakes; precise reductions are mandatory.

### Fourier-sampling template and abelian guarantee (line 132)

- **Correctness:** A coset state followed by group QFT yields annihilator/dual information for finite abelian groups. Measuring the function register is optional; discarding it produces the same first-register mixture.
- **Normalization/notation:** The state should sum over `$x\in G`; as written `$\sum_x` is inferable. If `$f(x)` labels are not orthonormal encodings, the oracle model must guarantee distinguishable output states.
- **Abelian complexity:** `$O(\log|G|)` samples/generators plus polynomial postprocessing is plausible under efficient decomposition/representation, group operations, and QFT. State dependence on input encoding length and success probability, not only group cardinality.
- **Nonabelian nuance:** Nonabelian QFT outputs irrep labels/matrix indices; weak/strong/entangled measurements have different power. Some nonabelian HSP families are efficiently solvable, so “wide open” should mean no general efficient solution and major cases remain unresolved.
- **Graph-isomorphism mapping:** GI reduces to specific HSP instances over a wreath-product/symmetric-group-related family, not simply arbitrary `$S_n` HSP. Name the group and clarify that an efficient solver for those instances would solve GI.
- **Dihedral status:** Kuperberg’s subexponential algorithms are important but have notable space variants/tradeoffs; cite exact asymptotics only if stated later.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** One coset-measure-transform recipe spanning several algorithms is a powerful abstraction; nonabelian representation theory deserves a precise boundary marker.

### Global-unification and 2026 research-frontier claim (line 134)

- **Major “most” overclaim:** “Most known exponential quantum speedups outside Hamiltonian simulation” is not established by examples. Linear-algebra algorithms under strong access models, quantum walks, topological/number-theoretic algorithms, sampling separations, forrelation, and other oracle constructions complicate any count. Define the corpus or say “many landmark number-theoretic/oracle speedups.”
- **Good exceptions:** Glued trees and forrelation are useful counterexamples showing HSP is not universal; their exact separation models should be named if used as evidence.
- **Time-sensitive claim:** Calling nonabelian HSP/new templates “one of the central questions … in 2026” is an editorial judgment and current-status claim. Date/source it or frame it as the authors’ perspective.
- **Research-map balance:** Modern quantum algorithm research also centrally studies block encodings/QSVT, Hamiltonian algorithms, optimization, learning, walks, cryptanalysis, and fault-tolerant resource reduction. Avoid implying HSP dominates the whole frontier.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Ending on an open frontier is exciting; a narrower claim would feel more authoritative.

## Chapter 15, §15.1 — Grover’s Algorithm (lines 11–46)

### Search problem, rotation formula, rounded iteration count, and guarantee (line 13)

- **Diffusion precision:** Inversion about the arithmetic mean describes computational-basis amplitudes for the uniform-state diffusion operator; geometrically it is reflection about `$|\psi\rangle`. The latter remains correct for complex amplitudes and general amplification.
- **Query count:** `$\Theta(\sqrt{N/M})` is correct for constant/high success in unstructured search when `$1\le M\le N` and the relevant access model is fixed. If `$M` is close to `$N`, zero queries plus random sampling may already have high success; constants/optimal policy depend on the target guarantee.

### Grover-iteration SVG reference (line 15)

- **Alt-text scope:** The alt text states a three-qubit iteration, oracle implementation `H–MCX–H`, diffusion, and approximately `(π/4)√N` repetitions. This describes the one-marked-item case; label `$M=1` explicitly.
- **Oracle implementation caveat:** `H–MCX–H` phase-flips `$|111\rangle` only with the correct target/control arrangement and phase convention. This requires structural/rendered inspection of `figures/grover-iteration.svg` later.
- **Generalization:** The figure’s oracle is problem-specific; arbitrary marked predicates require reversible verifier synthesis/uncomputation, often the dominant cost.
- **Deferred evidence:** The SVG is a separate tracked file and remains uncounted until structural plus visual review.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A geometric/circuit visual is ideal here, provided its oracle and one-solution scope are visibly labeled.

### Unknown `$M` and quantum minimum finding (line 17)

- **Correctness:** BBHT-style randomized iteration ranges avoid deterministic resonance/overshoot and find a marked item in expected `$O(\sqrt{N/M})` queries for `$M>0` under standard assumptions, with candidate verification.
- **No-solution defect:** For `$M=0`, “detected by repeated verification failure” is not a conclusive finite certificate. A fixed `$O(\sqrt N)`-scale budget can declare no solution with a specified bounded error when `$M>0` alternatives are considered; state the stopping rule and false-negative probability. With no marked item, verification failure itself is exact but indistinguishable from bad luck after finitely many attempts.
- **Known bounds:** “Unknown `$M`” may still assume a known domain size and phase oracle. Expected-query constants and confidence amplification should be stated/cited if claiming detection.
- **Minimum finding:** Dürr–Høyer minimum finding uses repeated searches against a changing threshold and achieves expected/ bounded-success `$O(\sqrt N)` query complexity. Clarify assumptions about distinct values/ties, value-oracle comparisons, and amplification.
- **Domain notation:** The minimum-finding function maps bit strings to an ordered value domain, unlike the Boolean search predicate. Define comparison-oracle cost.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Randomized stopping defeating a periodic quantum overshoot is a clever and memorable extension.

### What Grover is not, fault-tolerant cost, applications, and optimality (line 19)

- **Misleading NP sentence:** Grover *can* search an efficiently verifiable NP witness space in its square root, yielding `$O(2^{w/2})` verifier calls for `$w` witness bits. What it does not do is make generic NP-complete problems polynomial-time or exploit their structure automatically. Rewrite accordingly.
- **Correct speedup classification:** The improvement is quadratic in black-box search size, not exponential in input length; because `$N=2^n`, `$\sqrt N=2^{n/2}` remains exponential in `$n`.
- **Oracle-cost strength:** Reversible verifier/oracle synthesis, uncomputation, routing, error correction, and repeated logical depth can dominate; emphasizing fault-tolerant query cost is excellent.
- **Architecture qualification:** Toffoli/T/magic-state expense assumes a common Clifford+T/surface-code-like fault-tolerance stack. Non-Clifford realization and dominant resources vary; Chapter 19 should state the architecture.
- **“Current consensus” issue:** The usefulness claim for large spaces/cheap oracles is a dated expert judgment, not a theorem. Cite resource studies and define “useful”/crossover; branch-and-bound also has structured classical pruning that a coherent oracle may not import cheaply.
- **Cryptanalytic nuance:** Grover changes symmetric-key/preimage brute-force exponents under large coherent-depth requirements; parallelization, memory, circuit depth, and attack economics matter. Chapter 27 should provide actual resource estimates.
- **Optimality:** BBBV establishes `$\Omega(\sqrt N)` quantum query lower bounds for black-box search (with model/success assumptions); Zalka gives tight optimality refinements. Cite the precise theorem rather than a bare author string.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The anti-hype paragraph is valuable and concrete; the corrected NP wording would make it a model of responsible explanation.

### Three-qubit Qiskit implementation and sampled output (lines 21–45)

- **Iteration count:** For `$N=8,M=1`, `$\theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt8)` and the rounded optimum is `$k=2`; the loose floor formula happens to agree. The exact ideal success is `$\sin^2(5\theta)=121/128\approx94.53125\%`.
- **Oracle correctness:** `H`–`mcx`–`H` on target qubit 2 with controls 0 and 1 implements a CCZ/phase flip on `$|111\rangle`. This assumes Qiskit’s multi-controlled-X semantics and no open controls.
- **Diffusion sign:** The sequence `H^n X^n CCZ X^n H^n` implements `$I-2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|`, the negative of `$2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I`; this global sign per Grover iterate does not change measurement probabilities. Explain the convention so code and formula appear consistent.
- **Output distribution:** The seven unmarked states each have ideal probability `$(1-121/128)/7=1/128\approx0.78125\%`; the displayed counts are a plausible 1000-shot sample and sum to 1000.
- **Analytic-before-empirical:** State the exact `$121/128` probability and then explain stochastic count variation. This lets readers distinguish algorithmic probability from simulator sampling noise.
- **API/version risk:** The `StatevectorSampler` result path and default classical-register name `c` are Qiskit-version-sensitive. Validate with the repository’s pinned environment/example tests later.
- **Code style/accessibility:** Multiple semicolon-separated circuit calls compress important oracle/diffusion layers. Use helper functions (`phase_oracle_111`, `diffusion`) or one gate per line so the code mirrors the theory and can generalize.
- **Scalability caveat:** The hard-coded `mcx([0,1],2)` is only the three-qubit demo. Larger multi-controlled gates require decomposition/ancillas and can dominate fault-tolerant resources; connect back to the oracle-cost warning.
- **Shots/query accounting:** 1000 sampler shots execute two oracle calls each, totaling 2000 oracle invocations in the experimental batch, though algorithmic query complexity is two per independent run.
- **External reference scope:** `examples/grover.py` lies outside the requested `book/**` file review; later project example checks can verify consistency without counting it as a reviewed book file.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Watching one basis state rise to 94.5% after only two rotations is a compelling executable demonstration.

### §15.1 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section gives an unusually precise rounded iteration formula and lower success guarantee, then connects geometry, unknown-solution strategies, optimality, fault-tolerant cost, and executable output.
- **Highest-priority wording repair:** Say Grover quadratically accelerates generic NP witness search but does not make it polynomial; replace conclusive `$M=0` “detection” with a bounded-error stopping rule.
- **Highest-priority implementation repair:** Align diffusion sign conventions, expose exact probability, and separate per-run queries from total shots.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Strong mathematics, practical skepticism, and code make this an excellent section after two scope corrections.

## Chapter 15, §15.2 — Shor’s Algorithm (lines 47–55)

### High-level factoring/order-finding decomposition (lines 47–49)

- **Correctness:** Shor gives a randomized polynomial-time quantum algorithm for integer factoring by combining classical reduction/postprocessing with quantum order finding.
- **Complexity model:** “Polynomial time” should specify polynomial in bit length `$n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil`, with bounded success amplified by repetition, on a fault-tolerant uniform quantum circuit model.
- **Terminology:** Factoring is a function/search problem rather than a BQP decision language as such; decision versions/reductions place relevant languages in BQP. This matters after Chapter 13’s BQP framing.
- **Hybrid structure:** The classical–quantum–classical decomposition is clear and should be retained as the organizing spine for the next subsections; §15.3’s separate “Factoring” heading otherwise risks duplication.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The concise three-stage structure makes a daunting landmark approachable.

### Classical reduction and useful-order probability (line 51)

- **Preprocessing conditions:** Handle even `$N`, prime powers, and primality/perfect-power checks separately; assume an odd composite with at least two distinct prime factors for the familiar useful-order probability statement.
- **Random `$a` step:** Pick `$1<a<N` and compute `$d=\gcd(a,N)`. If `$d>1`, a factor is already found; only then assume `$a\in\mathbb Z_N^*` and order exists in the multiplicative group.
- **Probability placement defect:** Once the exact order is even and `$a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N`, the gcds yield nontrivial factors deterministically (one or both, under the standard argument). The probability `$\ge1/2` belongs to a random coprime `$a` satisfying the useful-order conditions under the stated class of `$N`, not to the gcd operation after those conditions hold.
- **Expected rounds:** A constant lower bound on useful choices implies expected `$O(1)` outer trials, but quantum order finding itself has bounded success and may need repeated Fourier samples. Separate these probabilities rather than collapsing them into “a few `$a`’s.”
- **Miller attribution:** The classical reduction/history attribution to Miller (1976) needs a precise primary citation and scope (including assumptions/results) rather than a surname/year.
- **Pedagogy:** The identity `$(a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1)\equiv0\pmod N` explains the gcd step in one line and should be shown.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Random modular order exposing factors through a difference of squares is a satisfying number-theoretic pivot.

### Quantum order-finding circuit, continued fractions, and gate complexity (line 53)

- **Critical initialization omission:** The second/work register must start in `$|1\rangle` for `$|x\rangle|1\rangle\mapsto|x\rangle|a^x\bmod N\rangle`. The paragraph states register sizes but never initializes it.
- **Unitary-domain defect:** `$|y\rangle\mapsto|a^xy\bmod N\rangle` is a permutation only on valid residues when `$\gcd(a,N)=1`; an `$n`-qubit register also contains basis states `$y\ge N`. Define the circuit’s reversible extension (often identity or another permutation on invalid states) to make `$U_a` unitary on the full Hilbert space.
- **“Query” wording:** Modular exponentiation is not one black-box query in an end-to-end Shor circuit. It is synthesized from controlled modular multiplications keyed by exponent bits. Call it a reversible modular-exponentiation unitary, then count its gates.
- **Register size:** A `$2n`-qubit phase register (`$Q=2^{2n}`) provides enough resolution for continued fractions in the textbook construction, but exact counts can be optimized/semiclassical. Explain `$N^2\le Q<2N^2` style conditions rather than treating exactly `$2n` as sacred.
- **QFT direction:** With the book’s negative-exponent convention, applying forward `$F_Q` to a period/coset state produces peaks near `$sQ/r`; this is consistent, subject to bit order and swaps.
- **Single-sample overclaim:** Continued fractions returns the true `$r` directly only when the measured approximation is sufficiently accurate and numerator `$s` is coprime to `$r`. It may yield a divisor `$r/\gcd(s,r)` or an unusable convergent. Verify candidates by modular exponentiation and combine/repeat samples (e.g. LCM/reduction) as needed.
- **Probability:** “With high probability” requires accounting for Fourier peak probability, coprimality `$\varphi(r)/r`, candidate verification, and repetition. It is not automatic from one measurement.
- **Gate-count evidence:** `$O(n^2\log n\log\log n)` from fast reversible arithmetic is a nontrivial model-dependent bound, as the text acknowledges. Cite the exact construction, ancilla count, gate set, approximation error, and whether reversibilizing Schönhage–Strassen preserves that bound. Textbook arithmetic is commonly `$O(n^3)`.
- **QFT cost comparison:** Exact ideal QFT is `$O(n^2)` arbitrary-angle gates, but finite-gate synthesis/approximation changes T/gate cost. Modular exponentiation generally dominates asymptotically and in resource studies, yet physical depth/qubits/factories depend on implementation.
- **Notation collision:** `$N` is the number to factor, while Chapter 14 used `$N` as Fourier dimension; define `$Q=2^{2n}` here to prevent ambiguity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The phase peaks-to-rational reconstruction pipeline is extraordinary, but its missing initialization and one-sample simplification are central.

### Cryptographic consequence and 2024 NIST standards (line 55)

- **Correct scope:** A sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor threatens RSA and discrete-log-based key exchange/signatures (finite-field DH/DSA and elliptic-curve variants). It does not break all public-key or symmetric cryptography.
- **Capability qualifier:** “Relevant scale” should mean logical qubit count, T/Toffoli resources, runtime, error rate, and cryptographic key size. “When (if)” is conversationally awkward; use “If cryptographically relevant fault-tolerant quantum computers are built.”
- **Migration motivation:** Quantum risk is a central motivation for PQC, together with long migration timelines and harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure; Chapter 27 should quantify these rather than imply a known arrival date.
- **Official verification (2026-07-23):** NIST confirms FIPS 203, 204, and 205 were finalized August 13, 2024. FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber; FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA, derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium; FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA, derived from SPHINCS+. Use NIST’s official announcement/FIPS pages as citations.
- **Terminology:** ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation/key-establishment mechanism, while ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are digital-signature standards. Calling the trio “post-quantum standards” is correct; calling all “encryption” would not be.
- **Current-maintenance note:** NIST’s FIPS 203 page carries a 2025 planning note for future errata/update. This does not undo standardization but illustrates why the book’s dated standards snapshot should link authoritative living pages.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Connecting period finding to real migration standards gives the mathematics immediate stakes without needing speculative quantum timelines.

### §15.2 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The classical–quantum–classical pipeline and resource warning make Shor legible without pretending modular exponentiation is free.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Initialize `$|1\rangle`, define a full-register unitary, move the `$\ge1/2` probability to useful random choices, and handle non-coprime Fourier numerators/repetition.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Source Miller reduction, fast reversible gate complexity, and use official NIST standards pages.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** High conceptual and real-world payoff; a few omitted conditions currently carry too much correctness weight.

## Chapter 15, §15.3 — Factoring Resource Snapshot (lines 57–72)

### Moving-target warning and snapshot date (lines 57–59)

- **Excellent epistemic labeling:** Explicitly dating physical-qubit/runtime estimates and instructing readers to re-verify them is essential. This is stronger than undated “current” claims elsewhere.
- **Date inconsistency:** The callout says “as of May 2026” while describing a May 2025 preprint and “best published sources as of 2026.” State the actual literature cutoff and search date separately; “published” should distinguish peer-reviewed papers from arXiv preprints.
- **“Best” criterion:** Define best as minimum physical qubits under specified superconducting/surface-code assumptions, not universally best runtime, volume, architecture, or confidence.
- **Predictive overclaim:** “Will keep moving” is plausible but not guaranteed; say estimates have changed rapidly and should be expected to change.
- **Draft wording:** If this remains in the published book, “If you are reading a draft” will age awkwardly. Make the re-verification instruction universal and link a maintained resource table.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The warning invites the reader into live research rather than presenting projections as settled engineering.

### Choice of resource metrics and RSA-2048 target (line 61)

- **Importance:** RSA-2048 is a relevant standardized/deployed-scale benchmark and makes abstract polynomial time concrete.
- **Incomplete metric pair:** Physical qubits and wall-clock hours alone conceal spacetime volume, code cycles, logical qubits, factory throughput, power/control/cryogenic requirements, connectivity, decoder latency, and success probability. Report at least physical-qubit-days plus assumptions.
- **“Realistic noise” wording:** The cited studies assume a stylized uniform physical error rate, cycle time, connectivity, and decoder/control reaction time. Call these explicit plausible target assumptions, not observed realistic operation at million-qubit scale.
- **Threat criterion:** A cryptographically relevant machine must outperform migration/attack economics and complete within the target key/data lifetime; “factor once” resource estimates are anchors, not arrival forecasts.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Converting Shor into qubits × hours supplies immediate stakes, provided the omitted dimensions remain visible.

### 2019/2021 Gidney–Ekerå anchor (line 65)

- **Primary-source verification:** The paper/preprint *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits* (arXiv `1905.09749`, later *Quantum*) supports the headline estimate under a planar nearest-neighbor superconducting model, `$10^{-3}` characteristic physical gate error, 1 μs surface-code cycle, and 10 μs reaction time.
- **Approximation language:** Use “estimated/projected” rather than presenting 20 million/8 hours as measured capability. The result is conditional on architecture, decoder, factory, error model, and repeated-attempt assumptions.
- **Magic-state claim:** Distillation/factories are major spacetime contributors, but “dominating the cost” should cite the paper’s breakdown and specify whether qubits, runtime, or volume is dominated.
- **Date label:** The preprint is 2019 and journal publication later; format as “Gidney–Ekerå (2019 preprint; 2021 journal)” rather than the ambiguous semicolon.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The memorable anchor is valuable, especially with assumptions attached immediately.

### 2025 Gidney sub-million-qubit anchor (line 66)

- **Primary-source verification:** arXiv `2505.15917`, *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, explicitly estimates under one million noisy qubits and under one week, retaining the 2019 grid, error-rate, cycle-time, and reaction-time assumptions.
- **Tradeoff:** The newer design reduces space while allowing much longer runtime and changes arithmetic, idle storage, and magic-state production. “`>20×` qubit reduction” is correct relative to 20 million, but it is not a free across-the-board resource reduction; compare spacetime volume and runtime too.
- **“Without weakening assumptions” overstatement:** The physical baseline assumptions are retained, but algorithm/code/factory choices and performance targets change. Say “under the same headline physical assumptions” and list the changed architecture/resources.
- **Attribution correction:** The 2025 abstract credits approximate residue arithmetic, yoked surface codes, and **magic-state cultivation**/less factory space; the manuscript says “smaller magic-state-distillation budget.” Use the paper’s actual cultivation terminology and cite the relevant 2024 work.
- **Publication status:** As of the cited date this is an arXiv preprint; do not call both anchors equally established “published” estimates without noting review status.
- **Chevignard source:** The approximate/residue-number arithmetic lineage is supported by Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher’s factoring work, but cite the final venue/version and distinguish their logical-qubit optimization from Gidney’s physical resource integration.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A 20× space shift in six years vividly shows why dated snapshots matter; the time/architecture trade prevents sensationalism.

### Logical-to-physical overhead explanation (line 68)

- **Order-of-magnitude plausibility:** The 2019 abstract gives roughly `$3n+0.002n\log n` logical qubits (about several thousand for 2048 bits); the 2025 construction is lower. “A few thousand” is a reasonable rough cross-estimate but should be split by paper rather than implying identical logical footprints.
- **Patch formula qualification:** Rough planar surface-code data patches scale like `$O(d^2)` physical data/measurement qubits per logical qubit, and `$2d^2` is a common rotated-patch rule of thumb. Layout, boundaries, lattice surgery, factories, routing, and yoked storage make one multiplier inadequate.
- **Distance claim:** “`$d` in the high twenties” depends on logical operation count, target failure probability, decoder, circuit noise, cycle time, and factory protocol. Quote each paper’s chosen distances rather than a generic value.
- **Causal simplification:** Surface-code overhead is a major source of millions of qubits, but factories/routing/storage strategies are part of that overhead and not captured by multiplying logical qubits by `$2d^2` alone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The logical-to-physical inflation is important intuition; one crude formula should be labeled as such.

### Trend, current-device comparison, and security-lifetime framing (line 70)

- **Trend evidence:** Resource estimates have fallen substantially through arithmetic and QEC/layout improvements, but “orders of magnitude over the last decade” needs a plotted, apples-to-apples series under comparable assumptions. The two displayed anchors show >20× qubit reduction, just over one order, with longer runtime.
- **Prediction:** “Will probably come down further” is explicitly speculative; attribute it as expectation and note estimates can also rise when neglected engineering/control costs are included.
- **Device-count overgeneralization:** “Current physical devices … `$10^2$–`$10^3` qubits” excludes/merges gate-model superconducting, ions, neutral atoms, photonics, and annealers. Qubit count and `$10^{-3}` error are not cross-platform scalar metrics; two-qubit, measurement, leakage, connectivity, and logical performance differ.
- **Evidence/date:** A 2026 hardware snapshot should cite specific systems and metrics, not one generic range. Cross-link Appendix F/Chapter 20 and avoid duplicating a rapidly aging inventory here.
- **“Degree, not kind” overclaim:** Scaling from thousand-device demonstrations to a million-qubit fault-tolerant system involves qualitative systems challenges—control, wiring, decoding, yield, correlated errors, factories, reliability—not merely more units. Physical principles permit it, but engineering feasibility/timeline is not proven by a resource estimate.
- **Harvest-now distinction:** Recorded encrypted sessions/data with long confidentiality life motivate harvest-now-decrypt-later. Root certificates and signing keys concern future forgery/authentication and migration, not decrypting previously recorded ciphertext in the same way. Separate confidentiality and signature threats.
- **TLS nuance:** Modern TLS often uses ephemeral (EC)DHE; a future discrete-log-capable adversary can derive recorded ephemeral shared secrets from public handshake material, subject to protocol/capture details. Do not imply RSA key transport is the only scenario.
- **“When not whether” rhetoric:** Cryptographically relevant fault-tolerant machines are physically plausible, but arrival is not established. Migration planning rationally treats uncertainty and long lead times; phrase as risk management, not certainty.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The migration stakes are compelling; nuanced threat categories and engineering uncertainty would improve trust.

### Variational and lattice-hybrid factoring alternatives (line 72)

- **Variational assessment:** Toy demonstrations without asymptotic advantage evidence are accurately characterized. Also ask whether classical preprocessing has already encoded/factored most of the instance and compare against state-of-the-art classical factoring.
- **Schnorr/Yan precision:** Name the exact Schnorr proposal/status and Yan et al. paper rather than relying on years. Claims about a few hundred qubits/RSA-2048 attracted published/preprint critiques.
- **Counterevidence:** Khattar–Yosri’s arXiv `2307.09651` reports that even a perfect optimizer in their implementation did not support the claimed scaling beyond small sizes; `2303.04656` likewise analyzes complexity pitfalls. Cite critiques and original response/revisions for balance.
- **“Consensus” defect:** “The consensus by 2025” requires a survey/poll/review and is too broad. Say independent analyses found no demonstrated relevant-size/asymptotic speedup and summarize the evidence.
- **Category:** These hybrid proposals do not replace Shor with a proven polynomial quantum factoring method; keep heuristic resource counts separate from cryptanalytic capability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Discussing tempting low-qubit alternatives is valuable, especially when the book teaches how their claims failed scrutiny.
