- **Modular exponentiation map:** `$|x\rangle|y\rangle\mapsto|x\rangle|y\oplus a^x\bmod N\rangle` needs define register widths and whether `$\oplus` is bitwise XOR or modular addition into a clean result register. Standard implementations compute/multiply reversibly.
- **Input sizes:** Complexity is polynomial in `$n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil` and exponent-register size, not polynomial in numeric `$N`.
- **Not an unknown-input oracle:** In Shor, `$a,N` are known classical inputs and modular exponentiation is an explicitly built subroutine, unlike a black-box oracle encoding an unknown function. This is exactly why a gate-level algorithm can be analyzed.
- **Time advantage epistemics:** Shor is polynomial versus the best known classical subexponential algorithms; no unconditional classical superpolynomial lower bound is proved. “Advantage survives” means algorithmic comparison under factoring hardness belief, not a theorem.
- **Other costs:** QFT, arithmetic width/depth, error correction, repetitions, and classical continued fractions must also be polynomial; oracle implementability is necessary but not sufficient.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Showing how a black box becomes modular arithmetic is the right bridge from query magic to executable algorithms.

### Random-oracle contrast (line 150, second half)

- **Random oracle meaning:** A uniformly random Boolean function on exponentially many inputs has no polynomial-size circuit with overwhelming probability by counting, so a succinct gate implementation is unavailable absent physical oracle access.
- **Not “no implementation” absolutely:** A finite random truth table can be implemented with exponential storage/gates; “no efficient implementation exists with overwhelming probability” is the precise statement.
- **Relativized role:** Oracle separations compare machines granted unit-cost access and reveal limits of proof techniques/class containments relative to that oracle; they need not describe a realizable standalone computational problem.
- **Quantum versus classical access:** A quantum oracle permits coherent superposition queries, a stronger physical interface than ordinary classical API calls; state this in claims.
- **Pseudorandom substitutes:** Efficient quantum-secure pseudorandom functions may instantiate some oracle-like hardness conditionally, but are not truly random and require cryptographic assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The reality check is essential and clean once “efficient” and probability are made explicit.

### Polynomial method (line 152, first part)

- **Correct degree fact:** For the standard Boolean query oracle, a `$T`-query algorithm's acceptance probability is a real multilinear polynomial of degree at most `$2T` in input bits (or related `$\pm1` variables).
- **Amplitude precursor:** Each final amplitude has degree at most `$T`; squaring/summing yields degree at most `$2T`. This two-step proof is short and illuminating.
- **Approximate degree:** For bounded-error computation, the acceptance polynomial approximates the target function on the promise domain; lower bounds use approximate degree, not necessarily exact representing degree.
- **Partial functions:** The polynomial only needs satisfy approximation constraints on promised inputs, which can greatly reduce degree.
- **One-way implication:** Approximate degree lower-bounds quantum queries by half, but low approximate degree does not by itself always give an equally low query algorithm for arbitrary partial functions.
- **Other outputs:** Relations/state generation require generalized polynomial arguments; do not imply this scalar theorem covers all queries.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Turning a quantum circuit into a low-degree polynomial is an elegant and surprisingly concrete lower-bound lens.

### Adversary method and tightness (line 152, second part)

- **Oversimplified description:** The adversary method uses a weighted matrix/progress measure over pairs of inputs with different outputs and bounds progress per query through coordinate-difference matrices; it is not merely “pairs differing in one position.” Pairs may differ in many positions.
- **Positive/negative weights:** Original spectral/weighted adversary bounds had limitations; allowing negative weights yields the general adversary bound and overcomes certificate barriers.
- **Tightness scope:** The general adversary bound characterizes bounded-error quantum query complexity up to constants for Boolean functions (including partial functions under standard formulations), with Reichardt/span-program and subsequent general state-conversion results. Cite exact theorem chain.
- **Algorithmic side:** Tightness is constructive in principle via span programs, though resulting time/gate complexity may be inefficient—another query/time gap.
- **Input costs:** Computing/implementing the optimal adversary/span-program witness may itself be hard.
- **“Tight bounds are norm”:** Query complexity is unusually mature, but many concrete problems, constants, time-efficient realizations, and nonstandard oracle models remain open. Soften the field-wide superlative.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** An adversarial progress meter that exactly characterizes quantum queries is a striking capstone; one OR example would anchor it.

### §17.6 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It assembles a memorable ladder of oracle separations and pairs it with the two central lower-bound methods plus a vital query-to-time warning.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Disentangle Fourier Checking/Forrelation chronology, define its oracle/count, and qualify near-tight logarithmic factors/Raz–Tal relation.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Define the oracle/error/promise model in a comparison table and give one short polynomial/adversary derivation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Fast, varied, and intellectually satisfying; precision would turn the catalog into a reliable reference.

## Chapter 17, §17.7 — Oracle Separations (lines 154–173)

### Definition and claimed non-relativization consequence (line 156)

- **Core definition:** An oracle `$O` relativizes each class by granting unit-cost access, and an inequality `$\mathcal C^O\ne\mathcal D^O` is an oracle separation.
- **Direction needed:** Equality/inequality can mean noncontainment one way or both. State whether a language lies in `$\mathcal C^O\setminus\mathcal D^O`, vice versa, or classes are incomparable.
- **Critical logic overstatement:** A single oracle separating C and D does **not** by itself show that every proof of unrelativized C≠D must be nonrelativizing; a relativizing separation proof could conceivably hold for all oracles. A barrier to resolving the question by relativizing techniques comes from incompatible oracle worlds (equality in one, separation/reversed containment in another) or an oracle counterexample to the proposed containment direction.
- **Relativizing proof:** Define a proof/technique as relativizing when it remains valid after giving all machines the same arbitrary oracle.
- **Oracle type:** Classical Boolean, random, quantum unitary, and algebraic oracles are not interchangeable. Tag every example.
- **Evidence versus barrier:** A separating oracle can provide evidence of possible power and establish a relativized theorem; paired worlds establish a technique barrier. Keep these claims distinct.
- **“Specific properties”:** Nonrelativizing methods may use arithmetization, interactive proofs, circuit lower bounds, algebraic/combinatorial structure, or non-black-box properties; give examples.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Alternate computational universes are a vivid concept, but the exact meta-logical lesson is the whole point.

### Baker–Gill–Solovay paired worlds (line 158)

- **Correct landmark:** BGS constructed oracles `$A,B` with `$P^A=NP^A` and `$P^B\ne NP^B`, showing no proof that relativizes uniformly can settle ordinary P versus NP.
- **This is the proper barrier pattern:** The equality and inequality worlds together directly support the conclusion that relativizing techniques alone cannot prove either universal equality or universal separation.
- **Date/source:** Give full title/publication; verify 1975.
- **Oracle intuition:** Briefly explain that an oracle can encode shortcuts or diagonalized hard information, so relativized worlds need not look physically natural.
- **Limit:** BGS does not imply P=NP is independent of standard axioms or unprovable; it constrains a family of proof techniques.
- **Later barriers:** Natural proofs/algebrization are separate barriers with different scopes; a practitioner sidebar could prevent “oracle barrier” from becoming a universal excuse.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Two worlds giving opposite answers is a memorable demonstration of why proof technique matters.

### BPP versus BQP oracle bullet (line 162)

- **Direction:** Since BPP⊆BQP unconditionally and relativizes for a common classical oracle, a separation means `$\mathrm{BPP}^O\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}^O`.
- **Bernstein–Vazirani attribution:** Identify the exact oracle problem/theorem (often recursive Fourier sampling or an early quantum-oracle separation) and whether the year is conference/preprint/publication.
- **Random-oracle citation unresolved:** The review's primary-source search did not recover support for “refined to a random oracle by Aaronson 2010.” Aaronson's arXiv `0910.4698` concerns BQP versus PH, including a relation-oracle result and conditional decision separation; do not cite it for random-oracle BPP/BQP without an exact theorem.
- **Random oracle definition:** State probability-one/with-high-probability over a sequence of independently random truth tables and whether quantum coherent access is allowed.
- **Relation versus language:** Some early/random oracle results separate relation/search classes rather than decision BQP/BPP. The chapter must not silently convert one into another.
- **Technique barrier:** To argue an unconditional BPP≠BQP proof must be nonrelativizing, also identify an oracle relative to which BPP=BQP (a PSPACE-complete oracle may be relevant under precise closure facts), not merely the separating oracle.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** This is a foundational evidence point, but uncertain attribution undermines confidence.

### Random-oracle NP not contained in BQP bullet (line 163)

- **Theorem precision:** BBBV's random-oracle result should state probability-one (or stated measure) over oracle choice and exact relativized language construction.
- **Model:** NP^O gets existential access to a verifier using `$O`; BQP^O gets coherent quantum queries to the same Boolean oracle.
- **Bad intuition phrase:** Oracle NP is not simply “structured search.” NP^O contains existentially quantified oracle predicates; the separation diagonalizes/uses search lower bounds across input lengths.
- **Grover role:** BBBV hybrid/search bounds show only quadratic improvement for locating marked items in an unstructured oracle, supporting the construction.
- **“Not exponentially”:** Grover's query reduction from `$N` to `$\sqrt N` is a quadratic reduction in `$N` but, when `$N=2^n`, it changes `$2^n` to `$2^{n/2}`—still exponential time while being an exponential numerical ratio. Use unambiguous language.
- **Relativized limitation:** This does not prove NP⊄BQP unrelativized; it shows a relativizing proof of NP⊆BQP cannot work for all oracles and supports incomparability beliefs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Random black-box worlds sharply expose why generic witness search remains hard quantumly.

### Raz–Tal BQP versus PH and NP^NP bullets (lines 164–165)

- **Main separation:** There exists `$O` with `$BQP^O\not\subseteq PH^O`; correct and already discussed in §17.5.
- **Redundancy:** Repeating the result is fine in a catalog, but link back rather than restate without definition/source.
- **Second-level consequence:** Since `$\Sigma_2^{p,O}` is one level inside `$PH^O`, the main separation implies a language outside it. But notation `$NP^{NP}` “relative to an oracle” is ambiguous.
- **Correct notation:** Write `$BQP^O\not\subseteq\Sigma_2^{p,O}` or `$BQP^O\not\subseteq NP^{NP,O}` under a declared oracle convention, not `$BQP\not\subseteq NP^{NP}` relative to something unnamed.
- **Strength ordering:** The NP^NP bullet adds no independent evidence beyond the stronger PH separation; use it pedagogically to connect §17.5's recursion or remove it.
- **Decision versus relation:** Raz–Tal's landmark result is a decision-oracle separation; distinguish it from Aaronson's earlier relation-oracle result.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Escaping the entire hierarchy remains the catalog's strongest quantum-class bullet; avoid diluting it with a redundant corollary.

### QMA versus QCMA oracle bullet (line 166)

- **Oracle kind:** Aaronson–Kuperberg's separation uses a **quantum oracle**, not necessarily an ordinary Boolean oracle. Highlight this because quantum-oracle relativization has different semantics and barriers.
- **Direction:** It supplies `$QMA^U\not\subseteq QCMA^U` for an appropriate unitary oracle while QCMA⊆QMA remains; state exact notation/model.
- **Evidence:** It suggests some quantum states can serve as short verifiable witnesses without comparable classical descriptions in that oracle world, but does not prove unrelativized strictness.
- **Later refinements:** Name exact classical-oracle/randomized-oracle separations if claimed; “oracles” plural currently hides differences.
- **Technique barrier:** A quantum-oracle separation may constrain fewer conventional proof techniques than a classical-oracle separation; calibrate the inference.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The example concretely tests whether quantum information itself is a stronger proof medium.

### “Closest real separations” framing and P versus EXP (lines 168–170)

- **Loaded terminology:** Unconditional hierarchy theorems are fully “real,” while oracle separations are also valid theorems in restricted models. Say “unrelativized class separations relevant to this diagram.”
- **P≠EXP:** Deterministic time hierarchy gives strict separation; correct.
- **Scope:** This is a classical separation, not specifically quantum complexity; it provides a coarse anchor.
- **Other unconditional results:** Query/depth/communication/circuit-class separations exist, so “mostly out of reach” should be scoped to broad uniform time classes like BPP/BQP/NP/QMA.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The rarity of broad separations is sobering, but scare quotes around “real” are unnecessary.

### BQP strict containment in EXPSPACE and BQP-versus-EXP note (line 171)

- **Valid chain:** BQP⊆PSPACE and PSPACE⊊EXPSPACE imply BQP⊊EXPSPACE: if BQP equaled EXPSPACE it would contain PSPACE, contradicting strictness; more directly BQP is a subset of the proper smaller PSPACE.
- **Space hierarchy:** State definitions of EXPSPACE and the space-hierarchy theorem; EXPSPACE was not introduced in §17.1.
- **Coarseness:** Calling it coarse is fair—the upper class permits exponentially more workspace than BQP's polynomial time permits.
- **BQP versus EXP:** Known BQP⊆PSPACE⊆EXP; strictness BQP≠EXP is unproved.
- **Equality implication:** If BQP=EXP, then EXP=BQP⊆PSPACE⊆EXP, so PSPACE=EXP; correct. Note it would also entail striking collapses/containments elsewhere.
- **“Equally open”:** PSPACE=EXP is open, though “equally momentous” is subjective; space/time hierarchy facts should be distinguished.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** This is a nice exercise in squeezing containments into a genuine strict result.

### Evidence for BPP≠BQP and conditional-separation conclusion (line 173)

- **Honest unknown:** No unrelativized proof BPP≠BQP is known; correct.
- **“No proof in sight”:** Sociological/time-sensitive; say no currently known technique establishes it as of the literature cutoff.
- **Candidate status:** Factoring/discrete log are in BQP and not known in BPP; Hamiltonian-dynamics decision tasks are BQP-complete but lie outside BPP only if the classes differ; sampling problems are not decision languages without reformulation.
- **Classical baselines:** Best-known algorithm gaps are evidence, not lower bounds. Structured Hamiltonians and sampling instances can be classically easy; specify hard families.
- **Cryptographic assumptions:** Factoring/discrete-log hardness against randomized classical algorithms can yield conditional separations for particular problems; other post-quantum assumptions support different quantum/classical relationships.
- **PH noncollapse:** Sampling-hardness arguments often show efficient classical sampling would collapse PH under average-case/#P and anti-concentration assumptions. They do not directly prove BPP≠BQP without all assumptions/reductions.
- **Overbroad “most”:** Current techniques also give unconditional separations in query, communication, space, depth, and restricted-circuit models. Say broad unrelativized polynomial-time class separation remains unavailable.
- **Missing experimental evidence nuance:** Experiments can demonstrate performance on finite instances but cannot prove asymptotic class separation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The evidence ledger is valuable and appropriately sober once every candidate is labeled by evidence type.

### §17.7 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It collects the oracle evidence shaping BQP/NP/PH/QMA intuitions and contrasts it with the very few broad unconditional separations.
- **Highest-priority logical repair:** Do not infer a nonrelativization barrier from one separating oracle; state paired-world/counteroracle logic precisely.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Resolve or remove the Aaronson-2010 random-oracle BPP/BQP attribution and distinguish classical, random, relation, decision, and quantum oracles.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Alternate oracle worlds are compelling, but this section must be exceptionally precise because it teaches how to interpret evidence rather than results alone.

## Chapter 17, §17.8 — Types of Quantum Speedup (lines 175–213)

### Taxonomy motivation (line 177)

- **Excellent premise:** “Speedup” is meaningless without specifying scaling variable, task, error, access model, and classical comparator; a taxonomy is highly useful.
- **Missing axes:** Categories should be a matrix, not one list: asymptotic ratio (constant/polynomial/superpolynomial/exponential), resource (queries/gates/time/space/samples/depth), evidence (proved/conditional/best-known/experimental), task (decision/function/relation/sampling/state preparation), and regime (worst/average case).
- **Overlap:** A speedup can be polynomial in precision, exponential in dimension, query-only, and conditional simultaneously. The current headings are not mutually exclusive.
- **Input-size normalization:** Always express runtimes in encoded input length `$n`; calling `$\sqrt N` polynomial or exponential depends on whether `$N` is list length or `$2^n` search space.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Taxonomy promises to turn hype words into a usable instrument; a multidimensional table would deliver that promise best.

### Polynomial-speedup heading and “provable, robust, ubiquitous” claim (line 179)

- **Provability scope:** Some listed query separations are proved; gate/time advantages over best classical implementations often are not. Do not let one adjective cover all layers.
- **“Robust”:** Polynomial advantages are especially vulnerable to constants, data loading, error correction, and classical algorithm improvements. Robustness must mean theorem under perturbation/model changes, not merely commonness.
- **“Ubiquitous”:** Sociological and unsupported. Polynomial improvements occur broadly, but not every domain or practical workload.
- **Error dependence:** Quadratic precision improvements can be decisive even when problem size is moderate; categorize separately from polynomial dimension speedups.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Energetic heading, but its confidence conflicts with the nuanced evidence lesson.

### Grover polynomial example (line 181)

- **Correct query scaling:** Unique/`$M`-marked unstructured search gives `$\Theta(\sqrt{N/M})` quantum versus `$\Theta(N/M)` randomized classical queries under standard promises.
- **Variable interpretation:** If `$N=2^n`, quantum runtime is still `$2^{n/2}`; the speedup factor is exponential in `$n` while the exponent is merely halved. This illustrates why labels need a denominator.
- **Gate lift:** Oracle and diffusion implementations add gates; SAT predicate evaluation can dominate but remains polynomial per query if the formula is explicit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Familiar and ideal for demonstrating taxonomy ambiguity.

### Quantum-walk examples (line 182)

- **Element distinctness:** Ambainis gives `$O(n^{2/3})` quantum queries versus `$\Theta(n)` classical randomized queries under a standard list oracle; quantum optimality is known. State `$n` is list length.
- **Triangle finding:** `$\widetilde O(n^{5/4})` must be dated, attributed, and labeled query versus time, with `$n` graph vertices and adjacency-matrix oracle. Chapter 15 already flagged this status claim for a 2026 check.
- **Classical comparator absent:** Triangle detection has fast algebraic and combinatorial classical algorithms under different models; quote both quantum query and actual time if claiming speedup.
- **Walk not sole ingredient:** Algorithms may combine learning graphs, nested searches, and algebra; “quantum walks giving” is acceptable shorthand after citation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Contrasting list collisions and graph triangles shows range, but mixed variables/models need a table.

### Monte Carlo polynomial example (line 183)

- **Ambiguous `$T`:** “`$O(\sqrt T)` speedups” could mean runtime becomes square root of a classical runtime, which is not a theorem without matched oracle costs. Define `$T` as classical sample/query complexity for a fixed error.
- **Precision form:** Classical mean estimation generally uses `$O(\sigma^2/\epsilon^2)` samples; quantum variance-aware/amplitude-estimation methods can use roughly `$\widetilde O(\sigma/\epsilon)` coherent queries under boundedness/oracle assumptions.
- **Montanaro scope:** *Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods* (2015) gives quadratic improvements for broad randomized algorithms under coherent implementation and moment/variance conditions; cite the exact theorem rather than one slogan.
- **Coherent access:** Need reversible sampler/payoff, inverses/reflections, and depth; this is not a black-box speedup for ordinary sample streams.
- **Confidence/range:** Failure probability and heavy tails introduce logarithms/truncation; `$\sigma` alone may not suffice.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Square-rooting sample complexity is practically evocative once variables are explicit.

### Amplitude-amplified subroutines (line 184)

- **Too vague to audit:** Name representative graph/number-theoretic algorithms, the amplified success probability, and full complexity before/after.
- **Composition:** If a subroutine succeeds with `$p`, amplitude amplification costs `$O(1/\sqrt p)` coherent uses versus `$O(1/p)` repetition, assuming reflections and inverse access.
- **No automatic end-to-end gain:** State preparation, checking, variable stopping times, and nested amplification can change complexity; variable-time amplification may be needed.
- **Number theory:** Avoid suggesting Shor's exponential advantage is merely amplitude amplification; use concrete algorithms such as collision/search components.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** A placeholder bullet adds little; a surprising concrete case would improve it.

### Claim that polynomial speedups survive gate/fault-tolerant lifting (line 186, first sentence)

- **False universal:** Some query speedups have no time-efficient oracle/algorithm; triangle/query algorithms and span-program constructions can have costly data structures. “These speedups survive” must be example-specific.
- **Realistic undefined:** Hardware connectivity, memory/QRAM, arithmetic, state preparation, precision, and output costs determine lifting.
- **Fault-tolerance overhead not constant:** Threshold theorems typically give polylogarithmic/architecture-dependent overhead in computation size and target logical error, with potentially huge constants and physical-qubit factories. Calling it “constant overhead” is incorrect.
- **Polynomial advantage resilience:** A polylog overhead can asymptotically preserve a sufficiently strong polynomial exponent gap, but finite crossovers may vanish.
- **Classical fault tolerance asymmetry:** Compare quantum physical runtime/cost with optimized classical hardware, parallelism, memory, and energy, not only logical gate counts.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The practical bridge is necessary, but confident generalization undermines the chapter's core skepticism.

### `$n\ge10^9` practical heuristic (line 186, second sentence)

- **Unsupported number:** No universal threshold makes square-root advantage practical. `$n` may count database records, oracle calls, paths, or dimension; per-item costs and parallelism differ by orders of magnitude.
- **Simple arithmetic incomplete:** `$10^9` versus `$\sqrt{10^9}\approx31623` looks large, but quantum coherent query cost, error correction, clock rate, setup, and repetitions decide crossover.
- **Classical baseline:** GPUs/distributed systems can issue many queries in parallel; Grover's sequential depth and limited quantum parallelization alter comparisons.
- **Oracle ratio:** “Oracle cheap relative to rest” is backwards/incomplete: quantum oracle must be cheap enough relative to classical query and fixed overhead; if non-oracle quantum work dominates, advantage vanishes.
- **Better tool:** Provide a crossover equation `$c_q\sqrt N+S_q<c_cN+S_c` with actual throughput/setup constants for scenarios rather than folklore `$10^9`.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Readers enjoy a number, but an unjustified number is sticky misinformation; an interactive crossover example would be better.

### Superpolynomial heading and Simon/Shor bullets (lines 188–191)

- **Evidence label:** Simon's query separation is unconditional in its oracle model; Shor's time separation from all classical algorithms is conditional/best-known. “Believed but not proved” should apply per bullet, not the whole category.
- **Simon:** `$O(n)` quantum versus `$\Omega(2^{n/2})` randomized queries under the Simon promise; correct after §17.6 model definition.
- **Shor terminology:** Polynomial quantum time versus best-known classical factoring/discrete-log algorithms that are superpolynomial/subexponential or exponential depending group; the speedup is not proved without classical lower bounds.
- **Assumption:** “No efficient classical factoring” establishes superpolynomial separation only if no polynomial classical algorithm; to compare exact best-known growth, state number-field-sieve complexity.
- **RSA:** Classical factoring hardness supports RSA specifically; discrete-log hardness supports DH/DSA/ECC families. Do not use RSA as evidence for both.
- **Cryptographic status:** RSA's historical security is evidence of practical classical hardness, not a complexity assumption of proved asymptotic form; attacks/parameter choices evolve.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Simon-to-Shor is a strong narrative pair and ideal for contrasting proved oracle versus conjectured time advantage.

### Abelian HSP bullet and claimed time lift (line 192)

- **Structural core:** Simon, order finding, factoring reductions, and discrete log fit abelian Fourier-sampling/HSP frameworks.
- **Not every abelian HSP automatically efficient:** Need an efficiently represented/decomposed finite abelian group, coherent group/oracle operations, efficient QFT, enough samples, and efficient classical postprocessing.
- **Query versus time:** Information/query efficiency can coexist with hard measurement/postprocessing or group decomposition in black-box settings. Cite exact general theorem/model.
- **“Group action”:** HSP oracle hides cosets via a function; group actions arise in related hidden-shift problems. Use correct interface.
- **Superpolynomial comparator:** State classical lower bound/best-known algorithm per concrete problem; a generic HSP family includes easy instances.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The unifying symmetry story is elegant, but “efficiently implementable action” is not the whole contract.

### Pell/principal-ideal bullet (line 193)

- **Task definition:** Pell's equation seeks/fundamental unit may have exponentially many output bits; Hallgren outputs a compact representation/solves regulator/principal ideal problems under precise number-field encoding.
- **Output-size issue:** A claimed polynomial-time algorithm cannot print an exponentially long minimal solution explicitly; state compact output and approximation.
- **Number fields:** Principal ideal algorithms may be polynomial for fixed-degree number fields or under specified degree/discriminant inputs; define scope.
- **Classical comparator:** “Super-polynomial” is relative to best known and assumptions, not an unconditional lower bound.
- **Precision:** Continuous/approximate Fourier sampling, regulator estimation, and success probability add technical conditions.
- **Citation:** Give Hallgren paper(s), year, theorem, and whether GRH/number-theory assumptions enter variants.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Pell's ancient equation becoming a quantum showcase is delightful; the compact-output twist is particularly engaging.

### QFT structural generalization and nonabelian-HSP status (line 195)

- **Commonality:** Abelian QFT/Fourier sampling is a genuine thread through Simon/Shor/Hallgren, though reductions and classical postprocessing differ.
- **“Outside sporadic”:** Overbroad; Hamiltonian simulation, quantum walks, amplitude estimation, sampling, and other algorithmic frameworks offer large conditional/query advantages outside abelian HSP.
- **Nonabelian is not uniformly unsolved:** Efficient algorithms/results exist for some nonabelian groups/promises; symmetric/dihedral cases remain important hard families. State specific open targets.
- **Dihedral significance:** Dihedral HSP connects to hidden shift and lattice problems; Kuperberg gives subexponential quantum algorithms, so it has not simply “resisted attack.”
- **Symmetric significance:** Efficient HSP over symmetric groups would have graph-isomorphism implications under standard reductions, but strong Fourier sampling limitations are known.
- **Generic query nuance:** Information-theoretically polynomial query/sample complexity may be possible while efficient joint measurement/time implementation is unknown; this is a valuable query/time lesson.
- **Aging:** “Two decades” should be replaced by literature-cutoff date and exact duration/source.
- **Centrality claim:** “One of central” is reasonable perspective but should be attributed or softened.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The unsolved symmetry frontier is compelling; mentioning Kuperberg and graph isomorphism supplies concrete stakes.

### Restricted-model Hamiltonian-simulation comparison (line 197, first half)

- **Not merely restricted cost:** Efficient quantum simulation of generic local dynamics versus brute-force state vectors is an exponential dimension comparison, but classical hardness is conditional/BQP-completeness-based and instance dependent.
- **State-vector baseline straw man:** Full `$2^n` vectors are a generic exact baseline, not always the best algorithm. The text correctly names tensor networks/Monte Carlo but should also include stabilizer methods, sign-problem structure, locality/light cones, and observable-specific algorithms.
- **Output matching:** Quantum hardware produces samples/observables, not a full state vector. Comparing quantum sampling to classical full-state output is unfair; match local observable/sample accuracy.
- **Monte Carlo caveat:** Quantum Monte Carlo is not uniformly applicable due to sign problems; tensor networks depend on entanglement/geometry/time.
- **BQP-complete families:** Use completeness to state that a universal efficient classical sampler/observable estimator would imply BPP=BQP under task assumptions, not that every Hamiltonian has exponential advantage.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The baseline correction is exactly the nuanced lesson readers need.

### Block-encoded linear algebra and dequantization preview (line 197, second half)

- **Dimension scaling:** QLSAs may have polylogarithmic dependence on matrix dimension under sparse/block/data access, favorable condition, state input, and quantum-state/observable output.
- **“Assumptions doing most work”:** Rhetorical and too universal. Some access models arise naturally from quantum subroutines or sparse formulas; quantify parameter contributions.
- **Dequantization:** Classical sample/query algorithms match dimension dependence for selected low-rank tasks while differing in rank, condition, precision, norms, and output. Do not imply all HHL successors are dequantized.
- **Cross-reference order:** §17.12 is later, so “made explicit” should be future tense (“will make explicit”).
- **Input construction:** Block encoding gate cost and normalization `$\alpha` are part of time, as Chapter 16 stressed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A good cautionary preview, though its verdict should await the actual parameter table.

### Sampling-complexity definition (line 199)

- **Core distinction:** Sampling from a distribution is not a decision problem and demands separate complexity/error definitions.
- **Input family:** Define distributions `$\mathcal D_x` indexed by an instance/circuit `$x`; a single fixed distribution can be hard-coded.
- **Approximation metric:** Specify exact sampling, total-variation distance, cross-entropy/fidelity proxies, multiplicative probability approximation, and allowed failure probability. Hardness changes dramatically.
- **Strong versus weak simulation:** Strong computes probabilities/amplitudes; weak generates samples. A strong-simulation lower bound does not automatically imply weak-sampling hardness.
- **Verification:** How does one validate samples without classically computing probabilities? Statistical tests can reject alternatives without certifying closeness to the ideal distribution.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The conceptual shift from answering a bit to reproducing a distribution is important and accessible.

### BosonSampling bullet (line 201)

- **Model:** Standard BosonSampling injects single photons into a passive linear-optical interferometer and photon-counts outputs; distinguish from Gaussian Boson Sampling used later.
- **Permanent relation:** Output probabilities involve squared permanents of submatrices; exact classical sampling hardness and approximate sampling arguments use different complexity assumptions.
- **Approximate hardness incomplete:** Aaronson–Arkhipov approximate-sampling evidence relies on conjectures such as Permanent-of-Gaussians average-case hardness and anti-concentration, plus PH noncollapse/Stockmeyer reasoning—not just “conjectured #P-hardness of approximating permanents.”
- **Formatting:** Use math `$\#P` rather than inline code ``#P`` and define #P.
- **Photon loss/distinguishability:** Experimental noise can change the distribution and classical simulability; connect to Jiuzhang cautiously.
- **Scale:** `$n` photons plus `$m` modes and collision regime determine hardness; one variable is insufficient.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Photons encoding permanents is a wonderful bridge between optics and complexity, deserving one formula.

### IQP sampling bullet (line 202)

- **Expansion:** Standard term is “Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time,” not merely “Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial.”
- **Circuit convention:** IQP circuits consist of commuting gates diagonal in a common basis (often X-diagonal acting on computational input and Z measurement, or equivalently Z-diagonal with surrounding Hadamards). State full preparation/measurement convention.
- **Hardness conditions:** Exact, multiplicative-error, additive/TV approximate sampling results differ and require average-case hardness/anti-concentration assumptions for robust experimental claims.
- **PH wording:** Efficient classical sampling plus the needed conjectures would collapse PH to a low level; PH noncollapse alone is not always sufficient.
- **Noise:** Constant local noise can make some IQP distributions classically simulable unless error correction or suitable observables/postselection are used.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** “Commuting yet hard to sample” is a delightful paradox; spell it out.

### RCS bullet (line 203)

- **Family:** Random circuits depend on architecture, gate ensemble, depth/cycles, qubits, and sampling/fidelity target; “RCS” is not one fixed distribution family.
- **Hardness chain incomplete:** Anti-concentration plus average-case #P-hardness of estimating output probabilities and Stockmeyer approximate counting under an efficient sampler lead to PH-collapse consequences under specified TV/multiplicative error. PH noncollapse is a conclusion-side assumption, not paired alone with anti-concentration.
- **Experimental metric:** Linear cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB) is a proxy and does not by itself certify total-variation closeness or ideal sampling hardness.
- **Noise:** At sufficient noise/depth, distributions may become easier or spoofable; experimental hardness must include fidelity/noise model.
- **Date:** Cite Google's 2019 primary paper and later larger circuits separately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Chaotic circuits as a benchmark are intuitive; a flowchart of assumptions would clarify the claim.

### Why sampling appeals for near-term demonstrations and conditional hardness logic (line 205)

- **Fault tolerance not strictly unnecessary:** Existing demonstrations run without full FT, but hardness at scale requires noise low enough that the experimental distribution stays in a classically hard regime. “Does not need” is empirical strategy, not theorem.
- **“Modest depth”:** Depth must be sufficient for anti-concentration/entanglement yet not so noisy as to wash out structure; define relative to architecture/size.
- **Load-bearing stack:** Correctly emphasizes conjectures, but also hardware fidelity, calibration, validation, and matched sampling metric are load bearing.
- **Logical chain:** Efficient approximate sampler → Stockmeyer estimates probabilities in FBPP^NP → with average-case #P hardness/anti-concentration yields PH collapse (under exact assumptions). Write this rather than a generic italic conditional.
- **Conjecture independence:** Correct that these assumptions are not equivalent to BQP≠BPP; sampling classes/problems do not map one-to-one to decision BQP.
- **Falsity:** If a hardness conjecture fails, the conditional argument disappears; it does not imply PH collapse. This is a valuable logical point.
- **Classical spoofing:** Passing selected validation statistics is weaker than sampling the target distribution; include this in “scrutiny.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The conditional proof stack is an excellent practitioner lesson and should be diagrammed premise by premise.

### “Supremacy” coinage, terminology shift, and definition (line 207)

- **Historical claim:** Verify Preskill's exact 2012 source/context for coining “quantum supremacy”; cite it rather than asserting chronology.
- **Original meaning:** It generally meant reaching a regime beyond feasible classical simulation for a specific task, not a formal class separation.
- **Terminology reason:** “Less politically loaded” is one factor; inclusivity/colonial-racial connotations and scientific precision have both been discussed. Avoid reducing the shift to one adjective without source.
- **Advantage definition:** “Faster than best known classical algorithm on best hardware” is an empirical performance claim, not proof no classical computer could replicate it. Distinguish demonstrated benchmark advantage from complexity-theoretic advantage.
- **Metric:** Faster may mean wall time, cost, energy, accuracy, throughput, or solution quality. Fix task and success/fidelity.
- **Usefulness:** Advantage demonstrations need not solve useful tasks; say so explicitly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The terminology history is useful, but a neutral evidence taxonomy matters more than politics shorthand.

### Google Sycamore headline and IBM response (line 209, first part)

- **Google primary claim verified:** The 2019 Sycamore paper reports roughly 200 seconds for one million samples from a 53-qubit random circuit and estimated about 10,000 years for its then-modeled classical benchmark.
- **Claim versus fact:** Keep “estimated/claimed”; the classical time was model dependent, not an observed 10,000-year run.
- **IBM response precision:** IBM proposed a Schrödinger-style/state-vector simulation using Summit's secondary storage and estimated about 2.5 days, not merely vague “days.” Verify whether tensor-network language accurately describes that proposal; it may be a full-state/storage strategy.
- **Not completed at response time:** Distinguish a proposed resource estimate from an executed classical reproduction.
- **Task matching:** Compare number of samples, circuit instance/cycles, XEB fidelity, correlations, energy, and preprocessing; “same task” is not automatic.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The rapid 10,000-years-to-days reversal is dramatic and a perfect baseline lesson when the methods are described accurately.

### 2021–2024 classical RCS progress and named teams (line 209, middle)

- **Citation overload:** “Pan–Zhang–Chen advances,” “USTC group,” Gordon Bell run, and 2024 GPU result each need full primary citations, hardware, circuit, sample, fidelity, and runtime fields.
- **Sunway 304-second claim unresolved:** The current review search did not recover a primary source confirming an exactly matched 304-second million-sample Sycamore task. Do not compare it to Google's 200 seconds until sample correlations/XEB/circuit and preprocessing are matched.
- **Award wording:** Verify the exact Gordon Bell Prize year/category/title through ACM/SC records; a run associated with an award paper is not automatically “the Prize run.”
- **“Chinese teams”:** Nationality is less informative than institutions/authors/hardware; name collaborations consistently.
- **Fixed-benchmark point:** Later classical algorithms can target the published circuit ensemble/instances, while quantum hardware advances to new scales. This is still a legitimate benchmark reassessment but not a timeless comparison.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The classical chase is gripping; a chronological table would prevent a blur of names and incompatible benchmarks.

### 1,432-GPU 2024 result (line 209, ending)

- **Primary support:** Zhao et al., *Leapfrogging Sycamore: Harnessing 1432 GPUs for 7× Faster Quantum Random Circuit Sampling* (arXiv `2406.18889`), reports uncorrelated samples with higher linear-XEB score and seven-times faster time-to-solution than the 53-qubit, 20-cycle Sycamore experiment.
- **Use exact factor:** Replace “several times” with the paper's reported 7×, while labeling it the authors' comparison.
- **Metric matching:** State sample count, XEB, circuit ensemble/instance, preprocessing, GPU model, wall time, and energy boundaries from the paper.
- **“Refute” caution:** The authors call it unambiguous evidence refuting the original advantage claim for that fixed benchmark; distinguish this from refuting RCS advantage at larger/deeper future parameters.
- **Publication status/date:** Track preprint versus peer-reviewed publication and version; results may update.
- **Energy:** The abstract also claims much lower energy than prior classical works, a relevant advantage metric if independently specified.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A classical machine literally leapfrogging a famous quantum benchmark is a memorable demonstration of moving baselines.

### Jiuzhang/Jiuzhang 3.0 status and “least-contested” claim (line 211, first half)

- **Model distinction:** Jiuzhang uses **Gaussian** Boson Sampling with squeezed states, not standard single-photon BosonSampling; connect but do not conflate hardness assumptions.
- **Primary Jiuzhang 3.0 evidence:** Deng et al., arXiv `2304.12240`, reports pseudo-photon-number-resolving detection up to 255 clicks, 1.27 μs sample time, and authors' exact-classical estimates (~600 years for a single ideal sample on Frontier; much larger for hardest events), plus validation against then-current mockups.
- **Exact versus noisy target:** Comparing experiment with exact ideal-distribution simulation can overstate advantage if noise/loss permits faster approximate simulation. Match the experimentally realized distribution and validation metric.
- **“Least-contested” is sociological:** It needs a systematic literature review and is especially unstable given continuing approximate/lossy GBS algorithms. The parenthetical admits this but does not source it.
- **Classical progress:** Primary work such as *Classical algorithm for simulating experimental Gaussian boson sampling* (arXiv `2306.03709`, later publication) explicitly targets Jiuzhang/Borealis-scale noisy experiments; incorporate rather than claiming low contest.
- **Hardness assumptions:** GBS probabilities involve hafnians/loop hafnians and approximate-sampling conjectures; “different from RCS” is true but insufficient.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The photonic scale and microsecond sampling are spectacular; noisy-target fairness is the essential counterweight.

### 2024–2025 moving-line summary (line 211, second half)

- **Cutoff inconsistency:** Current chapter framing mentions 2025–2026 literature, but the summary stops at 2024–2025 and ignores any verified 2026 developments. State a fixed May 2026 search cutoff and update.
- **Fixed benchmark:** Correct that original RCS gaps narrowed/closed while newer circuits can reset scale; this is a valuable distinction between a task instance and an architecture trajectory.
- **“Quantum advantage” threshold:** Define feasible classical wall time/cost and matched accuracy rather than a moving rhetorical line.
- **Dedicated response:** Benchmark claims intentionally stimulate classical innovation; publication latency and hardware availability affect comparisons.
- **No monotonicity:** Bigger/deeper/noisier circuits are not automatically harder; structure, noise, layout, and target fidelity matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The arms-race framing is compelling and appropriately provisional when dated rigorously.

### Three practitioner questions and cryptographic analogy (line 213)

- **Task question:** Excellent; add input distribution, instance generation, sample count, error/fidelity, and useful output.
- **Baseline question:** Strong versus weak simulation and tensor-network memory are crucial; also ask classical preprocessing, parallel hardware, energy/cost, and best algorithm as of what date.
- **Rebuttal question:** Valuable, but “rebutted” can imply binary invalidation. Ask whether matched classical cost estimates changed and which parts of the claim survive.
- **Unsupported frequency claim:** “Erosion has typically followed within a few years” is explicitly called folklore but should be removed or backed by a defined sample of claims/times. Labeling unsupported statistics folklore does not make them useful evidence.
- **Additional questions:** Is hardness proved or conditional? Does validation certify the target distribution? Is noise included? Is the task decision/useful or benchmark sampling?
- **Cryptographic analogy:** Apt in that security/advantage claims depend on best attacks and update over time; unlike cryptography, sampling benchmarks may lack an adversarially valuable task and formal security reduction. State the limits.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A strong actionable finish; expanding it to a checklist would make this a standout reference.

### §17.8 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It recognizes that “speedup” spans query theorems, conjectural time advantages, access-model gains, and empirical sampling races, then asks readers to audit baselines.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Remove universal gate/FT survival claims, the constant-overhead statement, generic abelian-HSP time guarantee, and incomplete sampling-hardness chains.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Replace `$n\ge10^9` folklore, unresolved Sunway matching, and “least-contested”/typical-erosion claims with sourced scenario tables; update through the declared 2026 cutoff.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** One of the chapter's liveliest sections, with an excellent moving-baseline narrative that needs a stricter multidimensional taxonomy.

## Chapter 17, §17.9 — What “Exponential Speedup” Really Means (lines 215–226)

### Overload framing and missing dimensions (line 217)

- **Strong premise:** Explicitly separating meanings of “exponential” is essential and follows naturally from §17.8.
- **Four is not exhaustive:** Also distinguish exponential improvement in precision/error, sample complexity, space/depth, parameterized complexity, communication, and output-size-limited tasks.
- **Formal versus empirical:** Each category needs a label: proved lower bound, oracle theorem, conditional complexity consequence, best-known comparison, or finite benchmark.
- **Input variable:** Define `$n` as encoded input length for every example; otherwise exponential in qubits/dimension/numeric value are confused.
- **Speedup ratio:** Ratios can be stretched exponential `$2^{n^c}` for `$0<c<1`, fully exponential `$2^{\Theta(n)}`, or superpolynomial but subexponential. Explain terminology conventions.
- **Error matching:** Both algorithms must solve the same task to the same accuracy/confidence; exponential precision claims often hide this mismatch.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The phrase deserves exactly this skeptical unpacking; a truth-label column would sharpen it.

### Meaning 1 — gate/time-model comparison and Shor versus GNFS (line 219)

- **Metric mismatch:** Classical algorithms are usually measured in bit/RAM operations, memory, and parallel time, not “gates” in the quantum circuit sense. Use comparable time/operation models or state conversion overhead.
- **Best-known is not complexity separation:** A ratio between best known algorithms is an empirical algorithmic gap, not a proved unrelativized lower bound. Label it “best-known unrelativized time comparison.”
- **Definition:** `$T_C/T_Q=2^{\Omega(n^c)}` for some `$c>0` captures stretched/full exponential ratios, but only if both runtimes use the same `$n`, output/error, and cost model.
- **Factoring variable:** For an `$N`-bit? Better: factoring an integer `$M` with bit length `$n=\log_2M`; GNFS heuristic runtime is `$\exp((c+o(1))n^{1/3}(\log n)^{2/3})`, while Shor is polynomial in `$n` under gate arithmetic. This is superpolynomial/subexponential classical time and a stretched-exponential ratio.
- **GNFS status:** Its standard complexity expression is heuristic/expected under assumptions about smoothness and implementation; distinguish proven algorithms/bounds.
- **Odd phrase:** “No quantum-resistant classical algorithm” is not standard—an algorithm is not quantum-resistant. Say “no polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm.”
- **Output:** Full factorization has polynomial output length in `$n`; no output-size obstruction.
- **Hardware:** Logical gate polynomiality does not imply near-term wall-clock advantage; fault-tolerant resources remain.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Writing the actual GNFS exponent would make the famous gap much more informative.

### Meaning 2 — exponential query separation and Simon (line 220)

- **Correct model claim:** Simon gives an unconditional bounded-error query separation under its promise: `$O(n)` quantum versus `$\Omega(2^{n/2})` randomized classical queries.
- **Oracle specification:** “Same gap” must refer to a promised oracle family, coherent quantum access, and output recovery; define it or link §17.6.
- **Free computation:** Query model ignores gate cost between calls, oracle implementation, and data construction, so the theorem is bulletproof only within that model.
- **Time lift:** Some structured oracles can be efficiently implemented; adversarial Simon oracles need not be. Do not imply query-only means inherently impractical.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A clean anchor for what an unconditional exponential statement actually looks like.

### Meaning 3 — restricted classical simulation baseline (line 221)

- **Output mismatch risk:** Classical state-vector simulation outputs/maintains exponentially many amplitudes; a quantum device usually produces samples or observables. Comparing full-state maintenance with one sample is not a matched task.
- **Generic baseline:** State vectors are a valid exact worst-case simulator, not necessarily the “classical algorithm” for a specific observable/state family.
- **Tensor networks:** Performance depends on entanglement, contraction width, geometry, depth, approximation, and observable. “Where tensor networks are good” is true but tautological; name scaling regimes.
- **Other simulators:** Stabilizer-rank, Monte Carlo/sign structure, neural/tensor representations, light-cone methods, and Schrödinger–Feynman hybrids also matter.
- **Hard-family statement:** BQP-complete local-dynamics tasks give conditional evidence no universal classical polynomial simulator exists unless BPP=BQP; this is stronger than comparing one restricted implementation.
- **Noise:** Noisy dynamics may be easier to simulate; match device noise versus ideal target.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The straw-baseline warning is excellent and broadly applicable.

### Meaning 4 — quantum-friendly input access and HHL (line 222)

- **Loaded asymmetry:** Saying the classical baseline is “denied the same access” implies deliberate unfairness. Quantum coherent amplitude/block access and classical sample/query access are different interfaces; define the closest operationally comparable capabilities and preprocessing.
- **Access construction:** Include cost to build QRAM/data structures, update them, prepare `$|b\rangle`, and implement `$U_A`; if data are generated coherently by a prior quantum process, the quantum interface may be natural.
- **Other parameters:** HHL/QLSA advantages depend on sparsity/block normalization, condition number, rank/norms, precision, state overlap, and limited quantum output—not access alone.
- **Dequantization scope:** Tang-style algorithms remove exponential dimension dependence for selected tasks/access regimes but often have worse polynomial dependencies; “often eliminates this kind” should point to exact pairs.
- **Amortization:** `$O(N)` preprocessing can be worthwhile across many queries; total lifecycle rather than one call decides savings.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Input-access sleight of hand is a vital lesson; neutral matched-interface language will persuade more effectively.

### Practitioner rule and evidence hierarchy (line 224)

- **Excellent first action:** Identify which meaning, resource, input variable, task, error, and baseline before evaluating any speedup claim.
- **“Bulletproof”:** Query lower bounds are rigorous under their exact oracle/promise/error model; they are not immune to changing the oracle or task.
- **“Say little about practice”:** Too broad. Grover bounds guide cryptographic key-size choices, and query algorithms can lift when oracle circuits are cheap. Say they are insufficient alone.
- **Product claim:** Building a product on a conditional time gap also requires hardware feasibility, end-to-end cost, market/task value, reliability, and stability against classical progress—not merely belief in classical hardness.
- **No-classical-algorithm trust:** One cannot establish absence by trust; articulate a named complexity/cryptographic assumption and monitor best algorithms.
- **Restricted-model value:** Such separations can identify bottlenecks and inspire algorithms even without practical advantage; “sometimes oversold” is fair but sociological.
- **Add evidence labels:** “Theorem / conditional theorem / best known / experiment / forecast” would turn the rule into a checklist.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Direct and actionable, with a few absolutes to soften.

### Input-origin and arbitrary-amplitude loading rule (line 226)

- **Core lower bound:** A generic arbitrary `$2^n`-amplitude classical vector contains exponential information, so explicitly reading/loading it cannot take poly(`$n`) time without structure, preprocessing, or an oracle.
- **Normalization/precision:** Number of classical bits is actually `$\Theta(2^n b)` for `$b`-bit amplitude precision, subject to normalization/global phase; state the accuracy model.
- **State-preparation theorem:** Generic amplitude preparation needs exponential data/operations, while sparse, formula-generated, tensor-network, Fourier, or quantum-native states may be efficient.
- **Overabsolute conclusion:** “Has not actually saved time” fails when preprocessing is amortized across many queries, the data are already in quantum memory, or the state arises naturally from a physical/quantum process. Say the loading cost must be included and may erase advantage.
- **QRAM nuance:** QRAM can offer polylog coherent queries after `$O(N)`-scale loading/building, but hardware, routing, fault tolerance, updates, and classical analogous data structures matter.
- **Output mirror:** The result also has to go somewhere; full classical readout of `$2^n` amplitudes is exponential, while targeted observables may remain efficient.
- **Cross-reference:** Chapter 16 discusses block encodings, but Chapter 26's exact QRAM treatment must be verified when reached; do not promise resolution unseen.
- **Most HHL applications:** “Most” needs a surveyed corpus. Replace with “many classical-data proposals.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** “The input has to come from somewhere” is one of the book's best maxims; the amortized/quantum-native exceptions complete it.

### §17.9 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It gives practitioners a compact vocabulary for separating theorem-level query gaps, best-known time gaps, restricted simulators, and access-model advantages.
- **Highest-priority formal repair:** Label meaning 1 as conditional/best-known, define bit-length/GNFS scaling, and match outputs/error/cost in meaning 3.
- **Highest-priority scope repair:** Replace denial/free-loading rhetoric with lifecycle accounting for coherent and classical data interfaces, including amortization and quantum-native inputs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Short, memorable, and highly useful once its absolutes become calibrated rules.

## Chapter 17, §17.10 — Query Complexity vs. Time Complexity (lines 228–249)

### Operational framing of query versus time (line 230)

- **Core contrast:** Query complexity isolates information acquisition; executable runtime includes oracle realization and every operation between calls. This is a crucial practitioner distinction.
- **“Time-model algorithm”:** Define uniform circuit gate complexity, depth, and classical/quantum RAM assumptions rather than using an undefined phrase.
- **Operationally narrow:** Query models can still be operational for APIs, cryptographic oracles, laboratory experiments, and expensive function evaluations; “abstract” does not mean irrelevant.
- **Why bite is lost:** State preparation, data movement, precision arithmetic, oracle workspace/uncomputation, and output sampling are the common failure points; preview them here.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** A strong practical pivot with a vivid “where results lose bite” hook.

### Efficient oracle implementation requirement (line 234)

- **Necessary but incomplete:** A `$Q(n)`-query algorithm with oracle gate cost `$G_O(n,\eta)` incurs roughly `$QG_O` plus inter-query gates, depth, and synthesis error. Merely saying each oracle is polynomial does not give the exponent/crossover.
- **Uniform construction:** Oracle circuits must be generated uniformly from the explicit input in polynomial classical time; otherwise their descriptions can hide advice/preprocessing.
- **Coherent interface:** Need controlled/superposition queries, inverses, clean garbage, reflections, and finite-precision arithmetic as required by the algorithm—not merely a classical function evaluator.
- **Error allocation:** Oracle approximation `$\eta` may need scale as total target error divided by query count; gate cost can then grow with `$\log(Q/\epsilon)`.
- **Preprocessing/amortization:** Data structures/QRAM/QROM may require large build cost that can be amortized across runs; include lifecycle.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Turning one “oracle call” into an actual subcircuit is the exact accounting move readers need.

### Compilation requirement (line 235)

- **Gate-set compilation:** Translate logical high-level gates/rotations to a fixed fault-tolerant/native set with an error budget; count synthesis gates, routing, swaps, and ancillas.
- **Hardware dependence:** Native connectivity, parallelism, measurement/feed-forward, calibration, and code operations mean two devices can have different depths for the same logical circuit.
- **Classical compiler time:** Usually offline/polynomial but can be substantial; exact optimization may be hard. Do not require globally optimal compilation to define time complexity.
- **Approximation:** Solovay–Kitaev is a class-level guarantee, while Clifford+T number-theoretic synthesis gives concrete rotation costs; distinguish asymptotic membership from resource estimation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Important but terse; one rotation-synthesis example would enliven it.

### Fault-tolerance compatibility requirement (line 236)

- **Correction relative to §17.8:** It is good that this line explicitly says overhead is not constant.
- **Threshold assumptions:** Fault-tolerance theorems require physical noise below threshold, locality/correlation assumptions, fresh ancillas, decoding/control, and a target total failure probability.
- **Overhead form:** Depending on code/noise/architecture and what resource is measured, overhead can be polylogarithmic or larger in circuit size/error; “polylogarithmic-to-polynomial” is too broad to guide scaling.
- **Scaling preservation:** A polynomial overhead can absolutely erase a polynomial quantum advantage if its exponent is large; even polylog overhead may dominate finite sizes. Compute the combined exponent/crossover.
- **Logical versus physical:** Complexity-theory time generally assumes ideal gates; fault tolerance is a physical realization layer, not a prerequisite for a mathematical query-to-gate lift.
- **NISQ/analog:** Some algorithms target error-mitigated or analog execution rather than FT; their noise/error scaling requires different analysis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The correction is welcome; code-specific examples would prevent “polynomial overhead” becoming another black box.

### What is needed for a formal or empirical separation (line 238)

- **Key distinction:** An unrestricted **formal time separation** needs a classical lower bound under a matched model; a best-known-baseline comparison supplies evidence/benchmark advantage, not a theorem.
- **Wording defect:** “A classical time lower bound or best-known-baseline argument … With all that the lift succeeds” conflates two epistemic outcomes. Split “proved separation” from “conditional/empirical advantage.”
- **Non-query costs:** Correctly names state preparation/readout; also include classical preprocessing/postprocessing, repetitions, confidence, output verification, and memory.
- **Shor:** Its quantum algorithm fully lifts to polynomial gate time, but the separation from all classical algorithms rests on the unproved absence of polynomial classical factoring. Say “the algorithm lifts; the speedup remains conditional.”
- **Input/output matching:** Factoring's classical input and output are explicit polynomial-size strings, making the comparison unusually clean.
- **Limited practical implications:** Query theorems can still rule out black-box improvements, guide oracle design, or establish optimal dependence; “limited” should not mean none.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Shor is the right positive example, and the proof-versus-baseline fork is an excellent teaching opportunity.

### Four-column resource-ledger framing (lines 240–245)

- **Useful start, not complete ledger:** Query count, logical gates, logical depth, and space are foundational but must be paired with error/success and classical resources.
- **Logical/physical mixing:** “Space” combines algorithm ancillas with “error-correction” qubits, conflating logical qubit count and physical qubit footprint. Use separate columns.
- **Gate count definition:** Count one-/two-qubit logical gates, rotations, measurements, resets, classical controls, and oracle calls consistently; a universal set may hide expensive arbitrary rotations.
- **Depth:** Wall time requires duration-weighted scheduled depth, not simply longest number of gates; measurement and lattice surgery have different cycle lengths.
- **Query:** “Conceptual equivalent” is too loose—time-evolution use, block-encoding query, data oracle, and function call have different controlled/adjoint costs.
- **Additional columns:** Input/preprocessing; target error/confidence; success/repetitions; T/CCZ count and depth; logical qubits; physical qubits; QEC cycles/spacetime volume; classical memory/time; output/verification; energy/cost.
- **Parallelism:** Report work and span/depth plus number of factories/QPUs; total count alone hides scheduling.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A ledger is exactly the right device; making it an actual table/template would be highly useful.

### Query-count row (line 242)

- **Oracle identity:** Specify exact unitary, precision, control/adjoint availability, and whether state-preparation calls count.
- **Equivalent ambiguity:** A time-evolution operator may itself be synthesized by many block queries; do not count both levels without a hierarchy.
- **Cost variance:** Oracle invocations can have data/parameter-dependent depth; worst-case/average/amortized convention matters.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Necessary but should link to a formal oracle contract.

### Gate-count row (line 243)

- **Chosen set:** State Clifford+T, Clifford+T+measurement, Toffoli model, or native analog gates; counts are not interchangeable.
- **Approximation:** Gate count depends on total error allocation and rotation-synthesis precision.
- **Oracle inclusion:** Correctly says include oracle and surrounding circuit, repairing common query-only reporting.
- **Count versus volume:** Gate count ignores qubit occupancy/duration and parallel execution; report spacetime volume when physical.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Clear but architecture labels are essential.

### Circuit-depth row (line 244)

- **Dependency definition:** Logical depth is the critical path after respecting qubit conflicts, controls, measurements, and classical feed-forward.
- **Coherence:** Under FT computation, physical coherence time is continually protected; total algorithm runtime matters through logical failure, not a bare device coherence window. “Coherence budget” fits NISQ more directly.
- **Clock cycles:** Convert each operation layer to code cycles/native duration; T-state availability and routing can stall nominal depth.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Good practical focus with a needed NISQ/FT distinction.

### Space row (line 245)

- **Logical categories:** Separate data, clean/dirty workspace, selector/signal, routing, distillation/factory, syndrome, and decoder/control resources.
- **Peak versus total:** Space is peak simultaneous qubits, while spacetime volume integrates qubit-cycles; both matter.
- **Physical mapping:** Code distance can vary across patches/time and depends on operation error budget; no fixed logical-to-physical multiplier.
- **Classical memory:** Classical simulators and quantum control/decoding use substantial memory; matched comparisons should include it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Ancilla bookkeeping becomes tangible when split by role.

### T-count, Toffoli/CCZ units, and Clifford/non-Clifford asymmetry (line 247, first half)

- **Architecture-specific importance:** T count is a major metric for Clifford+T surface-code designs, not a universal fifth metric that always dominates.
- **Correct nonconflation warning:** Toffoli count, T count, T depth, and CCZ/Toffoli-state consumption differ; the sentence rightly warns against direct conflation.
- **Decomposition variability:** Toffoli implementations trade T count/depth, measurements, clean/dirty ancillas, and relative phase; dedicated CCZ states change factory accounting.
- **Clifford cost:** Correctly notes Clifford gates are not free; surface-code lattice surgery/routing/measurements can dominate width/depth.
- **Transversality:** “Transversal in some codes” needs specify not all Clifford gates are transversal in every code and Eastin–Knill constrains universal transversal sets.
- **Magic states:** Distillation is common, but newer cultivation, catalysis, code switching, gauge fixing, and alternative code-native gates alter supply cost.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §8.10 actually details this resource asymmetry and uses terminology consistent with Chapter 15's cultivation discussion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The factory picture is vivid and practically important.

### Factory-dominance and true spacetime qualifiers (line 247, middle)

- **Overbroad dominance:** Magic-state factories often dominate selected large surface-code estimates, but memory, routing, reaction depth, data blocks, decoding, or Clifford operations can dominate other algorithms/architectures.
- **“Realistic noise rates”:** Give physical error, code cycle, target logical failure, decoder, and factory protocol; otherwise the phrase cannot be audited.
- **Correct multimetric caveat:** T depth, throughput, logical width, and routing jointly set cost; add code distance/cycles and classical feed-forward.
- **Spacetime unit:** Report physical-qubit-seconds or qubit-cycles rather than treating T count as a proxy without architecture mapping.
- **Failure budget:** More T states/cycles require lower logical error per operation and larger code distance, making cost nonlinear.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The caveat is strong; it should govern the paragraph rather than trail its superlative.

### RSA-2048 figures and 2019/2025 estimate linkage (line 247, ending)

- **Source/scenario:** Roughly `$3\times10^9` Toffolis and ~20 million physical noisy qubits/~8 hours correspond approximately to Gidney–Ekerå-era resource assumptions; cite exact table/version and use the paper's number rather than rounding across designs.
- **Not direct T conversion:** The physical estimate depends on reaction depth, modular-arithmetic layout, CCZ/T factories, surface-code cycle/error, routing, and failure allocation—not merely “the corresponding T-count.”
- **Logical versus physical:** Make explicit that 20 million is physical noisy qubits under assumed surface code, while Toffolis are logical operations.
- **2025 refinement tradeoff:** Gidney 2025's sub-million-qubit headline also changes runtime (roughly under a week versus hours) and resource-state/architecture assumptions. It is not a monotonic replacement using the same conversion.
- **Terminology:** The new work emphasizes magic-state cultivation/other design changes; do not describe every resource state as conventional distillation.
- **Comparability table:** Put physical error, cycle time, physical qubits, runtime, success probability, logical operations, factories, and code in side-by-side rows.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** RSA resource numbers are inherently gripping; scenario transparency prevents them becoming cargo-cult constants.

### T-count-as-practicality takeaway (line 249)

- **False dichotomy:** Query complexity can determine asymptotic interest, but gate/time/space/output structure also determines theoretical interest. T count alone does not determine practicality.
- **Near-future mismatch:** Near-term non-fault-tolerant devices do not execute logical Clifford+T circuits with distillation factories; T count is most relevant to projected fault-tolerant deployment.
- **Better question:** Ask for a complete logical and physical resource estimate with error model, not merely T count.
- **Algorithm dependence:** Analog, photonic, topological, measurement-based, neutral-atom, and non-Clifford-native architectures use different cost currencies.
- **Classical comparison:** Practicality also needs matched classical cost, value, data pipeline, and total wall-clock/energy.
- **Memorable repair:** “Query count sketches the algorithm; spacetime-and-error accounting prices the implementation.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The punchline is memorable but too single-metric for a section devoted to multidimensional accounting.

### §17.10 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It explicitly separates oracle theorems from compiled execution and offers a practitioner resource ledger with fault-tolerant context.
- **Highest-priority conceptual repair:** Separate formal lower-bound separation from best-known advantage, and logical resources from physical architecture resources.
- **Highest-priority resource repair:** Replace T-count determinism with full error-aware physical spacetime accounting; source RSA scenarios as distinct architectures/tradeoffs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Practical and highly relevant, with a ledger metaphor worth expanding into a reusable template.

## Chapter 17, §17.11 — Lower Bounds and Limits (lines 251–279)

### Opening claim about routine lower bounds (line 253)

- **Scope correction:** **Quantum query complexity** is unusually rich in lower bounds. Broad uniform quantum time/circuit lower bounds remain profoundly difficult, as line 263 itself says. Replace “quantum complexity” with the restricted area.
- **Model labeling:** A proof that no `$T`-query algorithm succeeds does not rule out algorithms with a different oracle/input representation; every “no algorithm” phrase must name model, error, promise, and output.
- **Two techniques:** Polynomial and adversary methods dominate Boolean query lower bounds, but hybrid arguments, information theory, communication reductions, representation theory, and no-fast-forwarding are also important. Say “two central general techniques.”
- **Cross-reference:** §17.6 already introduced them; this section should add worked consequences or limits rather than repeat slogans.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The promise of actual impossibility proofs is exciting; restricting it honestly to queries preserves credibility.

### Polynomial-method search lower bound (line 257)

- **Result:** Bounded-error quantum search/OR on `$N` bits needs `$\Omega(\sqrt N)` queries, matching Grover's `$O(\sqrt N)` asymptotically.
- **Method attribution:** The original BBBV hybrid lower bound predates/does not rely solely on the polynomial method; Beals et al. also derive polynomial lower bounds. Say which proof is meant.
- **Promise:** Unique marked item, zero-versus-one marked, or general OR have slightly different exact constants; specify bounded-error OR/unique search.
- **Approximate degree:** OR's approximate degree is `$\Theta(\sqrt N)`; because acceptance degree ≤`$2T`, this yields the query lower bound.
- **Constants:** “Up to constants” is correct; exact quantum query complexity/constants are a separate topic.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A one-line Chebyshev/approximate-degree intuition would make the proof feel tangible.

### Polynomial-method element-distinctness lower bound (line 258)

- **Result:** Element distinctness has bounded-error quantum query complexity `$\Theta(N^{2/3})` under a standard value-oracle model, matching Ambainis's walk algorithm.
- **Variable consistency:** §17.8 used `$n`; this line uses `$N`. Pick list length `$N` and distinguish item bit width/range.
- **Promise/range:** Inputs are lists/oracles over a sufficiently large alphabet; output decides whether all entries are distinct. Range size can affect reductions.
- **Attribution:** Aaronson–Shi established collision/element-distinctness-related polynomial lower bounds, with Shi refinements/history; cite exact theorem and publication rather than a compound surname only.
- **Time complexity:** Query optimality does not automatically imply gate-optimality; data structure/quantum walk update/check costs matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Matching a nontrivial walk exponent with an algebraic lower bound is a satisfying success story.

### Approximate-counting and Hamiltonian-simulation lower-bound shorthand (line 259)

- **Too vague to verify:** State the task, error parameters, oracle normalization, and exact lower/upper formulas for each.
- **Approximate counting:** Quantum query complexity depends on marked fraction/count, additive versus relative error, and success probability; amplitude estimation/counting has regime-dependent bounds.
- **Hamiltonian simulation:** Time/no-fast-forwarding lower bounds, precision log-over-loglog lower bounds, and sparse/block-oracle normalization arise from different constructions/methods. Do not attribute all generically to “the polynomial method.”
- **Polylog phrase:** “Within polylog factors” is weaker than Chapter 16's repeated “optimal” claims and may conflict. Reconcile exact theorem/model across chapters.
- **Gate caveat:** These are oracle-query lower bounds; block-encoding implementation and structure can allow fast-forwardable special families.
- **Citations:** Name Nayak–Wu/approximate counting and Berry et al./Hamiltonian simulation results as appropriate after exact verification.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** A vague miscellany is less useful than one fully worked bound.

### General adversary tightness claim (line 261)

- **Core theorem:** The negative-weight/general adversary bound characterizes bounded-error quantum query complexity up to constants under standard function-evaluation formulations.
