### Heading and code naming (lines 43–45)

- **Clarity:** “3-qubit bit-flip code” correctly signals a restricted-noise repetition code, not a full arbitrary-single-qubit-error code.
- **Plural heading:** The section presents one code; singular “The three-qubit bit-flip code” would match unless variants are added.
- **Notation:** This is often written as a $[[3,1,1]]$ quantum stabilizer code with restricted $X$-distance 3; introduce bracket notation only after defining it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Familiar now, but a necessary formal consolidation.

### Logical basis and encoding equation (lines 45–49)

- **Correct:** $|0_L\rangle=|000\rangle$, $|1_L\rangle=|111\rangle$, and linear extension to arbitrary $\alpha,\beta$ are correct.
- **Normalization/orthogonality:** The logical basis is orthonormal and the encoding preserves inner products; one sentence would identify it as an isometry.
- **No-cloning reminder:** The encoded superposition is not $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes3}$; this was just explained and need not be repeated at length.
- **Pacing:** These exact equations appeared in §§19.1–19.3. Repetition consolidates, but the chapter could reduce duplication by making §19.3 the informal preview and this the single formal definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Clean, though the third presentation slightly reduces momentum.

### Encoding circuit sentence (line 51)

- **Correct ideal construction:** With data on qubit 1 and ancillas on 2 and 3 in $|0\rangle$, CNOT$_{1\to2}$ and CNOT$_{1\to3}$ implement the encoding.
- **Circuit ordering:** The two CNOTs share a control and are sequential in standard circuit scheduling unless hardware permits a multi-target operation; do not imply parallelism.
- **Fault propagation:** An error on the unencoded data/control before or during encoding can spread to multiple qubits, so this naïve circuit is not a fault-tolerant state-preparation gadget.
- **Ancilla spelling:** “Ancillas” is more common in technical English than “ancillae”; standardize book-wide.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Concrete and implementable, with valuable fault-tolerance foreshadowing.

### Stabilizer generators introduction (lines 53–57)

- **Algebra check:** $Z_1Z_2$ and $Z_2Z_3$ are independent commuting generators whose simultaneous +1 eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{|000\rangle,|111\rangle\}$.
- **Terminology correction:** They are the two stabilizer **generators**, not all “the stabilizers.” The group also contains $I$ and $S_1S_2=Z_1Z_3$ (with phase convention).
- **Dimension preview:** Two independent commuting generators on three qubits leave dimension $2^{3-2}=2$, hence one logical qubit; this is an ideal place to foreshadow §19.8.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A compact algebraic replacement for enumerating codewords.

### +1-eigenspace explanation (line 59, first sentence)

- **Correct:** Each pair in $000$ and $111$ has equal computational-basis values, so $ZZ$ parity is even/+1; linearity extends to every logical superposition.
- **Phrase precision:** $Z\otimes Z$ has +1 eigenvalue on $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$, and -1 on $|01\rangle,|10\rangle$—include the latter to make parity explicit.
- **Global state:** The explanation should say the untouched third qubit does not affect the check eigenvalue.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The sign-product parity is easy to grasp and reuse.

### Anticommutation-to-syndrome rule (line 59, second sentence)

- **Correct:** $X_i$ anticommutes with a $Z$ on the same qubit and commutes with checks not containing it; applying it flips exactly the touched stabilizer eigenvalues.
- **General rule:** If $|\psi_L\rangle$ is stabilized by $S$, then $S E|\psi_L\rangle=\pm E|\psi_L\rangle$ according to commute/anticommute. Writing this one line generalizes the table.
- **“Encode which qubit” scope:** Unique identification holds for no error or one $X_i$; multiple $X$ errors can share/mimic syndromes and cause logical failure.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Anticommutation becoming a diagnostic bit is a satisfying conceptual leap.

### Syndrome bullet for no error and $X_1$ (line 61)

- **Values:** No error $(+1,+1)$ and $X_1=(-1,+1)$ are correct.
- **Presentation issue:** “No error or $X_1$: … vs …” compresses two table rows into an awkward bullet while others get one. Use a four-row table with error, commutation pattern, syndrome, recovery.
- **Identity ambiguity:** Stabilizer errors/nontrivial undetectable errors can also yield $(+,+)$; under the restricted at-most-one-$X$ model, it means no $X$ error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Correct but visually less clean than a table.

### Syndrome bullets for $X_2$ and $X_3$ (lines 62–63)

- **Values:** $X_2=(-1,-1)$ and $X_3=(+1,-1)$ are correct.
- **Binary convention:** Many decoders map $+1\to0$, $-1\to1$; showing $(00,10,11,01)$ or the chosen ordering would connect syndrome signs to classical bits.
- **Error order:** The Gray-code-like pattern is memorable and supports a compact correction lookup.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Gives the promised location information with minimal machinery.

### Stabilizer-measurement circuit (line 65, first sentence)

- **Correct ideal parity circuit:** Prepare an ancilla in $|0\rangle$, use the two data qubits as controls into the ancilla target, then measure ancilla in $Z$ to obtain $Z\otimes Z$ parity without resolving individual data values.
- **Direction must be explicit:** “CNOT cascade onto an ancilla” is ambiguous; reversing control/target measures a different interaction and changes fault propagation.
- **Separate ancillas/sequence:** Say whether each check uses its own ancilla and whether checks are sequential; a single reused ancilla must be reset.
- **Fault-tolerance caveat:** A $Z$ fault on a target ancilla can propagate backward through CNOTs to multiple data qubits, and measurement/preparation faults can corrupt syndrome. Verified cat states, flags, repeated rounds, or careful schedules address this later.
- **Logical nondisclosure:** The ancilla records only even/odd parity; because both logical basis states have even parity, it carries no information about $\alpha,\beta$ ideally.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The physical mechanism of “measure damage, not message” is highly rewarding.

### Recovery sentence (line 65, second sentence)

- **Correct under restricted model:** Apply $X_i$ for the decoded single-flip syndrome.
- **Pauli frame:** Often record the correction in a classical frame rather than physically apply it immediately; this reduces added operations and matters later for feed-forward.
- **Decoder ambiguity:** For multiple faults, the same syndrome may lead the minimum-weight decoder to a wrong correction and a logical $X_L=X_1X_2X_3$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Simple closure after the syndrome lookup.

### Restricted and full distances (line 65, third sentence)

- **Strong and correct distinction:** The smallest undetectable nontrivial $X$-type logical operator is $X_1X_2X_3$ (weight 3), so the restricted bit-flip distance is 3; a single $Z_i$ is a logical phase operation, so full distance is 1.
- **Convention warning:** CSS literature sometimes defines $d_X$ as minimum weight of an $X$-type logical operator (hence protection against $X$ errors) but readers may encounter conventions linking $d_X$/$d_Z$ to the opposite check family. Define explicitly.
- **Code parameters:** Calling it $[[3,1,1]]$ while separately stating $d_X=3,d_Z=1$ would prevent readers from treating it as a distance-3 quantum code.
- **Correction theorem:** Full $d=1$ means it cannot detect every arbitrary single-qubit Pauli error, even though it corrects the restricted set $\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** An unusually valuable nuance that many introductory accounts omit.

### Phase-error reminder (line 65, final sentence)

- **Correct:** It reinforces that this code is pedagogical/restricted.
- **Pacing:** The same fact was fully explained two paragraphs earlier; retain only if it prepares the immediate phase-flip construction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Useful orientation, mildly repetitive.

### Figure reference and alt text (line 67)

- **Alt text strength:** It describes encoding, named wires, parity checks, ancillas, and syndrome measurements rather than merely naming the figure.
- **Potential mismatch:** The prose calls the data qubits 1–3 while alt text calls them d0–d2; reconcile labels so equations and diagram map without mental offset.
- **Terminology:** The alt text says two CNOTs encode d0 “into d0–d2,” appropriately implying distribution rather than cloning.
- **Deferred artifact audit:** `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/bit-flip-code.svg` remains unopened during this one-manuscript pass and must later receive structural and visual review.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10 expected from the description.** This is exactly a circuit that benefits materially from a figure, subject to later verification.

### §19.4 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It derives syndrome signs from anticommutation and explicitly distinguishes restricted $X$ distance 3 from full quantum distance 1.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Rename $S_1,S_2$ as generators, specify CNOT directions/fault-propagation limits, and define the $d_X$ convention.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Replace syndrome bullets with a complete error–syndrome–recovery table and introduce Pauli-frame correction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Clear and satisfying, with just enough formalism to make the earlier miracle operational.

## Chapter 19, §19.5 — Phase-Flip Codes (lines 69–83)

### Heading and Hadamard-conjugation construction (lines 69–71, first sentence)

- **Elegant reuse:** Conjugating the whole code by $H^{\otimes3}$ turns the bit-flip code into a phase-flip code, avoiding a second derivation from scratch.
- **Meaning of conjugation:** Clarify that logical basis states, stabilizer generators, errors, encoding, and recovery are all transformed consistently—not merely that Hadamards are appended after storage.
- **Encoding circuit:** A concrete construction is encode the repetition code then apply $H$ to all three physical qubits (or commute basis changes into preparation/gates); include a circuit or sentence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A one-gate basis change swapping two kinds of protection is highly satisfying.

### $HXH=Z$ and $HZH=X$ identities (line 71, second sentence opening)

- **Correct:** Hadamard swaps $X$ and $Z$ under conjugation and maps computational to $X$ basis.
- **$Y$ nuance:** $HYH=-Y$; not needed for the construction, but worth noting when the chapter soon discusses arbitrary Pauli errors.
- **Prior reference:** If these identities were derived in the gates chapter, add a cross-reference rather than rely only on recall.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Compact algebra with immediate coding consequences.

### Protection-transfer claim (line 71, latter half)

- **Correct restricted statement:** Under global conjugation, a code correcting the set of $X_i$ errors becomes one correcting $Z_i$ errors.
- **Basis wording:** Error correction is not inherently “in the computational basis”; the bit-flip code’s stabilizers are $ZZ$, while the conjugated code’s are $XX$. Say the error set and code basis explicitly.
- **Noise transformation:** Physically applying Hadamards also transforms the representation of noise; it does not make a fixed device’s $Z$ noise disappear unless storage/recovery are designed in the conjugated basis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Strong conceptual transfer with a subtle physical interpretation.

### Logical basis states (lines 73–75)

- **Correct:** $H^{\otimes3}|000\rangle=|+++\rangle$ and $H^{\otimes3}|111\rangle=|---\rangle$.
- **Typography:** `|+\!+\!+\rangle` controls spacing but is visually nonstandard source. Check rendered output and consider $|+++\rangle$ if spacing is acceptable.
- **Logical superposition:** Explicitly include $\alpha|0_L\rangle+\beta|1_L\rangle$ to reinforce preservation of arbitrary logical amplitudes.
- **Orthonormality:** $|+++\rangle$ and $|---\rangle$ are orthogonal because $\langle+|-\rangle=0$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The basis-level symmetry with the previous code is visually pleasing.

### Stabilizer generators (lines 77–81)

- **Algebra check:** $X_1X_2$ and $X_2X_3$ stabilize both $|+++\rangle$ and $|---\rangle$, because paired $X$ eigenvalues multiply to +1. Correct.
- **Terminology correction:** These are two independent stabilizer generators; the group additionally contains $I$ and $X_1X_3$.
- **Derivation:** Show $H^{\otimes3}(Z_1Z_2)H^{\otimes3}=X_1X_2$ and similarly for $S_2$.
- **Dimension:** Two generators again define a two-dimensional code space/one logical qubit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Makes conjugation tangible at the operator level.

### Single-$Z$ action and syndrome (line 83, first sentence)

- **Correct:** $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$ and $Z|-\rangle=|+\rangle$; $Z_i$ anticommutes with each $X$-type generator containing qubit $i$, yielding the same sign table as $X_i$ in the prior code.
- **“In this basis”:** The physical $Z$ operator is unchanged; its interpretation as a basis flip occurs in the $X$ basis. The phrase is fine but should not imply a different operator.
- **Recovery omitted:** Apply $Z_i$ (or update an appropriate Pauli frame) based on the syndrome.
- **Measurement:** Measuring $XX$ checks requires a different ancilla preparation/control basis from $ZZ$ checks; a brief circuit relation via Hadamards would be useful.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Exact reuse of the syndrome map rewards understanding over memorization.

### Protection and failure distances (line 83, second sentence)

- **Correct:** It corrects one unknown $Z_i$ error and does not detect a single $X_i$, which acts as a logical phase/sign operation in the chosen logical basis.
- **Distance:** State restricted $d_Z=3$, $d_X=1$, and full quantum distance $d=1$, with the book’s convention defined.
- **Logical operators:** On the code space, any single $X_i$ acts equivalently as logical $Z_L$; $Z_1Z_2Z_3$ acts as logical $X_L$ (depending on naming convention). Showing this strengthens the symmetry.
- **Coherent bias:** Under independent phase noise, logical phase error starts at $3p^2-2p^3$ after correction; under bit noise it begins at order $p$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The mirrored strength/weakness is clear and memorable.

### “Neither code … useful” and combination question (line 83, final sentence)

- **Overstatement:** Neither code alone corrects an arbitrary single-qubit error, but repetition codes are useful under strongly biased noise, in experiments demonstrating suppression, as components/subsystems of larger codes, and for protecting one observable/logical basis.
- **Better wording:** “Neither alone is a general quantum memory; can we combine them to correct both bit and phase errors?”
- **Strong transition:** The combination question naturally motivates Shor’s concatenated nine-qubit code.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Excellent cliffhanger after removing the dismissive absolute.

### §19.5 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** Global Hadamard conjugation turns every element of the previous construction—codewords, checks, errors, and recovery—into its phase-error counterpart with minimal new machinery.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Call $S_1,S_2$ generators, state recovery and restricted/full distances, and replace “not useful” with “not general-purpose.”
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Show how to measure an $XX$ parity and how logical operators transform under $H^{\otimes3}$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Brief, elegant, and an excellent setup for combining protections.

## Chapter 19, §19.6 — Shor Code (lines 85–99)

### Heading and historical claim (lines 85–87, first sentence)

- **Historical core:** Shor’s 1995 nine-qubit code is conventionally recognized as the first quantum error-correcting code capable of correcting an arbitrary error on one physical qubit.
- **Citation required:** Cite Shor’s primary 1995 paper and distinguish proposal/preprint/conference/publication date if making a priority claim.
- **Scope:** “Arbitrary single-qubit error” means any channel/error operator supported on at most one of the nine modeled qubits, via the Pauli-span property; leakage outside the qubit Hilbert space is not automatically included.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A major historical milestone provides gratifying payoff.

### Concatenation description (line 87, second sentence)

- **Correct construction:** The outer phase-flip repetition code protects the three encoded blocks against a $Z$ error on an underlying qubit, while each inner bit-flip block protects against $X$ errors.
- **Concatenation terminology:** More formally, each physical qubit of the outer code is replaced by an inner-code block. State the order/rates: $3\times3=9$ physical qubits encode one logical qubit.
- **Error-type subtlety:** Outer “bit flips” in the $|+\rangle,|-\rangle$ basis correspond to physical $Z$ actions; keeping both basis and physical Pauli labels visible avoids confusion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Combining two incomplete protections into a complete code is deeply satisfying.

### Encoded $|\pm\rangle_b$ definition (line 87, third sentence)

- **Correct:** Applying the bit-flip encoding isometry to $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives $(|000\rangle\pm|111\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
- **Subscript:** Define `_b` explicitly as “inner bit-flip block,” not a standard basis label readers must infer.
- **Block tensor products:** The later juxtaposed parentheses mean tensor product; insert $\otimes$ between blocks at least once.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A compact bridge from the previous two sections.

### $|0_L\rangle$ codeword (lines 89–91)

- **Normalization:** Three normalized GHZ-plus blocks give factor $(1/\sqrt2)^3=1/(2\sqrt2)$. Correct.
- **Tensor notation:** As written, multiplication of kets in parentheses is informal. Use $\bigl(|000\rangle+|111\rangle\bigr)^{\otimes3}/(2\sqrt2)$ or explicit tensor symbols.
- **Expansion avoidance:** Keeping product/block form rather than expanding eight computational strings preserves the concatenation structure.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Visually exposes three identical protected blocks.

### $|1_L\rangle$ codeword (lines 93–95)

- **Normalization and signs:** The factor and three GHZ-minus blocks are correct.
- **Orthogonality:** Each plus/minus block is orthogonal, so the logical codewords are orthogonal; one-line verification would reinforce the construction.
- **Logical convention:** This choice makes physical/block operations produce logical operators that can look swapped ($Z$ products implement $\bar X$, $X$ products implement $\bar Z$); warn readers before the later paragraph.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The sign-only change elegantly carries logical information across blocks.

### Three-by-three block interpretation (line 97, first sentence)

- **Strong explanation:** The within-block/across-block division is the best way to read the code.
- **“Across groups” precision:** The outer phase-flip code treats each inner block as one effective qubit; its $X$-type checks compare pairs of entire blocks.
- **Visual opportunity:** A nested diagram with inner $ZZ$ checks and outer six-body $X$ checks would materially reduce cognitive load.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The spatial block picture makes nine qubits feel structured rather than arbitrary.

### Single-$X$ correction (line 97, second sentence)

- **Correct:** The two $ZZ$ checks inside an affected block locate one $X$ fault among its three physical qubits.
- **Across blocks:** Six check bits (two per block) show which block and which position under the at-most-one-error assumption.
- **Idealization:** Syndrome faults and propagation are ignored; fault-tolerant measurement will require repeated/verified extraction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Directly reuses the earlier lookup table.

### Single-$Z$ correction and block sign flip (line 97, third sentence)

- **Correct action:** A $Z$ on any one physical qubit maps GHZ-plus to GHZ-minus and vice versa for that block, so the outer phase-code syndrome locates the affected block.
- **Degeneracy omission:** The syndrome does **not** identify which qubit inside the block suffered $Z$. $Z_1,Z_2,Z_3$ within one block differ by inner $ZZ$ stabilizers and act equivalently on the code space. Identifying the block/equivalence class is sufficient.
- **Wording repair:** Replace “a $Z$ error anywhere is identified” with “the affected block is identified; the within-block location is intentionally degenerate.”
- **Recovery:** Applying any representative $Z$ in that block restores the logical state up to a stabilizer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Degeneracy is a fascinating feature, not a caveat to hide.

### Single-$Y$ correction (line 97, final sentence)

- **Algebra:** With the stated convention $Y=iXZ$, a $Y_i$ triggers both the relevant inner $ZZ$ syndrome and outer $X$-type syndrome. Correct up to global phase.
- **“Independently” nuance:** The $X$- and $Z$-type stabilizer checks commute and their syndrome bits diagnose the two Pauli components, but one physical $Y$ event is not two statistically independent faults.
- **Recovery:** The combined correction can be $Y_i$ up to phase or corresponding $X_i$/$Z_i$ representatives.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The two syndrome systems jointly recognizing $Y$ completes the construction elegantly.

### Stabilizer-generator count (line 99, first sentence)

- **Correct generators:** Six intra-block $ZZ$ generators plus two six-body $X$ generators across adjacent block pairs give eight independent commuting generators.
- **Terminology:** Say “eight independent stabilizer generators,” not “eight stabilizers”; the full group has $2^8$ elements (ignoring phases).
- **Explicit indices:** List or compactly define $Z_1Z_2,Z_2Z_3;Z_4Z_5,Z_5Z_6;Z_7Z_8,Z_8Z_9$ and $X_1\cdots X_6,X_4\cdots X_9$.
- **Dimension:** Nine qubits minus eight independent generators leaves $2^{9-8}=2$ dimensions, hence one logical qubit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The stabilizer count verifies the code rate immediately.

### Minimal logical $\bar X$ (line 99, second sentence first clause)

- **Correct representative:** $Z_1Z_4Z_7$ flips plus/minus in each block, mapping $(\mathrm{GHZ}_+)^{\otimes3}\leftrightarrow(\mathrm{GHZ}_-)^{\otimes3}$. Thus it acts as logical $X$.
- **Equivalent representatives:** Any one $Z$ chosen from each block differs by inner $ZZ$ stabilizers and implements the same logical operation.
- **Normalizer check:** It commutes with all stabilizers but is not in the stabilizer group.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The apparent $Z$-product acting as logical $X$ is a rewarding basis twist.

### Minimal logical $\bar Z$ (line 99, second sentence latter clause)

- **Correct representative:** $X_1X_2X_3$ swaps $000\leftrightarrow111$ inside block 1, fixing GHZ-plus and negating GHZ-minus; hence it fixes $|0_L\rangle$ and negates $|1_L\rangle$.
- **Equivalent representatives:** The triple-$X$ on any one block is equivalent modulo the six-body $X$ stabilizers.
- **Logical anticommutation:** $Z_1Z_4Z_7$ and $X_1X_2X_3$ overlap on one qubit, so they anticommute as logical $X,Z$ should.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The overlap proof gives a satisfying algebraic verification.

### Parenthetical operator corrections (line 99, parenthetical)

- **Distance:** Both chosen representatives have weight 3, supporting $d\le3$; together with correction of all weight-one Pauli errors this establishes $d\ge3$, hence $d=3$.
- **All-$X$ check:** $X_1\cdots X_9$ applies logical-$Z$ action on all three blocks; because three signs multiply to one minus on $|1_L\rangle$, it is indeed another $\bar Z$ representative, equivalent modulo stabilizers.
- **$Z_1Z_2Z_3$ check:** It anticommutes with $X_1\cdots X_6$ because of three overlaps, so it is outside the stabilizer normalizer and is not a logical operator. Correct and unusually careful.
- **Pacing:** The parenthetical is technically excellent but dense enough for a displayed “common operator confusion” box/table.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Expert-level myth prevention with real algebraic payoff.

### “Generate the relevant group” (line 99, third sentence)

- **Vagueness:** The eight stabilizer generators plus representatives of logical $\bar X,\bar Z$ generate the Pauli normalizer $N(\mathcal S)$ modulo phases (for this one-logical-qubit code), not the full nine-qubit Pauli group.
- **Destabilizers:** Generating the full Pauli group would also require operators conjugate to stabilizer generators.
- **Required rewrite:** Name the normalizer and quotient $N(\mathcal S)/\mathcal S\cong\mathcal P_1$; preview §19.8.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The structural claim is important but “relevant” hides exactly what readers need to learn.

### Parameters and arbitrary-error correction (line 99, fourth sentence)

- **Correct:** Eight generators encode $k=1$, and minimum logical weight 3 yields $[[9,1,3]]$, correcting every weight-one qubit Pauli/channel error.
- **Convention timing:** The parenthetical says §19.8 fixes $[[n,k,d]]$ later; briefly define it here as done, then give formal treatment later.
- **Degenerate code:** The Shor code is degenerate—some distinct low-weight errors have the same syndrome/equivalent action. Name this now because the preceding $Z$ behavior demonstrates it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The first full code parameters feel like a genuine milestone.

### Efficiency and concatenation close (line 99, final sentence)

- **Ambiguous efficiency:** “Not the most efficient nine-qubit code” could mean not minimum physical qubits for one-error correction (the five-qubit perfect code uses five), not highest $k$ among length-nine codes, or poor stabilizer weight/overhead. Specify metric.
- **Better phrase:** “It is not qubit-minimal—the $[[5,1,3]]$ code is—but its nested repetition structure is exceptionally transparent.”
- **Concatenation:** §19.19 should distinguish Shor’s one-level concatenation idea from the recursive concatenated-code threshold proof and its assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Ends by valuing explanatory structure over record efficiency, a good textbook choice.

### §19.6 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The nested block explanation and unusually careful logical-operator checks make the Shor code both intuitive and algebraically credible.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Call the eight operators generators, explicitly introduce degeneracy/block-only phase localization, name the generated normalizer, and specify the efficiency metric.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Add an indexed generator table and a nested diagram showing inner $ZZ$ and outer six-body $X$ checks.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Dense but exceptionally rewarding; the first complete arbitrary-single-error code earns its historical status.

## Chapter 19, §19.7 — Steane Code (lines 101–123)

### Heading and historical/parameter opening (lines 101–103, first sentence)

- **Correct core:** The Steane code is a seven-qubit distance-three stabilizer/CSS code encoding one logical qubit and correcting arbitrary weight-one qubit errors.
- **Historical citation:** Cite Steane’s 1996 primary work and clarify publication chronology if using “due to.”
- **Scope:** As before, arbitrary one-qubit errors means within the modeled qubit Hilbert space and ideal recovery, not arbitrary leakage/correlated operation faults.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A natural next efficiency milestone after Shor’s nine qubits.

### Shor comparison and CSS/transversality preview (line 103, second sentence)

- **Correct:** Both have $d=3$; Steane uses seven rather than nine physical qubits for one logical qubit.
- **Efficiency breadth:** Fewer qubits is not automatically lower full fault-tolerant overhead—check weights, ancilla verification, syndrome circuits, gate set, geometry, and decoder matter.
- **Structural advantage:** CSS structure and transversal Clifford generators are genuinely important for textbook fault-tolerant constructions.
- **“Admits transversal Clifford gates”:** Specify that logical single-qubit Clifford generators act qubitwise within a block and logical CNOT acts pairwise between blocks; phase conventions need care below.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Promises not merely storage efficiency but easier computation.

### Classical Hamming-code source (line 105)

- **Correct:** The binary Hamming $[7,4,3]$ code has length 7, dimension 4, and distance 3; its dual is the $[7,3,4]$ simplex code and is contained in it.
- **Missing dual-containing property:** This inclusion $C^\perp\subset C$ is what lets the same check structure define commuting $X$ and $Z$ stabilizers. State it before the matrices.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Classical structure becoming a quantum code makes the prior recap pay off.

### Hamming parity-check matrix (lines 107–109)

- **Matrix check:** The columns are $001,010,011,100,101,110,111$ when read top-to-bottom as most-to-least significant bits. Correct.
- **Convention:** Say explicitly which row is the high-order bit; “binary representations 1 through 7” otherwise depends on bit order.
- **Syndrome property:** Each single-bit error produces the corresponding nonzero column, hence a unique three-bit location label. This is the main reason to show the matrix and should be stated.
- **Row rank:** The three rows are independent, so the kernel has dimension $7-3=4$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The columns literally encoding error locations is a satisfying construction.

### “Two copies” CSS description (line 111)

- **Useful intuition:** One set of checks diagnoses $X$ faults and the other diagnoses $Z$ faults.
- **More precise algebra:** The stabilizer supports come from rows of the Hamming parity-check matrix, equivalently codewords of $C^\perp$. $Z$-type generators detect $X$ errors; $X$-type generators detect $Z$ errors.
- **Commutation:** Because the rows are mutually orthogonal over $\mathbb F_2$ (the dual is self-orthogonal/contained appropriately), every $X$ support overlaps every $Z$ support in even parity, so the generators commute.
- **“Encoded as quantum stabilizers”:** A binary row $h$ maps to $X(h)=\bigotimes_iX_i^{h_i}$ or $Z(h)$; writing this map would generalize cleanly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The same binary checks catching complementary quantum faults is elegant.

### $X$-type generator row (lines 113–115)

- **Index check:** Supports $4567$, $2367$, and $1357$ match the three rows of $H_{\rm Ham}$. Correct.
- **Terminology:** Label them independent $X$-type stabilizer generators.
- **Detection:** A $Z_j$ anticommutes with precisely the generators whose Hamming column has 1 at position $j$, producing its three-bit syndrome.
- **Weight:** Each generator has weight 4, relevant to ancilla circuit/fault propagation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Concrete and patterned enough to inspect.

### $Z$-type generator row (lines 117–119)

- **Index check:** The same supports with $Z$ are correct.
- **Detection:** These generators diagnose $X_j$ errors with the same Hamming-column syndrome.
- **Commutation check:** Matching weight-four supports overlap in 4 positions; distinct rows overlap in 2 positions, so $X$/$Z$ generators commute.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Symmetry makes the six checks easy to internalize.

### Six-generator dimension count (line 121, first sentence)

- **Correct if independence/commutation stated:** Six independent commuting Pauli generators with no $-I$ stabilize a space of dimension $2^{7-6}=2$, encoding one qubit.
- **Terminology correction:** “Six stabilizers” should be “six independent stabilizer generators”; the full group has $2^6$ elements.
- **Proof opportunity:** Each independent commuting constraint halves the Hilbert-space dimension; say this once for reuse.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A clean algebraic count replaces explicit 128-amplitude codewords.

### All-seven logical operators (line 121, second sentence)

- **Valid representatives:** $X^{\otimes7}$ and $Z^{\otimes7}$ commute with all stabilizer generators, are not stabilizers, and anticommute because they overlap on seven (odd) qubits.
- **Not minimal:** The code distance is 3, so weight-three logical representatives exist modulo stabilizers. The sentence does not call these minimal, but readers may infer all logical gates have weight 7.
- **Transversal role:** These all-seven representatives arise naturally from physical transversal $X$/$Z$ and are useful despite nonminimal weight.
- **Show equivalence:** Multiplying by a weight-four stabilizer gives a complementary weight-three representative, e.g. $X^{\otimes7}(X_4X_5X_6X_7)=X_1X_2X_3$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A satisfying connection between stabilizer equivalence and distance.

### Parameter statement and textbook-workhorse claim (line 123, first two sentences)

- **Correct:** $[[7,1,3]]$ follows from dimension and minimum normalizer weight.
- **Distance proof:** The text should show or cite why no weight-one/two normalizer element is logical and exhibit a weight-three representative; arbitrary single-error correction alone establishes $d\ge3$, and the representative gives equality.
- **“Workhorse” scope:** It is a workhorse of textbook examples and historical fault-tolerance schemes, not necessarily current hardware roadmaps. The phrasing already limits it to textbook fault tolerance, which is sensible but subjective.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Formal parameters consolidate the construction cleanly.

### Transversal Hadamard (line 123, first feature)

- **Correct:** $H^{\otimes7}$ swaps $X$- and $Z$-type generators on identical supports and swaps logical $X^{\otimes7}$ with $Z^{\otimes7}$, implementing logical Hadamard up to convention.
- **Fault-tolerance reason:** A transversal operation couples no two physical qubits within the same code block, limiting one physical fault to at most one error per block.
- **Terminology:** “Same classical code” is shorthand for the self-dual CSS check structure; dual-containing versus self-dual distinctions should be precise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A whole logical gate emerging from seven independent Hadamards is highly rewarding.

### Transversal $S,X,Z,$ and CNOT claim (line 123, second clause)

- **Broadly correct projectively:** The Steane code supports transversal representatives for Clifford generators; pairwise CNOT between corresponding qubits of two blocks implements logical CNOT.
- **Phase-convention subtlety:** Under displayed Hermitian logical $X^{\otimes7},Z^{\otimes7}$, conjugation by physical $S^{\otimes7}$ sends $\bar X$ to $-\bar Y$, corresponding to logical $S^\dagger$ rather than $S$ if signs are tracked; $(S^\dagger)^{\otimes7}$ realizes logical $S$. Some conventions absorb Pauli phases/projective Clifford action. State the actual physical/logical mapping.
- **“Entire Clifford group”:** The generators are transversal and their compositions remain blockwise transversal, but not every logical Clifford necessarily appears as one depth-one identical gate layer; distinguish transversal implementability from one-shot uniform gates.
- **CNOT orientation:** Pair physical control block qubit $i$ to target block qubit $i$; propagation remains at most one fault per block.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The computational power is exciting; exact phase mapping matters in a fault-tolerance chapter.

### General dual-containing CSS claim (line 123, final sentence)

- **Correct special construction:** If a binary $[n,k,d]$ code $C$ contains its dual $C^\perp$, using the same code/check structure for $X$ and $Z$ yields $[[n,2k-n,d_Q]]$.
- **Distance formula:** More exactly, $d_Q=\min\{\operatorname{wt}(c):c\in C\setminus C^\perp\}$ in this symmetric construction (or the minimum of the relevant $X/Z$ logical cosets in general). Thus $d_Q\ge d(C)$, with possible strict inequality if all minimum-weight codewords lie in $C^\perp$.
- **General CSS breadth:** The most general CSS construction uses two classical codes with an inclusion such as $C_2^\perp\subseteq C_1$ (conventions vary), yielding $k_Q=k_1+k_2-n$ and separate $d_X,d_Z$. Do not imply all CSS codes arise from one dual-containing code.
- **Phrase “contains its dual”:** Explicitly $C^\perp\subseteq C$, since “dual-containing” is easy to reverse.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A powerful generalization, dense enough to deserve its later full section.

### §19.7 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The Hamming columns, duplicated $X/Z$ checks, and transversal Hadamard make classical-to-quantum structure exceptionally transparent.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Call the six operators generators; explicitly prove commutation/distance; track transversal phase-gate conventions; and distinguish symmetric dual-containing CSS from the general two-code construction.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Show syndrome columns locating $X_j/Z_j$, weight-three logical representatives, and pairwise block CNOT in one diagram/table.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Algebraically elegant and computationally consequential; one of the chapter’s strongest sections.

## Chapter 19, §19.8 — Stabilizer Formalism (lines 125–141)

### Heading and shared-pattern opening (lines 125–127, first sentence)

- **Correct unification:** The preceding codes are all describable as simultaneous +1 eigenspaces of commuting Pauli checks.
- **Terminology:** A code is specified by a generating set; every element of the generated group is a stabilizer. Calling the small listed set “the stabilizers” perpetuates the earlier generator/group ambiguity.
- **“Small” qualification:** The number of independent generators is $n-k$, often extensive in $n$; it is small relative to the $2^n$ state description, not necessarily a constant.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The promised abstraction arrives at exactly the right moment.

### Gottesman attribution (line 127, second sentence)

- **Historical value:** Gottesman’s work/thesis systematized stabilizer codes, Clifford operations, and efficient simulation.
- **Citation/priority:** Cite the primary thesis/papers and acknowledge related Calderbank–Shor–Steane/additive-code developments if “due to” is meant as sole attribution.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** A named formalism gives historical anchor, needing evidence.

### Pauli-group definition (line 129, first sentence)

- **Substantive definition:** $\mathcal P_n=\{i^a P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_n:a\in\{0,1,2,3\},P_j\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}\}$ is the clearest explicit form.
- **Wording issue:** `$\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}$` already denotes tensor products rather than a conventional generator set. Say generated by single-qubit $X_j,Z_j$ and phases, or give the explicit set above.
- **Redundancy:** $Y=iXZ$, so $X_j,Z_j$ plus phase generate $Y_j$; including all is harmless.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Foundational bookkeeping, compact enough not to stall momentum.

### Commute-or-anticommute property (line 129, second sentence)

- **Correct:** Tensor-product Pauli operators commute or anticommute because the total sign is the parity of local anticommuting overlaps; global phases do not change this.
- **Derivation:** “$XZ=-ZX$ etc.” is correct but could state the parity rule explicitly, preparing binary symplectic representation.
- **Caveat:** Equality up to phases should be handled consistently; commutator sign remains $\pm1$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** A remarkably simple algebraic property powering the entire framework.

### Stabilizer-group definition (line 129, third sentence)

- **Correct standard conditions:** An abelian subgroup of $\mathcal P_n$ excluding $-I$ has a nonempty common +1 eigenspace.
- **Why exclude $-I$:** If $-I\in S$, the condition $-I|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle$ forces $|\psi\rangle=0$. State this immediate proof.
- **Hermiticity:** Under subgroup closure and exclusion of $-I$, elements used as +1 checks can be chosen Hermitian with phases $\pm1$; generators with $\pm i$ eigenvalues would not fit the displayed eigenspace definition.
- **Notation consistency:** Use $\mathcal S$ rather than $S$ if $S$ is also the phase gate elsewhere.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The forbidden $-I$ condition has a satisfying one-line reason.

### Code-subspace definition (lines 129–133)

- **Correct:** The joint +1 eigenspace definition is standard.
- **Linear subspace:** Each constraint is linear and commuting projectors can be multiplied; a projector formula $P_C=|S|^{-1}\sum_{g\in S}g$ would be a powerful later tool.
- **Zero vector:** The set notation technically includes the zero vector; a subspace does, though normalized code states are its unit vectors.
- **Typeface:** Distinguish the code $C(S)$ from classical code $C$ and operator $S$ consistently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Concise and formal without losing accessibility.

### Dimension and logical-qubit count (line 135)

- **Correct under hypotheses:** If $r$ commuting independent order-two Hermitian generators exclude $-I$, then $|S|=2^r$ and each independent constraint halves dimension, yielding $2^{n-r}$.
- **Independence definition:** No nonempty product of generators equals $I$ (up to the allowed phase convention). State this.
- **Logical count:** $k=n-r$ is correct; hence a $[[n,k]]$ stabilizer code has $n-k$ independent generators.
- **Constraint:** $r\le n$ follows from commuting independent Pauli structure.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A satisfying compression law central to code bookkeeping.

### Normalizer definition (line 137, first sentence)

- **Effective definition:** Within the Pauli group, the set commuting with every stabilizer is the centralizer and equals the Pauli normalizer of $S$ under the standard no-$-I$ convention.
- **Group-theory nomenclature:** The abstract normalizer is $\{P:PSP^\dagger=S\}$; define this first or explicitly say “for Pauli stabilizers this normalizer equals the centralizer.”
- **Notation:** Use $N_{\mathcal P_n}(S)$ if precision matters.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The operators invisible to syndrome checks are the natural next object.

### Why normalizer equals centralizer (line 137, second sentence)

- **Conclusion correct but proof incomplete:** If a Pauli $P$ anticommutes with some $g\in S$, then $PgP^\dagger=-g$. Because $-I\notin S$, $-g\notin S$, so $P$ does not normalize $S$. Therefore a Pauli normalizer element must commute with every $g$.
- **“Almost abelian”:** Informal and memorable; pair it with the exact conjugation argument above.
- **Phases:** Central Pauli phases normalize/commute trivially and later must be quotiented out.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** An elegant consequence of the Pauli sign algebra.

### Logical operators modulo stabilizers/phases (line 137, third sentence)

- **Correct idea:** Centralizer elements preserve the code space; stabilizers act as identity there; quotient classes in $N(S)/S$ (with Pauli phases handled) implement encoded Paulis.
- **Overstatement:** An element of $N(S)\setminus S$ such as $-g$ or $ig$ for $g\in S$ differs only by global phase and does not act nontrivially. The sentence’s “taken modulo phases” caveat repairs this, but formalize the quotient before saying every element is nontrivial.
- **Quotient:** For $k$ logical qubits, $N(S)/(\langle iI\rangle S)$ is isomorphic to the phase-free $k$-qubit Pauli group/symplectic vector space.
- **Logical Clifford gates:** Not every logical gate is a Pauli normalizer element within $\mathcal P_n$; this paragraph defines logical Pauli operators, not arbitrary logical unitaries.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The quotient elegantly explains why many physical strings are the same logical action.

### Global-phase example (line 137, parenthetical)

- **Correct:** $iI$ commutes with everything and acts by a global phase on state vectors, irrelevant to measurement probabilities.
- **Density matrices:** Global phases cancel exactly in $U\rho U^\dagger$, reinforcing why they are quotiented.
- **Potential confusion:** $-g$ for a stabilizer acts as global $-1$ on the code but is not an element of the chosen stabilizer group; “stabilizer up to phase” handles it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Useful guardrail against a common set-difference mistake.

### Distance definition (line 137, final sentence)

- **Correct stabilizer-code formula:** $d=\min\{\operatorname{wt}(P):P\in N(S)\setminus\langle iI\rangle S\}$ for $k>0$.
- **Weight:** Define Pauli weight as number of nonidentity tensor factors.
- **$k=0$ edge case:** A stabilizer state has no nontrivial logical Pauli; distance needs a separate convention/definition via detectable errors.
- **Subsystem codes:** Later gauge codes replace stabilizer quotient conditions; note formalism scope.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Turns logical vulnerability into a concrete minimization problem.

### $[[n,k,d]]$ notation (line 139, first two sentences)

- **Correct:** Double brackets distinguish quantum code parameters from classical $[n,k,d]$ notation.
- **Qudit extension:** Optional: $[[n,k,d]]_q$ for $q$-ary/qudit stabilizer codes.
- **“Lightest undetectable logical”:** Correct for stabilizer codes, but undetectable stabilizers are harmless; “nontrivial logical” properly excludes them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Compact notation now has enough algebra behind it.

### Three-qubit restricted-code clarification (line 139, third and fourth sentences)

- **Excellent correction:** Explicitly refusing to call the bit-flip repetition code $[[3,1,3]]$ as a full quantum code prevents a common misconception.
- **Terminology:** It can be described as an asymmetric/restricted code with $d_X=3,d_Z=1$, but the full $[[3,1,1]]$ parameters should be stated.
- **Logical $Z$:** Any single $Z_i$ commutes with the $ZZ$ stabilizers and is outside the stabilizer group up to phase, so distance 1 follows directly from the normalizer definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** One of the section’s strongest pieces of precision.

### Shor and Steane parameter examples (line 139, fifth sentence)

- **Correct:** $[[9,1,3]]$ and $[[7,1,3]]$ match the preceding constructions.
- **Evidence:** The prior sections should explicitly establish independent-generator counts and minimum logical weights so these do not appear as memorized labels.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Useful consolidation.

### Planar surface-code parameter formula (line 139, sixth sentence)

- **Common convention:** A standard unrotated planar patch of distance $d$ often has $d^2+(d-1)^2=2d^2-2d+1$ data qubits; a rotated planar patch often has $d^2$ data qubits, encoding one logical qubit under appropriate boundaries.
- **Layout dependence:** “Standard” hides boundary, check layout, hook-error schedule, and distance convention. Cite/illustrate the exact patch family.
- **Odd-$d$ restriction questionable:** Surface-code patches can be defined for even as well as odd $d$; odd distances are commonly chosen for symmetric correction/round conventions, but the formula itself is not inherently limited to odd $d$. Explain or remove.
- **Ancillas:** Good that ancilla counts are separated from code parameters; complete physical-qubit overhead must add syndrome ancillas, routing/spares, factories, and layout.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Gives a concrete forward glimpse of scaling, with convention risk.

### Distance-to-correction-radius statement (line 139, final sentence)

- **Correct ideal theorem:** A distance-$d$ code can correct every error supported on at most $t=\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor$ qubits because products $E_a^\dagger E_b$ then have weight at most $2t<d$ and satisfy detection/correction conditions.
- **Erasures:** It can correct up to $d-1$ known-location erasures under ideal assumptions; useful comparison.
- **Noise caveat:** This is adversarial bounded-weight correction, not a threshold statement about arbitrary channels with average error rate.
- **Degeneracy:** Degenerate codes may also correct selected higher-weight errors; the statement guarantees all up-to-$t$ errors, not an exact maximum for every pattern.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A clear operational meaning for distance.

### “Right language for everything” (line 141, opening)

- **Rhetorical overreach:** Stabilizers are the right language for the following stabilizer/CSS/surface-code material, but nonadditive, bosonic, subsystem, and non-Pauli noise may need broader frameworks—the roadmap already says so.
- **Better phrase:** “The main language for the stabilizer-code developments that follow.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Confident transition, slightly too universal.

### Code, syndrome, decoder, and success chain (line 141, first long sentence)

- **Correct pipeline:** Generators define checks, outcomes form a syndrome, decoder proposes a correction, and success requires combined error/recovery to act trivially on logical information.
- **Order convention:** If actual error is $E$ and correction is $R$, success means $RE\in\langle iI\rangle S$ (up to phase); “correction times actual error” matches this.
- **Coherent errors:** After an ideal syndrome branch, use a representative error/coset; the simple Pauli product statement assumes Pauli errors or a discretized branch.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Excellent end-to-end summary in one sentence.

### Degenerate same-syndrome parenthetical (line 141)

- **Strong defect:** Not all errors sharing a syndrome are corrected by the same recovery. Two same-syndrome Pauli errors differ by an element of $N(S)$; if that difference is a stabilizer they are benignly degenerate/equivalent, but if it is a nontrivial logical operator, one recovery succeeds for one class and fails for the other.
- **Correct decoder task:** Choose the most likely **logical coset/equivalence class** given the syndrome, summing probabilities of stabilizer-equivalent errors.
- **Required rewrite:** “Degenerate errors that differ by a stabilizer share a syndrome and are corrected by the same recovery; other same-syndrome classes differ by logical operators and create decoder ambiguity.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The corrected version makes decoding more interesting, not less.

### Transversality qualification (line 141, second sentence)

- **Excellent nuance:** Transversality is code/geometric and neither identical to nor coextensive with the Clifford group. Some codes have transversal non-Cliffords; some Clifford operations require other constructions.
- **Definition deferred:** Briefly define “tensor product of operations each touching at most corresponding positions/blocks” before relying on geometric intuition.
- **Eastin–Knill preview:** No finite code with standard assumptions has a universal set of transversal logical gates; this motivates magic states/code switching/lattice surgery.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Prevents a common stabilizer=Clifford=transversal conflation.

### Gottesman–Knill theorem statement (line 141, final sentence opening)

- **Major definition defect:** A pure stabilizer state is the unique joint +1 eigenstate of a maximal abelian Pauli stabilizer group with $n$ independent generators. “A state in $C(S)$ for some $S$” includes every state by choosing the trivial $S=\{I\}$ and includes magic states within nonmaximal code spaces.
- **Mixed/encoded variants:** Stabilizer mixed states/codes have related definitions, but arbitrary superpositions within a stabilizer code space need not themselves be stabilizer states.
- **Operations:** Clifford unitaries, Pauli-basis measurements (including computational $Z$), stabilizer preparation, and adaptive classically controlled Clifford operations are efficiently simulable in standard formulations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The theorem is striking; the state definition must be exact.

### Tableau update complexity (line 141, final clause)

- **Correct qualitative claim:** Stabilizer generators/tableaux provide polynomial-time classical simulation.
- **Complexity nuance:** Standard Aaronson–Gottesman-style tableau operations vary: Clifford gates can update $O(n)$ tableau entries; measurements may require $O(n^2)$ in basic implementations; $O(n^2)$ per operation is a safe coarse upper bound as stated.
- **Description size:** A tableau uses $O(n^2)$ bits for a pure $n$-qubit stabilizer state; distinguish storage from per-operation runtime.
- **Noise/mixtures:** Pauli stochastic noise can be sampled efficiently; arbitrary non-Clifford noise/states break the stabilizer closure unless decomposed/approximated.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The exponential state vector collapsing to a quadratic tableau is a powerful closing surprise.

### §19.8 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It develops generators, code dimension, normalizer quotient, logical operators, and distance in a compact chain, while carefully distinguishing restricted repetition distance from full quantum distance.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Fix the same-syndrome degeneracy statement and the overbroad stabilizer-state definition; formalize the phase/stabilizer quotient and normalizer=centralizer proof.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Add Pauli-weight definition, projector/dimension derivation, and a diagram of syndrome classes split into stabilizer-equivalent versus logical cosets.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Dense, elegant, and foundational; two definitional errors would otherwise propagate through every later decoder/simulation claim.

## Chapter 19, §19.9 — Syndrome Measurement (lines 143–155)

### Heading and opening definition (lines 143–145, first sentence)

- **Correct within stabilizer QEC:** Syndrome extraction measures stabilizer generators/checks to learn error information without measuring logical amplitudes.
- **“Detecting an error” scope:** Stabilizer measurement detects errors that anticommute with at least one check; stabilizer errors are harmless and logical normalizer errors are undetected. A zero syndrome is not proof of no physical/logical error.
- **Disturbance:** Ideal projective stabilizer measurement preserves states already in a syndrome eigenspace; for coherent superpositions of error sectors it intentionally projects the error syndrome while preserving logical information under correctability conditions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Directly answers the chapter’s “measure damage, not message” challenge.

### Stabilizer eigenvalues and code space (line 145, second sentence)

- **Correct for Hermitian Pauli stabilizers:** Generators have eigenvalues $\pm1$ and the code is their simultaneous +1 eigenspace.
- **Group versus generator:** Measuring an independent generating set suffices; measuring every $g\in S$ is redundant and products’ outcomes are determined.
- **Signs:** Stabilizer generators can be written with a minus sign (e.g. $-P$) while still defining +1 constraints; eigenvalue convention belongs to the full signed operator.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Concise and foundational.

### Pauli-error syndrome eigenspace (line 145, third sentence)

- **Correct for a Pauli $E$:** If $S_j|\psi_L\rangle=|\psi_L\rangle$, then $S_jE|\psi_L\rangle=(-1)^{[S_j,E]}E|\psi_L\rangle$, so commute/anticommute signs form the syndrome.
- **Non-Pauli caveat:** A general coherent error $E=\sum_a c_aP_a$ need not place the state in one joint eigenspace before measurement; it can be a superposition of syndrome sectors.
- **Normalizer exception:** A logical Pauli commutes with every stabilizer and remains in the +1 code space while corrupting logical information.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Anticommutation becomes a physical measurement signature cleanly.

### Syndrome definition and information content (line 145, final sentence)

- **Correct:** The ordered generator eigenvalues $(s_1,\ldots,s_r)$ are the stabilizer syndrome.
- **Ordering:** Syndrome bits depend on the chosen ordered generating set; equivalent generating sets relabel the same cosets.
- **Nonuniqueness:** A syndrome identifies a coset modulo the normalizer, not a unique physical error. Within it, stabilizer-equivalent errors are degenerate and logical cosets compete in decoding.
- **Binary conversion:** State $b_j=(1-s_j)/2$ if later decoders use 0/1 syndromes.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Compact enough to remember, rich enough to support inference.

### “One ancilla per generator” (line 147, first sentence)

- **Ideal baseline:** A separate ancilla per concurrently measured generator is a common schematic implementation.
- **Not universal:** Ancillas may be reused sequentially/reset, checks may use cat/flag ancillas, subsystem gauge checks, direct multi-body measurements, resonators, or hardware-native parity operations.
- **Fault-tolerance warning:** A single bare ancilla sequentially coupled to many data qubits can spread one ancilla fault into a correlated high-weight “hook” error. This must be stated before calling the implementation standard.
- **Parallel scheduling:** Neighboring checks share data qubits, so CNOT ordering/coloring matters.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Gives a concrete implementation, but ideal simplicity conceals the main engineering hazard.

### General Pauli-product setup (line 147, second sentence)

- **Correct operator form:** A Pauli-string stabilizer is a tensor product of $I,X,Y,Z$ (with an overall sign convention).
- **Hermiticity/sign:** Include possible overall $\pm1$ and ensure the controlled unitary corresponds to the signed stabilizer; controlling a global minus changes the ancilla phase.
- **Weight:** The number of nonidentity $P_i$ is check weight and controls circuit depth/fault propagation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** General enough to unify $ZZ$, $XX$, and mixed checks.

### Step 1: prepare $|+\rangle$ (line 149)

- **Correct Hadamard-test preparation:** $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ creates two paths, one applying $g$.
- **Preparation fault:** An $X/Z$ error on this ancilla has different effects on outcome/data propagation; fault-tolerant gadgets need verification/flags/order.
- **Implementation:** Usually prepare $|0\rangle$ then $H$, whose error belongs in the syndrome circuit model.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The interferometer analogy begins clearly.

### Step 2: controlled-$P_i$ sequence (line 150)

- **Ideal algebra:** With the ancilla as control, multiplying controlled-$P_i$ operations implements controlled-$g$ because the factors act on distinct data qubits/commute.
- **Controlled-$Y$ synthesis:** Hardware rarely offers native controlled-$Y$; basis changes plus CNOT implement it and add gates/errors.
- **Fault propagation:** An $X$ fault on the control ancilla can propagate $P_i$ faults onto every subsequent target; this bare circuit can turn one fault into an uncorrectable data error.
- **Ordering:** For CSS checks, standard circuits often choose data→ancilla CNOT direction for $Z$ checks and ancilla→data for $X$ checks, with basis changes. Schedule controls hook orientation relative to logical strings.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The general controlled-product trick is elegant, and its propagation failure is crucial.

### Step 3: $X$-basis ancilla measurement (line 151)

- **Correct ideal result:** If data is a $g$ eigenstate with eigenvalue $s=\pm1$, the ancilla becomes $|+\rangle$ or $|-\rangle$ and $X$ measurement returns $s$.
- **Projection:** For arbitrary data, this measurement projects onto $(I\pm g)/2$ eigenspaces, not merely reads a pre-existing classical value.
- **Readout mapping:** Define which classical bit corresponds to $\pm1$ and include assignment error later.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The phase-kickback payoff is immediate and satisfying.

### Interference explanation (line 153, first sentence)

- **Correct:** Controlled-$g$ phase kickback encodes an eigenvalue into the ancilla’s relative phase, and $X$ measurement reads it.
- **Terminology:** “Entangle” is true for a superposition of eigenspaces; for an eigenstate the ancilla/data remain separable after phase kickback. Say “correlate (or kick back the eigenvalue).”
- **Derivation:** Write $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle g|\psi\rangle)$ and substitute $g|\psi\rangle=s|\psi\rangle$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A short derivation would make the mechanism feel transparent.

### Nondisturbance claim (line 153, second sentence)

- **Reason is misstated:** A stabilizer generator commuting with the other stabilizers ensures compatible joint measurement, but logical nondisturbance follows because every code state has the same eigenvalue (+1) and the check reveals no logical-state information.
- **After error:** Measurement can disturb/project a coherent error superposition across syndrome sectors; it should preserve logical amplitudes within each correctable sector.
- **“Error subspace”:** There are multiple syndrome subspaces, and a logical error remains within code space. Replace the singular vague phrase.
- **Idealization:** Faulty ancilla interactions can disturb the encoded state even when the ideal observable is a stabilizer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The nondemolition miracle is central; its causal explanation should be exact.

### Noisy syndrome-circuit examples (line 155, first sentence)

- **Good reality check:** Ancilla preparation, entangling gates, and measurement all create syndrome/data faults.
- **Missing faults:** Reset leakage, hook propagation, idle errors, crosstalk, correlated measurement, data faults during extraction, and timing/drift matter.
- **Syndrome versus data:** A wrong syndrome bit and a propagated data fault have different spacetime signatures and decoder consequences.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The chapter appropriately refuses to let ideal correction end the story.

### “Repeated $d$ times” claim (line 155, second sentence)

- **Strong overgeneralization:** A quantum memory/computation repeats syndrome cycles for as long as protection is required. Running $d$ rounds is a common benchmark/logical-memory convention to balance temporal and spatial distances for a distance-$d$ surface-code experiment, not a universal extraction rule.
- **Single-shot codes:** Some code families/syndrome schemes can tolerate measurement noise with single-shot error correction (given extra check redundancy/dimensional structure), further disproving universality.
- **Decoder input:** Repeated noisy measurements are converted to **detection events** (changes relative to expected syndrome across rounds), not simply a majority history of raw syndromes.
- **Required rewrite:** “For 2D surface-code memory experiments one often studies about $d$ rounds; in computation extraction continues each cycle and spacetime distance depends on boundaries/schedule.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Repetition is intuitive, but the exact-$d$ rule will be misremembered as a theorem.

### Syndrome history and spacetime decoding (line 155, third sentence)

- **Correct core:** Measurement faults are separated from data faults by analyzing changes over time, turning decoding into a spacetime inference problem.
- **Dimensional scope:** A 2D surface code plus time gives 2+1 dimensions. A 1D repetition code gives 1+1; a 3D code gives 3+1; general stabilizer codes may lack a simple geometric dimension.
- **Boundary conditions:** Initial/final measurements, temporal boundaries, lattice surgery, and different check schedules alter the decoding graph.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Time becoming an extra code dimension is a powerful conceptual leap.

### Threshold-theorem closing claim (line 155, final sentence)

- **Correct high-level lesson:** Fault-tolerant QEC must tolerate faults in its own syndrome/recovery machinery, not assume perfect correction.
- **Theorem overstatement:** Threshold theorems assume fault-tolerant gadgets/noise conditions; they do not universally assume “repeat syndrome $d$ times” or the surface-code history protocol.
- **Other constructions:** Concatenated codes use verified ancillas, repeated/majority syndrome, exRecs, and recursive gadgets; single-shot/topological schemes differ.
- **Better bridge:** “Repeated/history-aware extraction is the surface-code realization of the general threshold requirement that one fault not spread into an uncorrectable error.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Strong handoff to fault tolerance after removing the construction-specific claim.

### §19.9 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The controlled-P Hadamard test makes nondestructive syndrome extraction concrete and naturally introduces spacetime history.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Distinguish Pauli eigenstates from coherent error superpositions; explain logical nondisclosure correctly; flag the bare ancilla’s hook-error propagation; and remove universal “repeat $d$ times/2+1D/threshold assumes this” claims.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical repair:** Derive phase kickback, show a fault-propagation diagram, and introduce detection events rather than raw repeated syndromes.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Operational and conceptually vivid; its ideal circuit must be labeled non-fault-tolerant before readers imitate it.

## Chapter 19, §19.10 — Decoding (lines 157–163)

### Heading and decoder definition (lines 157–159, first sentence)

- **Correct role:** A decoder consumes syndrome/detection information and proposes a recovery or Pauli-frame/logical-correction decision.
- **Output nuance:** Modern decoders may output corrections, frame updates, logical-observable predictions, erasure flags, confidence scores, or boundary matchings rather than a physical operation immediately.
- **Input:** With noisy repeated extraction, the input is a spacetime detection-event record plus metadata/priors, not one static syndrome vector.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Turns QEC into a concrete classical inference problem.

### Minimum-weight instruction (line 159, second sentence)

- **Conflated objectives:** Minimum Hamming weight is justified for iid symmetric low-rate Pauli noise; under nonuniform rates one uses weighted likelihood, and under correlations/degeneracy the most probable logical coset need not contain the single minimum-weight representative.
- **Phrase contradiction:** “Minimum weight (under the chosen noise model)” should be “minimum negative log-likelihood/weighted cost under a simplified noise model,” since weight itself is model independent unless weighted.
- **Syndrome ambiguity:** Many $E$ share the syndrome, partitioned into stabilizer-equivalent logical classes; choosing any minimum-weight $E$ can fail if a different class has larger total probability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Simple actionable rule, too readily mistaken for decoding’s definition.

### Applying $E^\dagger$ (line 159, third sentence)

- **Correct representative recovery:** For a Pauli estimate $E$, $E^\dagger=E$ up to phase, and applying/tracking it cancels the estimated representative.
- **Success condition:** If actual error is $F$, recovery succeeds iff $E^\dagger F$ is a stabilizer up to phase; if it is a logical normalizer element, syndrome is cleared but logical state is wrong.
- **Physical correction:** Often update a Pauli frame rather than apply gates, avoiding new faults and latency; non-Pauli/leakage recovery may require physical intervention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The distinction between clearing syndrome and restoring logic is crucial and engaging.

### Baseline/family organization (line 161, first sentence)

- **Useful structure:** Optimal reference versus scalable decoder families is a productive comparison.
- **Taxonomy:** MWPM is itself a practical family/reference, while maximum likelihood can be implemented approximately by tensor networks, Monte Carlo, or specialized exact methods. “Two baselines and families” is slightly artificial.
- **Comparison axes:** Add logical error rate, threshold, latency, throughput, memory, parallelism, training/calibration, model robustness, and hardware resource cost.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Prepares a useful algorithmic contest.

### Maximum-likelihood decoder definition (line 161, second sentence opening)

- **Probability object needs repair:** A decoder should choose a recovery/logical coset maximizing the conditional sum of probabilities of actual errors $F$ for which $RF\in S$, given syndrome $s$.
- **Current formula:** $\Pr(\text{recovery}\mid\text{syndrome})$ treats a chosen action as a random event. Better write
  $$R^*(s)=\arg\max_R\sum_{F:\,\mathrm{syn}(F)=s,\,RF\in S}\Pr(F\mid s).$$
- **Degeneracy:** Summing over stabilizer-equivalent errors, rather than selecting the most probable individual error, is the essential quantum distinction. The prose recognizes the sum and should make the classes precise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Optimal decoding as Bayesian coset inference is intellectually satisfying.

### Maximum-likelihood hardness/use claim (line 161, second sentence tail)

- **Complexity claim needs scope:** Exact optimal decoding is computationally hard for broad code/noise families, with #P-/NP-hard results under specific formulations. “Generally #P-hard” needs an exact problem, reduction, input encoding, and primary citation.
- **Not only benchmark:** Exact ML can be used for very small codes, structured models, offline analysis, tensor-network contractions, and likelihood calculations; impractical asymptotically does not mean never operational.
- **Approximation:** Near-ML decoders can provide useful benchmarks and may be tractable below bounded treewidth or for special codes/noise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The optimal-but-hard tension is compelling, with an unsupported blanket class label.

### MWPM attribution and mechanism (line 161, third sentence opening)

- **Historical structure:** Edmonds supplied matching algorithms; Dennis–Kitaev–Landahl–Preskill developed the topological-memory decoding/statistical-mechanics framework. Cite exact primary works and avoid implying one linear adaptation event.
- **Mechanism:** Under graphlike faults, syndrome detection events occur in pairs/boundaries; edge weights encode negative log probabilities, and MWPM chooses a minimum-cost pairing—not automatically the exact most likely error/coset.
- **Degeneracy/correlation:** Multiple paths and correlations can make minimum matching differ from ML unless weights/degeneracy corrections are included.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Turning defects into a geometric pairing problem is highly visual and memorable.

### MWPM runtime $O((nT)^3)$ (line 161, middle clause)

- **Coarse worst-case only:** Cubic complexity can describe generic blossom-style matching in number of graph vertices, but practical sparse/parallel/approximate implementations have different scaling and average behavior.
- **Variable mismatch:** The number of detection events can be far below $nT$ at low noise; decoding graph volume, vertices, and edges depend on check count, rounds, boundaries, and faults.
- **Memory/latency:** Online windowing changes both complexity and optimality; state a specific algorithm/implementation for a runtime bound.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Gives scale, but false precision around a broad family.

### “Canonical surface-code decoder” (line 161, next sentence)

- **Reasonable historical status:** MWPM is a canonical baseline and widely used surface-code decoder.
- **Time-sensitive plurality:** Union-find, correlated matching, tensor-network, belief propagation/ordered-statistics, neural, and specialized hardware decoders increasingly compete; say “a canonical baseline.”
- **Noise dependence:** Matching performs best for graphlike sparse faults; leakage/correlations/hyperedges require adaptations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A useful anchor, not a monopoly.

### Neural, union-find, and belief-propagation families (line 161, fourth sentence opening)

- **Useful breadth:** The list spans learned, geometric-cluster, and message-passing approaches.
- **Tradeoff overgeneralization:** They do not uniformly trade accuracy for speed; performance depends on code/noise/training/implementation, and some can outperform baseline MWPM for correlated/biased models.
- **Neural limitations:** Training data, generalization across distances/noise drift, interpretability, worst-case latency, and hardware implementation matter.
- **BP limitations:** Loops/degeneracy can cause convergence/pathology; ordered-statistics or degeneracy-aware enhancements are common for qLDPC.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The algorithmic diversity makes decoding feel like a live field.

### Union-find scaling and threshold competitiveness (line 161, final clause)

- **Plausible theorem/benchmark:** Union-find decoders have near-linear/almost-linear complexity in relevant graph size in standard analyses and can achieve competitive thresholds under selected phenomenological/circuit noise.
- **Evidence required:** Cite Delfosse–Nickerson and specify code, noise model, erasure/Pauli setting, threshold metric, and whether weighted/optimized variants are used.
- **“At threshold”:** Usually one compares threshold values or logical performance below threshold; “competitive with MWPM at threshold” is imprecise because all decoders’ curves cross/critical finite-size behavior needs definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Near-linear decoding offers a satisfying scalability counterpoint.

### Noisy-syndrome difficulty (line 163, first two sentences)

- **Correct:** Measurement faults can mimic data syndromes and cause a decoder to apply harmful corrections if time history is ignored.
- **Detection events:** The standard surface-code representation uses changes between consecutive check outcomes, including initial/final temporal boundaries, rather than raw wrong syndrome values alone.
- **Joint inference:** Decode data and measurement faults together in spacetime; repeated majority vote per check is insufficient under correlated faults.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The error corrector itself lying is a strong, intuitive challenge.

### “Extract for $d$ rounds” standard fix (line 163, third sentence)

- **Repeated universalization:** Approximately $d$ rounds is a common distance-matched surface-code memory experiment convention, not the standard fix for every QEC computation/code.
- **Runtime:** During computation, checks continue each cycle for the operation duration; temporal distance can be shaped by measurement schedules and lattice-surgery geometry.
- **Single-shot exception:** Some higher-dimensional/gauge/qLDPC constructions can infer measurement errors from redundant checks in one round under assumptions.
- **Required rewrite:** Refer to repeated extraction over an application-dependent temporal window and reserve $T=d$ for a named benchmark setup.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** The concrete rule is easy to remember—and therefore especially important to qualify.

### Space–time history growth (line 163, fourth sentence)

- **Correct for local repeated-check codes:** Adding time enlarges the decoding graph and problem size with rounds/distance.
- **Dimensional/model scope:** Use “spacetime” without asserting every code has a simple 2D lattice; graph/hypergraph structure can be irregular/nonlocal.
- **Scaling:** Heuristic decoder runtimes may be polynomial, but exact ML remains hard; “the decoding problem … only polynomially” conflates input-size growth with algorithmic complexity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The code becoming a spacetime inference volume is compelling.

### Real-time streaming-decoder claim (line 163, final sentence)

- **Important systems issue:** Decoder throughput/latency must keep pace with syndrome generation or support backlog/windowing/Pauli-frame dependencies.
- **Time-sensitive evidence:** “Keep up with real-time hardware in modern experiments” needs named primary demonstrations, code distance, cycle time, hardware platform, decoding hardware, batch/streaming distinction, and whether corrections affected live control.
- **Latency nuance:** Processing throughput can exceed data rate while worst-case feedback latency still misses logical branch deadlines; Pauli-frame deferral relaxes some but not all deadlines (e.g. non-Clifford feed-forward).
- **“Parallel and streaming” cost:** Requires hardware resources, communication, memory, and approximate/windowed decisions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The classical computer racing the quantum clock is inherently exciting; evidence must substantiate victory.

### §19.10 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It frames decoding as probabilistic logical-coset inference and introduces the rich algorithmic landscape from matching to learning/message passing.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Replace minimum-weight-as-definition with likelihood/coset objectives; scope hardness/runtime claims; remove universal $d$-round/polynomial-decoding language; and distinguish syndrome clearing from logical success.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Cite exact hardness theorems, MWPM/union-find results, and named real-time decoder demonstrations with latency/throughput metrics.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Compact and alive with algorithmic tension, but several headline complexities are too sweeping.

## Chapter 19, §19.11 — CSS Codes (lines 165–176)

### Heading and construction attribution (lines 165–167, first sentence)

- **Correct scope:** CSS codes are stabilizer codes built from compatible classical binary linear codes, separating $X$- and $Z$-type checks.
