- **Basis dependence:** $|0_L\rangle,|1_L\rangle$ are a chosen logical-$Z$ eigenbasis. The logical qubit is the encoded degree of freedom, not just those two named states.
- **Notation:** Write $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{|0_L\rangle,|1_L\rangle\}$ for a one-logical-qubit subspace code; this removes the grammatical ambiguity immediately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The concept is central and intuitive, but experts will catch “subsystem” instantly.

### Logical operators versus physical Paulis (line 230, middle)

- **Correct protective idea:** Logical Pauli operators preserve the code space and act nontrivially on encoded information; in a stabilizer code they are represented by normalizer elements modulo stabilizers.
- **False dichotomy:** A logical operator is itself a physical operation/operator on the constituent qubits, often represented by a product of physical Paulis. “Rather than through any single physical Pauli” should say no weight-one Pauli can be a nontrivial logical operator when $d>1$.
- **Equivalence classes:** $\bar X,\bar Y,\bar Z$ denote logical actions/classes, each with many physical representatives differing by stabilizers. This is worth stating because deformation and fault-tolerant implementation rely on that freedom.
- **Gate implementation:** Logical gates need not be applied as one monolithic Pauli string; transversal gates, lattice surgery, code deformation, teleportation, and gauge fixing implement encoded actions through fault-tolerant circuits.
- **$\bar Y$ relation:** For one logical qubit, $\bar Y=i\bar X\bar Z$ up to convention, so listing it is fine but not an independent generator.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The physical-versus-logical distinction is satisfying when the many-representatives idea is visible.

### Reliability and exponential suppression claim (line 230, closing)

- **Conditional, not “whole point” guarantee:** Exponential suppression requires a suitable code family, physical noise below the relevant threshold, repeated fault-tolerant syndrome extraction, and a decoder whose performance scales appropriately. QEC above threshold or under unhandled correlated/leakage errors can worsen with distance.
- **Metric needed:** Logical error may mean failure per QEC cycle, per logical gate, per unit time, per memory experiment, or per algorithm. The rest of the section moves among these units, so define one before writing $p_L$.
- **Exponential variable:** The decay is exponential in $d$ for common local stochastic models below threshold; it is not a universal theorem for every code/noise/decoder combination.
- **Error floor caveat:** Rare correlated events, leakage, drift, decoder approximation, and control/systematic errors can break the simple exponential at large $d$.
- **Style:** Italic “reliable” emphasizes the goal but risks sounding absolute; “can become increasingly reliable” better preserves the threshold condition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** This is QEC’s emotional payoff, and the conditions make it more—not less—impressive.

### Formal setup for the scaling law (line 232)

- **Insufficiently formal despite label:** Code distance and a scalar physical error rate do not determine $p_L$ without specifying circuit, syndrome rounds, boundary conditions, decoder, and noise distribution/correlations.
- **Threshold is scheme-specific:** $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ belongs to a family plus syndrome circuit, decoder, and noise model—not to an isolated distance-$d$ stabilizer code.
- **Finite family:** The statement should refer to a sequence of increasing-distance codes; a single code cannot establish a threshold or exponential scaling.
- **Physical-rate ambiguity:** Gate, measurement, reset, idle, leakage, erasure, and correlated error rates are generally heterogeneous. A one-parameter depolarizing model is acceptable if declared.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The promise of a usable formula is attractive, but “formally” raises an accuracy expectation the setup does not meet.

### Logical-error scaling equation (lines 234–236)

- **Common heuristic/fit:** $p_L\approx A(p/p_{\mathrm{th}})^{(d+1)/2}$ is widely used for odd-distance surface-code scaling under stochastic circuit noise, especially well below threshold.
- **Odd-distance assumption:** $(d+1)/2=\lceil d/2\rceil$ only for odd $d$; use $\lceil d/2\rceil$ or explicitly restrict to odd-distance patches.
- **Fault-count interpretation:** A distance-$d$ code corrects at most $t=\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor$ adversarial data errors under ideal recovery, so minimally uncorrectable patterns have $t+1=\lceil d/2\rceil$ faults. Circuit-level spacetime distance requires a detector model rather than only static code distance.
- **Prefactor concern:** Calling $A$ an $O(1)$ constant in $d$ is a phenomenological approximation, not automatic. The number of malignant fault sets and finite-size corrections can introduce distance dependence; fitted $A$ also depends on how $p$ and $p_L$ are normalized.
- **Near-threshold behavior:** A simple power law with fixed $A,p_{\mathrm{th}}$ is least trustworthy near the critical region and at small distances, precisely where the next sentence applies it.
- **Inequality symbol:** $\lesssim$ suggests a bound, whereas this expression is generally an empirical/asymptotic scaling ansatz. Use $\approx$ and cite a model-specific fit, or state conditions under which an upper bound is proved.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A compact scaling law gives the reader real leverage, provided it is labeled as a model rather than a universal theorem.

### Suppression factor $\Lambda\approx2$ (line 238, opening)

- **Definition missing:** Define $\Lambda=p_L(d)/p_L(d+2)>1$ (for a fixed number/unit of cycles and matched experiments). Under the displayed heuristic, $\Lambda\approx p_{\mathrm{th}}/p$.
- **Primary result, not generic plural:** Google’s Willow surface-code memory reported $\Lambda=2.14\pm0.02$ from distance 5 to 7, with logical error measured per error-correction cycle. Attribute this result rather than saying broadly “current experiments operate.”
- **“Near threshold” imprecise:** Within the heuristic, $\Lambda\approx2$ corresponds to $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}\approx1/2$, not arbitrarily close to threshold. Device correlations and the use of detection probability as a physical-error proxy further limit this inversion.
- **Temporal maintenance:** “Current” needs an as-of date and will age; §19.17 should report a milestone table rather than making this sentence carry the field status.
- **Primary evidence checked 2026-07-23:** [Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y) reports the distance-5/7 memory result and explicitly defines $\Lambda$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Connecting the formula to a real processor is excellent; the exact experiment makes the drama credible.

### “Cutting in half” and deep-below-threshold arithmetic (line 238, middle)

- **Arithmetic correct under the model:** If $\Lambda=2$, increasing odd distance by two halves the logical error; if $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$, it reduces it by a factor of ten.
- **Direction language:** Say “reduces by a factor of two,” not “cutting in half requires,” because the latter sounds like a universal resource law rather than a fitted ratio.
- **Fixed conditions:** The comparison assumes identical code geometry, cycle definition, decoder family, physical noise, and no error floor as distance changes.
- **Cost omitted:** Increasing $d$ by two increases patch area and often logical-operation duration; the logical-error improvement should be paired with the extra spacetime volume, not only qubit count.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The factor-per-two-distance rule is one of the chapter’s most memorable quantitative intuitions.

### Error target drives patch size (line 238, closing)

- **Good design principle for surface-code patches:** Target logical failure, physical noise, and allowed failure budget determine distance and hence patch size.
- **Overgeneralized wording:** “Code patch” is surface/topological-code language, while the setup claimed an arbitrary stabilizer code. Other codes use blocks and may have different $n(d)$ scaling.
- **Other drivers:** Runtime, number/type of logical operations, correlated-noise margin, factory throughput, connectivity, and desired confidence affect distance and allocation; not only “how much suppression.”
- **Adaptive allocation:** Data blocks and factories need not all use the same distance; space-time scheduling can vary code distance over the computation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** It lands the formula in engineering, though “spacetime cost” would be more powerful than “size.”

### Resource-estimation transition (line 240, first sentence)

- **Correct transition:** Choosing code distance from an algorithmic error budget is a central fault-tolerant resource-estimation task.
- **Broader problem:** Resource estimation also chooses algorithm/circuit, logical gate set, synthesis precision, distillation protocol, layout/routing, cycle time, factory count, parallelism, decoder latency, and success/retry strategy.
- **Opportunity:** Present a short dependency chain: algorithm $\to$ logical operations/qubits/depth $\to$ error budget $\to$ code/factory parameters $\to$ physical qubits and runtime.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The chapter pivots from coding theory to machine scale at exactly the right dramatic moment.

### RSA-2048 logical-gate count (line 240, second sentence opening)

- **Order-of-magnitude plausible but undefined:** “Logical gates” could mean Clifford gates, $T$/Toffoli gates, measurements, surface-code lattice-surgery operations, or total abstract operations. Resource estimates quote different counts and depths depending on arithmetic and cost model.
- **Primary concrete comparator:** Gidney–Ekerå’s 2021 construction gives, in its abstract circuit model, roughly $0.3n^3+0.0005n^3\lg n$ Toffolis and $3n+0.002n\lg n$ logical qubits; for $n=2048$, this supports a few-billion non-Clifford-operation scale and thousands of logical qubits, not an unexplained universal $10^{10}$ gate fact.
- **Algorithm variants:** Windowing, arithmetic design, approximate rotations, measurement-based uncomputation, coset representation, and tradeoffs among qubits/runtime change counts materially.
- **Citation required:** Name the estimate and assumptions; “a Shor-factoring run” is not one fixed circuit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** RSA-2048 supplies immediate stakes, but readers deserve to see where the huge number comes from.

### Per-operation success budget (line 240, second sentence remainder)

- **Union-bound logic:** For $N$ opportunities with failure probability at most $p_L$, total failure is at most $Np_L$. Setting $p_L\sim10^{-11}$ for $N\sim10^{10}$ yields a constant-order failure budget around $0.1$, not certainty.
- **Wording error:** An algorithm does not “terminate without a logical error” because each gate independently succeeds with a stated probability; logical failures can be correlated, detected/undetected, retried, or sometimes benign. Specify desired overall success probability and use a budget allocation.
- **Gate heterogeneity:** Memory cycles, Clifford operations, injection/distillation, measurement, routing, and decoder failures have different logical error rates and counts.
- **Synthesis errors:** Approximation error and algorithmic failure probability also consume the total error budget; QEC does not own all of it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The one-error-in-a-huge-circuit intuition is powerful, but probabilistic bookkeeping needs one more line.

### Distance $d\approx21$ back-of-envelope (line 240, third sentence opening)

- **Arithmetic checks under hidden assumptions:** With $A=1$, $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$, odd $d$, and a target $10^{-11}$ in the equation, $10^{-(d+1)/2}\le10^{-11}$ indeed gives $d\ge21$.
- **“Low-to-mid 20s” mismatch:** The simple result is exactly the low edge; the range only emerges after adding conventions and margins not contained in the formula.
- **$A$ omitted:** The calculation silently sets the declared decoder/noise prefactor to one. Even a modest prefactor changes the required distance by steps of two.
- **Model confidence:** Extrapolating from small-distance threshold fits over many orders of magnitude assumes no correlated-error floor or drift; this is a major engineering uncertainty, not a minor arithmetic detail.
- **Physical ratio assumption:** $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$ is ambitious and scheme-dependent; quote actual gate/cycle noise and a matched threshold when presenting a hardware estimate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Letting readers reproduce $d=21$ is excellent; surfacing the assumptions makes it an honest estimate.

### Spacetime-volume adjustment to $d\approx27$ (line 240, parenthetical)

- **Unit mismatch exposed:** If the formula estimates logical failure **per QEC cycle**, then a logical operation lasting $O(d)$ cycles has failure roughly $O(d p_L^{\text{cycle}})$ at small rates. If it already estimates failure per logical operation, multiplying again is wrong. Define the unit first.
- **Not every operation is $O(d)$ identically:** Lattice-surgery measurements, braids/deformations, transversal layers, idle storage, and factory protocols have different constants and sometimes different distance scaling.
- **Numerical derivation absent:** Show the inequality that produces 27, including $A$, number of cycles/operation, total spacetime locations, overall failure target, and safety margin. A rough $d$ factor alone does not uniquely imply 27.
- **Full accounting is much broader:** “Full spacetime-volume accounting” also includes thousands of simultaneously stored logical qubits, routing, distillation blocks, operation scheduling, failures/retries, and heterogeneous distances.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The correction is directionally valuable but currently looks like an unexplained authoritative adjustment.

### Surface-code physical qubits per logical (line 240, fourth sentence opening)

- **Convention-specific formula:** A rotated distance-$d$ surface-code memory patch commonly uses $d^2$ data qubits and approximately $d^2-1$ measurement qubits, totaling $2d^2-1$ in the particular layout used by the Willow paper. Other boundaries, extraction circuits, spare/routing qubits, and architectures change the constant.
- **Arithmetic correct:** $2(21)^2\approx882$ and $2(27)^2\approx1458$, supporting the rounded 1,000–1,500 range.
- **Resource label:** Say “data plus syndrome-measurement qubits in an idealized rotated memory patch,” not simply “physical qubits per logical qubit.” A computational layout needs tiles, boundaries, routing space, feed-forward, and possibly leakage-removal resources.
- **Logical operations:** Patch area alone does not price time or neighboring workspace required for lattice surgery.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The thousand-to-one translation is visceral and mathematically transparent.

### Magic-state factory overhead (line 240, fourth sentence closing)

- **Unsupported “comparable”:** Factory footprint depends on target output error/rate, distillation protocol, physical error, chosen logical gate set, parallelism, and whether one compares qubits, spacetime volume, or peak area. It may be smaller, comparable, or dominant.
- **Data/factory interaction:** Factories can use different code distances at different distillation levels and may dominate peak qubits when runtime is constrained.
- **Cross-reference:** §19.21 should provide a worked factory throughput/error calculation before this section asserts a ratio.
- **Alternatives:** Logical non-Clifford gates via code switching, transversal gates in another code, or other resource states alter the overhead, though none is automatically free.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Magic-state factories are intriguing, but “comparable” feels like a placeholder rather than insight.

### “Millions of physical qubits” conclusion (line 240, final sentence)

- **Does not follow from displayed factors alone:** Multiplying 1,000–1,500 physical qubits per logical by an unstated number of logical data/work qubits is necessary to reach millions. Add that logical-qubit count explicitly.
- **Primary estimate is more concrete:** Gidney–Ekerå estimate about 20 million noisy qubits and eight hours under specified assumptions: $10^{-3}$ gate error, planar nearest-neighbor superconducting layout, 1-$\mu$s surface-code cycle, 10-$\mu$s reaction time, factories/routing, and repeated attempts. Cite [How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/).
- **Plural “millions” is too broad to be informative:** Published estimates span orders of magnitude across assumptions and resource metrics. Give named baselines/year rather than “consistently quoted.”
- **“Refined steadily downward” is a progress narrative needing evidence:** Improvements are not monotonic across more realistic models; adding correlated noise, leakage, architecture constraints, classical latency, or stricter security/success targets can push estimates upward.
- **Cryptographic framing:** Factoring one RSA-2048 modulus under a chosen time target is not the same as immediately breaking all deployed RSA; key relevance, data capture, runtime/reliability, and system availability matter.
- **Cross-reference risk:** §19.18 must actually compare like-for-like resource studies; otherwise it cannot substantiate this trend claim.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The scale reveal is highly effective, but a named 20-million/8-hour scenario is more memorable and defensible than a floating consensus number.

### §19.16 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section builds an accessible numerical bridge from exponential distance suppression to code distance, patch area, and cryptographically relevant machine scale.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Define a logical qubit as an encoded degree of freedom/code-space span rather than two vectors as a subsystem; state the model/odd-distance limits of the scaling ansatz; and keep $p_L$ in one explicit unit throughout.
- **Highest-priority quantitative repair:** Derive the algorithm-wide error allocation and $d=21/27$ choices transparently, include the logical-qubit count, distinguish patch from computational-layout resources, and anchor the final figure to a named RSA estimate.
- **Highest-priority temporal repair:** Attribute $\Lambda=2.14$ to the Willow distance-5/7 memory result with its per-cycle metric and date, rather than generalizing it to “current experiments.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** This is one of the chapter’s strongest narrative sections because it turns abstractions into a million-qubit machine; a few unit/assumption repairs would make that excitement trustworthy.

## Chapter 19, §19.17 — Code Distance (lines 242–248)

### Heading and repetition (line 242)

- **Necessary concept, repeated late:** Distance has already been defined and used throughout the chapter. This section should either consolidate earlier fragments into the authoritative definition or be retitled around “Distance in spacetime and experiments.”
- **Progression opportunity:** Explicitly announce the move from static code distance to circuit/spacetime distance; otherwise the second paragraph appears to attach a universal round count to the static definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Distance is the chapter’s key quantitative lever, but another basic heading risks déjà vu.

### Normalizer definition (line 244, first clause)

- **Correct for a nontrivial stabilizer subspace code with conventions stated:** For a stabilizer $S$ in the $n$-qubit Pauli group, $d=\min\{\operatorname{wt}(P):P\in N(S)\setminus S\}$, modulo irrelevant phases, gives the minimum weight of a nontrivial logical Pauli for $k>0$.
- **Specify the ambient group:** “Normalizer” must be the Pauli normalizer/centralizer of $S$ within the Pauli group (for Paulis, commuting up to the phase convention), not the full unitary normalizer, whose elements include logical Cliffords of unrelated support notions.
- **Phase convention:** Stabilizer groups exclude $-I$ and are usually treated with phases quotienting appropriately. Without that convention, $-s\notin S$ can create a spurious member of $N(S)\setminus S$ with stabilizer support.
- **$k=0$ edge case:** A stabilizer state has no nontrivial logical Pauli, so the minimum set is empty; define distance separately or restrict to $k\ge1$ codes.
- **Subsystem-code caveat:** Subsystem codes have bare and dressed logical operators/distances because gauge operators matter. This definition is for subspace stabilizer codes, despite §19.16’s use of “subsystem.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The algebraic definition is compact and satisfying once the quotient/group is named.

### “Minimum number of physical qubits any logical operator must touch” gloss (line 244, middle)

- **Too broad:** The formula minimizes over logical **Pauli representatives**, not every conceivable logical unitary or every fault-tolerant implementation. A logical $H$, measurement, or lattice-surgery operation does not fit the simple Pauli-weight gloss.
- **Representative equivalence:** Logical Paulis are cosets in $N(S)/S$; multiplying by a stabilizer can deform support, and distance takes the minimum over every representative of every nonidentity coset.
- **“Touch” ambiguity:** Weight counts nonidentity tensor factors in the abstract operator, not necessarily qubits touched by a physical gate sequence or syndrome circuit.
- **Better gloss:** “The smallest support of any nontrivial logical Pauli representative.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The physical-support intuition is strong but should not overclaim all logical operations.

### Correction radius (line 244, second sentence opening)

- **Correct theorem:** A distance-$d$ quantum code corrects an arbitrary error acting on at most $t=\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor$ qubits, including coherent combinations, under ideal recovery.
- **Why half the distance:** For any pair $E_a,E_b$ of weight at most $t$, $E_a^\dagger E_b$ has weight at most $2t<d$ and cannot implement a nontrivial logical action; connect this directly to the Knill–Laflamme condition from §19.4.
- **Degeneracy:** Some errors above $t$ are also correctable, and degenerate errors may share a syndrome without harming recovery. The guarantee is “all errors up to,” not a sharp failure boundary.
- **Circuit-level distinction:** Weight in data qubits is not the same as number of circuit faults; a poorly designed syndrome circuit can let one fault spread to multiple data errors, motivating fault-tolerant gadgets and circuit distance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The half-distance rule is memorable and becomes more rewarding with its one-line proof.

### Detection radius (line 244, closing)

- **Mathematically conventional:** A distance-$d$ code detects every error of weight below $d$ in the quantum error-detection sense $PEP=c_EP$.
- **Syndrome-language nuance:** A stabilizer error of weight below $d$ produces no nontrivial syndrome but acts trivially on the code space; saying it is “detected” can mislead readers into expecting a flag. Distinguish “is detectable or harmless” from “always yields a nonzero syndrome.”
- **Non-Pauli errors:** The weight guarantee extends by linearity to operators supported on fewer than $d$ qubits, not only named Pauli errors, when detection is defined correctly.
- **Boundary:** Weight-$d$ errors are not uniformly undetectable; distance only guarantees that at least one weight-$d$ nontrivial logical Pauli exists.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The detect-versus-correct contrast is useful, though the word “detects” needs operational unpacking.

### “Two roles” framing (line 246, opening)

- **Useful organization:** Protection and time/depth cost are a productive pair for resource estimation.
- **Not exhaustive:** Distance also controls geometric patch dimensions, number of physical qubits, logical-operator support, deformation widths, and tolerance to erasures/defects; “two roles here” avoids implying exhaustiveness.
- **Different distances:** Static code distance, circuit distance, $X/Z$ distances, time-like distance, and effective distance under biased/correlated noise can differ. The framing should introduce these rather than collapse them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A clean dual-role frame makes an abstract integer feel operational.

### Protective scaling restatement (line 246, first role)

- **Repeats §19.16 too strongly:** The same heuristic is restated as fact without carrying over the odd-$d$, below-threshold, decoder, noise, and per-cycle qualifications.
- **Exponent:** Replace $(d+1)/2$ by $\lceil d/2\rceil$ or explicitly retain odd-distance surface-code scope.
- **“Exponentially suppresses” language:** A two-unit distance increase reduces $p_L$ by the constant factor $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}$ under the ansatz; exponential suppression describes repeated increases across the family, not a single step by itself.
- **Fixed conditions:** Physical error rate alone is insufficient; circuit, decoder, correlations, code geometry, number of rounds, and logical-error unit must also be held fixed.
- **Error floors:** Experimental rare correlated events can violate continued exponential scaling at high distance; the same primary Willow report observes a floor in high-distance repetition-code data.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The scaling remains exciting, but near-verbatim repetition brings less payoff the second time.

### “Distance-$d$ generally requires $d$ rounds” (line 246, second role)

- **Not a general code theorem:** A code of distance $d$ does not inherently require exactly $d$ syndrome rounds. Round count depends on the task, temporal boundaries, measurement-error model, syndrome circuit, decoder, desired circuit distance, and whether single-shot correction is available.
- **Common surface-code convention:** To build a roughly distance-$d$ spacetime memory/measurement experiment with noisy syndrome measurements, running about $d$ rounds is common because a time-like logical chain should also require $d$ faults.
- **Memory duration:** A logical memory may run for any number $T$ of cycles; if $T<d$ temporal boundaries can limit experiment distance, while a long computation runs far more than $d$ total rounds.
- **Logical gates:** A lattice-surgery parity measurement often uses $O(d)$ rounds for fault tolerance, but constants and protocols differ; some transversal operations take constant quantum depth followed by correction.
- **Single-shot counterexample:** Suitable higher-dimensional/gauge codes can infer measurement errors from one noisy syndrome round (plus classical processing/structure), directly defeating the blanket claim.
- **Repeated versus independent rounds:** Syndrome measurements are interpreted as changes/detection events in spacetime; simply repeating a static syndrome $d$ times is not the full decoder construction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The spatial-protection/time-cost duality is fascinating, but the universal phrasing hides its real spacetime geometry.

### Circuit depth grows with distance (line 246, closing)

- **Architecture/task dependent:** For surface-code memories and lattice surgery designed to maintain distance, syndrome-cycle count per protected logical measurement commonly scales as $O(d)$. This is not true of every logical operation or code family.
- **Depth unit:** Separate syndrome rounds from native two-qubit-gate depth per round and from wall-clock latency including measurement, reset, transport, and decoder feed-forward.
- **Parallelism:** Patch area grows as $O(d^2)$ while many checks run concurrently; total gate count, circuit depth, and spacetime volume scale differently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The cost warning is valuable but deserves a miniature area–time scaling table.

### “Practical surface-code distances” status range (line 248, opening)

- **Scope unclear:** Restrict this to repeated, full two-dimensional surface-code memory experiments with noisy checks. Repetition-code experiments have reached much larger nominal distances, and other QEC/code demonstrations cannot be summarized by 3–7.
- **“Practical” undefined:** Practical could mean physically realized, below threshold, real-time decoded, fault-tolerant logical gates, or application-ready. Use “reported in selected hardware memory experiments.”
- **Range is not a survey result:** Cite each endpoint/platform or give a compact table. As of the stated interval, Google reports distance 5 and 7 memories; a 2025 neutral-atom architecture reports distance-3/5 comparisons. That does not prove all practical experiments fall inside one meaningful range.
- **Publication-date ambiguity:** Google’s Willow work was posted/published online in December 2024 and appeared in a 2025 Nature volume; use one bibliographic convention consistently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Readers like a frontier scoreboard, but only if the event category is stable and comparable.

### Distance-scaling experiments and “exponential” (line 248, first sentence closing)

- **Below-threshold signature:** Lower logical error at larger distance under matched physical conditions is the crucial evidence that scaling helps.
- **Finite-point restraint needed throughout:** Two or three distances support below-threshold scaling and can fit the expected law; they do not empirically establish an asymptotic exponential over the distances needed for algorithms.
- **Matched comparison:** Subsampled smaller codes on the same chip may have different local component quality; experiments need averaging/modeling to disentangle size from spatial variation.
- **Metric:** State logical error **per cycle** and memory basis/decoder; $p_L$ without a unit conceals differences.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Watching errors fall as hardware grows is the right experimental climax.

### Google device/date description (line 248, second sentence opening)

- **Attribution mostly identifiable:** The primary paper reports distance-5 and distance-7 surface-code memories on Willow-generation superconducting processors, with lower-distance subsets used in scaling analysis.
- **“Google’s 2024 experiments”:** Better: “Google Quantum AI’s work posted online in December 2024 (Nature 2025).” Distinguish experiment date, preprint date, and journal issue rather than selecting one silently.
- **Processor wording:** The work used a 105-qubit processor for the distance-7 memory and a separate 72-qubit processor for the real-time distance-5 demonstration; “on a 105-qubit device” compresses distinct experimental configurations.
- **101 versus 105:** The distance-7 code used 101 physical qubits on a 105-qubit processor. Stating both avoids implying every device qubit participated.
- **Primary evidence checked 2026-07-23:** [Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Concrete device and patch sizes make the milestone vivid.

### Factor $\sim2.14$ per distance step (line 248, middle)

- **Overgeneralized measurement:** The headline $\Lambda=2.14\pm0.02$ is the suppression from increasing distance by two for the larger-memory comparison/fit, not necessarily an identical factor for every 3→5 and 5→7 transition under one homogeneous experiment.
- **Use uncertainty:** Since the prose gives two decimal places, retain the reported uncertainty and decoder/context or round to “about two.”
- **Metric:** It is logical error per error-correction cycle, not a generic logical-gate error.
- **Decoder dependence:** The paper reports different values with neural-network versus ensembled-matching decoding; name the quoted decoder/result.
- **Meaning:** $\Lambda>1$ establishes below-threshold behavior over the tested range; it does not mean the physical error rate itself fell when distance increased.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The factor is a superb headline metric once attached to its exact comparison.

### Relation to the 2023 distance-3/5 report (line 248, middle-to-late)

- **Useful historical continuity:** Google’s earlier Sycamore work compared distance 3 and 5 and found a modest average improvement, marking an initial scaling signal.
- **Bibliographic precision:** The preprint appeared in 2022 and journal publication was in 2023; cite it as [Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.06431) or its journal version.
- **Different hardware/noise:** The later Willow result should not be described as merely appending a third point to the same fixed-$p$ series; processor generation, calibration, circuits, decoder, and error-removal techniques changed.
- **Authorial caveat is excellent:** “Three points support the trend; they do not by themselves establish the asymptote” is exactly the epistemic restraint the surrounding “demonstrating exponential suppression” wording needs. Move this caution earlier and make all verbs agree with it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The progression from tentative to stronger evidence is a strong scientific narrative.

### Distance 21–27 as cryptographic regime (line 248, final sentence opening)

- **Distance alone does not define cryptographic usefulness:** Required distance depends on physical error relative to threshold, suppression factor/error floor, algorithmic spacetime volume, decoder, operation type, and allocated failure probability.
- **Cross-section inconsistency:** §19.16 obtains $d\approx21$ from the optimistic hypothetical $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$ and a $10^{-11}$ target. By contrast, the Willow paper projects distance 27 for about $10^{-6}$ logical error per cycle at its measured $\Lambda$ and assumptions. The same 21–27 range cannot be presented as hardware-independent.
- **“Cryptographically interesting algorithms”:** RSA-2048 factoring is one scenario; cryptographic relevance spans key sizes, algorithms, security models, and time/resource constraints. Name the scenario.
- **Fault-tolerant operations:** Demonstrating a distance-27 memory is not sufficient: computation also needs logical gates, magic-state production/non-Clifford resources, routing, sustained cycles, real-time decoding, and system-level reliability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A target distance gives the frontier a finish line, but the current finish line moves with the assumed suppression factor.

### “Major hardware milestone of the late 2020s” (line 248, closing)

- **Forecast without owner:** This is not an established field milestone or deadline. Attribute a vendor roadmap/research scenario and date, or say it is one illustrative scaling target.
- **Wrongly singular objective:** Hardware roadmaps may prioritize logical error, logical qubit count, gate fidelity, modularity, decoder throughput, or qLDPC blocks rather than a surface-code distance number.
- **Potential architecture mismatch:** IBM’s announced fault-tolerant path uses bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes, for which surface-patch distance and $2d^2$ accounting are not the roadmap’s organizing metric.
- **Better close:** Ask what combination of distance, suppression factor, cycle stability, logical operation fidelity, and factory throughput is needed to cross an application-level error budget.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Roadmap urgency is engaging, but an unattributed decade forecast will date the book quickly.

### §19.17 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section pairs the algebraic meaning of distance with both error suppression and spacetime cost, then grounds the idea in a landmark scaling experiment.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** State the Pauli-group quotient/phase and $k>0$ scope of the normalizer definition; distinguish static, circuit, spatial, and temporal distance; and replace the universal $d$-round rule with a surface-code/task-specific explanation.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Describe the Willow processors, code sizes, logical-error-per-cycle metric, decoder, uncertainty, and publication chronology precisely; do not treat changing hardware generations as one fixed-$p$ three-point series.
- **Highest-priority consistency repair:** Reconcile what distance 21–27 means under the hypothetical $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$ model versus Willow’s measured $\Lambda\approx2.14$, and avoid elevating one surface-code scenario into a universal late-2020s milestone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Distance is presented as a gripping bridge between theorem and hardware; careful metric and chronology fixes would make the experimental climax durable.

## Chapter 19, §19.18 — Physical-to-Logical Overhead (lines 250–258)

### Heading and scope (line 250)

- **Important system metric:** The heading correctly signals a shift from code theory to resources.
- **Singular metric risk:** “Overhead” can mean peak physical qubits, physical qubits per logical qubit, qubit-rounds per logical operation, gate count, runtime, wiring/control hardware, decoder cost, or total spacetime volume. The section must choose and label each metric.
- **Hyphenation:** “Physical-to-logical” is readable, but a ratio notation $n_{\rm phys}/k_{\rm log}$ would expose whether ancillas/factories/shared infrastructure are included.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Readers naturally want the price tag after learning how protection works.

### Definition of overhead (line 252, first sentence)

- **Too narrow for “implement”:** Counting physical qubits for one encoded memory patch is a space overhead; implementing a fault-tolerant logical qubit also requires syndrome ancillas, repeated cycles, decoder/control, routing neighbors, spare qubits, and resources for logical operations.
- **Target metric necessary:** “At a given logical error rate” must specify per what—cycle, logical gate, unit time, algorithm—and under which physical noise, code, decoder, and circuit.
- **Shared-resource problem:** Factories and routing fabric serve a computation or throughput target, not necessarily one logical qubit. Dividing total machine qubits by data-logical count produces workload-dependent overhead rather than an intrinsic code number.
- **Distance/rate distinction:** For a block encoding $k>1$ logical qubits, quote $n_{\rm data}/k$ plus syndrome ancillas and layout resources; a one-patch definition structurally favors the surface-code framing.
- **Better taxonomy:** Separate memory space overhead, operation spacetime overhead, and full-application resources.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A simple definition is welcome, but it promises comparability the later numbers do not have.

### “Headline number” and practical/speculative distinction (line 252, second sentence)

- **Overclaim:** No single qubit ratio distinguishes practical from speculative schemes. A low-rate code with local shallow checks and a fast decoder may be more implementable than a high-rate code requiring costly communication.
- **Missing axes:** Threshold, finite-size logical performance, syndrome circuit, connectivity, logical gates, decoder accuracy/latency, leakage handling, cycle time, factory throughput, and fabrication yield all matter.
- **Rhetorical effect:** “Headline number” accurately describes publicity but should be followed by a warning that headline ratios often compare unlike tasks.
- **“Speculative” tone:** The word can dismiss mathematically rigorous but not yet engineered approaches; “system-ready versus theoretical” with explicit readiness levels would be fairer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Competitive scoreboards are engaging, but a multidimensional scorecard is intellectually richer.

### Physical error $p\approx10^{-3}$ and threshold relation (line 254, opening)

- **Model ambiguity:** A single $p$ must be declared as uniform circuit-level depolarizing probability (or another exact model). Real gate, idle, reset, measurement, leakage, and correlated errors are not one scalar.
- **Threshold mismatch:** A circuit-level surface-code threshold around $0.7\%$–$1\%$ makes $10^{-3}$ roughly one order of magnitude below threshold, not generally “one to two.” A phenomenological/code-capacity threshold can be much higher but is not comparable to a physical two-qubit-gate rate.
- **Scheme dependence:** Threshold depends on layout, extraction circuit, decoder, and noise. The parenthetical cannot float independently of those choices.
- **Hardware versus assumption:** $p=10^{-3}$ is a standard resource-estimate assumption; do not conflate it with a complete experimental noise model merely because a device reports a similar average gate infidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A concrete physical-error anchor helps, though mixed threshold conventions will confuse careful readers.

### Target $p_L\approx10^{-10}$–$10^{-12}$ (line 254, first sentence middle)

- **Unit missing again:** State logical error per surface-code cycle, Toffoli, lattice-surgery primitive, or algorithmic operation. These targets are not interchangeable.
- **Budget derivation:** For about $10^{10}$ failure opportunities and an overall QEC failure allowance $\epsilon$, a uniform union-bound allocation is $p_i\lesssim\epsilon/10^{10}$; $10^{-11}$ corresponds to $\epsilon\sim0.1$. The range needs an explicit desired success margin and allocation.
- **Operation counts differ:** Memory locations across thousands of logical qubits can dominate “logical operations”; magic-state failures and synthesis error need separate budgets.
- **Cryptographic plural:** RSA factoring is one workload family; not every cryptographic-scale quantum computation has the same count or error allocation.
- **Broken self-reference:** “(§19.18)” points to the current section. It likely intends §19.16 or another resource-estimation section and should be corrected.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The stringent target conveys scale, but the self-reference and missing unit break confidence.

### Claimed distance 21–27 (line 254, first sentence closing)

- **Only reproducible under a chosen ansatz:** With $A=1$, odd $d$, $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}=0.1$, and $p_L$ in the chosen unit, $10^{-10}$ suggests $d\ge19$ and $10^{-12}$ suggests $d\ge23$, not automatically 21–27. Larger values can reflect prefactors, spacetime budgets, and margins, which must be shown.
- **If ratio differs, result moves sharply:** At the experimentally reported $\Lambda\approx2.14$, each $d+2$ gains only about a factor 2.14 rather than 10; the required distance can be far larger for the same starting error.
- **Noise “details” insufficient explanation:** The decoder, syndrome schedule, temporal extent, error unit, and confidence margin are first-order assumptions, not incidental details.
- **Cross-section repetition:** This repeats §19.16 without resolving its unit and $d=27$ derivation concerns.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A narrow distance band feels actionable but becomes false precision without the calculation.

### $2d^2$ and “data storage alone” (line 254, second sentence)

- **Direct contradiction:** In the common rotated surface-code memory layout, $d^2$ is the data-qubit count and about $d^2-1$ syndrome-measurement qubits bring the total to $2d^2-1$. Therefore $2d^2$ is *not* data storage alone.
- **Arithmetic:** $2(21)^2=882$ and $2(27)^2=1458$, so the rounded 900–1,500 range is correct for that particular total patch convention.
- **Even distance:** The earlier scaling uses odd distances, but the text describes a continuous 21–27 range. State selected odd $d$ values and layout.
- **Missing layout resources:** A computing patch may need boundaries, inter-patch spacing, surgery ancillas, routing tiles, spare/faulty-site margin, and leakage-removal hardware beyond the memory patch total.
- **Correct repair:** “About 900–1,500 data-plus-check qubits per isolated rotated memory patch; data qubits alone are about 440–730.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The square-law calculation is satisfying, but the resource label must be right.

### “Standard 15-to-1” magic-state premise (line 254, third sentence opening)

- **One protocol, not the standard universal baseline:** 15-to-1 Reed–Muller distillation is canonical for $T$ states, but modern estimates use multi-level factories, block-code protocols, catalysis, cultivation, CCZ factories, or application/gate-set-specific constructions.
- **Input/output error:** One 15-to-1 level suppresses suitable input error roughly cubically but may not reach $10^{-10}$–$10^{-12}$ from raw injection error near $10^{-3}$ once circuit faults are included; number of levels and code distances matter.
- **“Current circuit depths”:** Time-sensitive and undefined. Give a named factory layout, physical model, target output error, and throughput.
- **Cross-reference sequencing:** §19.21 has not yet supplied this model; the present numerical conclusion should not rely on a future section without a compact derivation here.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Distillation is inherently dramatic, but one named protocol should not stand for the whole factory design space.

### Factory multiplier 1×–4× of data-qubit budget (line 254, middle)

- **Unsupported generalization:** Factory peak area depends on $T$/Toffoli consumption rate, parallelism and runtime target, output error, protocol, physical error, code distances, and acceptance probability. There is no workload-independent “typical” multiplier.
- **Wrong normalization:** Factories are shared production infrastructure. Their cost per data logical qubit depends on how many data qubits and how much non-Clifford throughput the algorithm requires.
- **Space versus spacetime:** A small factory reused serially has low peak qubits and high runtime; many parallel factories reverse that trade. A scalar qubit multiplier hides the central scheduling choice.
- **Data budget itself mislabeled:** Since the preceding $2d^2$ already includes measurement ancillas but omits routing, the denominator is neither “data qubits” nor total data-block layout.
- **Need a worked design:** Give number of factories, output states/cycle, footprint, levels, acceptance, and target runtime for the RSA scenario before quoting a ratio.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** The factory-as-second-machine idea is engaging; an unexplained multiplier is not.

### Total 1,000–10,000 physical qubits per logical (line 254, middle-to-late)

- **Arithmetic inconsistency at the low end:** Starting from 900–1,500 and adding another 1×–4× that budget implies approximately 1,800–7,500 before routing/other resources. A lower total of 1,000 cannot follow from the stated premises except by changing protocols/base distance.
- **Range mixes architectures:** “Per logical qubit” divides shared factory resources across an unspecified number of data logical qubits. Different workload widths and factory counts can produce nearly any ratio.
- **False precision/order:** A tenfold interval already signals model uncertainty; bolding it as a stable practical range hides incompatible assumptions.
- **Memory versus computation:** Compare isolated memory overhead, data-block computational layout, and full-machine peak qubits in separate rows.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The bold reveal has punch, but readers who check the addition will lose trust.

### Cultivation/improved-distillation trend and “stable order” (line 254, closing)

- **Real active improvement:** Magic-state cultivation can reduce estimated qubit-round cost markedly under specified surface-code circuit noise, and newer distillation/scheduling ideas change the trade space.
- **Primary quantitative context:** Gidney–Shutty–Jones estimate cultivation at about an order of magnitude fewer qubit-rounds than prior methods to reach roughly $2\times10^{-9}$ under $10^{-3}$ uniform depolarizing circuit noise; at $5\times10^{-4}$ they estimate about $4\times10^{-11}$: [Magic state cultivation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17595).
- **Not merely “push low end”:** Cultivation changes protocol, postselection/acceptance, error range, and spacetime profile; a result at $2\times10^{-9}$ does not automatically satisfy every cryptographic allocation.
- **Contradictory stability claim:** If protocols move estimates by an order of magnitude and a 2025 RSA estimate drops peak qubits below one million, the claimed per-logical/full-machine “stable order” needs a matched longitudinal dataset.
- **Temporal caution:** Say “recent as of 2026” and distinguish peer-reviewed results, preprints, simulation estimates, and hardware demonstrations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Rapid factory innovation is exciting; declaring the endpoint stable prematurely dulls that story.

### “Three trends” framing (line 256, opening)

- **Helpful compression:** Decoder, hardware, and code-family improvements are indeed major levers.
- **Missing coequal trends:** Logical-gate protocols, magic-state production, circuit/algorithm optimization, biased/erasure noise conversion, modular connectivity, scheduling, and architecture-aware compilation can dominate.
- **Interactions:** These levers are not additive independent discounts; a decoder gain depends on the noise/code, and a new code may require a new circuit/connectivity/decoder.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A three-front race is lively, but the interactions should be the point.

### Decoder savings of 20%–30% (line 256, first trend)

- **No universal percentage:** A decoder changes logical error at fixed hardware/code; converting that into qubit savings requires re-optimizing discrete distance and layout. Savings vary from zero to a large step depending on the target and distance boundary.
- **Categories overlap/mislead:** “Neural,” “belief propagation,” and “parallel MWPM” describe model or implementation families with different accuracy/latency goals; parallelization by itself normally targets speed, not necessarily extracting more information.
- **Benchmark requirements:** Compare matched syndrome data/noise, accuracy, latency, throughput, training/calibration cost, hardware resources, scalability, and robustness to drift.
- **Neural caveat:** A more accurate decoder may be too slow or difficult to retrain for real-time high-distance use; the Willow paper explicitly separates real-time and higher-accuracy contexts.
- **Citation needed:** “Sometimes saving 20%–30%” must name the code, physical-error point, target $p_L$, baseline decoder, and whether saving means qubits or spacetime.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Software buying hardware is a compelling idea; a floating percentage reads like marketing.

### Better-physical-qubit examples (line 256, second trend)

- **Correct mechanism:** Lower physical error below threshold increases $\Lambda$ and can reduce required distance sharply at a fixed logical target, assuming other error mechanisms scale too.
- **Average gate infidelity is not model $p$:** Randomized-benchmarking/two-qubit-gate error, circuit-level depolarizing probability, detector rate, leakage, crosstalk, drift, and measurement/idle errors are different metrics.
- **Google claim needs metric/source:** Willow’s component errors and observed logical suppression should be quoted from the QEC experiment rather than reduced to “reaching $p\approx10^{-3}$ on two-qubit gates.”
- **IBM claim needs device/gate/source:** “IBM reaching similar in 2024–2025” is too vague to verify and compares no specified processor, layer fidelity, topology, or simultaneous operation.
- **Time sensitivity:** These vendor-status sentences need an as-of date and official/primary sources, or should be replaced by the timeless dependence on $p/p_{\mathrm{th}}$.
- **System bottleneck:** Improving only two-qubit gates may not lower required distance if measurement, leakage, rare correlated bursts, or stability dominates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The hardware race is engaging, but vendor name-checks need apples-to-apples evidence.

### IBM bivariate-bicycle example (line 256, third trend)

- **Use the exact code/result:** Bravyi et al. analyze the $[[144,12,12]]$ BB code with 144 data qubits and 144 syndrome ancillas. Under a standard circuit-noise model at $p=0.1\%$, they estimate 12 logical qubits stored for nearly one million cycles using 288 total qubits, versus nearly 3,000 in their matched surface-code comparison.
- **What “10×” means:** The paper reports about a tenfold encoding/total-memory overhead reduction for that finite modeled task. It is not simply “encoding rate at distance 12”: raw code rate is $12/144=1/12$, while the comparison also includes ancillas, target duration, logical performance, and circuit model.
- **Not an asymptotic result:** A finite $[[144,12,12]]$ comparison cannot establish that asymptotic computation overhead falls by the same factor. BB families here should not be conflated with the asymptotically good qLDPC constructions of §19.15.
- **Memory versus computation:** The 2024 result is an end-to-end **fault-tolerant memory** protocol; universal logical gates, routing, factories, and full computation can change the advantage.
- **Connectivity:** The proposed syndrome circuit needs degree-six, thickness-two connectivity and depth eight, not ordinary nearest-neighbor planar hardware. “If extraction can be realized” is appropriate but should mention these concrete requirements.
- **Experimental update:** By 2026, a 32-qubit processor experiment reported small distance-4/distance-3 BB variants, an important but far smaller and high-logical-error milestone: [Demonstration of low-overhead quantum error correction codes](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-025-03157-4). Do not leave “real hardware” as wholly hypothetical.
- **Primary baseline:** [High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07107-7).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A concrete 288-versus-3,000 contest is far more gripping than a vague asymptotic promise.

### “2025-era anchor” RSA scenario (line 258, opening)

- **Not one identifiable estimate:** The tuple “$10^6$–$10^7$ qubits, $10^{10}$ cycles, around a day” appears to blend different studies or configurations. Cite a single design whose table produces all three numbers.
- **“Fully fault-tolerant” needs scope:** State whether arithmetic, routing, distillation/cultivation, memory, reaction latency, retries, decoder, and classical postprocessing are included.
- **Key versus modulus:** One factors a 2048-bit RSA modulus, not “a 2048-bit RSA key” in the direct algorithmic object sense; clarify public modulus/key context.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A single end-to-end attack scenario is an ideal anchor—if it is genuinely single.

### Qubit, cycle, and wall-clock tuple (line 258, middle)

- **Dimensional sanity check:** $10^{10}$ cycles at a 1-$\mu$s surface-code cycle is about $10^4$ seconds (2.8 hours), not a day; a day implies an effective average around 8.6 $\mu$s per serial cycle or added reaction/scheduling latency. Show the conversion.
- **Cycles are not gates:** Parallel patches undergo cycles simultaneously; total qubit-rounds and critical-path rounds differ. “$10^{10}$ surface-code cycles” must mean depth/critical-path cycles, not sum over every patch.
- **Peak space–time trade:** Fewer factories reduce qubits but extend runtime. Quoting ranges without paired configurations obscures that Pareto frontier.
- **Physical assumptions:** Cycle time, reaction time, fabrication yield, connectivity, uniform error, and sustained calibration determine wall-clock plausibility.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Runtime makes the threat concrete; the arithmetic should invite rather than resist checking.

### Comparison with named RSA-2048 estimates (line 258)

- **2021 peer-reviewed baseline:** Gidney–Ekerå estimated 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours under $10^{-3}$ uniform gate error, 1-$\mu$s cycles, 10-$\mu$s reaction time, and planar nearest-neighbor assumptions: [How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/).
- **2025 preprint update:** Gidney estimated fewer than one million noisy qubits and less than a week under the same headline physical assumptions, trading more time/fewer factories and using approximate residue arithmetic, yoked storage, and cultivation: [How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917).
- **Current range conflict:** The latter falls below the manuscript’s stated $10^6$ lower endpoint and does not support “around a day”; the former exceeds its $10^7$ upper endpoint but runs under a day. The manuscript has combined the desirable ends of distinct tradeoffs.
- **Publication status:** Clearly label the 2025 result as a preprint/estimate if that remains its status at final fact-check.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The 20-million/8-hour versus sub-million/sub-week tradeoff tells a much more interesting optimization story.

### “Order of magnitude stable for nearly a decade” (line 258, closing)

- **Contradicted by cited progress:** The named estimates move peak qubits by more than twentyfold from 2021 to 2025, while earlier estimates were much larger; runtime and included realism also change.
- **No matched longitudinal series:** To claim stability, normalize algorithm, success probability, physical noise, cycle/reaction time, gate set, layout, and space–time objective across papers.
- **Exact dependencies incomplete:** Algorithm/arithmetic choice, logical qubit reuse/storage code, target runtime/factory count, synthesis/error budget, connectivity, and failure/retry policy matter alongside the three listed choices.
- **Better lesson:** Resource estimates lie on a moving Pareto frontier; report scenario, date, assumptions, peak qubits, runtime, and total spacetime volume together.
- **Section-reference inconsistency:** Earlier prose says estimates are “refined steadily downward,” while this sentence says the order has been stable. Choose evidence-based wording.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Stability sounds reassuring but erases the genuine drama of a rapidly moving frontier.

### §19.18 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section tries to give readers exactly what they want—an end-to-end conversion from physical error through distance and factories to an RSA-scale machine.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Separate data-only $d^2$, data-plus-syndrome $2d^2-1$, computational-layout, shared-factory, and full-machine resources; fix the impossible low-end addition and self-reference.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Replace floating decoder/vendor/factory percentages with named matched studies; present IBM’s exact $[[144,12,12]]$, 288-versus-nearly-3,000 memory comparison and its circuit/connectivity assumptions.
- **Highest-priority synthesis repair:** Do not splice 2021’s 20-million/8-hour and 2025’s sub-million/sub-week endpoints into a fictitious 1–10-million/one-day consensus. Show the Pareto tradeoff and publication dates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The stakes and numbers are highly engaging, but this is also the chapter section most vulnerable to false precision and apples-to-oranges arithmetic.

## Chapter 19, §19.19 — Threshold Theorem (lines 260–268)

### Heading and theorem identity (line 260)

- **Right capstone topic:** The theorem explains why all preceding engineering effort can scale in principle.
- **Not one unique theorem:** There are quantum accuracy-threshold theorems for different architectures, code constructions, locality constraints, and stochastic/coherent/non-Markovian noise models. Introduce a representative formulation rather than implying a single universal constant/result.
- **Distinguish threshold notions:** Code-capacity, phenomenological, circuit-level, pseudothreshold, and rigorous accuracy threshold are not interchangeable; this section should reconcile the chapter’s earlier numerical “thresholds.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** An existence theorem guaranteeing scalable computation is a natural conceptual climax.

### “Central existence result” characterization (line 262, opening)

- **Fair assessment:** The threshold theorem is foundational because it shows noisy components need not become arbitrarily accurate as computation grows.
- **What exists:** The result asserts a fault-tolerant simulation scheme with bounded physical noise strength and controlled overhead, not that every code or architecture has a useful threshold.
- **Historical opportunity:** Briefly credit the independent foundational threshold work and point to a modern rigorous construction/proof; this is one of the chapter’s few theorem-level historical landmarks.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** “Arbitrarily reliable from imperfect parts” is one of quantum computing’s best intellectual hooks.

### Existence of a constant threshold (line 262, first sentence middle)

- **Constant relative to problem size:** $p_{\mathrm{th}}>0$ is independent of circuit size/target accuracy but depends on the fault-tolerant scheme and assumed noise model.
- **Noise strength may not be a probability:** Stochastic local noise can use a fault probability parameter; coherent/local non-Markovian results may bound operator amplitudes or system–bath coupling strength instead. Do not define every theorem through $p$.
- **Rigorous versus simulated values:** Proved lower bounds for concatenated gadgets can be far below numerically estimated surface-code thresholds. A theorem’s existence constant is not automatically the familiar ~1% engineering threshold.
- **Primary examples:** Aliferis–Gottesman–Preskill prove an accuracy threshold for concatenated distance-3 codes under adversarial stochastic faults and extensions: [Quantum accuracy threshold for concatenated distance-3 codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0504218). Terhal–Burkard formulate a result for local non-Markovian noise using a coupling-strength measure: [Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation For Local Non-Markovian Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0402104).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A nonzero constant is deceptively simple; contrasting proof bounds and practical thresholds adds depth.

### “Every physical operation fails independently with $p$” implication (line 262, middle)

- **Missing correlation/locality hypothesis:** Marginal failure probability below a number is insufficient. Perfectly correlated global faults can destroy an entire block with probability $p$ regardless of distance. State local stochastic/independent fault assumptions or the bounded-correlation condition of the chosen theorem.
- **Location completeness is good:** Gates, preparations, measurements, and idles must all be fault locations; also include transport/reset/classical-feed-forward interfaces if present in the architecture.
- **Uniformity simplification:** Heterogeneous location rates can be bounded by a maximum or handled with weighted conditions, but “every operation” need not have identical $p$.
- **Leakage/non-Pauli faults:** A theorem needs gadgets/noise reduction that bring leakage and general faults into its correctable model; a per-operation average infidelity alone is not the required bound.
- **Spatial locality:** If long-range gates are unavailable, routing overhead and extra fault locations must be included in the simulated gadgets and threshold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The condition sounds wonderfully usable, but hiding correlations makes it dangerously magical.

### Arbitrarily long computation and arbitrarily small error (line 262, closing)

- **Correct existential conclusion under assumptions:** For any finite ideal circuit size and target total simulation error, one can choose sufficient encoding/protection to meet it below threshold.
- **Not an infinite run:** “Arbitrarily long” means every chosen finite length can be simulated with correspondingly increased resources, not that one fixed finite device runs forever with zero cumulative failure.
- **Total versus per-gate error:** The theorem controls a norm/distributional distance or total failure probability of the simulated computation; “logical error rate” sounds per-cycle and should be replaced by “overall simulation error at most $\varepsilon$.”
- **Classical reliability:** Classical decoding/control is usually assumed sufficiently reliable or itself fault tolerant; mention this hidden resource.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The finite-but-unbounded interpretation preserves the awe without suggesting immortality.

### Polylogarithmic-overhead statement (line 262, final phrase)

- **Precision parameter unclear:** Overhead is polylogarithmic in circuit size divided by target total error (for common concatenated constructions), not merely “desired precision” in isolation.
- **Metric:** State whether overhead is physical circuit size, depth, qubits, or per-logical-location gadget size. Exponents and locality penalties differ.
- **Multiplicative baseline:** Total work is the ideal circuit size times a polylog factor; saying simply “at an overhead polylogarithmic” can be read as total resource independent of $T$.
- **Modern constructions:** Some code families target constant space overhead under appropriate assumptions; the concatenated-code proof here establishes one sufficient scaling, not the unique optimum.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Polylog overhead is the theorem’s astonishing efficiency payoff, worth defining precisely.

### “$T$-gate computation” notation (line 264, opening)

- **Severe ambiguity:** In this chapter, $T$ also denotes the non-Clifford phase gate. “A $T$-gate computation” naturally means a computation made of $T$ gates, not a circuit containing $T$ elementary locations. Use $L$ or $N$ for ideal circuit size.
- **Operation versus gate count:** Preparations, measurements, idles, and classical control locations matter; define $L$ as the number of ideal locations and optionally width/depth separately.
- **Overall target:** Say the simulated output distribution/channel differs by at most $\varepsilon$ or the total failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$, according to the proof model.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** This notation collision is likely to stop exactly the readers who know what a $T$ gate is.

### $O(T\,\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon))$ operation count (line 264, first sentence)

- **Broadly correct concatenated-simulation form:** Allocate error about $\varepsilon/L$ per encoded location, use $O(\log\log(L/\varepsilon))$ concatenation levels, and obtain a polylog multiplicative size overhead.
- **Exponent/constants hidden:** If a level-$1$ gadget expands a location by $G$ and error exponent doubles, $G^\ell=(\log(L/\varepsilon))^{\log_2G}$ up to constants. Showing this makes “polylog” earned rather than asserted.
- **Depth/locality:** Total depth may also acquire polylog overhead, and enforcing geometrically local gates can change constants/exponents.
- **Circuit width:** Physical qubit count scales with ideal logical width times encoding/gadget overhead, not just “per logical qubit” independently of concurrent ancillas.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The scaling is powerful and becomes memorable with one explicit exponent derivation.

### “Ancilla blocks per logical qubit” guarantee (line 264, first sentence closing)

- **Nonstandard/unclear resource unit:** A theorem normally bounds physical qubits and circuit locations. “Ancilla blocks” depends on gadget design, verification, parallelism, and scheduling.
- **Missing ideal width:** If the ideal computation uses $W$ simultaneous qubits, total physical qubits scale roughly $W\,\mathrm{polylog}(L/\varepsilon)$ plus workspace, not merely a number “per logical qubit.”
- **Factory distinction:** Concatenated-code error-correction ancillas are not automatically magic-state factories; avoid linking this count silently to the previous overhead discussion.
- **Better statement:** Give total physical circuit size and maximum width/depth bounds in terms of ideal $L,W,D$ for the selected theorem.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The phrase sounds concrete but provides no countable architecture object.

### Distance-3 concatenation recurrence, first level (line 264, proof sketch)

- **Correct leading idea:** A fault-tolerant distance-3 gadget fails only when at least two suitably placed lower-level faults occur, yielding $p_1\lesssim C p^2$ below assumptions.
- **Malignant pairs, not all pairs equally:** $C$ bounds/counts malignant fault pairs (plus higher-order terms); gadget correctness ensures a single fault does not produce logical failure.
- **Inequality versus approximation:** Use $p_1\le C p^2$ within a proven regime or $\approx$ only as a heuristic. The tilde currently suppresses higher-order contributions and norm definitions.
- **Threshold from recurrence:** The simplified recurrence has threshold $p<1/C$; the full gadget analysis gives a more careful threshold/pseudothreshold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** “One fault tolerated, two required” makes double-exponential suppression beautifully intuitive.

### Two and $\ell$ levels algebra (line 264, middle)

- **Algebra checks:** Iterating $p_j=Cp_{j-1}^2$ gives $p_2=C^3p^4$ and $p_\ell=C^{2^\ell-1}p^{2^\ell}=(Cp)^{2^\ell}/C$, as written.
- **Index convention:** Define $p_0=p$ explicitly so readers can verify the recurrence.
- **Bound direction:** If the recurrence is an upper bound, preserve $\le$ through the iteration; equality/tildes should not convert a combinatorial bound into an exact rate.
- **Higher-distance generalization:** A code/gadget tolerating $t$ faults gives an exponent $(t+1)^\ell$, so the doubling is distance-3-specific.
- **Correlations:** The recurrence relies on the chosen local-noise condition making sets of faults sufficiently suppressed; arbitrary correlations invalidate the power.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** This is the section’s best derivation—short, checkable, and genuinely surprising.

### Solving for concatenation level (line 264, late)

- **Missing circuit-size factor:** To make total computation error below $\varepsilon$ over $L$ ideal locations, require encoded-location error $p_\ell\lesssim\varepsilon/L$, yielding $\ell=O(\log\log(L/\varepsilon))$, not just $O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
- **Below-threshold constant matters:** Solving uses $Cp<1$; near threshold, $|\log(Cp)|$ affects the additive/constant level count substantially.
- **Integer ceiling:** $\ell$ is discrete and small finite-level effects dominate practical resource estimates; asymptotic notation hides step changes.
- **Internal inconsistency:** The opening concrete bound correctly contains $T/\varepsilon$, then the proof drops $T$. Restore the same variable throughout.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Double-log levels are delightful, but the missing circuit size weakens the promised concrete connection.

### Constant expansion per level to polylog overhead (line 264, closing)

- **Correct argument:** If each recursive level multiplies physical size by a constant $G$, then $G^{O(\log\log(L/\varepsilon))}$ is a power of $\log(L/\varepsilon)$.
- **Gate count and qubit count constants differ:** Encoding block size, gadget size, ancilla verification, and time steps have separate expansion factors and thus separate polylog exponents.
- **Preparation/postselection:** Some gadgets can need retries or verified ancillas; expected versus worst-case overhead and failure-tail handling should be identified.
- **Classical decoding:** Concatenated syndrome processing also grows and may be parallelized; it is absent from the physical-operation count.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** This completes a remarkably accessible proof sketch once the variables are consistent.

### Noise-model dependence (line 266, first subtlety opening)

- **Correct and essential:** Threshold values are conditional on noise structure and metric.
- **Category mismatch:** “Independent stochastic Pauli,” “biased,” and “adversarial” are not mutually exclusive categories: noise can be independent and biased, or adversarial stochastic with locality bounds.
- **Broader distinctions:** Circuit-level versus data-only, erasure versus unlocated errors, coherent versus stochastic, Markovian versus non-Markovian, and spatial/temporal correlation length are important.
- **Decoder role:** A threshold quoted for optimal decoding differs from one for a particular efficient decoder.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The caveat turns one magic number into a map of physical regimes.

### “Standard 1% surface-code threshold” (line 266, first subtlety middle)

- **Needs exact standard:** Around 1% is associated with selected circuit-level depolarizing models, syndrome schedules, boundaries, and matching-like decoders. Other standard models produce ~10% data-only/phenomenological values or different circuit thresholds.
- **“Every gate” incomplete:** Measurement, reset, idle, and two-qubit locations may receive different channels/rates; some models assign uniform depolarizing faults after each circuit location.
- **Not theorem constant:** This numerical threshold is predominantly a simulation/decoder result, not the rigorous $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ guaranteed by the concatenated-code theorem just sketched.
- **Cross-reference:** Reconcile with §19.13’s threshold discussion and §19.18’s $p=10^{-3}$ ratio rather than repeating an unqualified 1%.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A familiar benchmark helps, but “standard” hides too many standards.

### Realistic noise “drops sometimes by 2× or more” (line 266, first subtlety closing)

- **Unsupported scalar claim:** Correlations, leakage, and crosstalk can lower a threshold modestly, create an error floor, alter scaling, or under sufficiently nonlocal/adversarial behavior eliminate the threshold assumptions entirely. There is no generic factor of two.
- **Can also improve with structure:** Biased or heralded-erasure noise exploited by tailored codes/decoders can raise thresholds substantially. “More realistic” is not synonymous with “uniformly worse.”
- **Metric issue:** An effective threshold under a multiparameter hardware noise model may be a boundary/surface, not one rescaled $p$.
- **Evidence:** Give matched studies for one correlation/leakage model if retaining a numerical factor; otherwise state the qualitative risk.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Concrete degradation sounds useful but is false precision without a model.

### Whole-construction dependence (line 266, second subtlety)

- **Strong point:** Threshold is jointly determined by code, syndrome circuit/gadgets, decoder, logical operations, architecture/connectivity, and noise.
- **Magic-state nuance:** A memory/Clifford QEC threshold can be defined without a magic-state protocol. A universal fault-tolerant architecture additionally needs injection/distillation/cultivation below its own acceptance/error conditions; this need not set the same threshold.
- **Hardware scheduling:** Hook-error orientation, parallel gates, idles, reset/measurement duration, leakage removal, and routing are part of the construction.
- **Terminology:** “The threshold” should always be indexed by the construction/model or accompanied by assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** This systems view is exactly the corrective to headline threshold numbers.

### Asymptotic nature (line 266, third subtlety opening)

- **Correct:** Threshold theorems prove scalable asymptotic suppression; they do not promise favorable constants at the first few code sizes.
- **Pseudothreshold/finite crossover:** Small codes can improve at physical error above or fail to improve below the asymptotic threshold depending on gadget balance. Introduce finite-size crossings explicitly.
- **Practical sufficiency:** Being below threshold only says increasing resources can help; useful logical error, qubit count, runtime, and error floors remain separate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The asymptotic-versus-useful distinction is a crucial dose of realism.

### “Three decades” and experimental crossing (line 266, closing)

- **Chronology needs an origin:** Three decades from Shor’s 1995 code/early threshold proofs to 2024 is reasonable rhetoric, but name the starting milestone.
- **“Crossed the line decisively” overstates scope:** Google’s 2023 distance-3/5 work gave an early modest scaling signal; the 2024 Willow work showed stronger below-threshold surface-code **memory** scaling through distance 7. Neither experimentally establishes arbitrarily long universal fault-tolerant computation or all theorem assumptions.
- **Other platforms/milestones:** Bosonic break-even, trapped-ion logical gates, neutral-atom codes, erasure correction, and code-switching offer different notions of “crossing.” Avoid crowning one universal line without metric.
- **Date conventions:** Earlier work was a 2022 preprint/2023 journal paper; Willow was online 2024/Nature 2025. Use bibliographic dates consistently.
- **Better claim:** “Finite devices have now demonstrated below-threshold memory scaling over several distances, a necessary but far from sufficient condition for theorem-scale computation.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The historical payoff is powerful; restraint makes the milestone more credible.

### Informal theorem blockquote (line 268, first sentence)

- **Useful recap:** The blockquote gives readers a memorable version after the derivation.
- **Carry the missing assumptions:** Add local/bounded-strength noise and a suitable fault-tolerant scheme; “physical error rate per operation” alone repeats the theorem’s biggest omission.
- **Overhead denominator:** “Polylog overhead per logical qubit and per logical gate” is ambiguous because total-error allocation depends on overall circuit size. Say multiplicative overhead polylogarithmic in $L/\varepsilon$ for the chosen construction.
- **Logical rate:** Replace “logical error rate can be made” by “overall simulation error can be made” or define the per-location rate whose union bound yields total error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A boxed takeaway is effective if it is safe to remember verbatim.

### “Above threshold, larger codes make things worse” (line 268, closing)
