- **Useful asymptotic intuition, false universal monotonicity:** Above the asymptotic threshold for a fixed family/decoder/model, increasing distance eventually fails to suppress logical error and often worsens it. Finite-size curves can be nonmonotonic and cross at pseudothresholds.
- **Threshold theorem does not prove the converse:** A theorem guaranteeing success below a sufficient bound does not imply impossibility above that proved bound. Numerical critical thresholds for a fixed scheme have a different status.
- **“Errors introduced faster than corrected” heuristic:** Decoding is not necessarily a temporal service queue; failure arises because likely error chains/classes become logically ambiguous. Rephrase as intuition, not mechanism.
- **Alternative scheme:** Being above one construction’s threshold does not preclude switching code, decoder, noise tailoring, or gadgets with a higher threshold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The reversal is memorable, but its theorem/converse distinction is important.

### §19.19 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The distance-3 concatenation recurrence gives a compact, genuinely illuminating explanation of double-exponential suppression and polylogarithmic overhead.
- **Highest-priority theorem repair:** State explicit local-noise/correlation assumptions, distinguish noise probability from general noise strength, and frame this as one representative accuracy-threshold theorem rather than a universal scalar criterion.
- **Highest-priority derivation repair:** Rename circuit size $L$ to avoid collision with the $T$ gate; consistently require $p_\ell\lesssim\varepsilon/L$; derive $\ell=O(\log\log(L/\varepsilon))$ and identify each overhead metric.
- **Highest-priority empirical repair:** Separate rigorous threshold bounds, simulated ~1% circuit thresholds, finite experimental below-threshold memory scaling, and realization of arbitrarily long universal fault tolerance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The theorem and recurrence are among the book’s most entertaining technical ideas; the current simplifications mainly risk teaching an invalid converse and an assumption-free “magic number.”

## Chapter 19, §19.20 — Fault-Tolerant Gates (lines 270–282)

### Heading and scope (line 270)

- **Natural progression:** After memory, thresholds, and resource costs, the chapter correctly turns to computation on protected data.
- **Beyond unitary gates:** Fault-tolerant computation also needs state preparation, measurement, reset, syndrome extraction, transport, classical feed-forward, and code conversion. The heading is fine if the opening acknowledges these operations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Manipulating information without destroying its protection is an inherently strong question.

### “Encoding is only half” opening (line 272, first sentence)

- **Effective motivation:** The sentence cleanly distinguishes passive/active storage from protected computation.
- **Encoding itself must be fault tolerant:** A naive encoding circuit can propagate a single fault into a correlated logical error; state injection and verified preparation are part of the same problem. “Preparing and storing encoded states is only part” is safer.
- **Error correction is ongoing:** Logical gates are interleaved with or integrated into QEC cycles; the two halves are not independent stages.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The pivot is concise and creates immediate tension.

### Definition of fault-tolerant implementation (line 272, second sentence)

- **Good core intuition:** One physical fault should not spread into an uncorrectable pattern or logical failure.
- **Not sufficient as a full definition:** Fault-tolerant gadgets must handle both incoming errors and new faults. Standard criteria bound output errors when the input contains up to $s$ errors and the gadget contains up to $r$ faults with $r+s$ within the code’s correction capability.
- **Higher-distance scaling:** For a distance-$d=2t+1$ construction, up to $t$ suitably local faults should not cause logical failure, not only one fault.
- **Logical error may occur without propagation:** A single fault at an unprotected measurement/feed-forward/injection location could directly flip a logical outcome even if it never spreads spatially; verification and repeated measurement matter.
- **Fault model:** “Physical error” should be a fault at a circuit location under the threshold theorem’s local-noise assumptions, not just a pre-existing Pauli on one data qubit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The one-fault rule is memorable, but a slightly richer criterion avoids becoming a misconception.

### Transversal-gate definition (line 274, opening)

- **Core definition:** A transversal operation partitions physical subsystems so that no component couples two subsystems belonging to the same code block; for multiple blocks, each component may couple corresponding positions across blocks.
- **“Same gate” is unnecessarily restrictive:** A transversal logical operation can apply different one-qubit gates $U_i$ at different coordinates, permutations, or coordinate-wise multi-block gates. Bipartite $S/S^\dagger$ patterns are an immediate example.
- **Block length:** Corresponding-qubit pairwise gates assume compatible block structures; more general transversal partitions need not be literal identical index pairs.
- **Physical implementation:** Simultaneous execution is not required by the algebraic definition, though scheduling faults and idle errors affect practical fault tolerance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The vertical-across-blocks image is elegant and would benefit greatly from a two-block diagram.

### Why transversality limits error spread (line 274, middle-to-closing)

- **Correct within-block principle:** Since no elementary component couples two subsystems of the same block, one component fault cannot create errors on multiple coordinates within that block.
- **Two-block nuance:** A faulty pairwise gate can create one error in each participating block; this remains correctable if each block’s error budget permits it.
- **Pre-existing propagation:** A CNOT propagates control $X$ to target and target $Z$ to control, so an existing error can spread *between* blocks even though it does not multiply within one block.
- **Leakage/crosstalk caveat:** A physical pair gate may produce correlated leakage or crosstalk beyond its formal support. Transversality is automatically spread-limiting only under the assumed local fault model.
- **Temporal repetition:** A persistent faulty/leaked qubit can affect later operations and rounds; leakage-reduction and error correction remain needed.
- **“Automatically fault-tolerant” too absolute:** Transversality supplies a key propagation property; state preparation, measurement, correction, decoding, and gadget composition must also satisfy fault-tolerance criteria.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The geometric reason is wonderfully intuitive; realistic exceptions make the engineering more interesting.

### Code dependence (line 276, opening)

- **Correct organizing fact:** Transversal logical gates arise from a code’s algebraic/geometric symmetries and differ sharply among families.
- **Representative versus exhaustive:** The listed physical layers should be verified as logical actions modulo stabilizers and phases; do not infer a gate merely because it preserves check type.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Comparing codes by the gates they make cheap is a strong design lens.

### Steane-code transversal Clifford claim (line 276, first example)

- **Correct for Steane with convention details:** Bitwise $H$, a uniform phase layer with $S$ or $S^\dagger$ logical orientation depending on conventions, and bitwise inter-block CNOT furnish encoded Clifford generators; logical Pauli representatives complete the group.
- **“Full Clifford group” notation:** The set $\{\bar H,\bar S,\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}\}$ is a generating set (with preparations/Paulis as appropriate), not the full group itself. Braces around three gates should be labeled “generated by.”
- **Single- versus multi-logical scope:** Steane encodes one qubit per block; multi-qubit Clifford circuits use multiple blocks and transversal CNOT plus single-block layers.
- **Physical phase:** Whether $S^{\otimes7}$ realizes logical $S$ or $S^\dagger$ follows weight/phase conventions. “Up to Pauli corrections” needs an explicit correction or should be omitted; a logical inverse is not merely an unspecified Pauli correction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Seeing a whole protected Clifford toolbox emerge from bitwise layers is gratifying.

### “Any self-dual CSS code” generalization (line 276)

- **False as stated:** Weak self-duality ($X$- and $Z$-check spaces matched) supports transversal Hadamard, and CSS structure supports bitwise inter-block CNOT, but transversal phase requires additional weight/divisibility structure (for example doubly-even conditions and appropriate logical action).
- **Terminology:** “Self-dual CSS” can mean different relationships between classical codes/check spaces; define weakly self-dual versus a classical self-dual code.
- **Counterexample risk:** Readers may infer $S^{\otimes n}$ preserves every CSS stabilizer whenever $H^{\otimes n}$ does; conjugation $X\mapsto Y=iXZ$ introduces support-dependent phases and $Z$ factors.
- **Repair:** State the Steane result specifically, then list the extra conditions required to generalize each gate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A broad symmetry rule would be elegant, but the incorrect breadth is pedagogically costly.

### Surface-code CNOT description (line 276, second example opening)

- **Terminology tension:** Algebraically, a bitwise CNOT between two identical CSS code blocks can be transversal if corresponding data qubits can interact. Two planar surface-code patches on strictly local 2D hardware generally cannot perform all those cross-patch pairings straightforwardly.
- **Usual implementation:** Lattice surgery implements logical parity measurements and CNOT with local operations; braiding/code deformation/teleportation are other routes. Calling ordinary patch CNOT “transversal-like” needs a defined circuit.
- **“Only” omits logical Paulis:** String/Pauli-frame operations and some measurement operations are fault tolerant too; the intended claim is about nontrivial Clifford unitary layers under a chosen layout.
- **Separate abstraction from hardware:** Say what is transversal at the abstract code-block level versus geometrically local in a planar architecture.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The algebra-versus-layout distinction is exactly the kind of subtle tradeoff readers enjoy.

### Surface-code $\bar H$ and $\bar S$ routes (line 276, second example closing)

- **Overcompressed alternatives:** Logical $H$ can be realized through transversal physical $H$ followed by patch rotation/relabeling/code deformation, or through surgery/teleportation protocols; logical $S$ often uses an injected/distilled phase resource or dedicated twist/surgery construction. They should not be bundled as identical procedures.
- **“Fold-and-rotate” needs definition/citation:** Fold-transversal Clifford proposals use nonlocal pairings/folded layouts; rotation may refer to swapping rough/smooth boundaries. The compound phrase is not standard enough to stand unexplained.
- **Lattice surgery is a primitive family:** It chiefly measures joint logical Pauli parities; a gate circuit also needs ancilla patches, feed-forward/Pauli frames, and $O(d)$ rounds.
- **Architecture dependence:** Fast transversal/folded operations trade extra connectivity and decoder complexity for time; recent work on decoding across transversal surface-code Clifford gates reinforces that this is not a settled one-line taxonomy.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Patch gymnastics are visually compelling; a figure or circuit would make this a highlight.

### 3D color-code transversal $T$ statement (line 276, final example)

- **Construction-specific:** Certain three-dimensional color/code variants (including tetrahedral/3D color-code or related Reed–Muller structures) admit transversal third-level logical gates such as $T$ or CCZ, with the exact layer and logical action depending on lattice, boundaries, and convention.
- **Eastin–Knill setup:** Do not imply the same fixed code has a universal transversal Clifford+$T$ set. A code with transversal $T$ generally lacks some complementary transversal Clifford operation; code switching/gauge fixing can combine capabilities.
- **“Third dimension is the obstacle” too singular:** Check weight, syndrome circuits, boundaries, decoding, connectivity, fabrication, code switching, and finite-size overhead are obstacles; 3D geometric embedding is only one.
- **Virtual/nonlocal realization:** A 3D code complex can be emulated with nonlocal connectivity or measurement-based constructions, so physical three-dimensional hardware is not a strict logical prerequisite—overhead is the issue.
- **Cross-section consistency:** Carry over §19.14’s Eastin–Knill and code-switching qualifications rather than restoring the unqualified claim here.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A third spatial dimension unlocking a higher-hierarchy gate is extremely engaging when paired with the no-go constraint.

### Eastin–Knill transition (line 278)

- **Strong dramatic pause:** Giving the theorem its own short paragraph effectively signals a fundamental limitation.
- **“Unavoidable” scope:** The obstruction applies to exact QEC with the relevant local-error-detection condition and transversal unitary gate set. Approximate codes, code switching, pieceable fault tolerance, measurements, and changing code blocks navigate around—not violate—the theorem.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** This is excellent pacing.

### Eastin–Knill theorem hypothesis (line 280, first sentence)

- **Missing essential hypothesis:** “Non-trivial code space” alone is insufficient. The original theorem assumes the code can detect arbitrary errors on each single physical subsystem (equivalently, exact correction of a single-subsystem erasure in the relevant setting). A distance-1/unencoded code can have a nontrivial space and universal one-qubit gates.
- **Finite-dimensional/exact setting:** State finite physical subsystems and exact error detection/transversal unitaries. Approximate Eastin–Knill tradeoffs permit approximate correction/universality with nonzero error.
- **Multiple blocks:** Define transversal partitions when gates act across several encoded blocks; universality may involve encoded multi-qubit gates.
- **Primary statement checked 2026-07-23:** Eastin and Knill’s abstract states precisely that detection of arbitrary error on any single physical subsystem is incompatible with a universal transversal encoded gate set: [Restrictions on Transversal Encoded Quantum Gate Sets](https://www.nist.gov/publications/restrictions-transversal-encoded-quantum-gate-sets).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The theorem is powerful; the correct hypothesis teaches why error protection and continuous logical symmetry conflict.

### “Equivalently, any stabilizer code has a finite transversal group” (line 280, second sentence)

- **Not presented as a justified equivalence:** The original Eastin–Knill theorem is general and rules out universality under an error-detection condition. Finiteness/classification of transversal logical groups for stabilizer/additive codes involves added structure/results; cite it as a strengthening/corollary under stated assumptions, not casually “equivalently.”
- **Distance-1 exception:** “Any stabilizer code” includes trivial/unprotected stabilizer encodings unless restricted; those do not satisfy the needed single-subsystem detection condition.
- **Modulo phases and trivial actions:** A physical transversal group may contain continuous phases or operations acting trivially on the code. The finite statement must concern induced nontrivial logical operations modulo global phase/kernel.
- **Closure issue:** A finite set of available transversal gates and the group it generates are different if products cease to be transversal under the chosen block partition; define the object.
- **Dense subgroup target:** Universal $k$-logical-qubit unitary computation concerns density in $PU(2^k)$/$SU(2^k)$ up to global phase, usually with entangling gates across blocks. The current single expression hides those conventions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The finite-versus-dense contrast is striking but mathematically too compressed.

### Cake metaphor and universality gap (line 282, opening)

- **Effective plain-language summary:** It makes the tradeoff memorable after a formal theorem.
- **Slight logical precision:** The theorem forbids a universal set composed entirely of transversal encoded gates for one fixed exact code; it does not require the missing resource itself to be a gate on that same code.
- **Alternatives:** Magic-state injection/distillation, code switching/gauge fixing, pieceable fault tolerance, teleportation, lattice surgery, braiding, and measurement-based schemes can supply missing operations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The metaphor is familiar but lands well here.

### “For surface and color codes” magic-state generalization (line 282, middle)

- **Too broad for color codes:** Standard 2D color codes may use magic states for non-Clifford gates, but 3D/gauge color-code proposals can use transversal non-Cliffords plus code switching/gauge fixing. The previous paragraph itself highlighted this alternative.
- **Surface-code mainstream:** Magic-state injection plus distillation/cultivation and teleportation is a leading surface-code route, though alternative non-Clifford schemes exist.
- **Distillation versus injection:** Distillation produces a higher-fidelity resource from noisy resource states using Clifford operations; gate teleportation/injection consumes the output to enact the logical gate. Keep the stages distinct.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Turning a special state into computational fuel is a great idea; family-specific routes make it richer.

### Magic-state definition and gate teleportation (line 282)

- **Define the state:** Give a convention such as $|T\rangle=T|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$; “non-stabilizer” alone includes many states not directly usable for a $T$ injection.
- **Protocol sketch:** A joint Clifford parity interaction/measurement, measurement, and conditional Clifford/Pauli-frame correction consumes the ancilla and applies $T$ (convention-dependent). Calling this simply “teleport” without a circuit can feel magical.
- **Why distill:** Raw preparation error must be below a protocol threshold, Clifford/QEC operations also fail, and output infidelity must meet the algorithmic allocation.
- **Terminology:** Magic-state injection and gate teleportation overlap in usage; establish the book’s chosen names consistently with Chapter 8.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** State-as-fuel is one of fault tolerance’s most entertaining concepts and deserves a tiny circuit.

### “Each $T$ costs one magic state” (line 282, late)

- **Correct for basic $|T\rangle$ injection:** One successful standard injection consumes one suitable encoded $|T\rangle$ resource, with conditional correction.
- **Not universal accounting:** Distillation consumes many noisy input states per accepted output; failures/postselection add expected cost. Catalysis, phase-gradient states, synthesized rotations, CCZ/Toffoli resources, and batched protocols change the one-to-one gate accounting.
- **$T$ versus arbitrary rotations:** Clifford+$T$ synthesis approximates rotations with a $T$ count dependent on precision; algorithms expressed natively with Toffolis/CCZs may be cheaper under different factories.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A consumable unit cost is memorable, provided the factory input cost is not hidden.

### “Entire overhead reduces to $T$-count” closing claim (line 282)

- **Strongly false absolute:** Total fault-tolerant resources also include logical data qubits, memory cycles, Clifford operations, syndrome extraction, routing, measurements, feed-forward, decoder latency, state preparation, factory footprint, and algorithmic/synthesis errors.
- **$T$-depth and parallelism:** Runtime/number of factories depends on the $T$-depth and width/consumption profile, not only total count. Two circuits with equal $T$ count can require radically different peak qubits and duration.
- **Factory cost is nonlinear:** Target output error, raw injection error, protocol levels, acceptance probability, code distance, and throughput determine cost per state.
- **When $T$ count is useful:** In a Clifford+$T$ cost model where Clifford operations are much cheaper, $T$ count is an important proxy for non-Clifford spacetime volume—but never the entire overhead.
- **Chapter 8 continuity:** Ensure Chapter 8 distinguishes $T$ count, $T$ depth, synthesis precision, and Toffoli/CCZ counts before relying on that cross-reference.
- **Better close:** “Non-Clifford resource production often dominates and makes $T$ count/$T$ depth central optimization metrics, alongside data-block and routing costs.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The dramatic reduction to one number is seductive; explaining why it is only a proxy yields a more useful design lesson.

### §19.20 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The progression from error propagation to transversal gates, code-dependent gate sets, Eastin–Knill, and magic-state fuel is exceptionally well structured and narratively strong.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Replace “any self-dual CSS code has full transversal Clifford” with gate-specific algebraic conditions; state Eastin–Knill’s single-subsystem-error-detection hypothesis; and separate the original theorem from stabilizer-group finiteness claims.
- **Highest-priority fault-tolerance repair:** Define transversal operations without “same gate,” explain one-error-per-block propagation for multi-block gates, and make clear that transversality is a spread-limiting property within a complete gadget—not automatic end-to-end fault tolerance.
- **Highest-priority resource repair:** Distinguish injection from distillation, acknowledge color-code switching alternatives, and demote $T$ count from “entire overhead” to one central proxy alongside $T$ depth, data blocks, routing, and QEC cycles.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** This is among the chapter’s most entertaining sections; its conceptual arc is excellent, while a handful of attractive absolutes create the main technical risk.

## Chapter 19, §19.21 — Magic State Distillation (lines 284–300)

### Heading and relation to prior section (line 284)

- **Direct payoff:** The heading immediately answers Eastin–Knill’s missing-resource question.
- **Scope split:** The section covers three distinct stages—magic-state definition, gate injection/teleportation, and state purification/factory architecture. Subheadings would keep these from collapsing into one “magic” mechanism.
- **Cross-reference:** §19.20 already introduces the same state and consumption claim; either shorten that preview or let this section be the first formal definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** “Magic state” is memorable terminology and the resource-theory idea is intrinsically engaging.

### Magic-state definition (line 286, opening)

- **Useful qubit/stabilizer intuition:** A pure state outside the set of stabilizer states is a magic resource relative to Clifford/stabilizer operations.
- **Orbit wording is malformed:** Say “outside the Clifford orbit of computational-basis stabilizer states,” not “outside the orbit of any Pauli–Clifford operator on the computational basis.” The Pauli group is contained in the Clifford group, and an operator acts on states rather than “on the computational basis” as one object.
- **Multi-qubit stabilizer set:** Stabilizer states are Clifford images of $|0\rangle^{\otimes n}$ (equivalently suitable computational-basis states), including entangled stabilizer states; make the $n$-qubit scope clear.
- **Mixed-state nuance:** For mixed states, magic means lying outside the convex stabilizer polytope/resource-free set, not merely outside a pure-state orbit.
- **Resource theory dependence:** “Magic” is relative to a free-operation set (usually stabilizer operations). Different qudit dimensions/gate sets have subtleties such as bound magic/non-distillable regions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The outside-the-stabilizer-world picture is compelling; one clean resource-theory sentence would sharpen it.

### “Any non-stabilizer consumed implements a non-Clifford gate” implication (line 286, closing)

- **Too broad as a definition:** A resource state must have a specified injection gadget and sufficient quality; not every arbitrary non-stabilizer state directly implements a desired non-Clifford gate with one copy and a fixed stabilizer circuit.
- **Pure-qubit versus general setting:** For pure single-qubit states, non-stabilizerness is closely tied to universality/distillability under suitable protocols; mixed, correlated, qudit, and restricted-operation cases are more nuanced.
- **Determinism:** Injection may require measurement-dependent corrections, postselection, or yield a probabilistic gate; “implements” should include those conditions.
- **Better definition:** A magic state is a non-free ancillary state that, together with stabilizer operations, enables operations/computation unavailable to stabilizer circuits alone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The fuel metaphor works best when it is not mistaken for a one-state/one-arbitrary-gate law.

### Canonical $|T\rangle$ formula (lines 286–290)

- **Correct convention:** With $T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})$ and $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, the displayed state follows.
- **Convention warning:** Literature also uses $|A\rangle$, $|T\rangle$, or a different Bloch-axis “$T$-type” state; declare this book’s convention and retain it in Chapter 8.
- **Normalization/phase:** The expression is normalized and global phase is fixed naturally.
- **Why non-stabilizer:** Its Bloch vector lies at $45^\circ$ in the equatorial plane rather than on a Pauli eigenaxis; a one-line observation would make “magic” visible.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** A simple, beautiful state formula gives the abstract resource a face.

### Eigenstate statement (line 292, opening)

- **Correct:** Since $X|+\rangle=|+\rangle$, $|T\rangle=T|+\rangle$ is the $+1$ eigenstate of $TXT^\dagger=(X+Y)/\sqrt2$ under the stated convention.
- **State the eigenvalue/operator:** Writing “the +1 eigenstate of $(X+Y)/\sqrt2$” is more informative than leaving the conjugated operator unevaluated.
- **Not a Pauli stabilizer:** This observable is Hermitian/unitary but not a Pauli; contrasting it with Pauli-eigenstate stabilizers explains why the state is non-stabilizer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The rotated-axis interpretation adds geometric elegance.

### One-state $T$-gate injection (line 292, middle)

- **Correct resource count for the basic ideal gadget:** One $|T\rangle$, one CNOT, one single-qubit measurement, and a measurement-conditioned Clifford correction can implement $T$ on an arbitrary input.
- **Circuit orientation essential:** Specify which wire controls the CNOT, which wire is measured, and in which basis. For one common convention, data controls the magic ancilla, the ancilla is measured in $Z$, and one outcome yields $T|\psi\rangle$ while the other yields $T^\dagger|\psi\rangle$ up to phase, repaired by $S$.
- **Correction convention:** Depending on circuit/state orientation the conditional correction may be $S$, $S^\dagger$, or tracked in a Clifford frame. A diagram removes ambiguity.
- **Encoded implementation:** The CNOT, measurement, resource, and feed-forward must themselves be fault tolerant; “lifted” is not automatic when code blocks/layouts differ.
- **Latency:** Conditional correction can often be frame-tracked, but later non-Clifford operations may require resolved feed-forward.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10.** This deserves a circuit figure; it is the section’s most satisfying operational trick.

### Gate-teleportation attribution (line 292, closing)

- **Attribution likely imprecise:** Nielsen and Chuang are a canonical textbook source, but gate teleportation/fault-tolerant constructions are historically associated with work such as Gottesman–Chuang. Distinguish textbook exposition from original attribution.
- **Terminology:** Some authors call this state injection rather than full gate teleportation. Establish the vocabulary and cross-reference Chapter 8’s circuit.
- **Citation:** Cite the actual circuit/protocol being drawn, not an undifferentiated textbook name.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Historical anchoring helps, but only if it is accurate.

### Imperfect encoded-state motivation (line 294, first two sentences)

- **Correct core problem:** An imperfect resource injected into data transfers some resource-state error into the logical operation.
- **Preparation path too narrow:** Practical raw states may be injected from an unencoded physical state, prepared in a small code and grown/switched, or produced by a noisy logical circuit—not only “on encoded qubits.”
- **Circuit errors matter:** Faults in injection CNOT, measurement, correction, storage, transport, and distillation Clifford operations also contribute; output error is not simply inherited input $p$.
- **Error channel dependence:** Different Pauli/coherent components propagate differently through injection; twirling/randomization may justify a scalar input error model at a cost.
- **Detected failure:** Some protocols flag/reject bad states rather than silently “inflict” every error, so distinguish accepted-output logical error from rejection probability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The dangerous-fuel premise gives distillation a clear reason to exist.

### Distillation definition and “exponential” suppression (line 294, closing)

- **Correct high-level transformation:** Stabilizer operations consume several noisy resource states and, conditional on acceptance, output fewer states of higher fidelity when inputs lie below a protocol threshold.
- **Not unconditional:** Above the distillation threshold or with adversarial/correlated/coherent errors, fidelity may not improve; success probability and output correlations matter.
- **Exponential in what:** For fixed small input error, concatenated levels give an error exponent growing exponentially in level (for 15-to-1, roughly $p^{3^\ell}$), often called doubly exponential suppression in level. State the variable.
- **No physical cooling analogy:** “Distillation” is postselected error detection/resource concentration, not purification of arbitrary noise without assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Turning many dirty resources into one clean one is intuitive and dramatic.

### 15-to-1 provenance and code (line 296, opening)

- **Canonical attribution:** Bravyi and Kitaev’s 2005 work is the correct foundational source for magic-state distillation and the 15-to-1 family; cite [Universal quantum computation with ideal Clifford gates and noisy ancillas](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0403025).
- **Code naming:** Identify the quantum $[[15,1,3]]$ punctured Reed–Muller code and what transversal/non-Clifford property underlies the protocol.
- **Triorthogonal chronology:** Calling the code triorthogonal is mathematically reasonable retrospectively, but the general triorthogonal-matrix framework/term is associated with later Bravyi–Haah work. Avoid implying Bravyi–Kitaev introduced that terminology.
- **“Not the Steane code”:** Helpful because both are Reed–Muller/CSS-related in reader memory, but explain the crucial difference (15-qubit code supports the relevant transversal $T$-type operation) rather than only negating.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The code-within-the-factory connection rewards the chapter’s earlier coding theory.

### Input-error model (line 296, first sentence middle)

- **Scalar $p$ requires definition:** After Clifford twirling into the $|T\rangle,|T^\perp\rangle$ basis, model each input independently as the orthogonal erroneous state with probability $p$.
- **Logical versus physical:** These are already prepared logical resource states in an idealized logical-level protocol; factory circuit locations may still be noisy in a surface-code implementation.
- **Independence is strong:** Common preparation circuitry can correlate inputs, and coherent errors can invalidate the simple cubic coefficient unless randomized/handled.
- **Twirling overhead:** Twirling is a randomized stabilizer operation and can discard exploitable bias/coherence; say whether it is performed physically or assumed analytically.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The model is manageable, but readers need to see what “an error with probability $p$” actually means for a state.

### Postselection and acceptance (line 296, middle)

- **Correctly acknowledged:** Explicitly saying acceptance is below one and belongs in the budget is excellent.
- **Quantify leading behavior:** Under the simple independent input model, give the acceptance polynomial or at least its leading $1-15p+O(p^2)$ behavior, subject to protocol convention.
- **Conditional output:** $35p^3+O(p^4)$ is the error probability conditioned on acceptance; place “conditional” directly beside the formula.
- **Expected consumption:** Expected raw-state cost includes failed batches and potentially correlated factory restarts, not merely 15.
- **Circuit-level rejects:** Noisy stabilizer measurements/Clifford gates introduce additional rejection and accepted logical faults; ideal-code analysis is only a first layer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Rejected batches add useful realism and a casino-like tension to factory throughput.

### Cubic output formula (line 296)

- **Correct leading coefficient under the stated idealized model:** The canonical 15-to-1 protocol has leading accepted-output error $35p^3$ for independent, appropriately twirled input errors.
- **Why cubic:** Distance three detects one- and two-error patterns relevant to the protocol, while 35 weight-three patterns contribute undetected logical error; this one sentence would explain the coefficient.
- **Denominator:** Because the result is conditional on acceptance, the exact expression is a ratio of bad accepted probability to total acceptance probability; $O(p^4)$ hides that expansion.
- **Output convention:** Logical Clifford corrections may map the output to the manuscript’s chosen $|T\rangle$ convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** “Fifteen noisy copies turn linear error into cubic error” is an excellent quantitative payoff.

### Cascading $\ell$ levels (line 296, late)

- **Exponent structure right at leading order:** Repeated cubic suppression produces an input exponent $3^\ell$.
- **Coefficient omitted:** With recurrence $p_{j+1}\approx35p_j^3$, the leading coefficient is $35^{(3^\ell-1)/2}p^{3^\ell}$, not simply $p^{3^\ell}$. Suppressing it is fine only with explicit asymptotic shorthand and sufficiently subthreshold $p$.
- **Cost is more than $15^\ell$:** That is the ideal number of level-0 inputs per final attempt. Expected consumption includes acceptance at every level; physical spacetime also includes Clifford circuits, syndrome extraction, routing/storage, and potentially different code distances by level.
- **“Cost in qubits” inaccurate:** Inputs can be produced serially/reused in space; $15^\ell$ is a state/input-count scaling. Peak qubits, qubit-rounds, and latency depend on scheduling.
- **Asymptotic perspective:** Since output log-infidelity grows as $3^\ell$ while inputs grow as $15^\ell$, ideal input overhead is a power of $\log(1/\varepsilon)$, not exponential in desired precision. “Exponential cost” without its variable sounds worse than the threshold theorem’s polylog story.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The tower of factories is vivid; distinguishing level, target error, peak space, and spacetime makes it genuinely useful.

### “Better protocols” taxonomy and 5–10× claim (line 296, closing)

- **Block-code direction is real:** Higher-output triorthogonal/block protocols can improve yield and asymptotic/logical-level overhead; cite a specific family and target regime.
- **Cultivation is not merely a better distillation block:** Magic-state cultivation combines small-code error detection, growth/grafting/code conversion, postselection, and QEC; distinguish it from concatenating noisy input magic states through a conventional distillation code.
- **Date wording:** The cultivation preprint appeared in 2024; “introduced 2024” should cite its authors and publication status.
- **Unsupported universal factor:** Improvements depend on physical noise, target infidelity, footprint versus qubit-round objective, cycle assumptions, and baseline factory. The cited cultivation work estimates roughly an order-of-magnitude qubit-round improvement over selected prior methods in a specified regime, not a universal 5–10×.
- **Not identical asymptotic structure:** Cultivation/error-detecting growth and postselection can have different finite-size and scaling behavior from $15^\ell$ concatenation; “same” must identify the intended broad many-noisy-resources-to-fewer-clean-resources principle only.
- **Primary context:** [Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17595) estimates about an order-of-magnitude fewer qubit-rounds for selected targets/noise and should be described with those assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A rapidly improving factory ecosystem is compelling; a comparison table would outperform a floating factor.

### 2026 cost anchor: distance 17 and 5,000–20,000 qubit-cycles (line 298, opening)

- **No identifiable source/configuration:** Distance alone does not determine factory cost. Name protocol, physical error model, target output infidelity, raw-state error, acceptance, layout, cycle definition, decoder, and throughput.
- **Unit terminology:** “Physical-qubit-cycles” should be defined as the sum over occupied physical qubits per QEC cycle (often qubit-rounds). Peak physical qubits and elapsed cycles are separately important.
- **One $T$ gate versus one accepted state:** Include injection/consumption circuit and conditional correction, not just state factory output, if calling it full gate cost.
- **Range precision:** A fourfold range without configurations is neither a reproducible estimate nor a robust order of magnitude.
- **As-of framing:** “In 2026 numbers” needs named sources dated through a stated cutoff; otherwise it ages immediately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A price per $T$ would be valuable, but this one currently feels invented from nowhere.

### Comparison to Clifford cost (line 298, middle)

- **Acknowledged scenario dependence is good:** The parenthetical correctly notices the fatal ambiguity.
- **But headline precedes its retraction:** “Tens to hundreds” remains asserted despite admitting no universal denominator. A transversal single-qubit Clifford, Pauli-frame update, lattice-surgery CNOT, and logical measurement have radically different spacetime costs.
- **Distance consistency:** Compare both operations at matched logical error, physical noise, and architecture; factories may use multiple distances internally.
- **Cultivation counterpoint:** The named cultivation work’s title/claim targets roughly CNOT-like qubit-round cost in selected regimes, directly showing why a universal tens-to-hundreds ratio is unsafe.
- **Throughput:** Amortized state cost at a saturated pipeline differs from startup/latency and peak factory footprint.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** “Magic is expensive” is a good lesson; a concrete CNOT-versus-$T$ pair would make it honest.

### Algorithm bottleneck claim (line 298, late)

- **Often true in Clifford+$T$ surface-code estimates:** Non-Clifford resource production can dominate peak area or critical-path time for high-throughput circuits.
- **“Gated entirely” is false absolute:** $T$ depth/dependency, measurement feed-forward, routing, logical memory, decoder/reaction latency, arithmetic depth, and classical postprocessing can bottleneck instead.
- **Algorithm examples too broad:** Shor-resource designs have specific Toffoli/CCZ profiles; quantum chemistry algorithms vary widely by representation and can be limited by data loading, logical width, or rotation synthesis. “Most large-scale circuits” has no defined population.
- **Metric distinction:** High $T$ count drives total resource-state consumption; high $T$ depth/peak rate drives runtime/factory count.
- **Grammar/style:** Use “Shor’s algorithm” or “factoring circuits,” not “Shor’s” as a standalone plural-like item.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The factory bottleneck gives algorithms an industrial feel, but dependency graphs are more interesting than total counts alone.

### “More factory qubits than algorithm qubits” (line 298, closing)

- **Scenario, not general law:** Fast-runtime designs provision many parallel factories and may be factory-area dominated; space-minimized designs reuse fewer factories and run longer.
- **Recent counterpressure:** The 2025 sub-million-qubit RSA preprint explicitly reduces factory allocation through cultivation and trades for longer runtime, while yoked storage changes the data-block side. This illustrates a Pareto frontier, not a stable majority rule.
- **Denominator ambiguity:** “Algorithm’s own logical qubits” are logical, while “more qubits on factories” appears physical. Compare physical footprint allocated to factory versus data regions.
- **Need paired figures:** Quote factory peak area, data peak area, output rate, and runtime from one architecture.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Factories outweighing the computer is a memorable image; it needs an actual floor plan.

### Recent-progress list structure (line 300)

- **Useful attempt at frontier synthesis:** Organizing improvement paths into protocol, code primitive, and hybrid checking directions is sensible.
- **Categories are unstable/overlapping:** Cultivation is encoded primitive plus postselected preparation; code switching can itself produce magic states; catalysis/recycling modifies resource conversion. Use named protocols rather than improvised bins.
- **Temporal status:** Mark theory, simulation, and experiment separately as of 2026.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The field feels alive, but clearer taxonomy would make the frontier legible.

### “Smaller distillation,” cultivation, and “T-state recycling” (line 300, item a)

- **Cultivation classification:** It is better described as an alternative fault-tolerant preparation protocol, not simply a smaller distillation circuit.
- **“Recycling” undefined:** Some protocols use catalysis, reusable catalyst states, synthillation, or resource-state conversions. State exactly which protocol and whether a $T$ state is consumed, returned approximately, or replaced by another resource.
- **No-cloning/resource monotone caution:** “Recycling” can sound like a consumed magic state is freely recovered. Explain catalyst degradation/correlation/error accumulation and net resource balance.
- **Lower overhead requires metric:** Peak qubits, qubit-rounds, raw injections, latency, and accepted-state cost can rank protocols differently.
- **Experimental update opportunity:** A late-2025 preprint reports cultivation on a superconducting processor; if included, distinguish demonstrated small-scale ingredients/output bounds from scalable factory performance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Reusing magical fuel is an irresistible hook, so vague naming is especially risky.

### Direct $T$ through 3D/gauge color codes (line 300, item b)

- **Broad research direction correct:** Certain 3D color-code-like constructions admit transversal non-Clifford gates, and gauge fixing/code switching can combine complementary gate sets.
- **Not “direct” without protocol:** State preparation, syndrome extraction, switching/gauge fixing, decoding, and return/transfer to the computational code carry faults and overhead.
- **Dimension jumping needs definition:** Dimensional code switching can relate 2D and 3D code structures, but not every 3D/gauge color-code proposal uses the same mechanism.
- **Eastin–Knill consistency:** No one exact static code gains a universal transversal gate set; complementary Clifford operations may be supplied in another code/gauge.
- **“Sidestepping distillation”:** These schemes can avoid conventional magic-state distillation in principle, but may instead use costly code conversion or can be deployed as alternative magic-state preparation factories. Compare total spacetime/error, not labels.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Changing code/dimension to manufacture a gate is one of the field’s most inventive ideas.

### “Magic state mixing” item (line 300, item c)

- **Nonstandard/undefined category:** The phrase does not identify a recognized protocol sufficiently for review. It could refer to mixing resource types, parity checking, correlated multi-output factories, heterogeneous fidelity allocation, or randomized mixtures.
- **“Low-fidelity factories” odd:** Factories generally *produce* improved states from raw inputs; combining factories with on-the-fly checking needs a concrete circuit and error model.
- **Potential intended ideas:** If the intent is magic-state parity checking, catalysis, block protocols, or just-in-time distillation, name and cite the method.
- **Error correlations:** Combining outputs can introduce correlated failures; on-the-fly checks may trade rejection/latency for fidelity.
- **Recommendation:** Remove until a specific primary protocol and quantitative benefit are supplied.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The phrase sounds intriguing but leaves no mental model.

### “Below 10× by 2030” open question (line 300, closing)

- **Undefined ratio:** Ten times which Clifford operation, at what distance/target error, under what protocol, physical noise, and resource metric? The preceding parenthetical already concedes these choices.
- **Unattributed popularity claim:** “One of the most-watched” needs survey/roadmap evidence or should be presented as the author’s chosen engineering question.
- **Arbitrary deadline:** 2030 is a forecast marker without a named roadmap and will date the book.
- **Existing claimed regime conflict:** Cultivation already claims roughly CNOT-like physical-gate/qubit-round cost in selected simulations, so “whether below 10×” may already be yes under some definitions and no under others.
- **Better open question:** “For a specified application and hardware noise model, which non-Clifford strategy minimizes the Pareto frontier of peak qubits, runtime, and total spacetime at the required accepted error?”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** A race against a deadline is dramatic, but an ill-defined finish line cannot sustain scrutiny.

### §19.21 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section gives a clear resource state, an elegant consumption gadget, and a memorable 15-to-1 cubic-suppression calculation, then connects it to system bottlenecks.
- **Highest-priority definition repair:** Define stabilizer states/free operations cleanly; do not equate every non-stabilizer state with a direct one-copy gate resource; draw the injection circuit and state correction convention.
- **Highest-priority quantitative repair:** Make $35p^3$ conditional on acceptance and the twirled independent-input model; carry recurrence coefficients, acceptance, circuit faults, and qubit-round versus peak-space accounting through concatenated levels.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Replace the unsourced distance-17/5,000–20,000 and tens-to-hundreds claims with one named factory layout; treat cultivation, catalysis/recycling, code switching, and any “mixing” as distinct cited protocols.
- **Highest-priority forecast repair:** Remove the undefined 10×-by-2030 scoreboard and compare non-Clifford strategies on a stated error/space/time Pareto frontier.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Magic-state distillation is one of the book’s most entertaining topics; the canonical core is strong, while the contemporary cost/trend paragraphs need substantial evidence discipline.

## Chapter 19, §19.22 — Lattice Surgery (lines 302–315)

### Heading and conceptual role (line 302)

- **Well-placed implementation topic:** After transversal gates and magic resources, lattice surgery shows how protected patches actually interact on local hardware.
- **Term deserves intuition:** “Surgery” refers to changing measured checks/boundaries so code surfaces merge and split, not physically cutting qubits. A one-sentence metaphor would orient newcomers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The geometric, almost tactile name creates immediate curiosity.

### Surface-code operational primitive claim (line 304, opening)

- **Major/common primitive, not singular:** Lattice surgery is a leading way to implement multi-patch logical Pauli measurements and gates in planar surface-code architectures. Braiding, code deformation, transversal/folded layers, teleportation, twist-based operations, and modular links are alternatives.
- **Primitive is measurement:** The core operation is fault-tolerant joint logical Pauli measurement through temporary check changes; CNOT and other logical gates are compiled from those measurements plus preparations/readouts/frame updates.
- **Architecture dependence:** “Used” should be “commonly proposed/used” unless the book adopts a specific architecture for all subsequent resource estimates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Joint measurement as computation is a strong conceptual turn.

### Historical attribution (line 304)

- **Correct journal attribution/year:** Horsman, Fowler, Devitt, and Van Meter published the lattice-surgery proposal in 2012 in *New Journal of Physics*; the arXiv preprint dates to 2011.
- **Primary citation checked 2026-07-23:** [Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery](https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/14/12/123011).
- **“Introduced” scope:** Earlier code-deformation/joint-measurement ideas form context, but this named four-author work is the standard source for the lattice-surgery method/term.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Naming the inventors gives a crisp historical anchor without slowing the section.

### Claimed replacement for transversal CNOT (line 304, middle)

- **Wrong requirement for transversal CNOT:** A bitwise CNOT between two surface-code blocks requires pairwise interactions between corresponding data qubits. Merely placing two planar patches adjacent along one edge does not provide those pairings; one may need stacked layers, folding, transport, SWAPs, or nonlocal couplers.
- **Original motivation:** Lattice surgery avoids transversal inter-block operations that would destroy strict 2D nearest-neighbor locality, replacing them with boundary-local check measurements.
- **Orientation nuance:** Logical boundary type/orientation matters for which parity can be measured locally, but “identically oriented” is not the defining obstacle to an abstract transversal CNOT.
- **Quotation marks:** Quoting “transversal CNOT between patches” suggests a known primitive, but the physical-access model should be stated explicitly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The local-boundary-versus-all-to-all-pairing contrast is more visually compelling than the current adjacency explanation.

### “Any two patches sharing a boundary” (line 304, closing)

- **Too permissive:** The shared boundaries must have compatible type, adequate length/effective distance, suitable seam checks, available measurement ancillas/connectivity, and a fault-tolerant schedule.
- **Adjacency remains required locally:** Basic lattice surgery does not connect arbitrary distant patches; routing space, intermediate/bus ancillas, patch motion, teleportation, or long-range surgery is needed.
- **Geometry:** Corners, twists, unequal distances, irregular defects, and rotated/unrotated layouts change the seam and decoder.
- **Better formulation:** “Two compatibly oriented adjacent boundaries can be coupled locally; routing layouts extend this to nonadjacent logical qubits at additional space/time cost.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Flexibility is real, but constraints make the floor-plan puzzle interesting.

### “Two primitives” list setup (line 306)

- **Good organization:** Merge and split are intuitive verbs and naturally support the figure.
- **Not operationally complete:** Preparation, destructive logical measurement, boundary deformation/extension, Pauli-frame updates, and classical decoding are also primitives in common tile/lattice-surgery calculi.
- **Inverse misconception risk:** A split is not a unitary inverse of a merge; both are measurements/isometries with random outcomes and frame information.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The two-verb grammar is easy to remember.

### Merge geometry and code-space change (line 308, opening)

- **Broad picture correct:** Temporarily replacing boundary checks with checks across a seam joins the syndrome complex and projects the two logical qubits onto a joint-parity eigenspace.
- **“Single larger patch” hides logical dimension:** Two one-logical-qubit patches carry two logical qubits; after a parity measurement/merge the merged code typically carries one remaining logical degree of freedom plus a classical parity outcome. State that information mapping explicitly.
- **Check schedule:** One stops/modifies some original boundary checks and begins measuring new seam-crossing generators/gauge checks; it is not simply additive measurement of all old and new stabilizers if they anticommute.
- **Ancilla/seam qubits:** Depending on layout, intervening data/measurement qubits are initialized and incorporated. “Without physically moving” is true for a provisioned adjacent layout, not a claim of zero new hardware/action.
- **Decoder:** Faulty seam outcomes are decoded jointly with pre-merge/post-merge syndrome history.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Watching two code spaces become one is fascinating; explaining where the second logical degree goes is essential.

### Joint logical parity and boundary convention (line 308, middle)

- **Convention appears consistent:** Under the stated convention, a smooth-boundary merge measures $\bar Z_1\bar Z_2$ and a rough-boundary merge measures $\bar X_1\bar X_2$; many sources use the rough/XX and smooth/ZZ pairing.
- **Convention dependence:** Boundary naming and patch orientation vary across literature. The promised §19.12 convention note must define which anyon/string terminates on which boundary and match the figure.
- **Outcome construction:** The logical parity is inferred from the product of appropriate new boundary-check outcomes (and decoded syndrome history), not from any one stabilizer.
- **Projection:** The measurement entangles/projectively correlates patches; it does not by itself apply a deterministic two-qubit unitary.
- **Sign/frame:** The random $\pm1$ outcome becomes classical frame information used in later corrections.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** A global logical parity emerging from local seam checks is the section’s key delight.

### $O(d)$ seam-measurement rounds (line 308, closing)

- **Common fault-tolerant scaling:** Measuring the new seam for roughly $d$ rounds is a standard way to preserve a distance-$d$ spacetime measurement against faulty syndrome outcomes.
- **Not exact/universal:** Required/optimal rounds depend on patch distances, seam length/separation, temporal boundaries, measurement versus data error rates, decoder, and target failure. Recent analyses find optima can be above or below $d$ in specified phenomenological models.
- **Circuit distance:** Explain that repetition protects the measurement outcome against time-like fault chains; the static patch distance alone does not impose exactly $d$.
- **Constant factors:** Initialization, final readout/split, and boundary re-stabilization add cycles. “$O(d)$” is asymptotically safe but not a resource estimate.
- **Primary contemporary nuance:** [Characterization of errors in a CNOT between surface code patches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05337) studies round-count optimization and explicitly notes that “usually $d$” is not always optimal.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The seam becoming a spacetime object is intellectually rich and deserves one diagram dimension.

### Split description (line 309)

- **Substantially incomplete:** A split generally measures a line/region of data qubits in an appropriate basis, stops merged checks, reinstates separate boundary checks, and processes those data/check outcomes to define two daughter-code states and Pauli frames.
- **Not merely stopping checks:** Simply ceasing boundary measurements does not initialize the new boundaries, disentangle the code, or determine the logical-state map fault tolerantly.
- **Rough versus smooth split:** The measured basis and mapping of logical $X/Z$ observables differ; parallel the merge list’s convention detail.
- **State transformation:** Splitting one logical patch creates correlated/entangled logical outputs depending on the input and measurement outcomes; it does not clone an arbitrary logical state.
- **Distance danger:** The original 2012 source explicitly notes that splitting geometry can reduce code distance (for example, a symmetric split of a square can halve it). Patch dimensions must be provisioned so daughter patches retain target distance.
- **Rounds/decoder:** Post-split syndrome history and measurement errors require fault-tolerant decoding, not an instantaneous topology switch.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Splitting is just as interesting as merging, but the current one-line description makes it look trivial.

### Lattice-surgery figure and alt text (line 311)

- **Deferred asset review:** `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/lattice-surgery.svg` must be inspected later both structurally and visually under the SVG pass; no judgment about drawn seams, labels, color contrast, or geometry is made from the Markdown reference alone.
- **Alt-text scope too narrow:** It describes only a $Z_1Z_2$ example while the prose introduces both smooth/ZZ and rough/XX merges. This is acceptable if the figure explicitly labels itself as one example.
- **Outcome language:** “Pauli correction conditioned on the outcome” should clarify whether the correction is physically applied or recorded in a Pauli frame.
- **Round wording:** “Measured for d rounds” inherits the convention/model qualification above.
- **Accessibility:** The alt text describes the sequence well but should state which boundaries meet and how the parity is inferred, if length permits.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10 anticipated from concept; visual score deferred.** A merge–measure–split sequence is exactly where a diagram materially helps.

### Logical-CNOT measurement sequence (line 313, first sentence)

- **Correct measurement-based skeleton:** An ancilla logical patch, a control–ancilla $ZZ$ measurement, an ancilla–target $XX$ measurement, and an ancilla logical measurement implement a teleported CNOT up to outcome-dependent Pauli corrections.
- **Ancilla preparation omitted:** The ancilla must be initialized in the appropriate logical state (commonly $|+_L\rangle$ for the stated convention/sequence); include this as part of the circuit.
- **Ancilla final basis:** Name the final logical measurement basis and give the correction truth table or Pauli-frame update; “measure out” and “three outcomes” are not enough to verify the CNOT.
- **Merge-and-split equivalence:** Each joint parity measurement can be implemented through merge/split, but modern lattice-surgery descriptions may treat multi-patch Pauli measurement directly; do not imply a unique physical sequence.
- **Outcome correlations:** Corrections depend on combinations of outcomes and convention; a circuit diagram would prevent sign/control-target errors.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10.** A deterministic entangling gate assembled entirely from parity measurements is a standout idea.

### CNOT time and ancilla area (line 313, second sentence)

- **Asymptotic scaling plausible:** A constant number of distance-preserving parity-measurement stages, each $O(d)$ cycles, gives total $O(d)$ time; the constant may be several $d$-round windows.
- **Do not confuse one stage with whole gate:** Resource tables need explicit time steps/cycles for initialization, both joint measurements, final measurement, and re-stabilization, including opportunities for overlap.
- **Comparable-size patch condition:** To avoid the ancilla becoming a low-distance fault path, its relevant dimensions/boundaries must support the target distance; area is then commonly $O(d^2)$ but elongated routing ancillas can cost $O(Ld)$.
- **Layout/routing:** Control, ancilla, and target must expose compatible boundaries; spare routing tiles can dominate peak area.
- **Correlated logical channel:** Joint operations can introduce correlated control/target errors and should be decoded/benchmarked as a gate, not two independent memories.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The clean area–time scaling is useful, but constants are the architecture.

### Logical-$T$ via lattice surgery (line 313, final sentence)

- **Correct broad principle:** An encoded magic resource can be coupled to data through a joint logical measurement, then measured/consumed with feed-forward to inject a non-Clifford gate.
- **“Similar” hides the key circuit:** Specify resource convention, joint Pauli measurement, ancilla final measurement, and conditional $S$/Clifford-frame correction, matching §19.21’s injection circuit.
- **Factory versus injection:** Preparing a high-fidelity encoded $|T\rangle$ patch is the expensive prior stage; surgery is the consumption interface, not the distillation protocol itself.
- **Adaptive correction:** A conditional $S$ is not always a Pauli-frame update; architectures may use selective teleportation/auto-corrected injection to manage time-critical feed-forward.
- **Distance matching:** Resource patch, surgery seam, and injection circuit need error budgets/distances appropriate to the target gate error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Magic fuel entering through a geometric seam is a strong unification of the last two sections.

### “Standard model” status (line 315, opening)

- **Fair as a mainstream abstraction:** Lattice-surgery/tile models dominate many surface-code resource estimates because they preserve planar locality and make space–time tradeoffs explicit.
- **Avoid monopoly language:** Other surface-code computational models—braiding holes/defects, twist networks, transversal/folded operations, measurement-based/foliated schemes—remain relevant.
- **Theory versus deployment:** Experimental demonstrations exist at small scale, but “standard model” mostly describes architectural/resource-estimation practice, not a single standardized hardware protocol.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Showing how a research primitive became a planning language gives satisfying context.

### Patch categories and spacetime accounting (line 315, middle)

- **Useful architectural vocabulary:** Data/logical, ancilla/routing, and factory patches are common conceptual allocations.
- **Categories overlap:** A “logical patch” is generic; factory and ancilla patches are also logical/code patches with roles that change over time.
- **Incorrect cost reduction:** Spacetime cost is not merely the sum/count of merge-and-split operations. One tracks occupied tiles/patch area over time, number/duration of code cycles, operations, idling/storage, routing, and factory throughput—often tile-time or qubit-round volume.
- **Physical gates still matter:** Threshold/logical-error models and hardware schedules compile each syndrome cycle into native gates, measurement, reset, and idles. Logical abstraction postpones rather than eliminates physical-gate accounting.
- **Parallelism:** A sum of operations ignores concurrent surgeries; critical path determines runtime, while integrated occupied area determines volume.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Patch economics is engaging when space and time remain two axes.

### Litinski 2019 and logical-block diagrams (line 315, closing)

- **Correct influential reference:** Daniel Litinski’s *A Game of Surface Codes* was published in *Quantum* in 2019 and presents a tile-based lattice-surgery framework with explicit space–time tradeoffs.
- **Primary citation checked 2026-07-23:** [A Game of Surface Codes: Large-Scale Quantum Computing with Lattice Surgery](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2019-03-05-128/).
- **Exact abstraction:** A tile occupies $O(d^2)$ physical qubits and a time step conventionally corresponds to $d$ code cycles in the model; layouts are compared using tiles and time steps, not “logical block diagrams” alone.
- **Compilation claim too automatic:** Mapping arbitrary circuits to Pauli measurements/lattice surgery requires Clifford+$T$/Pauli-rotation compilation, routing, scheduling, magic-state supply, and dependency handling. The paper supplies a framework/strategies, not a push-button direct compiler guarantee.
- **Singular citation grammar:** “Architecture papers (Litinski 2019…) layer this” makes one paper stand for a literature. Either cite multiple works or write “Litinski’s 2019 paper develops…”
- **Space–time examples:** The source explicitly demonstrates trading more qubits for shorter runtime; mentioning that Pareto lesson would connect back to §19.18/§19.21.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The idea of playing surface-code computation as a tile game is exceptionally accessible and deserves a small example.

### §19.22 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section turns global logical parity into a local boundary operation and then assembles CNOT/$T$ injection from measurements, giving the chapter a concrete computational geometry.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Explain why transversal blockwise CNOT conflicts with planar pairwise access; restrict “any shared boundary” to compatible distance-preserving seams; and replace the split-as-stopping-checks description with its data measurement, boundary restoration, decoding, and state map.
- **Highest-priority circuit repair:** Add ancilla initialization/final basis and the three-outcome correction table for CNOT; give the exact magic-state injection measurement/correction rather than “similar.”
- **Highest-priority accounting repair:** Define tile, time step, code cycle, qubit-round, peak area, and critical path; do not replace physical-resource accounting with a count of merge/split labels.
- **Asset follow-up:** Structurally and visually inspect `lattice-surgery.svg` during the dedicated SVG pass and reconcile its boundary/parity/round/correction labels with the fixed prose.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Lattice surgery is exceptionally visual and conceptually satisfying; the current section has excellent bones but underdescribes split and feed-forward mechanics.

## Chapter 19, §19.23 — Logical Gate Implementation (lines 317–340)

### Heading and promised synthesis (line 317)

- **Appropriate capstone:** The section promises to integrate compilation, code choice, layout, gates, decoding, tooling, experiments, and exercises.
- **Heading narrower than content:** Much of the section concerns full-stack architecture, resource estimation, and experimental outlook, not only logical-gate implementation. “From algorithm to fault-tolerant hardware” would better match.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A full-stack walkthrough is exactly the payoff readers need after many specialized components.

### Full-pipeline opening (line 319)

- **Strong integrative intent:** Mapping abstract algorithms to encoded physical operations is the right systems perspective.
- **Pipeline is not always Clifford+$T$:** Architectures may target Clifford+CCZ/Toffoli, Pauli rotations, native logical gates, code switching, bosonic operations, measurement-based primitives, or analog blocks. Present Clifford+$T$ surface-code compilation as one representative stack.
- **“Physical gates on encoded blocks” omits measurements/control:** Fault-tolerant execution is a schedule of gates, preparations, measurements, resets, idles/transport, decoding, and classical feed-forward.
- **Feedback loops:** Code/layout/noise/resource choices feed back into algorithm synthesis; this is not a purely one-way pipeline.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Seeing the abstraction ladder collapse toward hardware is highly satisfying.

### Step 1: compile with Solovay–Kitaev/GridSynth (line 321)

- **Two unlike methods:** Solovay–Kitaev is a general theorem/algorithm for approximating gates from a dense finite set with polylog sequence length but poor practical exponents/constants. Grid-based number-theoretic Clifford+$T$ synthesis (for suitable rotations/unitaries and conventions) is much more specialized and efficient.
- **Slash is misleading:** “Solovay–Kitaev / gridsynth” makes them interchangeable implementations. Explain when each applies and favor modern exact/near-optimal synthesis for Clifford+$T$ rotations.
- **Tool naming/capitalization:** Identify the exact GridSynth implementation/algorithm and current maintenance source; a generic lower-case “gridsynth” may be read as a package guarantee.
- **Input structure:** Algorithms often contain Toffoli/CCZs, arbitrary rotations, oracle arithmetic, measurements, and classical controls—not a list of arbitrary one-qubit unitaries.
- **Approximation budget:** Rotation-synthesis error consumes part of the algorithm’s total error budget; choosing precision changes $T$ count and must happen jointly with QEC allocation.
- **Ancilla-assisted alternatives:** Repeat-until-success, phase-gradient/catalysis, table lookup, native CCZ resources, and arithmetic redesign can change non-Clifford costs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Compilation is a rich optimization story; the slash currently turns it into a button press.

### Step 1 output as explicit $T$ count (line 321, closing)

- **Necessary but insufficient output:** Also retain logical qubit width, Clifford count/depth, measurements, feed-forward dependencies, $T$ depth, per-time-layer $T$ demand, rotation error, and connectivity graph.
- **Factory sizing:** Total $T$ count governs consumption/volume; $T$ depth and temporal demand govern throughput, factory parallelism, and runtime.
- **Circuit optimization:** Commuting Pauli rotations, cancellation, phase-polynomial synthesis, and Toffoli/CCZ grouping should occur before treating $T$ count as fixed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A visible non-Clifford budget gives readers a concrete optimization target.

### Step 2: choose a code (line 322)

- **Choice is preempted:** The colon immediately says “surface code,” so this is selecting a surface-code distance rather than choosing among codes.
- **Broader criteria:** Code choice depends on hardware connectivity/native gates, noise bias/erasures/leakage, measurement speed, decoder, logical gate set, block rate, qubit movement, fabrication defects, target workload, and maturity—not only $p$ and $p_L$.
- **Code concatenation/hybrids:** Bosonic inner codes plus surface/outer codes, heterogeneous data/factory codes, and code switching may be optimal.
- **Distance is not one global scalar:** $X/Z$ distances may differ; data blocks, factories, buses, distillation levels, and different computation phases can use different distances.
- **Error-budget unit:** Target logical error must be per memory cycle/operation and allocated over total spacetime; §19.16 does not yet provide a reliable one-number derivation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Code–hardware co-design is exciting; presenting a foregone choice loses that richness.

### Step 3: logical layout (line 323, first clause)

- **Correct for a planar surface-code architecture:** Data patches must be placed with compatible boundaries, routing/ancilla space, measurement access, and connectivity.
- **Physical lattice is not abstract:** Defects/yield, coupler topology, control/readout wiring, crosstalk constraints, chip/module boundaries, and communication links affect placement.
- **Dynamic layout:** Patches can expand, contract, move/deform, switch roles, or be teleported; layout is a spacetime schedule, not one static placement.
- **Missing storage/workspace:** Algorithm ancillas, routing buses, spare patches, injection ports, logical measurements, and defect margin need space beyond data and factories.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The floor-plan problem makes fault tolerance feel like real architecture.

### Step 3: factories “scaled to $T$-count throughput” (line 323, closing)

- **Conflated metrics:** $T$ count is a total quantity; throughput is states per unit time. Required factory count depends on the $T$-consumption profile/$T$ depth, target runtime, protocol latency/yield, buffering, and accepted output rate.
- **Space–time trade:** A single factory can eventually supply a large count; parallel factories shorten runtime at higher peak qubit cost.
- **Reliability:** Factory distance/levels and rejection/retry policy depend on output error allocation, not only demand.
- **Routing:** Moving resource states (or consuming via remote parity measurements) can throttle delivery even if production rate is sufficient.
- **Better wording:** “Size and schedule factories to the non-Clifford demand profile and chosen space–time point.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Factory logistics are compelling; count-versus-throughput is the key lesson.

### Step 4: Clifford operations (line 324)

- **Broad split is useful:** Some codes exploit transversal Clifford layers; planar surface-code architectures use measurement/code-deformation techniques.
- **Steane-style imprecision:** Name the code properties and gates, given §19.20’s false “any self-dual CSS” generalization.
- **Lattice surgery does not implement every Clifford identically:** It naturally implements joint logical Pauli measurements/CNOT-like operations; logical Paulis can be frame updates, and $H/S$ may use patch rotation, twist/surgery, teleportation, or resource states.
- **Compiler representation:** Clifford frames can be tracked classically, reducing physical layers; distinction from Pauli frame matters after logical $H/S$.
- **Fault tolerance:** Each primitive needs scheduling/decoding and a logical error model; “where possible” should be quantified in the selected architecture.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Cheap symmetry gates versus geometric surgery gives a useful code comparison.

### Step 5: $T$ gates (line 325)

- **Mainstream surface-code route:** High-fidelity magic-state preparation followed by measurement-based injection through surgery is a standard architecture.
- **Not every $T$ is separately distilled:** Factories distill/cultivate a stream/batch of resource states; each standard injection consumes an accepted output, but protocols can produce multiple outputs or use CCZ/catalytic resources.
- **Alternative routes:** Code switching/gauge fixing, transversal gates in complementary codes, pieceable gates, and other resource states should remain visible.
- **Distance/protocol heterogeneity:** Factory levels and injection interface may use distinct distances and error budgets.
- **Terminology:** “Teleporting each $T$” should align with §19.21’s exact injection circuit and correction convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The factory-to-data supply chain is a strong synthesis of the chapter.

### Step 6: real-time decoding (line 326, opening)

- **Essential requirement:** Syndrome must be processed quickly enough that frames/feed-forward needed by future operations are available without unbounded backlog.
- **Not one final step:** Decoding runs continuously and co-designs the syndrome schedule; compilation/layout provide detector models/observable mappings before execution.
- **Latency versus throughput:** A decoder can have high average throughput but excessive tail latency, or process in windows with delayed commitment. Both matter.
- **Correlated gates:** Surgery/code deformation changes detectors and logical observables dynamically; decoder state must cross operation boundaries.
- **Classical hardware:** Bandwidth, memory, power, reliability, calibration updates, and integration at cryogenic/room-temperature layers are missing resources.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The hidden classical supercomputer racing the QPU is an excellent systems story.

### Pauli-frame explanation (line 326, closing)

- **Correct core:** Known Pauli corrections can often be stored as classical frame bits and propagated through Clifford circuits rather than physically applied.
- **“Corrections only apply physically when they propagate” is backwards/unclear:** Propagation through Clifford gates is exactly when frames are efficiently updated classically. Trouble arises before non-Clifford gates, non-Pauli-sensitive measurements, or when hardware/control conventions require an adaptive basis/correction.
- **Measurement reinterpretation:** Final Pauli measurements can often absorb the frame by flipping/interpreting outcomes, so no physical correction is ever needed.
- **Clifford frames:** Injection schemes may generate conditional $S$ corrections, motivating a richer Clifford frame or selective teleportation; not everything fits a Pauli register.
- **Bookkeeping spelling/style:** “Bookkeeping” is normally one word; more importantly, define one example such as tracking an $X$ through CNOT.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Virtual corrections feel clever and practical; the propagation sentence needs inversion.

### Claim that modern tooling automates steps 3–6 (line 328, opening)

- **Major overstatement:** No listed combination universally automates physical layout, fault-tolerant logical synthesis, factory design, detector construction, real-time decoder deployment, Pauli-frame control, and hardware execution from arbitrary algorithms.
