- **Good canonical entry:** Resonantly driven two-level dynamics is the natural first control model.
- **Stack wording:** The actual bottom includes DAC reconstruction, mixers, transfer functions, fields, device coupling, and open-system physics; Rabi dynamics is the effective-model layer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Turning a waveform into motion on the Bloch sphere is immediately satisfying.

### Bloch-vector arc (line 13)

- **Correct ideal picture:** Under a resonant fixed-phase drive, the state rotates about an equatorial axis.
- **State restriction:** A Bloch vector represents a two-level density matrix; leakage into $|2\rangle$ makes the visualization incomplete.
- **Detuning:** Off-resonance adds a $Z$ component, tilting the rotation axis rather than only changing an equatorial arc.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The geometric picture is one of the section’s strengths.

### Speed set by amplitude (line 13)

- **Correct in calibrated linear/RWA regime:** Rabi rate is proportional to the field matrix element and amplitude.
- **Nonlinearity:** Mixer compression, amplifier saturation, device response, AC Stark shifts, strong-drive/Bloch–Siegert effects, and amplitude-dependent leakage break simple proportionality.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** An intuitive control knob with useful caveats.

### Axis set by drive phase (line 13)

- **Correct for resonant $X/Y$ control:** Carrier phase chooses an equatorial rotation axis relative to the chosen frame.
- **Reference-frame requirement:** Phase has meaning relative to local oscillator, qubit frame, prior virtual-$Z$ updates, and channel skew; absolute hardware phase is not enough.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Phase becoming geometric direction is elegant.

### “The gate is that arc” (line 13)

- **Effective but slightly state-centric:** A gate is the unitary/channel acting on all input states; one Bloch-vector trajectory illustrates it but does not define process fidelity or leakage.
- **Improvement:** Say the pulse generates the rotation whose action moves every Bloch vector accordingly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Strong phrase, worth preserving with precision.

### Exception parenthesis (line 13)

- **Good anti-absolutism:** Virtual $Z$, adiabatic, geometric, and composite gates usefully delimit the canonical model.
- **Placement:** The long parenthesis interrupts the opening momentum; a short note/callout after the core derivation would read better.
- **Missing examples:** Measurement-induced gates and frame-tracked Pauli corrections further show that not all “gates” are physical rotations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Interesting exceptions, densely packed.

### Virtual $Z$ takes “zero physical time” (line 13)

- **Common abstraction, needs qualification:** A phase/frame update has no pulse duration and can be compiled instantly, but controller instruction/metadata processing is not literally zero wall-clock time; scheduling may absorb it.
- **Physical effect:** It changes phases of subsequent drives/measurement interpretation rather than rotating the qubit through a standalone Hamiltonian.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A gate done by changing the coordinate system is highly engaging.

### Rotating-frame/two-level/RWA setup (line 13)

- **Good explicit assumptions:** The sentence responsibly names the approximations.
- **Conventions missing:** State $hbar=1$, whether the frame rotates at carrier frequency, angular-frequency units, and the sign definition of detuning.
- **Strong-drive limitation:** RWA and two-level approximations are precisely stressed by fast pulses, so connect them to the shaping motivation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Assumption transparency is rewarding for technical readers.

### Displayed driven Hamiltonian (lines 15–17)

- **Standard form under conventions:** $\frac12\Omega(\cos\phi X+\sin\phi Y)+\frac12\Delta Z$ is valid up to detuning/frame/sign definitions.
- **Time dependence:** The equation writes $\phi(t)$ but constant $\Delta$; rapidly changing phase is equivalent to frequency modulation and can contribute an effective detuning in a phase-tracking frame.
- **Units:** $Omega$ and $\Delta$ are angular frequencies; add $hbar$ if $H$ is energy rather than angular-frequency Hamiltonian.
- **Likely rendering defect:** Source uses doubled `\\,` before thin spaces. Replace with single `\,` and render-test; the same defect recurs in the time-ordered exponential.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Compact and central, provided conventions are visible.

### Rabi-frequency definition (line 19)

- **Correct:** $Omega(t)$ is the calibrated coupling/rotation rate, often proportional to envelope voltage over a limited regime.
- **Calibration distinction:** AWG amplitude is filtered/mixed/attenuated before becoming field amplitude; the proportionality constant is frequency-, channel-, and qubit-dependent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Connect the symbol to the real voltage chain.

### Drive phase definition (line 19)

- **Correct but frame-dependent:** State its reference oscillator/frame and whether IQ imbalance/skew has been calibrated.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Useful, slightly terse.

### Detuning definition (line 19)

- **Ambiguous sign:** “Between” does not say $Delta=\omega_q-\omega_d$ or $omega_d-\omega_q$; the displayed $+\Delta Z/2$ depends on that choice.
- **Dynamic reality:** Stark shifts, drift, chirps, and phase ramps can make effective detuning time-dependent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** A simple definition prevents later sign confusion.

### Gate as envelope/phase choice (line 19)

- **Correct optimal-control viewpoint:** Controls determine the propagator.
- **Incomplete control set:** Detuning/frequency, multiple quadratures/channels, flux/coupler controls, constraints, and system drift may also be optimized.
- **Open-system caveat:** Real evolution is a quantum channel, not exactly a unitary; target equality is ideal calibration intent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** “Draw a waveform, synthesize a unitary” is the section’s core fascination.

### Time-ordered exponential (line 19)

- **Correct general expression:** Time ordering is necessary when Hamiltonians at different times do not commute.
- **Missing $hbar$ convention:** Explicitly say $hbar=1$.
- **Global phase:** Good to state it is physically irrelevant for an isolated gate, though relative phases in controlled subspaces and frame conventions still matter.
- **Rendering:** The integral contains doubled `\\,dt`; repair.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Gives mathematical closure to pulse design.

### Square on-resonance Bloch “circle” (line 19)

- **Geometry wording:** For a generic initial state, the Bloch vector follows a circle around the rotation axis; for an eigenstate of the axis it does not move. “Traces a circle” is not universal.
- **Angular speed:** $Omega_0$ under the stated Hamiltonian and angular-frequency convention is correct.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Good visual after state qualification.

### $X_\pi$ duration $\pi/\Omega_0$ (line 19, closing)

- **Correct under resonance, constant phase $phi=0$, square amplitude, and stated factor-of-two convention.**
- **Calibration:** Hardware amplitude-to-$\Omega$ mapping and finite rise/fall alter naive duration; pulse area is the robust ideal relation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Clean derivation/payoff.

### “Square pulses ... operationally bad” (line 21)

- **Directionally right, overly categorical:** Square/rectangular pulses can be useful for calibration, bang-bang/fast control, and systems with large spectral separation; real electronics cannot make infinite-bandwidth edges anyway.
- **Improvement:** Say they are often spectrally inefficient and leakage/crosstalk prone in weakly anharmonic systems.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Strong transition, slightly theatrical.

### Abrupt edges and broadband Fourier content (line 21)

- **Correct:** A finite rectangular envelope produces sinc-like spectral sidelobes; smoother derivatives reduce high-frequency leakage.
- **Pedagogical opportunity:** Show time-domain square/Gaussian beside spectra, defining bandwidth–duration tradeoff.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Seeing sharp time edges become broad frequency tails is an excellent insight.

### Exciting transmon $|1\rangle\to|2\rangle$ (line 21)

- **Correct leakage mechanism:** Once amplitude occupies $|1\rangle$, drive spectral weight/coupling near $omega_{12}$ can populate $|2\rangle$.
- **Matrix elements:** Transmon ladder coupling strengths differ (approximately harmonic-oscillator scaling), so bandwidth alone is not the whole leakage probability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Direct connection between spectrum and leakage is strong.

### Anharmonicity $\alpha/2\pi\approx-200$ MHz (line 21)

- **Plausible representative value:** Chapter 20 used $-200$ to $-300$ MHz; the single $-200$ value should be marked example and made consistent.
- **Units/rendering:** Source again contains doubled `\\,` before `\mathrm{MHz}`; repair.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Concrete spectral separation helps.

### Spectator-qubit coupling (line 21)

- **Broadband spectral content can contribute:** But spectator errors also arise through microwave crosstalk, shared couplers, Stark shifts, frequency collisions, control-line leakage, and nonlinear mixing.
- **Improvement:** Separate direct spectral overlap from spatial/electrical crosstalk.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** One pulse disturbing neighbors makes control feel realistically crowded.

### Smooth-envelope list (line 21)

- **Representative:** Gaussian, raised-cosine, and sech are valid families.
- **Missing central technique:** DRAG/IQ-quadrature correction is standard for transmon leakage/phase error; merely smoothing one quadrature is not the full remedy.
- **Other methods:** Cosine-series, Slepian/DPSS, Blackman, optimized numerical pulses, Wah-Wah, echoed/composite and derivative-based shapes may matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** A list needs shape/spectrum plots to become memorable.

### Truncation and renormalized pulse area (line 21)

- **Correct only in restricted case:** For a resonant fixed-phase two-level drive, commuting Hamiltonians give rotation angle $\theta=\int\Omega(t)dt$. With detuning, time-varying phase, multilevel dynamics, Stark shifts, and transfer distortion, area alone does not guarantee target rotation.
- **Edge issue:** Truncation itself can reintroduce discontinuities unless endpoints/derivatives are sufficiently small or smoothly closed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Area-under-curve equals angle is satisfying when scoped.

### Typical Gaussian 20–60 ns (line 21)

- **Plausible transmon range:** Device, fidelity target, anharmonicity, drive power, and parallel/crosstalk conditions vary.
- **Current architecture diversity:** Some systems use cosine/DRAG or much faster/slower pulses; do not imply Gaussian is universal.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Concrete timing anchors the theory.

### Gaussian $\sigma$ near one quarter total length (line 21, closing)

- **Potential endpoint problem:** A total window of $4\sigma$ corresponds to truncation at roughly $\pm2\sigma$, where a Gaussian is still $e^{-2}\approx13.5\%$ of peak before baseline adjustment; many implementations use offset Gaussians, derivative constraints, or wider truncation.
- **Definition missing:** Is total duration $4\sigma$, pulse centered in window, and endpoint offset subtracted? Without convention the advice is not reproducible.
- **Improvement:** Give the exact formula including truncation, baseline subtraction, normalization, and DRAG quadrature.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Specific recipe is useful but presently underdefined.

### “For trapped ions story is similar in shape” (line 23)

- **Partly true:** Envelopes/phases shape spectral selectivity, robustness, Stark shifts, and motional closure.
- **Different objectives:** Ion pulses also manage optical phase, motional sidebands/modes, spontaneous scattering, beam pointing, Doppler effects, and composite/global addressing—not merely transmon leakage analogues.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Cross-platform analogy works when differences receive equal weight.

### Laser tuned to electronic or hyperfine transition (line 23)

- **Oversimplified:** Hyperfine gates are often two-photon Raman transitions with beat-note difference tuned to the splitting, or direct microwave/RF; optical qubits use direct narrow optical transitions.
- **Improvement:** Map encoding → carrier(s) → modulator → effective Hamiltonian.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The frequency-comb/beat-note story would be more engaging.

### Microsecond Raman hyperfine gates (line 23)

- **Plausible:** Representative single-qubit operations span a few to tens of microseconds depending on power/fidelity; microwave high-fidelity gates can also be microseconds to tens of microseconds.
- **Source example:** Recent $^{43}$Ca$^+$ work studies roughly 4.4–35 $\mu$s single-qubit gates; state protocol/benchmark if quoted.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Useful scale.

### Millisecond direct-optical transitions (line 23)

- **Misleading as representative:** Direct optical-qubit rotations are commonly microsecond-scale; a 2023 integrated-modulator experiment reports 5.5 and 11.6 $\mu$s gates. Millisecond durations may arise in weak-drive/special spectroscopy but should not define the architecture.
- **Possible confusion:** Metastable-state *lifetime* is around a second; do not convert narrow linewidth into necessarily millisecond coherent gates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **6.6/10.** The false scale contrast distorts the platform.

### Ion Hamiltonian reduces to driven two-level form (line 23)

- **Correct for isolated single-qubit carrier control under approximations:** But Raman schemes require adiabatic elimination and include differential Stark shifts/scattering; optical transitions include laser phase noise; motion may couple through Lamb–Dicke factors/sidebands.
- **Improvement:** State the effective Hamiltonian and the terms discarded.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Reusing one mathematical skeleton across platforms is powerful.

### Envelope/phase “live in the AOM” (line 23, closing)

- **Metaphorical and incomplete:** Electrical RF waveforms from DDS/AWG/RFSoC drive an AOM; diffraction controls optical amplitude/frequency/phase, while optical paths, AOM response, amplifiers, and laser lock also shape the field.
- **Alternatives:** EOMs, integrated photonic modulators, direct microwave electrodes, and electro-optic beam steering exist.
- **Not instead of AWG:** An AOM is often controlled *by* an AWG/DDS, so “rather than in a microwave AWG” creates a false opposition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The acoustic grating steering light is fascinating and deserves accurate explanation.

### §21.1 source-verification note (checked 2026-07-23)

- **Optical-ion gate-time counterexample:** *High-fidelity trapped-ion qubit operations with scalable photonic modulators* reports optical-qubit single-gate times of 5.5 $\mu$s with a Mach–Zehnder modulator and 11.6 $\mu$s with an AOM, contradicting milliseconds as the representative direct-optical scale: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41534-023-00737-1
- **Fast-ion breadth:** Trapped-ion entangling gates as short as 480 ns have been demonstrated in specialized low-fidelity/speed regimes, underscoring that gate type, method, and fidelity must accompany duration: https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06952

### §21.1 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It makes amplitude, phase, pulse area, Bloch rotation, and spectral leakage form a coherent introductory chain.
- **Highest-priority mathematical repair:** State $hbar$, angular units, detuning sign, frame convention, and the restricted conditions for the pulse-area rule.
- **Highest-priority content repair:** Add DRAG/quadrature control, transfer-function/predistortion effects, bandwidth–duration–leakage plots, and process/channel fidelity.
- **Highest-priority cross-platform repair:** Replace the false AOM-versus-AWG opposition and correct direct optical ion gate times.
- **Highest-priority rendering repair:** Fix repeated doubled backslashes in TeX and render-test every formula/unit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10 potential, 8.4/10 current.** Bloch geometry and Fourier leakage are excellent; omitted DRAG and inaccurate ion scale leave the lesson incomplete.

## Chapter 21, §21.2 — Microwave and RF Control (lines 25–31)

### Heading and RF/microwave boundary (line 25)

- **Useful scope:** It signals a move from effective Hamiltonian to classical signal chain.
- **Terminology:** RF and microwave bands overlap by convention; explain that low-frequency flux/control, IF, microwave qubit drive, and readout occupy different bands/functions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Concrete engineering layer, ready for a block diagram.

### “Across superconducting platforms” 3–8 GHz claim (line 27)

- **Contradicted by Chapter 20:** Conventional transmons commonly occupy roughly 3–8 GHz, but heavy fluxonium computational transitions may be 0.1–0.5 GHz; other superconducting qubits/readout/control transitions vary.
- **Improvement:** Say “Typical transmon $f_{01}$ values lie around 3–8 GHz” and separate qubit, readout-resonator, coupler, and higher-transition bands.
- **Notation/rendering:** Define $f_{01}=\omega_{01}/2\pi$; source again contains doubled `\\,` before units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** A frequency map would be more memorable than a range.

### Direct DAC generation is possible but bandwidth-hungry (line 27)

- **Broadly correct historically and currently:** Direct RF synthesis demands sample rate, analog bandwidth, ENOB/SFDR, memory/data throughput, filtering, and clock quality.
- **Current trend:** RF DACs/RFSoCs and direct digital synthesis increasingly generate multi-GHz signals directly; IQ mixing remains common but is not the only conventional path.
- **Improvement:** Compare direct-RF and heterodyne chains in a table: bandwidth, images, LO leakage, calibration, channel density, power, latency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The trade between digital speed and analog complexity is compelling.

### IQ upconversion as conventional path (line 27)

- **Correct representative architecture:** Two quadratures plus an LO synthesize arbitrary amplitude/phase around a carrier.
- **Architectural variants:** Homodyne/zero-IF, low-IF, single-sideband digital IF, direct RF, and channelized/multiplexed schemes differ.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Two slow waveforms steering one fast carrier is elegant.

### AWG produces $I$ and $Q$ “sidebanded” at a few-hundred-MHz IF (line 27)

- **Mixed terminology:** At zero IF, $I(t),Q(t)$ are complex baseband envelopes. At finite IF, the AWG digitally modulates them at $omega_{IF}$ before analog upconversion. Say which architecture is meant.
- **Range variability:** IF may be zero, tens/hundreds MHz, or higher depending on DAC/channelization/readout; “few hundred” is illustrative.
- **Control equations:** Give $I(t)=A(t)\cos(\omega_{IF}t+\phi)$ and $Q(t)=A(t)\sin(\omega_{IF}t+\phi)$ with sign convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** The phasor construction would be highly teachable with a diagram.

### Mixer “multiplies them against” LO (line 27)

- **Conceptually correct:** An IQ mixer combines multiplication with quadrature LO paths and summation, yielding upper/lower sidebands.
- **Imperfections:** DC offsets cause LO leakage; gain/phase imbalance leaves image; mixer nonlinearity creates spurs; LO phase noise transfers to the qubit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Frequency translation is satisfying when imperfections are shown in a spectrum.

### Output expression $\Omega(t)\cos(\omega_{LO}t+\phi(t))$ (line 27)

- **Inconsistent with finite IF prose:** If the AWG waveform is at $omega_{IF}$ and the upper sideband is selected, carrier is $omega_d=\omega_{LO}+\omega_{IF}$ (or lower with minus sign), so the expression needs $omega_d$, not bare $omega_{LO}$.
- **Amplitude units:** $Omega(t)$ earlier denotes Rabi angular frequency, but here it multiplies an RF cosine as though it were voltage/field amplitude. The transfer from voltage $V(t)$ to Rabi rate $Omega(t)$ must be separated.
- **Phase:** Include LO phase, IF/digital phase, mixer skew, cable delay, and qubit-frame convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Central equation, currently conflating control domains.

### “Arrives at qubit’s drive port” (line 27)

- **Too direct:** The signal passes filters, attenuators, cables, connectors, packaging, wirebonds/bumps, on-chip lines, reflections, and crosstalk; the qubit sees a local field through a coupling transfer function.
- **Drive port terminology:** A chip/channel has a drive line/port; the qubit itself is capacitively/inductively coupled, not necessarily a matched port.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The physical journey is precisely what the chapter should reveal.

### Mirror image at $\omega_{LO}-\omega_{IF}$ (line 27)

- **Correct for upper-sideband target:** Sign swaps if lower sideband is desired.
- **Other spurs:** LO feedthrough at $omega_{LO}$, higher mixing products, DAC images, harmonics, and intermodulation should be mentioned.
- **Impact:** Images can drive spectator qubits/transitions or corrupt multiplexed readout.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A ghost tone mirrored around the LO is memorable.

### Single-sideband/image-rejection calibration (line 27, closing)

- **Correct:** IQ amplitude/phase/DC calibration suppresses unwanted sideband and LO leakage.
- **Dynamic caveat:** Frequency-dependent imbalance and drift require calibration across bandwidth/time; digital predistortion may be needed.
- **Terminology:** An IQ mixer operated/calibrated for SSB is more precise than implying a distinct universal “single-sideband mixer.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Calibrating away a spectral mirror is a good engineering vignette.

### “Microwave engineering quietly governs the rest” (line 29)

- **Strong transition:** It conveys how invisible infrastructure controls fidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Excellent cadence and thesis.

### Drive line as 50-ohm transmission line end-to-end (line 29)

- **Overstatement:** Cables/connectors/instruments are designed near 50 $\Omega$, but chip launches, bond wires, package modes, coupling structures, filters, attenuators, and the qubit termination are not a perfectly matched 50-ohm load end-to-end.
- **Physical point:** The qubit is weakly coupled to a control line; it is not power-matched like a resistor, because that would strongly load/decohere it.
- **Improvement:** Say the classical feed network is designed around a 50-ohm environment up to an intentionally weak/reactive device coupling.
- **Rendering:** Doubled `\\,` appears before $\Omega$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Impedance matching becomes interesting when the endpoint exception is explained.

### Discontinuity reflects power and creates ripple (line 29)

- **Correct:** Reflection coefficient, standing waves, group delay, and multiple echoes distort amplitude/phase and can create long pulse tails.
- **Calibration nuance:** Predistortion can compensate a stable linear transfer function only within bandwidth/dynamic-range limits; drift/nonlinearity remain.
- **Improvement:** Give $Gamma=(Z_L-Z_0)/(Z_L+Z_0)$ and connect time-domain echo to frequency ripple.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** A cable mismatch echoing into a quantum gate is an excellent cross-layer lesson.

### Isolators/circulators protect from amplifier noise (line 29)

- **Correct for readout chains:** Nonreciprocal elements route outgoing readout toward the amplifier and attenuate amplifier backaction toward the device.
- **Placement clarity:** This is a readout-output chain, not “the rest” of the drive line; separate schematics.
- **Multiple stages:** Several isolators/circulators may be cascaded, with insertion loss degrading measurement efficiency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** One-way microwave traffic is intuitively appealing.

### Ferrite-based nonreciprocal three-port devices (line 29)

- **Taxonomy correction:** A circulator is typically three-port; an isolator is commonly a circulator with one port terminated, effectively a two-port component.
- **Operating requirements:** Ferrites, magnetic bias, bandwidth, insertion loss, isolation, power handling, and size matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Magnetic one-way routing is interesting; exact port distinction helps.

### “Bulky and lossy at millikelvin” (line 29)

- **Directionally correct:** Commercial ferrite components occupy substantial cryogenic volume and add insertion loss, magnetic fields, and integration constraints.
- **Loss tradeoff:** Loss before the first amplifier directly reduces measurement efficiency, yet isolation can improve qubit environment/readout stability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Protection itself consuming signal is a good tradeoff.

### “Newer designs increasingly replace them” on chip (line 29)

- **Premature deployment claim:** Josephson/kinetic-inductance nonreciprocal devices are active research and limited deployments; ferrite isolators remain standard in many systems.
- **Replacement criteria:** On-chip alternatives must meet bandwidth, isolation, insertion loss, saturation/dynamic range, pump leakage, noise, yield, magnetic compatibility, and multiplexing.
- **Improvement:** Say “seek to replace or reduce,” with dated demonstrated system examples.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Shrinking a ferrite can into a pumped superconducting circuit is exciting.

### Josephson/kinetic-inductance circulators and nonreciprocal parametric amplifiers (line 29)

- **Valid research categories:** But distinguish passive/magnetless circulators, directional amplifiers, reservoir-engineered nonreciprocity, and traveling-wave devices; they do not all perform identical isolation/amplification roles.
- **Pump/control cost:** Parametric devices need pump tones that can leak, heat, intermodulate, or saturate neighboring channels.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Engineered nonreciprocity is rich material.

### Directional couplers for pump injection/attenuation (line 29)

- **Pump injection is clear:** Directional couplers combine/sample traveling waves with finite directivity.
- **“Tailored attenuation” ambiguity:** Attenuators and couplers play different roles; specify whether coupled-port termination/filtering supplies attenuation/routing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Concrete but dense.

### Reciprocal directional-coupler warning (line 29)

- **Excellent correction:** Directionality of power coupling is not nonreciprocity/isolation; scattering reciprocity remains.
- **Pedagogical opportunity:** A four-port S-matrix sketch would settle this common confusion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Precisely the kind of subtle misconception worth surfacing.

### First amplifier “typically a TWPA” (line 29)

- **Overgeneralized:** Many systems use JPAs, JPCs, TWPAs/JTWPAs/KITs, TWPAs of different nonlinear materials, or no quantum-limited preamp; choice depends on bandwidth, multiplexing, saturation, noise, and pump complexity.
- **Improvement:** Say “often a quantum-limited parametric amplifier—JPA/JPC for narrowband or TWPA for broadband/multiplexed readout.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Amplifying microwaves without drowning them in noise is compelling.

### TWPA at mixing chamber (line 29)

- **Representative placement:** First-stage parametric amplifiers are near base temperature to precede lossy/noisy stages, though exact stage and thermal anchoring vary.
- **Backaction:** Pumps, reverse gain, saturation, and isolation placement matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Good physical anchor.

### HEMT at 4 K (line 29)

- **Correct standard chain:** A cryogenic HEMT provides robust high gain after quantum-limited first-stage amplification.
- **Noise/system:** Give noise temperature, gain, compression, and why preceding gain suppresses its referred-to-input noise via Friis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Friis cascade would make the architecture mathematically satisfying.

### Total gain 40–60 dB before room temperature (line 29, closing)

- **Plausible, chain-dependent:** HEMT alone often supplies tens of dB and parametric stage adds more; some room-temperature amplification follows.
- **Reference point:** State frequency band, component gains/losses, and whether quoted total includes parametric plus HEMT.
- **Rendering:** Source uses doubled `\\,` in dB units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Useful number, needs a gain/noise budget.

### Separate flux-control channel (line 31)

- **Correct:** Tunable qubits/couplers use mutual inductance into SQUID loops, distinct from XY microwave drive.
- **Taxonomy:** DC bias, fast $Z$/flux pulses, coupler modulation, and parametric AC flux are related but distinct channels.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A second control axis rounds out the stack.

### “DC + fast-pulse current driven into SQUID loop” (line 31)

- **Circuit wording:** Current flows in a nearby flux-bias line and couples magnetic flux via mutual inductance; it is not generally injected into the superconducting SQUID loop itself.
- **Electronics:** Voltage source/AWG plus bias tee, resistive/inductive line impedance, filters, and current conversion define the pulse.
- **Improvement:** Write $Phi(t)=M I_{line}(t)$ and map flux to frequency/coupling.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** One equation would make magnetic control tangible.

### Modulating inductance (line 31)

- **Correct:** Flux changes the SQUID’s effective Josephson energy/inductance and hence qubit/coupler frequency/coupling.
- **Nonlinear periodic response:** Frequency is a nonlinear periodic function of flux; sweet spots, hysteresis (design-dependent), crosstalk, pulse distortion, and flux noise matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Magnetic flux retuning a circuit is intuitive and interesting.

### Flux-line band DC to few hundred MHz (line 31)

- **Too narrow as a platform statement:** Fast flux gates and parametric modulation can require hundreds of MHz to GHz-class analog bandwidth/tones, while DC bias paths may be intentionally heavily filtered.
- **Separate bands:** Bias, baseband fast flux, and RF parametric flux lines may use different wiring/filtering.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** One range hides meaningful design variants.

### Different cryogenic filtering from drive lines (line 31, closing)

- **Correct:** Flux lines balance low-frequency accuracy/fast edges against thermal noise; XY lines use microwave attenuation/filtering, readout outputs use isolation/amplification.
- **Missing distortion:** Bias tees, skin effect, reflections, eddy currents, filters, and package transfer functions distort flux pulses; deconvolution/predistortion is central.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Filtering as both protection and waveform distortion is an excellent tradeoff.

### Missing §21.2 artifacts and concepts

- **No signal-chain diagram:** The prose urgently needs separate XY input, flux input, readout input, and readout output paths with temperature stages and component symbols.
- **No thermal-noise calculation:** Use attenuator cascade/Johnson noise or photon occupation to show why attenuation is distributed thermally.
- **No mixer calibration example:** Plot desired sideband, image, LO leakage before/after IQ calibration.
- **No noise/gain budget:** Apply Friis to parametric amplifier + loss + HEMT and connect measurement efficiency to readout fidelity.
- **No phase-noise/jitter account:** LO/AWG clock phase noise, channel synchronization, sampling jitter, and reference distribution directly affect gates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** These artifacts would turn dense component prose into one of the book’s most visually satisfying sections.

### §21.2 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It connects IQ mixing, reflections, nonreciprocity, amplification, and flux control in a compact hardware tour.
- **Highest-priority correctness repair:** Scope 3–8 GHz to transmons; fix finite-IF output frequency; separate voltage envelope from Rabi rate; correct current coupling into—not through—the SQUID loop.
- **Highest-priority maturity repair:** Do not imply on-chip nonreciprocal elements generally replace ferrites or that TWPA is universally the first amplifier.
- **Highest-priority systems repair:** Split the four line types and add temperature-stage, gain/noise, attenuation, and transfer-function budgets.
- **Highest-priority rendering repair:** Fix doubled TeX spacing escapes throughout.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10 potential, 8.2/10 current.** Ghost sidebands, pulse echoes, one-way components, and quantum-limited gain are excellent; prose density and universal claims obscure them.

## Chapter 21, §21.3 — Pulse-Level Programming (lines 33–39)

### Heading and present-versus-historical scope (line 33)

- **High-value topic:** It connects language abstractions to controller actions.
- **Currency problem:** The most famous public API discussed has been removed; the section should distinguish historical interfaces, standards syntax, current lab/vendor tooling, and current public cloud access.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Programmers seeing beneath gates is compelling, but obsolete code needs explicit archival framing.

### “Programming model has caught up” narrative (line 35)

- **Overly linear progress story:** Pulse access expanded, then major public providers restricted/removed it; standards grammar and actual hardware portability remain far apart.
- **Improvement:** Present stages as competing layers—language representation, compiler calibration metadata, controller IR, lab API, and cloud policy—not inevitable convergence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Evolution is interesting when reversals are included.

### OpenQASM 3 “added native syntax” (line 35)

- **Broadly correct:** OpenQASM 3 includes timing constructs and calibration declarations/blocks, with companion calibration grammars such as OpenPulse.
- **Version precision:** Cite a specific OpenQASM release/live-spec date; syntax and companion grammar status evolve.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** A circuit language reaching down to timing and calibration is a strong bridge.

### `cal` blocks (line 35)

- **Correct concept:** Inline calibration blocks contain implementation/calibration-grammar statements at program scope/context as specified.
- **Grammar dependence:** Their contents are not defined solely by core OpenQASM; a `defcalgrammar`/companion grammar determines syntax/semantics.
- **Improvement:** Show a complete, version-valid example and its declared grammar.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Embedded low-level control is interesting if runnable.

### `defcal` gate-to-pulse definitions (line 35)

- **Directionally correct:** `defcal` specializes calibration implementations for operations/qubits/parameters.
- **Not inherently “gate-to-pulse”:** A body could use a chosen calibration grammar and backend semantics; portability is not guaranteed.
- **Dispatch detail:** Explain matching by operation signature, parameter types, and physical qubits, including ambiguity/overload rules.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Overloading a gate with its physical realization is highly relevant to software readers.

### `delay` in real-time units (line 35)

- **Correct:** OpenQASM 3 includes `duration`/timing constructs and delays.
- **Hardware discretization:** Requested durations may need alignment to backend clock cycles/granularity; simultaneous channel/resource constraints matter.
- **Semantics:** Delay can mean idle evolution, dynamical-decoupling opportunity, or explicit schedule occupancy—not “nothing happens” physically.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Time as a first-class program value is a strong concept.

### `extern` “binds into the control system” (line 35)

- **Mischaracterized:** The OpenQASM spec declares external *classical functions* and explicitly leaves their definition/registration unspecified. They may run on a global processor concurrently; they are not specifically pulse/control bindings.
- **Scheduling side effects:** Extern latency/concurrency and state changes complicate deterministic real-time use.
- **Improvement:** Describe extern as implementation-provided classical functionality, then separately explain any vendor control binding.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.2/10.** The current phrase sounds more hardware-specific than the standard warrants.

### `defcal x $0` example claim (line 35)

- **No actual example follows:** The prose says it “looks like” a DSL but supplies no code block, so readers cannot validate syntax or understand timing/channel operations.
- **Physical-qubit literal:** `$0` denotes a physical qubit in OpenQASM calibration context; explain why logical qubit syntax differs.
- **Improvement:** Add a complete example with `defcalgrammar "openpulse"`, port/frame declarations, waveform, `play`, timing, and return/capture if relevant.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.0/10.** A promised code example that never appears is a noticeable letdown.

### Waveform/channel/frame/pre-post-correction DSL description (line 35)

- **Reasonable OpenPulse intuition:** Ports, frames, waveforms, play/capture, phase/frequency/timing are core concepts.
- **Backend dependence:** Channel/port resources, sample rate, supported parametric waveforms, collisions, phase conventions, and correction semantics vary.
- **Pre/post correction:** Virtual phases may be compiler-frame bookkeeping rather than emitted analog waveform.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The components form a satisfying low-level language model.

### “Same information compiler would otherwise generate from calibration database” (line 35, closing)

- **Partly true:** Compiler/scheduler uses target instruction definitions, durations, errors, calibrations, channel maps, and constraints.
- **Overstatement:** A user `defcal` may override only an operation realization; calibration databases include transfer functions, frequencies, amplitudes, mixer corrections, qubit state, validity timestamps, provenance, and safety constraints not reproduced in source.
- **Security/ownership:** Providers often prohibit arbitrary pulses precisely because safe/current calibration context is server-owned.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Good compiler connection, oversimplified database model.

### Historical Qiskit Pulse framing (line 37)

- **Tense problem:** “In Qiskit, Qiskit Pulse exposed” is grammatically historical but still reads like usable current guidance until the parenthesis. Lead with “Until Qiskit 1.x...” and mark code archival.
- **Object model:** Qiskit Pulse used `Schedule` and later `ScheduleBlock`/builder abstractions; naming only `Schedule` understates its final public shape.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.5/10.** Valuable history, likely to cause copy-paste confusion.

### `Play(Gaussian(...), DriveChannel(0))` example (line 37)

- **Illustrative, not runnable as shown:** Imports/namespaces and exact constructor signatures/version are absent; Qiskit examples commonly use `pulse.play(pulse.Gaussian(...), pulse.DriveChannel(0))` inside a builder.
- **Semantic overclaim:** `DriveChannel(0)` is a logical controller resource mapped by backend configuration, not proof the analog waveform arrives only at qubit 0.
- **Units:** `duration`/`sigma` are samples or backend time units depending API; `amp` is normalized complex amplitude with constraints.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Code helps, but a non-runnable fragment in a removed API needs a version badge.

### `ShiftPhase`, `SetFrequency`, `Delay` “complete instruction set” (line 37)

- **False completeness:** Pulse also included acquisition, measurement channels, control channels, frequency/phase shifts/sets, calls, barriers/time blocks, snapshots in simulation, waveform playback, memory/register targets, and more.
- **Improvement:** Say “illustrate the core frame/timing controls.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.1/10.** “Complete” invites immediate correction.

### Qiskit 1.3 deprecation and 2.0 removal (line 37)

- **Correct and well dated:** Official IBM release notes confirm deprecation in 1.3 and complete removal in 2.0.
- **Stronger current fact:** IBM’s migration guide says removal was *without replacement* in Qiskit, and migration of Pulse to Qiskit Dynamics was put on hold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The lifecycle reversal is important for practitioners.

### IBM withdrew pulse access from cloud QPUs (line 37)

- **Supported:** IBM documentation says all IBM Quantum processors ceased/offered removal of pulse-level access and points common uses toward fractional gates.
- **Exact timing/access:** State deprecation/removal dates and whether any private/on-prem/lab path remains rather than treating all IBM hardware identically.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Crucial practical constraint.

### OpenQASM `defcal` and vendor stacks “cover parts” (line 37)

- **Good caution:** Syntax capability is not a cross-vendor execution service.
- **Need examples:** Name a currently runnable backend/toolchain that consumes OpenPulse `defcal`, or readers may mistake a specification for deployed interoperability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Standards-versus-implementation gap is important.

### No drop-in cross-vendor replacement (line 37)

- **Plausible and consistent with IBM docs:** But substantiate via surveyed current APIs and define “same abstractions.”
- **Cross-reference:** §23.5 must be checked for the same 2026 status and should not resurrect removed Qiskit workflows.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Honest warning saves readers time.

### Cirq has no comparable public pulse API (line 37)

- **Supported by current public docs only indirectly:** Google documentation exposes circuits, gate/device specs, jobs, and calibrations; no comparable public pulse layer surfaced in the official search.
- **Access nuance:** Google Quantum Engine itself is not generally public and requires approved/sponsored access, so “public API” has two meanings: documented interface versus open hardware availability.
- **Avoid unverifiable internal claim:** “Pulse-level access is internal” requires a direct Google source or should be phrased “not documented as a public user interface.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** Useful ecosystem contrast, carefully evidence-limited.

### IQM Cocos as analogous ecosystem layer (line 37)

- **Unverified current claim:** No current official public Cocos pulse-programming documentation surfaced in targeted search. Cocos may be internal/proprietary control software rather than a user-facing analogue to historical Qiskit Pulse.
- **Improvement:** Cite exact product/API docs, version, access class, supported objects, and whether users can upload arbitrary envelopes/calibrations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **6.3/10.** Name-dropping without a documented interface adds uncertainty.

### Channels abstraction (line 37)

- **Useful common model:** Logical sinks/resources for drive, control, measurement stimulus, and acquisition support scheduling.
- **Example correction:** “Measurement readout for qubit 5” may involve a shared multiplexed resonator/feedline/channel rather than one channel per qubit.
- **Physical mapping:** Logical channels map many-to-many through electronics and crosstalk; they are not guaranteed isolation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Resource-channel mapping is clear and useful.

### Frames abstraction (line 37)

- **Correct and central:** A frame tracks frequency/phase reference and can absorb software phase changes.
- **Granularity:** Frames may attach to ports/channels/qubits/oscillators with implementation-dependent sharing; frequency changes alter phase accumulation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Computation via bookkeeping in a rotating coordinate system is elegant.

### Waveforms abstraction (line 37, closing)

- **Correct:** Sample arrays and parametric envelopes are common.
- **Constraints:** Sample rate, granularity, alignment, amplitude norm, bandwidth, memory, interpolation, quantization, and supported shape set are part of the type/target contract.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Typed waveforms nicely connect software and DAC hardware.

### “Two capabilities” payoff (line 39)

- **Useful organization:** Virtual phases and custom operations are major reasons for low-level access.
- **Not exhaustive:** Custom measurement/acquisition, dynamical decoupling, spectroscopy, calibration experiments, error characterization, analog simulation, and timing research also matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Clear, but falsely exhaustive.

### Virtual $Z$ by frame phase $-\theta$ (line 39)

- **Correct under a common convention:** The sign depends on rotation/frame definitions and how subsequent $X/Y$ pulse phases transform.
- **Not a physical pulse:** It updates phase bookkeeping and may be merged into later operations/readout interpretation.
- **No-later-pulse edge case:** A final virtual $Z$ can matter only through measurement basis/compiled downstream operations; explain semantic realization.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** This is one of the chapter’s most delightful ideas.

### Zero physical time (line 39)

- **Good gate-duration abstraction:** It consumes no scheduled analog pulse duration.
- **Literal caveat:** Controller/compiler state updates have finite processing but can occur off critical path; call it zero *quantum schedule duration*.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Worth precise wording.

### “Almost every modern compiler” emits virtual Z for all Z rotations (line 39)

- **Overbroad:** Applies strongly to microwave-controlled superconducting qubits and many rotating-frame systems, but hardware/encodings, native gates, control restrictions, conditional timing, and compiler choices vary.
- **Physical-Z cases:** Flux/phase accumulation, trapped-ion phase operations, logical FT gates, and calibrated composite operations may implement $Z$ differently.
- **Improvement:** Scope to platforms with phase-coherent equatorial control and frame tracking.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Good practical insight, universalized.

### “Reserves physical pulses for X and Y family” (line 39)

- **Simplification:** Two-qubit, reset, measurement, leakage removal, flux, coupler, and non-equatorial/adiabatic operations also use physical controls; $Y$ is often the same calibrated $X$ pulse with phase shift rather than a separate family.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.7/10.** Clear shorthand, incomplete.

### Custom gates when library is “wrong” (line 39)

- **Loaded wording:** A library may be non-native/inefficient for a workload, not wrong. Calibration ownership and target validity are deliberate abstractions.
- **Risk:** Arbitrary custom pulses can violate amplitude/bandwidth/safety limits, corrupt calibrations, increase crosstalk, or become invalid with drift.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Empowering, should teach responsibility.

### Fractional controlled phase example (line 39)

- **May not require pulses:** Many vendors expose arbitrary-angle/fractional native entanglers directly; the paragraph later notes this.
- **Algorithmic value:** Avoiding decomposition can reduce duration/error and preserve parameter structure.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Good bridge to current fractional-gate APIs.

### Bespoke parametric two-qubit gate (line 39)

- **Valid research use:** Frequency/amplitude/phase modulation can activate tailored interactions.
- **Calibration burden:** Requires Hamiltonian identification, spectator/leakage checks, phase compensation, waveform predistortion, and benchmarking across pairs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Custom interaction engineering is inherently interesting.

### Custom echoed cross-resonance example (line 39)

- **Historically valid for IBM-like fixed-frequency transmons:** But current IBM Heron generations emphasize different coupler/gate implementations; avoid making ECR the universal present path.
- **Parameter access:** IBM’s removal of pulse access makes this example unavailable to ordinary IBM cloud users today; label lab/historical context.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Concrete but dated relative to the stated ecosystem.

### Pulse programming as “most direct” expression (line 39)

- **Often true at a lab-controller layer:** But user waveform is still transformed by controller, mixer, transfer function, and device; Hamiltonian/optimal-control descriptions may be more direct semantically.
- **Portability tradeoff:** Direct physical expression is maximally backend-specific and fragile under recalibration.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** The power/portability tradeoff is valuable.

### Alternative parameterized gates/calibration overrides/services (line 39, closing)

- **Excellent current correction:** This is now central, not a subordinate caveat—IBM explicitly recommends fractional gates for common former pulse use cases.
- **Need provider matrix:** Name current systems, operation families, parameter domains, calibration ownership, access level, and portability.
- **Optimization claim:** “Avoiding generic decomposition overhead” should be measured in gate count/duration/error for an example.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Shows how higher-level APIs can preserve hardware efficiency.

### §21.3 source-verification note (checked 2026-07-23)

- **OpenQASM standard:** The OpenQASM 3 specification includes timing, calibration constructs, and an OpenPulse companion grammar; `extern` is defined as an implementation-provided classical function mechanism, not specifically a pulse binding: https://openqasm.com/versions/3.0/language/index.html and https://openqasm.com/versions/3.0/language/classical.html
- **Qiskit lifecycle:** Qiskit 1.3 deprecated `qiskit.pulse`; Qiskit 2.0 removed it, calibration data structures, channel APIs, scheduling, and related transpiler passes: https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/api/qiskit/release-notes/1.3 and https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/api/qiskit/release-notes/2.0
- **No-replacement/fractional-gate path:** IBM’s migration guide states removal was without a Qiskit replacement and recommends fractional gates for common uses: https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/migration-guides/qiskit-2.0 and https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/migration-guides/pulse-migration
- **Google public layer:** Current Google documentation presents Cirq/Quantum Engine as circuit, gate-set, job, device-spec, and calibration-metric APIs; it does not document a comparable public pulse DSL, and hardware API access is restricted: https://quantumai.google/cirq/google/engine
- **IQM caution:** The Cocos equivalence remains unverified from current official public documentation and should not survive revision without a direct source.

### §21.3 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** Channels, frames, waveforms, virtual $Z$, and custom operations give programmers a useful conceptual model of low-level control.
- **Highest-priority standards repair:** Separate core OpenQASM syntax from companion calibration grammar and correct `extern` semantics.
- **Highest-priority current-API repair:** Lead with Qiskit Pulse’s removal, mark code historical, elevate fractional/parameterized gates, and document actual 2026 access paths.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Rephrase Google’s internal-access claim and source or remove IQM Cocos.
- **Highest-priority example repair:** Supply complete versioned runnable examples instead of pseudo-code fragments, with units/constraints and expected schedules.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10 potential, 8.0/10 current.** Virtual gates and pulse DSLs are fascinating; historical/current ambiguity makes the section less useful than it could be.

## Chapter 21, §21.4 — Control Electronics Architecture (lines 41–47)

### Heading and architectural level (line 41)

- **Appropriate scope:** It promises component roles and data/control flow.
- **Missing architecture figure:** A rack/clock/trigger/data-flow diagram is essential; prose cannot clearly show which processing occurs in instrument FPGA, central sequencer, host, runtime service, or QPU.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Systems architecture is inherently engaging when visualized.

### “Modern control rack” as tightly coupled hybrid (line 43)

- **Broadly correct:** Waveform generation, acquisition, frequency references, real-time processing, synchronization, and host orchestration cooperate closely.
- **Packaging trend:** Functions may be discrete rack instruments, integrated all-in-one controllers, modular chassis, RFSoCs, ASICs, or cryogenic electronics; “rack” is representative, not architectural essence.
- **Missing clock/trigger:** Reference clock, trigger/marker distribution, timing fabric, calibration database, network, and host/accelerator are central enough to include in the opening list.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A classical machine wrapped around a quantum chip is a strong image.

### AWGs, digitizers, LOs, FPGA controller list (line 43)

- **Good canonical blocks:** But mixers/up/downconverters, filters, switches, amplifiers, bias sources, trigger fanout, reference oscillators, and RF front ends are also architectural rather than incidental.
- **Integration:** An SHFQC/OPX-class unit may integrate generator, analyzer, sequencer, and processing, so avoid implying one box per noun.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Useful inventory, slightly schematic without a picture.

### AWG produces I/Q pairs (line 43)

- **Architecture-specific:** An AWG may produce complex baseband/IF I/Q pairs for an external mixer, or a direct-RF DAC may synthesize the carrier; integrated RF instruments may not expose physical I/Q outputs.
- **Channel accounting:** Two DAC channels per IQ path affects density unless digital upconversion/direct RF is used.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Links naturally to §21.2.

### AWG sample rate 1–10 GS/s (line 43)

- **Plausible market envelope, not a representative operating point:** OPX+ official specs are 1 GS/s; direct-RF products can be many GS/s. Sample rate must be paired with analog bandwidth, interpolation, oversampling, number of channels, and waveform memory/streaming.
- **Nyquist is insufficient:** Reconstruction images, filter roll-off, timing granularity, and effective update bandwidth determine usable control.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Concrete but nameplate-centric.

### AWG 14–16-bit vertical resolution (line 43)

- **Nominal bits are misleading alone:** ENOB declines with output frequency/sample rate; SFDR, noise floor, integral/differential nonlinearity, glitch energy, and channel crosstalk determine actual pulse fidelity.
- **Range pairing:** High sample rate, high channel count, and 16 bits are not automatically simultaneous across systems.
- **Control mapping:** DAC quantization at room output is attenuated and transformed; relate voltage LSB/noise to Rabi-rate/phase error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Turning one DAC bit into gate error would be a satisfying worked example.

### ADC at “comparable rates” (line 43)

- **Not generally necessary:** With analog downconversion to IF/baseband, ADCs may sample near 1 GS/s or lower while direct-RF acquisition needs higher rates. OPX+ official input is 1 GS/s/12 bit while its output is 1 GS/s/16 bit.
- **Acquisition metrics:** Analog input bandwidth, ENOB, noise, full-scale range, channel count, aperture jitter, and decimation/integration are essential.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** A vague symmetry between DAC and ADC hides different requirements.

### FPGA real-time demodulation and discrimination (line 43)

- **Correct:** Digital downconversion/integration and classification are common low-latency tasks.
- **Pipeline detail:** ADC samples → NCO/reference mixing → weighted integration/matched filter → rotation/normalization → threshold or multistate classifier → feedback register.
- **Beyond threshold:** Linear discriminants, matched filters, multistate/leakage classification, adaptive thresholds, and some ML/accelerator paths exist.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A noisy waveform collapsing into one control bit is a compelling pipeline.

### LO as fixed-frequency low-phase-noise source (line 43)

- **“Fixed” is misleading:** Synthesizers are tunable/configurable but often remain phase-continuous/fixed during a pulse/program while digital IF selects tones.
- **Reference distribution:** Multiple LOs and instruments must share a stable 10 MHz/reference clock/trigger; phase noise and drift map into gate/readout error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** A shared clock giving the rack one notion of phase is a strong systems idea.

### Mixers/LO distribution in shielded enclosures (line 43, closing)

- **Reasonable engineering practice:** Shielding, layout, filtering, grounding, isolation, and connector quality reduce leakage/crosstalk.
- **Not sufficient:** LO leakage mainly also arises from mixer DC offsets/imbalance and coupling paths; digital calibration/cancellation is necessary.
- **Terminology:** Enclosures suppress electromagnetic coupling/radiation; they do not by themselves eliminate carrier feedthrough inside the mixer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Invisible RF leakage is interesting when its paths are shown.

### Decade-long orchestration shift (line 45, opening)

- **Broadly correct trend:** Controllers increasingly support resident real-time programs, parameter updates, branching, looping, acquisition, and feedback.
- **Historical nuance:** Sequencers, conditional triggers, and hardware feedback predate the last decade; the change is integration, programmability, latency, and scale.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** From tape player to real-time computer is a memorable evolution.

### Preloaded AWG sequence caricature (line 45)

- **Useful baseline, oversimplified:** Traditional AWGs already supported sequence tables, triggers, loops, markers, and conditional/event modes.
- **Improvement:** Contrast host-orchestrated instruments with unified controller-time instruction execution rather than “no program” versus “program.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Clean contrast, historically compressed.

### Real-time program branches/loops/feedback (line 45)

- **Correct modern capability:** Deterministic timing and local classical decisions avoid host/network latency.
- **Constraints:** Real-time arithmetic types, memory, instruction set, branch latency, loop bounds, synchronization, and data streaming are limited compared with a CPU.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Tiny programs running at qubit timescales are compelling.

### Quantum Machines OPX example (line 45)

- **Supported:** OPX+/QUA exposes pulse, measurement, control flow, and low-latency feedback; official material gives 224 ns conditional feedback and 272 ns parametric update figures.
- **Current-family naming:** By 2026 OPX1000 also exists; “OPX-class” should distinguish generation/spec.
- **Evidence grade:** Vendor latency is a defined product benchmark, not a modality-wide result.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Good concrete example.

### Zurich Instruments SHFQC example (line 45)

- **Supported in architecture:** Current manuals document internal/ZSync feedback messages, sequencer branching, conditional command-table playback, and multistate discrimination.
- **Need exact latency:** The manuscript’s later generic “few hundred ns” should cite a specified SHFQC+/PQSC protocol path and boundary rather than borrow OPX timing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Useful second implementation.

### IBM/Google/Rigetti internal systems “follow same shift” (line 45)

- **Plausible but unsourced umbrella:** Published QEC/dynamic-circuit performance implies real-time control, but architecture, FPGA/ASIC split, programmability, and user exposure differ.
- **Improvement:** Cite technical architecture papers/docs per vendor and avoid implying the same control-language/runtime topology.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.0/10.** Brand roll call adds little without contrasts.

### User-facing differences transition (line 45)

- **Excellent point:** Access policy/API is as important as internal hardware capability.
- **Axes:** Arbitrary waveform upload, calibration overrides, parameterized gates, branching/arithmetic, measurement result availability, latency guarantees, safety restrictions, and simulator parity should be tabulated.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Exposes a genuinely important systems boundary.

### OPX exposes procedural pulse program (line 45)

- **Supported:** QUA is a procedural hybrid pulse/measurement/classical-control DSL.
- **Compiler detail:** Users write a hardware-aware DSL compiled to controller execution; they do not necessarily write FPGA instructions or HDL.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Clear example.

### Rigetti Quil-T exposure (line 45)

- **Supported with constraints:** Rigetti currently documents Quil-T analog pulse instructions and says all QPU programs lower through Quil-T.
- **Important limitations omitted:** Pulse programs must be manually nativized, Quil-T is unsupported by `quilc` and QVM, many classical instructions are unsupported live, some frame/flux settings cannot be altered, and final machine code is encrypted.
- **Improvement:** Present “exposed” as a constrained target interface, not unrestricted hardware control.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** A real surviving pulse API is valuable after Qiskit’s removal.

### Qiskit Runtime above control stack (line 45)

- **Correct and important:** Runtime is a managed classical execution/service layer, not Qiskit Pulse’s replacement.
- **Dynamic-circuit nuance:** Which real-time branches/loops are accepted and their controller lowering vary by backend/runtime primitive/version.
- **Terminology:** Separate client–service session/job latency from within-shot controller feedback.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Prevents a common layer confusion.

### Procedural sequence content (line 45)

- **Good abstraction:** Pulses, measurements, classical operations, and conditions form hybrid timelines.
- **Resource semantics:** Concurrency/collisions, alignment, acquisition windows, frame state, register lifetime, and deterministic deadlines need explicit semantics.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Makes dynamic experiments feel programmable.

### “Controller compiles” program to FPGA sequencer instructions (line 45)

- **Layer imprecision:** Usually a host/vendor compiler translates DSL to instrument/sequencer machine code; the real-time controller then executes it. The controller itself need not perform compilation.
- **Not always FPGA:** RFSoCs, CPUs, ASICs, DSP blocks, and proprietary PPUs may participate.
- **Improvement:** Diagram source → host compiler → binary/configuration → sequencer/FPGA execution.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Important pipeline, wrong actor verb.

### Deterministically on FPGA (line 45)

- **Broad intent:** Hardware-timed execution offers bounded timing/jitter.
- **Qualification:** Data-dependent paths can have specified different latency; cross-instrument links, filters, queues, DMA, and synchronization add deterministic or bounded delays.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Determinism at nanosecond scale is compelling.

### Measurement-to-gate “few hundred ns” (line 45)

- **Supported for a defined controller interval:** OPX+ advertises 224 ns from last acquired analog input sample to first conditional analog output; this excludes physical readout integration duration, resonator ring-up/down, qubit response, and gate pulse duration.
- **Protocol dependence correctly noted:** Active reset, analog-to-digital output, parametric calculation, inter-controller routing, discrimination complexity, and filters change latency.
- **End-to-end requirement:** Report measurement start → classification → conditional pulse at device, not only controller internal boundary, when comparing QEC cycle time.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A quantified reflex arc is excellent once measurement boundaries are defined.

### “Instead of software round-trip” (line 45, closing)

- **Correct:** Host/cloud/network round trips are typically far too slow and nondeterministic for within-coherence feedback.
- **Hierarchy:** FPGA/local controller handles hard real-time; host handles near-real-time calibration/batching; cloud/runtime handles jobs/sessions; offline systems handle analysis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Timescale separation is a strong lesson.

### FPGA workload transition (line 47)

- **Good emphasis:** The “simple interface” hides significant signal processing/state management.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Effective reveal.

### Real-time demodulation against reference (line 47)

- **Correct:** Digital mixing/weighted integration extracts I/Q.
- **Reference details:** NCO phase must align with waveform/readout frame and compensate cable/time-of-flight phase; multiplexed tones require parallel digital channels.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Phase-coherent extraction is satisfying.

### Threshold IQ discrimination (line 47)

- **Correct simple classifier:** A rotated line/threshold separates state clusters.
- **Beyond binary:** Multilevel leakage/qutrit discrimination, matched filters, nonlinear classifiers, assignment matrices, drift adaptation, and confidence outputs matter.
- **Error budget:** Separation, amplifier noise, integration time, state transitions, thermal population, and classifier drift determine assignment error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Turning two clouds into a bit is visually teachable.

### Lookup-table waveform generation (line 47)

- **One implementation:** Controllers also stream stored samples, evaluate parametric envelopes, use NCOs/DDS, command tables, interpolation, and on-the-fly scaling/rotation.
- **Resource tradeoff:** LUT memory versus compute, bandwidth, upload time, and parameter-update latency should be explained.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** A useful hardware/software tradeoff.

### Per-channel phase tracking (line 47)

- **Correct:** NCO/frame accumulators implement virtual phases and preserve continuity.
- **Shared resources:** Channels/qubits may share LO/NCO/reference; phase resets, frequency switches, trigger alignment, and cross-channel skew must be controlled.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Reinforces virtual $Z$ physically.

### Arbitration between playback and feedback branches (line 47)

- **Correct systems function:** Scheduler/sequencer resolves resources and branch-dependent commands.
- **Need collision semantics:** What happens when two branches/channels request shared waveform engines, outputs, or readout units?
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Resource arbitration makes the controller feel like a real computer.

### Custom HDL “rarely written by end users” (line 47)

- **Reasonable for vendor controller users:** Most use DSLs/APIs and fixed gateware.
- **Audience caveat:** University/lab controller developers, QEC-control teams, instrumentation vendors, and FPGA researchers do write HDL/HLS; “end user” must be defined.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Useful expectation setting.

### Vendor compiler “emits gateware and sequencer instructions” (line 47)

- **Likely incorrect conflation:** A compiler commonly emits sequencer instructions/program binaries/configuration, not a newly synthesized FPGA bitstream (“gateware”) per user program. Gateware is usually prebuilt/signed firmware.
- **Internal exceptions:** Partial reconfiguration/HLS/custom frameworks exist but are not the normal path described.
- **Improvement:** Replace “gateware” with “machine code, command tables, waveforms, and instrument configuration” unless a specific platform truly synthesizes hardware.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.0/10.** Misuse of a precise FPGA term will distract hardware readers.

### Typical users never see FPGA configuration (line 47)

- **Broadly true for commercial systems:** Abstraction and safety protect timing/IP/hardware.
- **Debuggability:** Users still need visibility into timing diagrams, compiled schedules, resource use, logs, latency, and versioned firmware to reproduce experiments.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Good abstraction boundary.

### Exotic extensions list (line 47)

- **Strong examples:** New discriminators, feedback rules, and decoupling engines motivate lower access.
- **Supported features first:** Weighted integration, threshold configuration, command tables, real-time arithmetic, GPU links, and user functions may cover many needs without HDL.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Gives experts a reason to care.

### Control engineers with hardware access (line 47)

- **Correct:** Low-level modifications require timing closure, verification, analog co-design, safety, firmware signing, and hardware access.
- **Team breadth:** FPGA/embedded, RF, control, calibration, systems, and experimental physicists collaborate; avoid one-role simplification.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Realistic division of labor.

### Supported framework rather than reflashing (line 47, closing)

- **Good practical statement:** Vendor extension frameworks preserve safety/timing/support.
- **Tension with “compiler emits gateware”:** If users rarely reflash and compiler emits instructions, earlier gateware claim should be removed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Strong closing boundary.

### §21.4 source-verification note (checked 2026-07-23)

- **OPX+ specifications:** Official product material lists 1 GS/s, 16-bit analog outputs, 1 GS/s, 12-bit inputs, 400 MHz baseband bandwidth, and 224 ns conditional-feedback latency: https://www.quantum-machines.co/products/opx/
- **Latency-boundary caution:** Quantum Machines defines feedback from the last point of an acquired input pulse through processing to conditional output, so total measurement-plus-feedback is longer: https://www.quantum-machines.co/technology/make-your-quantum-circuits-truly-dynamic/
- **Zurich feedback architecture:** SHFQC+/PQSC manuals document internal/ZSync feedback words, conditional command-table playback, branching, masking/shifting, and multistate discrimination: https://docs.zhinst.com/shfqc_user_manual/news/24_07/flexible_feedback_processing.html
- **Rigetti current interface:** QCS docs confirm native Quil-T pulse control, manual nativization requirements, restricted live classical instructions/settings, translation, and encrypted machine code: https://docs.rigetti.com/qcs/guides/the-lifecycle-of-a-program

### §21.4 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section clearly explains the shift from host-triggered playback to deterministic local hybrid control and enumerates the hidden real-time pipeline.
- **Highest-priority specification repair:** Replace generic simultaneous AWG/ADC nameplate ranges with named products and ENOB/bandwidth/jitter/channel metrics.
- **Highest-priority pipeline repair:** Correct compiler/controller roles and remove “gateware” unless FPGA synthesis truly occurs.
- **Highest-priority latency repair:** Define start/end points and include acquisition/integration/device/cross-controller time before comparing feedback.
- **Highest-priority access repair:** Document the constraints around Quil-T/QUA/SeqC rather than reducing them to exposed/not-exposed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10 potential, 8.4/10 current.** A controller’s nanosecond reflex and hidden signal-processing work are excellent; spec compression and layer conflation limit precision.

## Chapter 21, §21.5 — DAC/ADC Interfaces (lines 49–55)

### Heading and interface plurality (line 49)

- **Good focus:** Converters are the numerical/physical boundary.
- **Scope expansion:** Include RF DAC/ADC, baseband converters, digital up/downconversion, sample clocks, reconstruction/anti-alias filters, front-end gain/attenuation, and data movement.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Translating bits into volts and photons back into bits is a strong interface story.

### “Small zoo” whose limits become qubit limits (line 51)

- **Effective rhetoric:** It emphasizes that classical errors propagate into quantum operations.
- **Overcausal:** Converter errors are filtered/attenuated/calibrated and combine with mixer, clock, amplifier, cable, package, and device errors; they do not map one-to-one.
- **Improvement:** Build an error-transfer budget from digital code to field to Hamiltonian to gate/readout metric.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Strong hook with a clear cross-layer payoff.

### 2 GS/s, 14-bit DAC example (line 51)

- **Valid illustrative specification:** But identify whether real or complex/IQ sampling, interpolation mode, number of active channels, and output frequency.
- **Nameplate versus effective:** Nominal resolution does not equal ENOB at high frequency; pair the example with a real data-sheet curve.
- **Rendering:** Doubled `\\,` appears in GS/s units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Concrete example helps.

### First Nyquist zone to 1 GHz (line 51)

- **Correct for a real-valued 2 GS/s DAC:** The first zone is 0 to $f_s/2=1$ GHz.
- **Architecture nuance:** Complex/IQ sampling and digital interpolation/NCOs alter usable spectral representations; RF DACs can intentionally use higher Nyquist zones.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A simple sampling-theory connection is satisfying.

### Usable bandwidth smaller due to reconstruction filter/rolloff (line 51)

- **Correct:** Zero-order-hold sinc response, analog output network, reconstruction filter, transformer/balun, mixer, and cables shape usable bandwidth.
- **Not always merely smaller:** Images in higher zones may be intentionally selected in RF synthesis.
- **Improvement:** Plot DAC sinc/images and filter response.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The gap between mathematical Nyquist and usable analog spectrum is valuable.

### Ideal quantization SNR formula and 86 dB (line 51)

- **Arithmetic correct:** $6.02(14)+1.76=86.04$ dB for an ideal uniformly quantized full-scale sine under standard assumptions.
- **Assumptions:** Ideal quantizer, uncorrelated uniform quantization error, full-scale sine, no clipping, and Nyquist-band noise integration; oversampling/process gain changes in-band SNR.
- **Do not call dynamic range generically:** SNR, SINAD, ENOB, SFDR, and noise spectral density are distinct.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Excellent small calculation when assumptions are visible.

### Effective dynamic range is lower (line 51)

- **Correct:** Thermal/device noise, nonlinearity, mismatch, reference noise, clock jitter, and spurs reduce performance.
- **ENOB definition:** $\mathrm{ENOB}=(\mathrm{SINAD}-1.76)/6.02$ under sine-test conventions; it already folds noise and distortion, so avoid listing it as an independent physical eater alongside its causes.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The fall from ideal bits to useful bits is instructive.

### Clock-jitter contribution (line 51)

- **Important but undeveloped:** For a sine at $f_{in}$ and RMS jitter $\sigma_t$, jitter-limited SNR is approximately $-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)$.
- **System clock:** Reference source, PLL, aperture jitter, LO phase noise, cross-channel synchronization, and trigger jitter have distinct impacts.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Picoseconds turning into amplitude/phase noise is a compelling quantitative link.

### “Enough headroom” for −30 dBm drive and −50 dBc spurs (line 51)

- **Unsupported inference:** Quantization SNR does not by itself guarantee SFDR, and a −30 dBm tone’s meaning depends on DAC full scale, 50-ohm load, frequency, attenuation, mixer conversion, and reference plane.
- **Qubit-plane confusion:** −30 dBm at AWG/mixer output is vastly different from power after cryogenic attenuation/on chip.
- **Spur danger:** A −50 dBc spur may still be harmful if resonant with a sensitive spectator; harmless if far detuned/filter-suppressed. Absolute power and susceptibility matter.
- **Improvement:** Use a real gain/attenuation chain and convert dBm → voltage → chip field/Rabi rate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.4/10.** Specific numbers feel authoritative but are not tied together.

### DAC SFDR and harmonic distortion (line 51)

- **Correct metrics:** SFDR measures largest spur relative to carrier over a specified band; THD aggregates harmonics under test conditions.
- **Frequency dependence:** Both vary with output frequency, amplitude, sample rate, interpolation, load, and channel configuration.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Good vocabulary with an opportunity for a spectrum figure.

### Spurs show up as “off-resonant drive tones” (line 51)

- **Not necessarily off-resonant:** Harmonics/images/intermodulation can coincide with qubit, spectator, coupler, resonator, $1\to2$, two-photon, or parametric conditions.
- **Error types:** Spurs can cause coherent rotations, AC Stark shifts, heating, leakage, and crosstalk even without resonant population transfer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** One spectral line becoming an unintended gate is a strong systems lesson.

### High-purity DAC plus image-reject mixing (line 51)

- **Good combination:** Converter quality and IQ calibration/filtering both matter.
