- **Plausible but unsourced/device-specific:** Backend topology, disabled elements, and generation determine actual diameter/path.
- **“Far corner” depends on embedding, not graph invariant:** Identify the specific backend and timestamp, then compute graph diameter/shortest path.
- **Current availability:** Historical 127-qubit devices and current maps may differ; avoid a floating current-sounding example.
- **The text correctly says read from actual coupling map:** Follow that advice by supplying code/output rather than the prose estimate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A real map/path would be compelling; vague “low tens” is not reproducible.

### Worst-pair remote CNOT costs a few dozen CNOTs (line 33)

- **Toy arithmetic plausible:** $3(L-1)+1$ native CNOTs if one endpoint moves, no restoration, CNOT is available in both directions, and compilation uses literal SWAPs.
- **Could be roughly twice with restoration, or much less/different with mapping/bridge/native-gate choices:** State assumptions.
- **Fidelity is multiplicative/channel-dependent:** “Tens of times one entangler” in count does not directly yield tens times error because errors/coherence/correlation differ.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Dramatic overhead is useful when the derivation is explicit.

### Layout-specific metrics (line 35)

- **Strong point:** Global averages fail to capture embeddings and local bottlenecks.
- **Name useful metrics:** Workload interaction-graph embedding cost, weighted shortest paths, edge betweenness/congestion, maximum matching/parallelism, defective-region detours, and layout yield.
- **Compiler dependence:** Initial placement, routing heuristic, direction correction, gate synthesis, and optimization level change observed overhead.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** This is where graph theory becomes a practical compiler problem.

### Heavy-hex “long spokes between dense vertices” (line 35)

- **Topologically misleading:** Heavy-hex is formed by inserting degree-two vertices along edges of a hexagonal-type lattice; its vertices are degree two or three, not “dense,” and “long spokes” is not a standard structural description.
- **Likely intended intuition:** Degree-two nodes lengthen routes between degree-three junctions and reduce connectivity/collision pressure.
- **Repair with diagram/formal definition:** Show original hex edges subdivided by degree-two qubits and label node degrees.
- **Official supporting description:** IBM’s dynamic-circuit tutorial constructs heavy-hex by placing a degree-two ancilla between each pair of hex-lattice data vertices: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/tutorials/dc-hex-ising
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.7/10.** “Spokes/dense vertices” gives a vivid but wrong mental picture.

### Spoke-end versus same-hex routing cost (line 35)

- **Cannot evaluate without a defined graph/path:** “Spoke end” is undefined in heavy-hex terminology and individual distances depend on coordinates.
- **Correct underlying lesson:** Local placement within a small connected region can avoid long paths; graph-aware layout matters.
- **Replace with measured pair:** Choose two labeled pairs on a real coupling map and compute shortest weighted paths/compiled gate counts.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Concrete contrast could work, but invented geometry language blocks verification.

### QED-C suite deliberately mixes near/far pairs (line 35)

- **Unsupported/maybe false characterization:** Public QED-C descriptions emphasize application-oriented algorithm circuits, volumetric width/depth sweeps, fidelity, resource counts, and time to solution; no reviewed evidence here establishes a deliberate physical near/far-pair probe.
- **Abstract circuit versus hardware mapping:** Benchmarks generally specify logical interactions; compiler/layout may choose physical qubits, so physical distance is not fixed unless the protocol constrains placement.
- **Do not postpone source to §22.13:** Cite the exact benchmark/circuit/configuration that forces pair distances or remove the claim.
- **Official suite description checked 2026-07-23:** https://quantumconsortium.org/publication/application-oriented-performance-benchmarks-for-quantum-computing/ and repository https://github.com/SRI-International/QC-App-Oriented-Benchmarks
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** It sounds authoritative but currently lacks protocol support.

### All-to-all connectivity story “uninteresting” (line 37)

- **Dismissive and false:** Edge fidelity/time uniformity, simultaneous-gate conflict graph, addressing/crosstalk, mode crowding, calibration scaling, transport, and dynamic availability remain rich connectivity questions.
- **Nominal graph is only one layer:** Complete logical connectivity may be implemented through shared modes or shuttling with nonuniform weighted costs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** The sentence throws away exactly the nuance this chapter should teach.

### “Every pair is a single gate” (line 37)

- **May be true at the exposed ISA level for some ion systems:** A native entangler can be requested between arbitrary pairs.
- **Not necessarily one physical operation of equal cost:** Transport, zone scheduling, pulse compilation, refocusing, mode selection, and calibration can occur underneath.
- **Gate locality versus execution locality:** A complete API graph does not imply all pairs can gate simultaneously or without motion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Useful distinction if reframed as logical/ISA connectivity.

### Costs move to gate-time blow-up, crosstalk, shuttling (line 37)

- **Good instinct:** Connectivity benefits can trade against mode density/control complexity and physical transport.
- **“Gate-time blow-up with system size” is not universal:** Architecture, segmentation, mode engineering, parallel zones, and selected pair determine scaling; cite a model/data.
- **Other costs:** Laser power/beam steering, motional heating/recooling, calibration pairs, zone congestion, sympathetic cooling, and parallelism.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Moving hidden cost elsewhere is a valuable systems lesson.

### Absence of routing overhead as a metric (line 37)

- **Valid operational advantage:** Fewer inserted SWAPs can reduce depth/error and simplify compilation.
- **Measure it on workloads:** Report post-routing two-qubit count/depth inflation, not a binary absence claim; logical all-to-all systems may still perform transport/refocusing internally.
- **Compiler accounting boundary:** Vendor-compiled native gate may hide movement/pulses from user circuit metrics.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** “What overhead is hidden below the ISA?” is an excellent follow-up.

### Ion vendors emphasize all-to-all “correctly” (line 37)

- **Fair recognition of a real benefit, avoid endorsement without metric scope:** Check physical implementation, pair uniformity, concurrency, and scaling.
- **Vendor marketing should be interrogated consistently:** The chapter should not treat one modality’s headline as self-validating while labeling all sheets adversarial.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Balanced praise is welcome; apply the same audit checklist.

### Connectivity has two alleged meanings (line 39)

- **Important ambiguity, wording imprecise:** Topology/adjacency and *usable-edge fraction* are distinct fields, not two interchangeable definitions of connectivity.
- **Other meanings:** Full/linear/nearest-neighbor connectivity, connected-component size, routing overhead, pair reachability, and network/link connectivity are also used.
- **Require schema:** Nominal graph + per-edge gate/type/direction/error/time/timestamp + thresholded usable graph.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** This is exactly the semantic audit the chapter should perform.

### Fraction of pairs above threshold $X$ (line 39)

- **Denominator ambiguous:** All $N(N-1)/2$ pairs, nominal coupling edges only, tested pairs, or enabled edges?
- **Threshold incomplete:** Fidelity protocol, confidence, calibration age, simultaneous context, gate family/direction, and duration must accompany $X$.
- **A scalar can hide fragmentation:** A high passing-edge fraction can still sever the graph if failures hit bridges; a lower fraction can retain a large robust component.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A percolation/bridge-edge example would make this memorable.

### “Two coincide exactly when every nominal edge passes” (line 39)

- **Category error:** A graph topology and a scalar fraction never “coincide.” What becomes equal is the thresholded usable-edge graph and the nominal coupling graph when every nominal edge passes.
- **If denominator is all possible pairs:** Even every nominal edge passing does not make the fraction equal a topology descriptor unless the nominal graph is complete.
- **Repair notation:** Define $G_0=(V,E_0)$ and $G_X=(V,\{e\in E_0:F_e\ge X\})$; then $G_X=G_0$ iff all nominal edges pass.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** One line of set notation would remove a substantial conceptual error.

### “Uniform calibration, not sparsity, is operative” (line 39)

- **False contrast:** Edge yield/uniformity and graph sparsity/topology answer different questions and jointly determine routing.
- **Uniformity need not mean all above threshold:** A uniformly mediocre graph can fail every edge; a nonuniform graph may retain excellent usable paths.
- **Weighted view beats thresholding:** Error/duration distributions and topology-aware path costs preserve more information than pass/fail.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** The intended nuance instead creates another misleading binary.

### Partially calibrated 1000-qubit usable-pair fraction (line 39)

- **Could be informative, not “more honest” alone:** Report numerator/denominator, largest connected component, weighted map, missing-edge locations, simultaneous behavior, and time distribution.
- **Again uses an unsupported generic 1000-qubit scenario:** Label hypothetical or cite a named device snapshot.
- **Threshold gaming:** Choosing $X$ changes the fraction; workload-specific sensitivity should set the threshold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Good practical direction if accompanied by topology rather than replacing it.

### Missing §22.2 artifacts and metrics

- **Graph comparison:** Same $N$ and average degree but different diameter, bottlenecks, and routing cost.
- **Weighted coupling map:** Edge gate family, direction, duration, error/leakage, timestamp, and simultaneous-conflict color.
- **Routing worked example:** One interaction graph mapped to heavy-hex, grid, and complete logical graph; report two-qubit count/depth, movement, fidelity estimate, and compiler settings.
- **Failure/percolation example:** Equal passing-edge fractions with fragmented versus robust topology.
- **Parallelism:** Maximum matchings, edge coloring/control conflicts, shuttling zones, and actual simultaneous layer capacity.
- **Dynamic/effective connectivity:** Nominal physical, calibrated thresholded, compiler/ISA, and workload-time graphs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10.** Connectivity is inherently visual and algorithmic; this section should exploit that fully.

### §22.2 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It correctly links hardware adjacency to compiler routing and warns that nominal topology is insufficient without calibration quality.
- **Highest-priority topology repair:** Replace the inaccurate heavy-hex spoke/dense-vertex story with its degree-two-edge-subdivision structure and a real map.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Remove or substantiate the QED-C near/far-pair claim and the 127-qubit low-tens path example.
- **Highest-priority metric repair:** Distinguish nominal graph, thresholded usable graph, usable-edge fraction, weighted cost graph, and largest connected component.
- **Highest-priority routing repair:** Scope $L-1$ SWAPs/three-CNOT SWAP to a toy gate set and account for restoration, native gates, global mapping, congestion, and hidden transport.
- **Highest-priority modality repair:** Treat all-to-all as an ISA/logical advantage with weighted/concurrency/transport costs, not an uninteresting solved story.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10 potential, 8.4/10 current.** Graph paths and routing explosions are naturally engaging; incorrect geometry and overcompressed metrics impair trust.

## Chapter 22, §22.3 — Gate Fidelity (lines 41–67)

### Section title and scope (line 41)

- **Central metric, correctly prioritized:** Gate quality is indispensable to circuit-depth planning.
- **Plural needed conceptually:** Average fidelity, entanglement/process fidelity, diamond distance, unitarity, leakage, Pauli/coherent components, context dependence, and logical effect are not one interchangeable “gate fidelity.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** This section can teach why one comforting decimal hides many error channels.

### Ideal gate versus noisy channel setup (line 43)

- **Correct mathematical framing:** An intended unitary channel is implemented by a completely positive trace-preserving map in the simplest in-subspace model.
- **Notation ambiguity:** $G_{\rm ideal}$ is called a gate/unitary while $\mathcal G$ is a channel; use $\mathcal U_G(\rho)=G\rho G^\dagger$ for type consistency.
- **Leakage/non-trace-preserving caveat:** If analysis projects onto the computational subspace or postselects loss, the effective map may not be trace preserving and standard formulas require care.
- **Time/context:** The channel may depend on neighboring operations, drift, initial leakage, and non-Markovian history rather than being one stationary map.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Ideal operation versus physical channel is a clean conceptual start.

### “How close” language (line 43)

- **Good intuitive question, metric dependent:** Different distance/fidelity measures order channels differently and have different worst-case/compositional meaning.
- **Average versus worst case:** A high average fidelity can coexist with a comparatively large coherent worst-case error/diamond distance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** This is an ideal moment to show two channels with equal average fidelity but different algorithmic damage.

### Operational random-state description (line 43)

- **Conceptually correct definition of average state fidelity relative to a unitary:** Haar-average the output-state overlap over pure inputs.
- **Not normally implemented by literal Haar sampling:** RB/2-designs/other protocols infer related quantities without preparing a continuum of random states.
- **Mixed/entangled reference:** Average single-system state overlap does not directly display action on half of an entangled state; entanglement fidelity provides that link.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Randomly probing all directions is intuitive; clarify definition versus experiment.

### Average-gate-fidelity integral (lines 45–47)

- **Formula is correct for comparing channel $\mathcal G$ with target unitary $G$:** $\langle\psi|G^\dagger\mathcal G(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)G|\psi\rangle$ is the ideal-frame output overlap.
- **State assumptions:** Pure normalized Haar inputs over the $d$-dimensional computational subspace and a trace-preserving channel are implicit.
- **Notation consistency:** The text calls the target $G_{\rm ideal}$ then the equation uses $G$; define once.
- **LaTeX/rendering:** The equation contains doubled `\\,` spacing commands around $G^\dagger$ and $\mathcal G$; verify build output.
- **Accessibility:** Define Haar average as uniform over pure states (unitarily invariant), not merely name the measure afterward.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Compact and useful; a Bloch-sphere single-qubit interpretation would help.

### “Averaged over Haar measure” explanation (line 49)

- **Correct:** Haar measure supplies the unitarily invariant uniform average.
- **Finite-design connection:** Clifford groups form unitary 2-designs (with appropriate dimensions/settings), explaining why finite randomized protocols access the average.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The symmetry connection would make an abstract measure more satisfying.

### “Number reported by most vendors” (line 49)

- **Unsupported prevalence and label ambiguity:** Providers report RB error per Clifford, error per gate, Pauli error, XEB/cycle error, process/tomography fidelity, median/typical/max infidelity, or model-derived values.
- **Extraction matters:** A displayed “gate fidelity” may be $1-$reported error, converted from Clifford decay under composition assumptions, or averaged over qubits/pairs.
- **Reader action:** Require metric definition, protocol, conversion, aggregation, and timestamp.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Useful warning opportunity; current sentence falsely standardizes the ecosystem.

### Average gate error $\varepsilon=1-F_{\rm avg}$ (line 49)

- **Definition correct:** Often called average gate infidelity/error rate in informal reporting.
- **Do not equate with stochastic failure probability:** It is a metric derived from average overlap, not necessarily the probability that “the gate failed” on a run.
- **Composition:** Coherent/systematic errors can accumulate quadratically in sequence length in some regimes despite the same average infidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** This distinction is essential for the later thousand-gate example.

### Process fidelity described as process overlap (line 49)

- **Needs a convention:** “Process fidelity” variously means normalized Choi-state fidelity/overlap, entanglement fidelity relative to target, or process-matrix overlap; formulas differ with normalization and purity.
- **For a unitary target:** The relation shown uses entanglement/process fidelity $F_e$ (normalized Choi overlap) for a trace-preserving channel.
- **“More fundamental” is unjustified:** Average fidelity, entanglement fidelity, diamond distance, unitarity, and error generators answer different operational questions; one is not universally more fundamental.
- **“Insensitive to which states are tried” is misleading:** The mathematical Choi overlap is input-ensemble independent, but estimating it experimentally still depends on preparation/measurement/protocol assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The whole-process perspective is useful; convention slippage is dangerous in a metrics chapter.

### Relation $F_{\rm avg}=(dF_{\rm pro}+1)/(d+1)$ (lines 49–52)

- **Correct under stated missing assumptions:** Target is unitary, $\mathcal G$ is trace preserving on a $d$-dimensional space, and $F_{\rm pro}$ is normalized entanglement/Choi overlap.
- **Leakage/loss/postselection:** If the map is trace-decreasing after projection or includes leakage outside modeled dimension, use generalized treatment and report survival/leakage separately.
- **Dimension:** $d=2^n$ is correct for $n$ computational qubits without leakage levels.
- **LaTeX/rendering:** Doubled `\\,` appears around $F_{\rm pro}$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Excellent conversion equation once its convention is locked down.

### Numerical conversion 0.99 to 0.9933 (line 55)

- **Arithmetic correct for $d=2$:** $(2\times0.99+1)/3=0.993\overline3$.
- **Error perspective:** Process infidelity is 1%, average infidelity is about 0.667%; that is a factor of 1.5, not necessarily “small” in an error budget.
- **Dimension dependence:** For two qubits, $F_{\rm avg}=(4F_{\rm pro}+1)/5$; provide both to prevent one-qubit conversion reuse.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Concrete conversion is valuable.

### “Differ by a small constant factor” (line 55)

- **Imprecise:** Fidelities are affinely related, while *infidelities* satisfy $1-F_{\rm avg}=\frac{d}{d+1}(1-F_{\rm pro})$.
- **Dimension-dependent, not one constant:** Factor is $2/3$ for one qubit, $4/5$ for two, and approaches one with dimension.
- **Small absolute difference can be large relative error:** At high fidelity, reporting/conversion mistakes materially affect claims about improvements or thresholds.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** This phrase encourages exactly the casual metric swapping the chapter warns against.

### Vendor ambiguity between the two fidelities (line 55)

- **Valid concern:** “Process fidelity,” “gate fidelity,” and “RB fidelity” labels are often used inconsistently across sources.
- **Need evidence rather than general accusation:** Quote named examples or frame it as a verification checklist.
- **Conversion cannot rescue unknown protocol:** Tomography/SPAM, RB, leakage, and aggregation differences remain even after algebraic conversion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Useful skepticism.

### “The larger is usually printed” (line 55)

- **Unsupported motive/prevalence claim:** No dataset or source establishes systematic selection of the larger convention.
- **Average fidelity is often printed because RB estimates it naturally, not necessarily because it is numerically larger.**
- **Rewrite:** “Do not infer the convention from which value looks more flattering; locate the protocol definition.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Cynical punchline weakens evidence-based tone.

### RB called “the standard measurement protocol” (line 57)

- **Broadly prominent, singular too strong:** Standard RB is widely used, alongside interleaved/simultaneous/leakage RB, cycle benchmarking, XEB, gate-set tomography, purity/unitarity benchmarking, and platform-specific protocols.
- **What it estimates:** Under assumptions, decay yields an average Clifford error parameter rather than a complete gate channel.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A random-sequence decay is an approachable benchmark.

### Increasing-length Clifford sequences (line 57)

- **Correct core protocol:** Sample many random sequences at several lengths, append an inversion, repeat shots, and fit averaged survival.
- **Sampling detail:** One sequence per length is insufficient; sequence-to-sequence variation and shot statistics matter.
- **Compilation:** Each Clifford decomposes into native gates; compilation distribution affects “error per Clifford” and any primitive-gate conversion.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Random walks that should return home are intuitive.

### “Unique Clifford” inversion (line 57)

- **Mathematically unique group inverse up to representation/global phase:** The product has an inverse Clifford mapping the ideal state back.
- **Physical decomposition is not unique:** Different native sequences have different duration/error; compiler convention matters.
- **State-specific RB variants:** If only return to a measurement state is required, multiple logical operations can yield the same ideal measurement outcome; distinguish group inverse from observable success.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Fine shorthand with one caveat.

### Return to $|0\rangle$ and survival fit (line 57)

- **Correct single-qubit cartoon:** Multi-qubit RB returns to a known computational basis state/projector under the inversion.
- **Fit model:** Commonly $A p^m+B$ under gate-independent Markovian assumptions; SPAM enters $A,B$.
- **Nonexponential data is diagnostic:** Leakage, drift, gate dependence, non-Markovian noise, and correlations can invalidate one exponential.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The decaying chance of finding home is a strong visual.

### Decay constant gives average error per Clifford (line 57)

- **Needs formula:** In dimension $d$, depolarizing parameter $p$ maps to $r=(d-1)(1-p)/d$ under the standard model.
- **Not automatically error per primitive gate:** Dividing by average primitives/Clifford is an approximation requiring stochastic/gate-independent small errors; exact conversion depends on composition.
- **Uncertainty:** Fit confidence, sequence sampling, length selection, heteroscedastic/binomial likelihood, and drift should be reported.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** One equation would make the metric reproducible.

### RB “insensitive to SPAM” (line 57)

- **Overstatement:** Standard RB’s decay parameter is designed to be robust to time-independent SPAM because SPAM is absorbed into fit constants, but poor/drifting/correlated SPAM reduces signal and biases fits.
- **Not self-calibrating:** RB does not separately identify SPAM or guarantee that it is irrelevant.
- **Use “relatively robust” rather than “insensitive.”**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Important advantage, but absolutes are hazardous.

### Clifford twirl to depolarizing channel of equal average fidelity (line 57)

- **Correct ideal group-theoretic result:** Twirling a fixed channel by a unitary 2-design yields a depolarizing channel preserving average/entanglement fidelity.
- **RB implementation caveat:** Clifford gates themselves are noisy; gate-dependent, time-dependent, leakage, non-Markovian, and context-dependent noise means the experiment is not a literal twirl of one fixed channel.
- **Averaging hides structure:** Coherent versus stochastic, bias, leakage, and correlated errors can share the same decay/average fidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Turning arbitrary noise into one symmetric decay by randomized conjugation is elegant and deserves a small derivation.

### Averaging as RB weakness (line 59)

- **Correct central criticism:** One scalar suppresses gate, direction, context, time, and error-channel structure.
- **Other weaknesses:** Assumption violations, leakage, coherent-error interpretation, drift, sequence compilation, finite sampling, long-sequence saturation, and scalability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The strength-becomes-weakness turn is effective.

### Average over Cliffords versus algorithm gate noise (line 59)

- **Good warning:** Algorithmic gate mix and context may differ from the randomized Clifford ensemble.
- **“Channel algorithm applies” wording:** An algorithm applies a sequence of native/compiled operations with time/context-dependent noise, not one channel.
- **Magnitude “substantial factor” needs example:** Coherent axis error, bad edge, simultaneous crosstalk, or rare leakage can demonstrate it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Workload mismatch is exactly what developers need to understand.

### Cycle benchmarking and interleaved RB grouped together (line 59)

- **Interleaved RB description is broadly right:** Alternate a target gate with random reference Cliffords and compare decay under assumptions to estimate target-gate error.
- **Cycle benchmarking is mischaracterized:** CB characterizes a repeated multi-qubit cycle using randomized Pauli dressing/twirling and can estimate Pauli error rates/process fidelity; it is not simply a target gate inserted into RB sequences.
- **Neither fully solves context:** IRB can suffer gate-dependence/reference-bound issues; CB depends on cycle definition, twirling/randomized compilation, SPAM treatment, and scalable observable sampling.
- **Rewrite separately:** One paragraph per protocol with target, assumptions, output, and blind spot.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Naming advanced methods is useful; conflating their mechanisms defeats the purpose.

### Direct fidelity estimation (line 59)

- **Overbroad:** DFE encompasses state/process variants that estimate fidelity to a known target using importance sampling of observables, often efficient for suitable states/unitaries.
- **Assumptions/cost:** Requires ability to prepare/sample specified inputs/observables and know target coefficients; experimental SPAM and dimensional scaling/target structure matter.
- **Not necessarily vendor gate benchmark:** Explain when used and how it differs from RB/tomography.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The shortcut is intriguing but too compressed to be useful.

### Process tomography (line 59)

- **Broadly correct:** It reconstructs a process representation from an informationally complete set and is costly/SPAM-sensitive in ordinary implementations.
- **Scaling:** Parameter/setting cost grows exponentially (roughly $d^4$ process degrees before constraints), making it unsuitable for large gates/systems.
- **Physicality/gauge:** Reconstruction requires statistical estimation/constraints; gate-set tomography addresses SPAM self-consistently but has gauge and scaling issues.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Full channel reconstruction is a useful contrast; quantify the cost.

### “Two numbers typically reported per device” (line 61)

- **Overcompression:** Gate metrics are normally per qubit/edge/gate and aggregated as median/mean/best/worst/quantiles; one $F_{1q}$ and one $F_{2q}$ hide yield/topology.
- **Devices also report SPAM/readout, coherence, leakage, layer/cycle metrics, and durations.**
- **Timestamp:** Live calibration properties can update often.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Convenient but teaches a scoreboard rather than a distribution.

### Superconducting $F_{1q}=0.9995$–$0.99995$ (line 63)

- **Plausible range for selected high-performing contemporary results, not a stable “best devices” interval:** Metric, gate set, isolated/simultaneous context, device-wide aggregation, and date differ.
- **Upper/lower semantics:** Does the interval span device medians, pair of named systems, or qubit distributions?
- **Records and current products move beyond/around it:** Source each named system’s exact table/metric rather than synthesize an opaque range.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Five decimal places demand much better provenance.

### Named Google Willow (line 63)

- **Primary device/source exists:** Willow’s 105-qubit below-threshold experiment and spec sheet provide component errors, but use the exact reported metric/aggregation rather than generic “fidelity.”
- **Pauli error versus average fidelity:** The Nature paper reports component Pauli errors in QEC context; conversion/comparison to RB fidelity must be explicit.
- **Primary source checked 2026-07-23:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y and Google spec sheet https://quantumai.google/static/site-assets/downloads/willow-spec-sheet.pdf
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Named hardware helps; exact metric labeling is mandatory.

### Named “IBM Heron r2” (line 63)

- **Identity/source unclear:** Give full product/backend/generation name, qubit cohort, live/static dataset, and retrieval date; “r2” is not self-explanatory.
- **Current metrics are often live distributions:** A single range can age between calibrations and processor revisions.
- **No supporting primary result located in the narrow official search:** Do not retain the named endorsement without a direct official/primary citation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Unexplained revision shorthand feels like insider lore.

### Ion $F_{1q}=0.9999+$ and Quantinuum H2 (line 63)

- **Directionally supported:** Quantinuum’s H2 datasheet lists typical one-qubit infidelity $3\times10^{-5}$ (fidelity 0.99997) and max $2\times10^{-4}$ under its definitions.
- **Use infidelity as reported:** Converting to fidelity is easy but protocol/“typical/max” must remain attached.
- **Current lineup stale:** Quantinuum’s system reference now lists Helios (98 qubits) as available since 2025-11-05, so calling H2 the “best ion trap” in a May 2026 snapshot requires an explicit benchmark rationale or update.
- **Official sources checked 2026-07-23:** H2 datasheet https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/data_sheets/Quantinuum%20H2%20Product%20Data%20Sheet.pdf ; current system reference https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/support/system_reference.html
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Good modality comparison, already stale in product selection.

### Single-qubit headline “rarely limits algorithms” (line 63)

- **Reasonable common hierarchy, overgeneralized:** Two-qubit/readout errors are often larger, but algorithms may contain many single-qubit/idle operations; coherent calibration errors, control crosstalk, DD pulses, and non-Clifford synthesis can matter.
- **Modality/circuit dependence:** Algorithms with mostly one-qubit rotations, long idles, or stringent phase accuracy can be limited differently.
- **System bottleneck:** High average $F_{1q}$ does not ensure simultaneous or worst-qubit performance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Useful rule of thumb if framed probabilistically.

### $F_{2q}$ as binding constraint “on most devices” (line 65)

- **Often true in gate-model NISQ circuits:** Entanglers generally have higher error and dominate compiled depth.
- **Not universal:** Readout/reset, loss, state preparation, idle/dephasing, transport, leakage, calibration instability, and classical latency can dominate by modality/workload.
- **Correlated context:** Pairwise fidelity can look strong while simultaneous entangling layers fail due to crosstalk.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Strong practical heuristic with scope caveat.

### Superconducting $F_{2q}=0.995$–$0.999$ “best” (line 65)

- **Already outgrown at upper endpoint by selected 2026 demonstrations:** A current PRX Quantum report demonstrates CZ above 99.9% in one superconducting device.
- **Lower endpoint may describe large-device medians rather than “best”:** Separate record pair, device-wide typical/max, and simultaneous-layer figures.
- **Protocol mismatch:** CZ XEB/RB/cycle figures should not be mixed as one range.
- **Current counterexample checked 2026-07-23:** https://journals.aps.org/prxquantum/abstract/10.1103/n86s-2b88
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** A “current best” range that excludes current results damages the chapter’s central promise.

### Ion $F_{2q}=0.998$–$0.9995$ (line 65)

- **Plausible selected-system range, metric/coverage still needed:** Pair distribution, gate angle, all-pair versus selected pair, isolated/parallel, and benchmark protocol matter.
- **H2 official typical:** Datasheet typical two-qubit infidelity is $10^{-3}$ (0.999 fidelity), maximum $3\times10^{-3}$; this supports one point, not the whole “best ion traps” range.
- **Current systems:** Helios availability again makes a May 2026 H2-only framing incomplete.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Useful scale, insufficiently sourced.

### Hundreds to thousands of two-qubit gates (line 65)

- **Plausible for many NISQ workloads, too vague:** Circuit width/depth, compilation/routing, algorithm, optimization, and problem instance determine count; useful/fault-tolerant algorithms can require vastly more.
- **Count versus depth:** Parallel gates experience time/crosstalk differently; total count alone is not runtime or accumulated error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Concrete enough to motivate compounding, but name a workload.

### $0.999^{1000}\approx0.37$ arithmetic (line 65)

- **Arithmetic correct:** Approximately $e^{-1.0005}\approx0.368$.
- **Average fidelity is not a literal independent survival probability:** The product only illustrates a toy model where each gate independently preserves the desired result with probability 0.999 and any failure destroys circuit success.
- **Depolarizing/error-model mapping:** Even independent stochastic Pauli errors can cancel or leave an observable unchanged; average gate infidelity is not directly “no-error probability.”
- **Coherent errors:** Systematic unitary errors can add coherently, oscillate/cancel, or scale much worse than the product.
- **Correlated/nonstationary errors:** Crosstalk, drift, leakage, and common events invalidate independence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The 37% alarm is memorable; bold-label it a deliberately pessimistic/illustrative proxy, not circuit survival.

### The prose’s own “deliberately naive model” caveat (line 65)

- **Excellent self-awareness:** It explicitly names coherent/correlated failure of the model and cross-references Chapter 18.
- **Still incomplete:** The primary conceptual error is also treating average fidelity as success probability; add that before composition assumptions.
- **“Right order-of-magnitude alarm” is not guaranteed:** Observable/circuit/error structure can yield much better or worse outcomes; the alarm is that per-gate error must be interpreted compositionally, not that 0.37 is generally near truth.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Caveat helps, but does not fully repair the equation’s semantics.

### Cross-vendor RB comparison trap (line 67)

- **Excellent warning:** Gate set, Clifford sampling/decomposition, fit model, SPAM handling, leakage, cohort, simultaneous context, and aggregation impede fine comparison.
- **Also require duration and native operation:** Equal error with radically different gate time/parallelism changes workload impact.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** This directly fulfills the chapter’s stated mission.

### Different Clifford constructions/generators/fits (line 67)

- **Correct factors:** Native decomposition and average primitives per Clifford materially change EPC-to-EPG conversion.
- **Protocol version/code:** Random seeds, sequence lengths/counts, shots, fitting likelihood, confidence method, drift randomization, and outlier policy should be reported.
- **Dimensionality:** One- and two-qubit RB, simultaneous RB, subsystem RB, and direct RB are different experiments.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** This is valuable fine print, well placed.

### “Not directly comparable at fine grain” (line 67)

- **Good nuanced phrasing:** Broad orders may inform, but small decimal differences do not establish device ranking.
- **Could be stronger mathematically:** Harmonize target gate, protocol, native decomposition, cohort, timing/context, and uncertainty before estimating an effect difference.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Responsible and clear.

### No universal “noise” threshold for differences (line 67)

- **Correct:** Statistical resolution depends on shot/sequence sample size, model, effect variance, drift, and systematic comparability.
- **Terminology:** Separate statistical uncertainty from physical noise and systematic protocol bias.
- **Controlled studies:** Paired/interleaved randomized order across devices/times can reduce confounding but cannot erase different native gates/architectures.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Strong scientific literacy point.

### Demand confidence intervals/protocol/cohort/isolation status (line 67)

- **Excellent minimum checklist:** These are essential.
- **Add timestamp/calibration distribution:** One run’s confidence interval does not capture day-to-day drift.
- **Add metric/conversion:** EPC/EPG, leakage, gate duration, direction/angle, SPAM handling, postselection/mitigation, and exclusions.
- **Add reproducibility:** Raw sequence data/code/seeds and independent validation when possible.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Concrete demands turn skepticism into practice.

### Missing §22.3 artifacts and analytical depth

- **Metric map:** Average/entanglement fidelity, infidelity, depolarizing $p$, error per Clifford/native gate, Pauli error, diamond distance, unitarity, leakage, and when conversions hold.
- **Equal-fidelity counterexample:** Coherent overrotation versus stochastic depolarization over repeated depth, showing different accumulation.
- **RB fit:** Plot $A p^m+B$ with SPAM constants, uncertainty, residuals, and a nonexponential failure case.
- **Protocol table:** Standard/interleaved/simultaneous/leakage RB, cycle benchmarking, XEB, DFE, process/GST by output, assumptions, scale, SPAM, and blind spots.
- **Device distributions:** Per-qubit/edge time series and simultaneous degradation rather than two headline numbers.
- **Composition exercise:** Compare naive product, depolarizing observable decay, coherent overrotation, and leakage for equal one-gate $F_{\rm avg}$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.9/10.** This section can turn one decimal into a fascinating error-channel detective story.

### §22.3 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It gives a valid average-fidelity definition and strongly warns against fine-grained cross-vendor RB rankings.
- **Highest-priority mathematical repair:** Define $F_{\rm pro}$ as normalized entanglement/Choi fidelity with trace-preserving/unitary-target assumptions; treat leakage separately.
- **Highest-priority RB repair:** Replace “SPAM-insensitive” with robust-under-static-SPAM, state the decay-to-EPC formula/assumptions, and separate cycle benchmarking from interleaved RB.
- **Highest-priority composition repair:** Do not equate $F_{\rm avg}$ with independent circuit-survival probability, even inside the deliberately naive example.
- **Highest-priority currency repair:** Update named devices/ranges (including Helios and >99.9% superconducting CZ) or centralize dated data in Appendix F.
- **Highest-priority reporting repair:** Replace two device numbers with distributions by gate/qubit/pair/time/concurrency and exact protocols.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10 potential, 8.7/10 current.** Random walks returning home, noise twirling, and thousand-gate compounding are excellent material; protocol conflations and stale decimals are serious in a metrics chapter.

## Chapter 22, §22.4 — Coherence Time (lines 69–89)

### Section title and opening (lines 69–71)

- **Essential metric family:** Coherence constrains idle storage and contributes to gate error.
- **“A qubit left untouched eventually decoheres” is physically practical, not universally mathematical:** An ideal isolated eigenstate need not; real open systems and control references drift/couple to environments.
- **“Untouched” is ambiguous:** Idle qubits may receive dynamical decoupling, frame updates, spectator drives, measurement crosstalk, or always-on coupling.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Direct opening, with room to distinguish ideal isolation from operational idling.

### “Two timescales summarize” decay (line 71)

- **Good Bloch-model entry:** $T_1$ and $T_2$ are standard summaries.
- **Overcompression:** $T_2^*$, echo/DD times, leakage, nonexponential relaxation, quasistatic drift, correlated noise, motional heating, loss, and state-dependent rates require more than two scalars.
- **Fit-model dependence:** Stretched exponentials, Gaussian Ramsey envelopes, oscillations/beating, telegraph jumps, and multi-exponential decay cannot always be summarized faithfully by one time constant.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The later protocol taxonomy repairs part of this; qualify “in the simplest model.”

### $T_1$ definition (line 73)

- **Correct standard meaning:** Longitudinal/energy relaxation describes population returning toward thermal equilibrium.
- **Ground-state-only wording assumes a cold bath:** At nonzero effective temperature, upward and downward transitions drive population toward $p_1^{\rm eq}$ rather than exactly zero.
- **Multi-level systems:** Transmons/ions can leak or decay through multiple states with branching, producing more than one rate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** An energy-level decay diagram would make the meaning immediate.

### Prepare–wait–measure protocol (line 73)

- **Correct experiment skeleton:** Prepare $|1\rangle$, vary delay, measure excited population, fit.
- **SPAM/thermal offset:** Fit $P_1(t)=P_1^{\rm eq}+[P_1(0)-P_1^{\rm eq}]e^{-t/T_1}$ in the simple two-rate model, not necessarily $e^{-t/T_1}$ from one to zero.
- **Preparation/readout bias:** Imperfect $X$, relaxation during readout, assignment asymmetry, and drift enter amplitude/offset.
- **Time sampling/uncertainty:** Randomize delay order to reduce drift bias and report fit residuals/confidence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Simple and experimentally concrete.

### Pure exponential claim (line 73)

- **Model-dependent:** Markovian time-homogeneous relaxation produces an exponential; TLS coupling, nonstationarity, quasiparticle bursts, spectral structure, and multilevel cascades can create nonexponential behavior.
- **Metric reporting:** Median/mean $T_1$ over repeated fits differs from fitting an averaged decay when rates fluctuate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Deviations from the straight semilog line make an excellent diagnostic story.

### Environmental-mode explanation (line 73)

- **Correct open-system intuition:** Coupling at the transition frequency to dissipative/noisy degrees of freedom sets downward/upward rates.
- **Spectral density:** Fermi’s golden-rule picture links matrix elements and environmental noise density; add one qualitative formula.
- **Control/environment boundary:** Readout resonator, package modes, control lines, dielectric defects, quasiparticles, and radiation are engineered environment components.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A qubit leaking energy into specific modes is vivid and causal.

### Transmon $T_1$: Purcell plus dielectric loss (line 73)

- **Important mechanisms, incomplete list:** Quasiparticles, TLS resonances, conductor/surface/interface loss, package/seam modes, control-line loss, radiation, vortices, phonons, and nonequilibrium photons can contribute.
- **Purcell nuance:** Readout/coupling resonators and filters alter the electromagnetic density of states; Purcell filtering can suppress decay without removing readout coupling.
- **Device variability:** Dominant mechanism changes with frequency, design, fabrication, temperature, shielding, and cooldown.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The same resonator used to observe a qubit becoming an escape route is compelling.

### Ion $T_1$: spontaneous emission and off-resonant scattering (line 73)

- **Encoding/illumination dependent:** Optical metastable qubits have radiative lifetime constraints; hyperfine/Zeeman ground-state populations can be extraordinarily long-lived.
- **Off-resonant scattering is generally drive-induced:** It occurs under Raman/control/cooling light, not necessarily during a truly dark untouched idle.
- **Other population-loss mechanisms:** Background-gas collisions, trap loss, state-changing collisions, laser leakage, blackbody-driven transitions, and imperfect shelving matter by species/setup.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Natural atomic lifetimes provide a strong contrast once encodings are separated.

### Motional heating separated from internal $T_1$ (line 73)

- **Excellent distinction:** Motional bus heating can degrade entangling gates without relaxing the internal qubit population.
- **Indirect memory effects:** Residual spin-motion coupling, magnetic/AC-Stark gradients, transport, and recooling operations can still affect stored internal coherence.
- **Metric implication:** Report motional heating rate (quanta/s), mode coherence, cooling/transport overhead separately from internal-state $T_1$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Distinguishing the qubit memory from its shared mechanical bus is excellent pedagogy.

### $T_2$ definition (line 75)

- **Correct:** Transverse coherence is decay of off-diagonal density-matrix elements/phase contrast in a specified frame/protocol.
- **Not always one exponential:** Ramsey/echo contrast may be Gaussian, stretched, oscillatory, or noise-spectrum dependent.
- **Reference oscillator:** Measured phase coherence includes local-oscillator/control-reference noise as well as the qubit.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Coherence as retaining a phase relationship is clear.

### $T_2\le2T_1$ called a fundamental bound (line 75)

- **Correct in the standard two-level Markovian Bloch model:** $1/T_2=1/(2T_1)+1/T_\phi$ with nonnegative pure-dephasing rate.
- **“Fundamental” needs assumptions:** Non-Markovian/nonexponential dynamics, time-varying rates, different fit protocols/time windows, leakage, encoding, and measurement uncertainty can yield apparent violations or incomparable fitted constants.
- **Protocol synchronization:** $T_1$ and $T_2$ should be measured under comparable conditions/times before invoking the bound.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The factor-of-two ceiling is memorable; the rate equation should be shown.

### Equality when relaxation is only decoherence channel (line 75)

- **Correct in the same model:** With $1/T_\phi=0$, transverse amplitude decays at half the population-relaxation rate.
- **Thermal bath nuance:** Upward and downward rates contribute to longitudinal/transverse relaxation; define the low-temperature convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A concise physical result.

### Low-frequency dephasing examples (line 75)

- **Plausible:** Flux noise affects flux-sensitive superconducting qubits; magnetic-field fluctuations affect field-sensitive ion transitions.
- **Not universal per modality:** Sweet-spot fixed-frequency transmons may be limited by photon/charge/TLS/control noise; clock-state ion qubits suppress first-order magnetic sensitivity and can be laser/reference limited.
- **Noise bands:** “Low frequency” is relative to experiment duration/control filter function.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Cross-platform comparison is useful if encoding sensitivity is specified.

### Several $T_2$ numbers warning (line 77)

- **Excellent and central:** A coherence time is inseparable from pulse/filter/fit protocol.
- **Add pulse count/spacing and envelope model:** The section later does so partly.
- **Terminology:** Some vendors report Hahn-echo simply as “$T_2$,” making schema/version scrutiny essential.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** This is exactly the metric-literacy lesson promised.

### Ramsey $T_2^*$ protocol (line 79)

- **Correct basic sequence:** Two nominal $\pi/2$ pulses separated by free evolution create/read interference.
- **Phase/detuning omitted:** The second pulse phase and deliberate detuning set fringes; fit contrast envelope separately from oscillation frequency.
- **SPAM/drive errors:** They affect contrast/offset but should not automatically be interpreted as decoherence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Interference as a clock is compelling.

### Quasistatic offsets between runs (line 79)

- **Correct source of inhomogeneous dephasing:** Slowly varying detuning produces ensemble/run-to-run phase spread.
- **Within-run noise also contributes:** Ramsey filter function samples a continuum; not all decay is quasistatic.
- **Single-shot/real-time tracking:** Tracking detuning can convert apparent $T_2^*$ into longer conditioned coherence without changing physical noise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A stable qubit appearing incoherent because its frequency wanders between shots is a valuable insight.

### $T_2^*$ “typically shortest” (line 79)

- **Reasonable common ordering, not guaranteed:** Echo/DD pulse errors, resonant noise, high-frequency noise, state orientation, heating, or short $T_1$ can erase/reverse gains.
- **The section later caveats CPMG but should qualify here too.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Useful rule of thumb with one “often.”

### Hahn echo protocol (line 81)

- **Correct:** A midpoint $\pi$ pulse reverses phase accumulated from approximately static detuning.
- **Pulse axes/phases:** Initial/final $\pi/2$ phases and echo axis matter for pulse-error rejection and measured quadrature.
- **Finite pulse effects:** Noise/control during pulses and pulse imperfection are not refocused ideally.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Time reversal of static phase is elegant and accessible.

### “Insensitive to mean detuning” (line 81)

- **Correct ideal intuition:** Constant detuning accumulated before and after an instantaneous perfect echo cancels.
- **“Mean” ambiguous:** A deterministic constant offset cancels; noise varying during the sequence, pulse detuning/error, and higher-order effects remain.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A phase-vector animation would make it memorable.

### No sharp cutoff/filter-function explanation (line 81)

- **Strong correction to simplistic high-pass language:** Echo sensitivity is frequency-dependent with lobes/zeros.
- **“Passes noise near $1/t$ and above” is too broad:** Exact filter peaks depend on angular-frequency convention and sequence; sensitivity does not monotonically pass all higher frequencies, and finite pulses/bandwidth matter.
- **Noise convention:** The filter weights dephasing spectral density; “passband” means noise there contributes to decoherence, potentially counterintuitive.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Filter functions are rich visual material.

### Echo several times Ramsey on low-frequency-noise devices (line 81)

- **Plausible, unsourced/general:** Ratio can be near one, several, or orders depending on spectrum and drift.
- **Prefer diagnostic ratio examples:** Name a device and simultaneous $T_1,T_2^*,T_2^{\rm echo}$ dataset with fit forms.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Concrete ratios help if sourced.

### CPMG pulse train (line 83)

- **Correct broad description:** Repeated refocusing pulses alter the filter function and suppress selected low-frequency dephasing.
- **Meiboom–Gill specificity:** Pulse phases/state orientation are chosen to reduce accumulation of certain rotation errors; arbitrary-state preservation may require XY-family sequences.
- **Pulse count notation:** Report $N_\pi$, total duration, spacing convention, and pulse width.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A train of flips as spectral engineering is engaging.

### “Passband to higher frequencies” (line 83)

- **Directionally captures filter peak movement with shorter spacing:** CPMG samples/suppresses noise differently as pulse repetition increases.
- **Terminology caution:** The filter-function peaks are frequencies where noise contributes strongly, while low-frequency components are rejected; call it sensitivity band rather than signal passband.
- **Resonances:** Coupling to narrow spectral features can shorten coherence at particular spacings, as the prose usefully notes later.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Noise spectroscopy by varying pulse spacing is a strong addition.

### CPMG usually longest $T_2$ (line 83)

- **Common under low-frequency dephasing, no universal order:** Pulse errors, heating, high-frequency/resonant noise, finite bandwidth, and $T_1$ ceiling can reverse it.
- **Pulse-number optimization:** More pulses do not guarantee longer lifetime; plot coherence versus $N_\pi$.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The included reversal caveat is good.

### Controlled-memory lifetime, not intrinsic constant (line 83)

- **Excellent metric discipline:** CPMG performance belongs to a control protocol and resource cost.
- **Add algorithm compatibility:** DD pulses consume schedule/bandwidth and may conflict with gates, measurement, crosstalk, frame, or QEC cycles.
- **Report pulse error/heat:** Long protected memory uses many imperfect operations and control power.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** One of the section’s strongest sentences.

### Coherence ratios reveal noise spectrum (line 85)

- **Useful qualitative diagnostic, inverse problem is nonunique:** A few scalar lifetimes cannot reconstruct a spectrum; filter-function spectroscopy across durations/pulse counts is needed.
- **Fit form and nonstationarity:** Ratios can reflect drift/fit choices rather than stationary spectral density.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Treat as clues, not a full diagnosis.

### Echo much greater than Ramsey means low-frequency refocusable noise (line 85)

- **Reasonable inference:** Quasistatic/low-frequency detuning is implicated.
- **Other explanations:** Run-to-run calibration/reference drift and ensemble inhomogeneity can produce the same ratio; these are operationally related but not identical microscopic noise.
- **Quantify “much greater”:** Uncertainty and fit definitions matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Good diagnostic shorthand.

### Recalibration and DD address “exactly that component” (line 85)

- **Overstatement:** Recalibration removes predictable/trackable drift, not stochastic low-frequency fluctuations faster than tracking; DD filters selected spectra during compatible idles.
- **Neither is exact:** Calibration estimation latency/noise and pulse/filter imperfections leave residuals.
- **Other mitigations:** Sweet spots, shielding, materials, reference stabilization, robust control, encoding, and feedback.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Helpful action mapping, too absolute.

### “Neither repairs noise during gates” (line 85)

- **False absolute:** Dynamically corrected/composite gates, robust optimal control, echoed gates, real-time tracking, randomized compiling, and error correction can mitigate gate-time noise.
- **Valid narrower point:** Idle DD sequences cannot simply be inserted through an arbitrary active gate without redesign.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The distinction is useful if rewritten narrowly.

### Echo approximately $2T_1$ means relaxation-limited (line 85)

- **Correct in the standard model under comparable measurements:** Pure dephasing is small for that echo protocol/time regime.
- **Approximation/uncertainty:** Require simultaneous/repeated $T_1$ and echo fits, compatible envelope definitions, and confidence intervals.
- **Protocol-specific wording is good:** It does not imply all gates/states are relaxation-limited.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** A practical stopping criterion for DD optimization.

### “Further software tricks cannot help” (line 85)

- **Far too absolute:** QEC/error detection, encoding/decoherence-free subspaces, shortening/scheduling operations, measurement/reset, algorithm redesign, and improved control can improve computational outcomes even if idle DD cannot exceed a relaxation limit.
- **Narrow truth:** No unitary refocusing pulse can reverse irreversible amplitude damping of one unencoded qubit in the Markovian model.
- **Hardware $T_1$ improvement can help:** Correct but not the sole route at system/logical level.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** A precise impossibility statement would be powerful; “software tricks” is dismissive and wrong broadly.

### 2025 superconducting cohort $T_1=100$–300 μs (line 87)

- **Plausible for selected large transmon processors, not a general current range:** Device-wide distributions include shorter values; research devices now demonstrate millisecond lifetimes.
- **Cohort undefined:** Vendor/device, qubit count, median/best, frequency, sample size, date, and loaded operating condition are missing.
- **Current counterexample checked 2026-07-23:** A 2025 Nature paper reports millisecond lifetimes/coherence in 2D transmons: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09687-4
- **Rendering:** Doubled `\\,` occurs in units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** An unsourced cohort range cannot support comparison.

### Superconducting $T_2^{\rm echo}=80$–300 μs (line 87)

- **Same cohort/aggregation problem:** Protocol, pulse axes, fit envelope, simultaneous conditions, median/best, and timestamp are needed.
- **Can exceed this in research devices:** Millisecond coherence results again make the range non-frontier.
- **Do not compare independently selected $T_1$/$T_2$ ranges:** The $2T_1$ bound is per qubit/condition, not across endpoints from different devices.
- **Rendering:** Doubled `\\,` appears.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Specificity without provenance is fragile.

### Hyperfine-ion $T_1$ beyond experimental timescale (line 87)

- **Directionally correct for magnetic-insensitive ground-state encodings:** Radiative population lifetime can be extremely long.
- **Not “trapped-ion qubits” generically:** Hyperfine/Zeeman/optical/metastable encodings differ, and technical state-changing processes set operational lifetime.
- **Define measured lower bound:** “Beyond” should cite observation duration/confidence and distinguish population $T_1$ from phase $T_2$ and trap survival.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Atomic ground states provide a striking contrast.

### Background-gas collision/trap loss limit (line 87)

- **Plausible operational limits:** Collisions can eject ions or change internal/motional state.
- **Other limits:** Laser leakage/scattering, microwave leakage, magnetic/reference noise, heating, chemical reactions, and control schedules.
- **Trap lifetime is erasure/loss, not necessarily internal $T_1$:** Report separately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A stable atomic state lost because the particle leaves the machine is a useful metric distinction.

### Optical-transition $T_1$ “roughly a second” (line 87)

- **Reasonable for some metastable quadrupole optical qubits, not typical across species/transitions:** Lifetimes range substantially, and some optical/clock encodings differ.
- **The prose appropriately says species-/transition-dependent but still gives an unanchored typical.**
- **Named example needed:** Specify ion, states, natural lifetime, and whether repumping/leakage is included.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Atomic-level specificity would improve both rigor and interest.

### Ion echo coherence multi-second to minute (line 87)

- **Broadly demonstrated, enormous protocol/encoding spread:** Hyperfine, Zeeman, optical/metastable, clock sensitivity, laser/local-oscillator stability, DD, sympathetic cooling, and magnetic shielding matter.
- **Primary examples show labels are essential:** $^{43}$Ca$^+$ hyperfine achieved $T_2^*=50$ s without DD: https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.1524 ; a $^{137}$Ba$^+$ metastable qubit achieved 136(42) s with tuned CPMG, sympathetic cooling, and leakage monitoring: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.111.L020601 ; other single-ion memory work estimates coherence beyond an hour under specialized control: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-20330-w
- **Do not mix Ramsey/echo/CPMG:** The passage specifically labels $T_2^{\rm echo}$ but cited-style records may be Ramsey or CPMG.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Extraordinary values are fascinating when the preservation machinery is disclosed.

### “Five to seven orders more coherent per shot” (line 87)

- **Arithmetic/scope unstable:** Comparing 100 μs to 1–100 s gives four to six orders, not generically five to seven; specialized minute/hour results extend it, but protocols and encodings differ.
- **“Per shot” is undefined:** Coherence time is a duration/decay parameter, not coherence “per shot.”
- **Unfair protocol comparison:** A DD-protected ion memory versus a bare/echo transmon must use matched control definitions if the ratio is meant operationally.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** The dramatic contrast is attractive but numerically/sloppily framed.

### Ion gates 100–1000 times longer (line 87)

- **Reasonable order for many high-fidelity two-qubit comparisons, not universal:** Ion gates span submicrosecond to hundreds of microseconds; superconducting gates span tens to hundreds of nanoseconds.
- **Operation matching:** Compare one- versus two-qubit gates separately, include transport/cooling, and report fidelity/context.
- **Counterexample:** Sub-2-μs high-fidelity ion entanglement narrows the ratio for slower superconducting gates: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25737
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Good balancing point, needs named pairs.

### Coherence-to-gate-time “gate count budget” (line 87)

- **Useful dimensionless heuristic:** $T_{\rm coh}/t_g$ estimates how many serial gate-duration intervals fit within a coherence time.
- **Not a literal executable gate count:** Gate errors, idles, parallelism, control crosstalk, measurement/reset, transport, DD, algorithm structure, and fault tolerance dominate before simple expiry.
- **Choose matching coherence:** Ramsey, echo, CPMG, driven/dressed coherence, or $T_1$ should match what happens during the operation/schedule.
- **Terminology collision:** “Gate count budget” could be confused with fidelity-based error budget; call it coherence-limited depth ratio.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Dimensionless normalization is exactly the right instinct once scoped.

### Raw $T_2$ comparison versus normalized budget (line 87)

- **Excellent comparative principle:** Absolute lifetimes alone mislead across platforms with different operation speeds.
- **Extend beyond ratio:** Include gate fidelity, connectivity/routing, parallelism, measurement/reset, clock cycle, loss, and workload.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** This is the section’s strongest cross-platform idea.

### Single unlabeled $T_2$ is underspecified (line 89)

- **Correct and important:** Protocol, pulse count/spacing, fit form, state/axis, qubit cohort, timestamp, and uncertainty must be given.
- **Also ask whether value is $T_2^*$, Hahn echo, DD, or model-derived and whether $T_1$ was measured concurrently.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Directly actionable checklist.

### Algorithm planning uses matching DD protocol (line 89)

- **Strong operational principle:** Use coherence under the schedule/control actually applied.
- **Not sufficient:** Gate-time noise, DD/gate conflicts, pulse errors, crosstalk, measurement, reset, and calibration drift need circuit-level modeling/benchmarking.
- **Compiler reality:** Verify that requested DD is supported, inserted after scheduling, fits idles, and survives transpiler/conditional-control constraints.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Connects a laboratory metric to compilation decisions effectively.

### Missing §22.4 artifacts and statistical rigor

- **Decay plots:** $T_1$ with thermal offset/nonexponential example; Ramsey/echo/CPMG contrasts with explicit fit models/residuals.
- **Rate equation:** $1/T_2=1/(2T_1)+1/T_\phi$ with assumptions and apparent-violation caveats.
- **Filter functions:** Ramsey, echo, CPMG versus frequency and a narrow spectral feature that reverses ordering.
- **Protocol report schema:** Pulse sequence/count/spacing/width, fit envelope, qubit/state, timestamp, repetitions, uncertainty, concurrent $T_1$, DD cost.
- **Cross-platform matched table:** Named encoding/device, memory protocol, $T_1$, $T_2^*$, echo/DD, one-/two-qubit gate time/error, transport/readout, $T/t_g$.
- **Time variation:** Distributions/Allan-style drift rather than one calibration snapshot.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10.** Echoes, filter spectra, thermal asymptotes, and minute-long atomic memories are excellent visual stories.

### §22.4 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It distinguishes Ramsey, Hahn echo, and CPMG and correctly insists that coherence belongs to a protocol.
- **Highest-priority physics repair:** Add the thermal asymptote/nonexponential caveat to $T_1$ and assumptions/rate equation behind $T_2\le2T_1$.
- **Highest-priority control repair:** Replace claims that recalibration/DD “exactly” fix low-frequency noise and that no software can help once relaxation-limited.
- **Highest-priority currency repair:** Replace the unsourced 2025 cohort ranges with named, protocol-matched distributions; millisecond transmon and specialized ion results already exceed the prose ranges.
- **Highest-priority comparison repair:** Remove “per shot” orders claim and compute matched $T/t_g$ ratios for named operations without treating them as literal gate budgets.
- **Highest-priority modality repair:** Separate hyperfine/Zeeman/optical/metastable ion $T_1/T_2$ and dark idle versus laser-induced scattering.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10 potential, 8.9/10 current.** Echo/filter-function physics and cross-platform timescales are compelling; absolutes and unnormalized ranges are the main weaknesses.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.5 “Gate Speed” (lines 91–105)

### Section title: “Gate Speed” (line 91)

- **Clear and searchable, but narrower than the operational subject:** The section actually discusses pulse duration, scheduled makespan, throughput, parallelism, coherence exposure, and neutral-atom rearrangement. “Gate duration, scheduling, and throughput” would better advertise the distinction the prose wants readers to learn.
- **Terminology opportunity:** Define *latency* (time for one operation/dependency chain) versus *throughput* (completed work per unit time). “Speed” invites readers to collapse them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Immediate and practical, though generic.

### “Wall-clock cost of one gate” equals gate time / pulse duration (line 93)

- **Useful first approximation, not a stable definition:** A reported gate duration may include or exclude pulse ramps, echo/cancellation lobes, coupler settling, buffers, transport, phase compensation, resonator depletion, and controller timing granularity.
- **Counterexample:** Virtual-$Z$ or frame-change operations can have essentially no physical pulse duration, although they remain logical/compiler operations and may affect later pulse phases.
- **Not always one pulse:** Entangling gates may be composite sequences, share a bus or motional mode, or require simultaneous control tones; “how long the pulse takes” singular is too platform-specific.
- **Suggested repair:** Define an interval from the earliest physical control action to the earliest safe start of dependent operations, and separately report nominal waveform duration and scheduler-reserved duration.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Concrete opening, with a satisfying systems flavor once endpoints are made explicit.

### Critical-path duration of a scheduled circuit (line 93)

- **Strong central correction:** Wall-clock runtime is governed by dependencies and concurrency, not the arithmetic sum of all gates. This is one of the chapter’s most useful antidotes to spec-sheet reasoning.
- **DAG wording is slightly incomplete:** Resource conflicts are normally constraints imposed during scheduling, not necessarily pre-existing edges in the logical instruction DAG. A resource-constrained schedule can add ordering decisions between otherwise independent operations.
- **Dependencies extend beyond quantum gates:** Measurement and feed-forward latency, reset, transport, sympathetic cooling, classical branching, waveform upload, synchronization barriers, and shared control/readout resources can all lie on the critical path.
- **Heterogeneous exposure:** The global makespan is not automatically the relevant decoherence duration for every qubit. Each qubit has its own live interval, idle intervals, driven intervals, reset points, and noise environment.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The “longest path” mental model is crisp and memorable.

### “This is what must fit inside the coherence budget” (line 93)

- **Overbroad for physical circuits:** What must remain tolerable is accumulated state-dependent error over each relevant quantum dependency path, not necessarily the entire job’s wall-clock duration beneath one scalar $T_2$.
- **Fault-tolerant exception:** Logical computations are designed precisely to run much longer than a physical qubit’s coherence time through repeated syndrome extraction, correction, and refresh.
- **Reset/measurement exception:** Mid-circuit measurement, reset, teleportation, and fresh ancillas break the assumption that every qubit preserves one coherent state from beginning to end.
- **Suggested repair:** Say an uncorrected coherent dependency chain must remain within an empirically validated error budget under its actual active/idle control schedule.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Intuitive but liable to plant an oversimplified rule.

### Inverse gate time and CLOPS (line 93)

- **Dimensional bridge is legitimate but weak:** $1/t_g$ is a nominal serial operation rate for one chosen gate; CLOPS is an end-to-end benchmark throughput and cannot be inferred from that inverse alone.
- **CLOPS scope needs explicit separation:** It incorporates circuit layers, parameter updates, runtime overheads, and hardware-aware execution conditions. IBM’s current description defines updated CLOPS using layers of a hardware-aware 100-qubit-by-100-layer circuit per unit time: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/announcements/product-updates/2023-11-21-new-and-updated-system-metrics
- **Parallelism reverses the intuition:** A processor can execute many operations during one gate interval, while control, reset, compilation, communication, or queueing can make observed application throughput far lower than $1/t_g$.
- **Suggested repair:** Introduce $1/t_g$ as a physical-control timescale, then state that CLOPS measures a specified system workflow and is not “operations per second” in the generic sense.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The connection is motivating if the non-equivalence is emphasized.

### Superconducting single-qubit gates: $20$–$50\,\mathrm{ns}$ (line 95)

- **Plausible representative pulse range, not a platform envelope:** Shorter and longer calibrated pulses occur depending on qubit, drive strength, leakage suppression, desired robustness, controller sampling, and gate family.
- **Virtual gates omitted:** $Z$ rotations are commonly implemented as frame updates, so a blanket single-qubit duration range is misleading unless it means microwave-driven $X/Y$ rotations.
- **Benchmarking mismatch:** Duration should be paired with angle/gate, fidelity, leakage, and simultaneous-operation condition; an $X_{\pi/2}$ pulse and arbitrary compiled one-qubit Clifford are not interchangeable units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Concrete numbers are welcome but need named operations.

### Ion-trap single-qubit gates: $1$–$30\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (line 95)

- **Plausible but architecture-dependent:** Microwave, Raman, quadrupole/optical, addressed, and global operations have different speed/selectivity/crosstalk tradeoffs.
- **Range lacks a comparison contract:** Specify species, encoding, rotation angle, addressed versus collective control, and achieved simultaneous fidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Useful scale contrast, presently too anonymous to teach cause and effect.

### Superconducting two-qubit gates: $30$–$300\,\mathrm{ns}$ (line 95)

- **Reasonable headline range, not exhaustive:** Demonstrations exist outside both ends; speed depends on coupling architecture, pulse shape, leakage constraints, and whether echoed/cancellation components and buffers are counted.
- **Native-gate list mixes mechanism and unitary label:** Cross resonance is an interaction/control mechanism often compiled into an echoed entangling operation, while iSWAP and CZ name unitary families; tunable-coupler CZ, echoed CR, parametrically activated exchange, and direct-coupling gates should be compared on equal footing.
- **“Qubit modality” is vague here:** If the intended distinction is transmon, fluxonium, fixed-frequency, tunable-frequency, or coupler architecture, name it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The named gates create texture but currently suggest a taxonomy that is not quite parallel.

### Fluxonium parenthesis (line 95)

- **True but under-informative:** Saying fluxonium has “its own gate schemes” signals heterogeneity without explaining what changes in speed, selection rules, coupling, leakage, or fidelity.
- **Editorial suspicion:** This reads like a defensive exception inserted after review rather than a teaching unit. Add one named comparison or remove it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **6.8/10.** Intriguing name, no payoff.

### Ion-trap two-qubit gates: $30\,\mu\mathrm{s}$–$1\,\mathrm{ms}$ (line 95)

- **Covers many routine high-fidelity regimes but is not a demonstrated envelope:** Ballance et al. report entangling-gate durations from $3.8$ to $520\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ with the best fidelity near $100\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, illustrating the speed–error tradeoff: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04600
- **Fast-gate counterexample:** Schäfer et al. demonstrated Bell-state entanglement in less than $2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, including a $480\,\mathrm{ns}$ setting, so the stated lower bound is not generally valid: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25737
- **Do not compare duration alone:** Motional-mode preparation, transport, sympathetic cooling, addressing constraints, and parallel gate capacity can dominate system timing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The orders-of-magnitude contrast is compelling; the fast-gate counterexample would make it richer.

### Neutral atoms “sit somewhere in between” for Rydberg gates (line 95)

- **Directionally plausible, insufficiently precise:** Experimental Rydberg entangling gates can operate on submicrosecond-to-microsecond scales, but species, excitation scheme, pulse optimization, blockade strength, geometry, fidelity, and parallelism matter.
- **High-value omitted evidence:** Evered et al. demonstrated $99.5\%$ CZ fidelity on as many as 60 atoms in parallel, making neutral atoms a direct counterexample to any speed comparison that ignores concurrency: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06481-y
- **Named products are not equivalent evidence:** Product names should be tied to supported operation modes and dated specifications, not used as proxies for the entire platform.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Neutral atoms provide an excellent third-way comparison, but “somewhere in between” wastes the story.

### QuEra Aquila and Pasqal as gate-time examples (line 95)

- **Category error for Aquila:** Aquila’s public interface natively implements analog Hamiltonian simulation, not a user-facing digital circuit composed of individually timed two-qubit gates. AWS’s official device documentation describes its parameterized time-dependent Hamiltonian: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/braket/latest/developerguide/braket-quera-submitting-analog-program-aquila.html
- **Pasqal needs product/version specificity:** “Pasqal” denotes a company/platform family with analog and digital-analog claims; a gate-time statement needs the exact machine, access mode, date, and native instruction.
- **Suggested repair:** Separate analog evolution duration from digital entangling-gate duration, then use a published experimental gate implementation for the latter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Recognizable names help orientation, but the incorrect comparison could confuse precisely the reader who benefits most.

### “Large overhead for atom rearrangement between cycles” (line 95)

- **“Cycle” is fatally ambiguous:** It might mean experimental shot, algorithm layer, error-correction round, job, loss-repair round, or loading cycle. Those have radically different timing models.
