## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.11 “Mid-Circuit Measurement, Reset, and Feedforward Latency” (lines 183–193)

### Section title (line 183)

- **Excellent systems grouping:** Measurement, reset, and conditional control form a dependency chain and belong together.
- **Title mixes operations and one metric:** “Latency” grammatically modifies feedforward but not clearly reset fidelity or measurement disturbance. Consider “Mid-circuit measurement, reset, and feedforward: fidelity and latency.”
- **Missing spectator dimension:** The defining challenge is often preserving unmeasured qubits, especially in atomic platforms; signal it in the title or opening.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Dynamic circuits feel active and consequential.

### Link back to Chapter 9 (line 185)

- **Good continuity:** It reminds readers that logical primitives require physical implementations.
- **Self-containment opportunity:** Briefly define feedforward as using a measured classical bit to select a later operation so readers need not reopen Chapter 9.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Efficient bridge, not much payoff by itself.

### “How fast and how cleanly” (line 185)

- **Excellent two-axis framing:** Latency and fidelity/disturbance must be reported together.
- **“Cleanly” needs decomposition:** Assignment error, demolition/QND character, leakage, spectator dephasing/accidental measurement, reset error, branch error, and conditional-gate error are distinct.
- **Include parallelism:** How many qubits can be measured/reset/conditioned simultaneously and which neighbors must idle can matter more than a single-channel time.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Plain language accurately identifies the engineering contest.

### “Three numbers govern this” (line 185)

- **False compression:** The prose itself invokes measurement latency, measurement fidelity, reset time, reset fidelity, feedforward delay, spectator disturbance, and coherence; at least six values plus context are needed.
- **Capability is categorical as well as scalar:** Supported branch expressions, fanout, nesting, register width, loop limits, decoder location, Pauli-frame support, and conditional native gates matter.
- **Suggested repair:** Call these three *metric families* and give a small schema for each.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The promise of three numbers is appealing but misleading.

### Mid-circuit measurement-latency definition (line 187)

- **Useful endpoint definition:** Starting at measurement pulse and ending when the bit reaches control is much better than quoting integration time alone.
- **Start boundary remains ambiguous:** Does “start” include state mapping/shelving, resonator ring-up, premeasurement basis rotation, or only acquisition?
- **End boundary remains insufficient for scheduling:** A bit can be “available” to one controller before decoded logic, fanout, synchronization, waveform selection, and the dependent gate can start.
- **Report a latency chain:** measurement command → analog response/integration → digitization/classification → controller availability → decision complete → dependent pulse start.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Timing endpoints invite a satisfying pipeline diagram.

### Superconducting MCM latency $1$–$5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (line 187)

- **Plausible order for some full readout/control stacks, not a stable platform range:** Raw integration can be tens-to-hundreds of nanoseconds, while scheduler reservation, resonator depletion, classification, transport through controllers, and conditional synchronization can extend the interval.
- **Operation and product must be named:** Qubit/backend, readout mode, simultaneous width, fidelity, QND/leakage, spectator effect, controller endpoint, and date are required.
- **Potential double counting:** The later paragraph adds feedforward delay; ensure this $1$–$5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ stops exactly at bit availability and excludes decision/dispatch.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Concrete scale is useful; anonymous bands are fragile.

### “Dispersive integration plus discrimination” (line 187)

- **Incomplete latency budget:** Include pulse/ring-up, analog chain/group delay, digitization, digital filtering, threshold/classifier, resonator ring-down/depletion, synchronization, and controller communication.
- **Classifier complexity matters:** Simple threshold, matched filter, neural classifier, and leakage-aware multistate discrimination have different accuracy/latency/resource tradeoffs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A signal racing through electronics is inherently visual.

### Ion-trap MCM latency $50$–$500\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (line 187)

- **Can describe fluorescence-detection windows in selected demonstrations, but not the complete mid-circuit operation generally:** Data-qubit hiding, ion separation/transport, state mapping, recooling, reset, recombination, and spectator protection can dominate.
- **Direct counterexample to the claimed envelope:** A recent trapped-ion implementation reports current mid-circuit measurement around **30 ms** and reset 1.7 ms, showing that complete operation latency can far exceed fluorescence time: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12848042/
- **Short detection is achievable:** Neighbor preservation above 99.6% during an 11-μs detection beam has been demonstrated, but that is a component result rather than an end-to-end register MCM: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11298003/
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The enormous component-versus-system gap is a compelling engineering lesson.

### Shelving/state mapping and recooling “add separately” (line 187)

- **Good recognition, but it undermines the headline range:** If mandatory steps are excluded, call $50$–$500\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ fluorescence collection/detection time rather than MCM latency.
- **Spectator isolation belongs centrally:** Resonant fluorescence can accidentally measure neighboring ions; hiding, multiple species, focused beams, or shuttling are correctness requirements, not optional footnotes.
- **Heating/recoil dependence:** Whether recooling is required depends on detection scheme, ion species, architecture, and later motional gates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Shelving and hiding qubits make the hardware feel ingenious.

### Coherence-time/measurement-latency ratio (line 187)

- **At best a rough spectator-idle ratio, not a count of measurements one shot can absorb:** The measured qubit is projected and may be reset; different qubits participate at different times; measurement errors and spectator disturbance accumulate separately.
- **Numerator mismatch:** Use coherence under the actual spectator protection/idle schedule, not a generic Ramsey or echo $T_2$.
- **Fault-tolerance exception:** Repeated syndrome measurement is intended to continue beyond physical coherence through correction; cycle error and decoder throughput matter more than fitting a shot under one $T_2$.
- **Ratio can still help:** Label it “spectator coherence-to-MCM-latency ratio” and never interpret it as successful MCM count.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Dimensionless comparison is attractive after careful renaming.

### Measurement disturbs measured qubits (line 187)

- **Correct but incomplete:** Whether demolition matters depends on reuse; QND fidelity, leakage/erasure, reset, and repeated-readout agreement quantify it.
- **Measurement is supposed to project the target:** The engineering concern is unintended transition/leakage and disturbance of spectators, not projection itself.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Useful conceptual distinction could be sharper.

### Spectators idle and dephase (line 187)

- **Correct and central:** Also include relaxation, crosstalk, measurement photons, AC Stark shifts, common-mode disturbance, and DD compatibility.
- **Idle is not inevitable:** Some architectures can operate disjoint regions or apply DD during parts of the measurement window; concurrency must be measured.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The image of the rest of the computer waiting makes latency tangible.

### Coherence is a decay constant, not a deadline (line 187)

- **Excellent qualification:** Preserve this language; it corrects a common mental model.
- **Extend it:** The allowed time depends on target error probability and decay envelope, not merely the $1/e$ time.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Crisp and scientifically mature.

### Reset fidelity/time definition (line 189)

- **Necessary pair of metrics:** Time without final-state error, or fidelity without duration/input distribution, is incomplete.
- **Define initial ensemble and target:** Reset from known $|0\rangle$, known $|1\rangle$, thermal steady state, leakage states, or arbitrary postmeasurement state can yield different fidelity.
- **Include residual excitation/leakage and spectator effects:** Computational-basis ground-state population alone may miss leakage and correlated disturbance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Practical and easy to motivate.

### Active reset as conditional $X$ (line 189)

- **One common protocol, not the definition of active reset:** Driven dissipation, resonator/coupler swaps, unconditional reset pulses, repeated measurement-feedback, optical pumping, and teleport/reset-by-replacement also exist.
- **Conditional reset may use a Pauli-frame/state-tracking choice in some contexts rather than a physical $X$, but actual qubit reuse generally needs physical preparation.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Measurement-then-flip is intuitive; alternatives add valuable variety.

### Active-reset fidelity as product of measurement and $X$ fidelity (line 189)

- **Mathematically incorrect in general:** Reset success depends on the input-state distribution, conditional assignment errors, measurement backaction/QND transitions, latency relaxation/excitation, conditional gate error, leakage, and the no-$X$ branch.
- **Even a simple binary model is a weighted sum, not one product:** For input probabilities $p_0,p_1$, success includes the correctly assigned/no-flip $|0\rangle$ branch and correctly assigned/flipped $|1\rangle$ branch, plus state transitions during the sequence.
- **Repeated feedback changes the model:** Multiple measurement/reset rounds can suppress one error source while accumulating others.
- **Suggested repair:** Give a two-branch probability tree or confusion-channel composition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10 potential, 7.8/10 current.** A probability tree would be both rigorous and approachable.

### Passive reset as waiting through $T_1$ (line 189)

- **Correct basic mechanism:** Excited population decays approximately exponentially toward thermal equilibrium.
- **Thermal floor omitted:** Passive waiting approaches the equilibrium excited-state population, not perfect $|0\rangle$; quasiparticles and nonexponential decay can matter.
- **Leakage levels differ:** $|2\rangle$ and other states may have different transitions/times, so one $T_1$ is not sufficient.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Natural decay provides a simple contrast to active intervention.

### Passive reset takes $5$–$10T_1$ (line 189)

- **Mathematically interpretable if a target residual is stated:** Pure exponential decay leaves $e^{-5}\approx0.0067$ or $e^{-10}\approx4.5\times10^{-5}$ of the excess excited population.
- **Not a universal prescribed range:** Required wait follows the target initialization error, starting population, equilibrium floor, and nonexponential dynamics.
- **Add formula:** $p_e(t)=p_e^{\rm eq}+[p_e(0)-p_e^{\rm eq}]e^{-t/T_1}$ under the simple model.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The exponential residual calculation is satisfying.

### 200-μs transmon gives 1–2 ms passive reset (line 189)

- **Arithmetic correct:** $5$–$10\times200\,\mu\mathrm{s}=1$–$2\,\mathrm{ms}$.
- **Representative, not generic:** $T_1$ varies by device, qubit, time, and operating point; use it as a worked example.
- **“Per shot” depends on scheduling:** Repetition delay may overlap classical work or other partitions, but it remains a major throughput limiter for that qubit/register.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Good concrete throughput consequence.

### Active reset is standard, fidelity around 0.99 (line 189)

- **Overgeneralized and unsourced:** Availability differs across providers/backends and between initialization, user-visible reset, mid-circuit reset, and leakage reset.
- **Performance range is protocol-specific:** A fluxonium feedback demonstration achieved 99.4% in about 1.5 μs: https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06814 ; driven reset demonstrations exceed 99% with very different mechanisms/times.
- **Standard practice may include fixed repetition delay instead:** IBM’s 2026 documentation still exposes backend-dependent repetition delays, underscoring that passive waiting has not vanished: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/announcements/product-updates/2026-02-10-rep-delay-max-increase
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Useful operational conclusion, too sweeping.

### Feedforward-delay definition (line 191)

- **Good clean separation from measurement latency:** Outcome-ready to dependent-operation start is the right additional interval.
- **Decision complexity matters:** A bit test, parity, table lookup, decoder, arithmetic, loop condition, and multi-bit branch have different latency/resource requirements.
- **Fanout/synchronization matters:** Sending a decision to one local channel differs from coordinating many qubit controllers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** This is classical computing on the critical quantum path.

### Classical decoding/logic plus pulse generation (line 191)

- **Correct components, incomplete pipeline:** Include data movement, buffering, clock-domain crossing, branch scheduling, waveform selection/cache, controller fanout, and synchronization.
- **Decoder latency can be pipelined/backlogged:** Average completion time, worst-case time, throughput per syndrome round, and backlog probability are distinct.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** A race against decoherence is naturally dramatic.

### Willow/Heron conditional dispatch $100$–$500\,\mathrm{ns}$ (line 191)

- **Unsupported named-device claim:** No primary/official evidence found tying both named systems to this common conditional-dispatch band under the section’s endpoint definition.
- **Willow counterevidence/category mismatch:** The published Willow distance-5 real-time decoder averaged **63 μs** latency with a **1.1 μs** QEC cycle; this is decoder latency, not simple branch dispatch, but it directly shows why the named latency type must be specified: https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/handle/20.500.11850/723955?show=full
- **IBM documentation confirms dynamic-circuit support and warns about control-computation latency but does not support this numeric Heron band in the cited public material:** https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/guides/dynamic-circuits-considerations
- **Remove or replace:** Use a named benchmark with exact start/end points, branch operation, hardware/firmware, and date.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Exciting number, currently trust-damaging.

### Full round trip equals measurement plus dispatch (line 191)

- **Additivity is a useful first model if intervals are disjoint and definitions align.**
- **Missing conditioned-gate start/settling and scheduling:** “Round trip” may include the conditional pulse duration or only its start; define it.
- **Parallel/pipelined paths:** Some classification/decision work can overlap late measurement processing, so simple addition is not always the implementation critical path.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Clear systems arithmetic.

### Teleportation-style Pauli corrections within coherence (line 191)

- **Misleading necessity:** Pauli corrections can often be tracked in a Pauli frame and propagated/classically interpreted later rather than physically applied immediately.
- **What must be timely:** The outcome must arrive before a later noncommuting/adaptive dependency or before classical interpretation is needed—not necessarily before a physical Pauli pulse.
- **Success is not guaranteed by latency alone:** Measurement/assignment, entanglement, idling, reset, conditional-control, and gate errors determine teleportation fidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Teleportation is a great example; Pauli-frame subtlety improves it.

### Ion-trap round trip and coherence-normalized budget (line 191)

- **Qualitative tradeoff is real:** Atomic coherence can offset slower measurement/control in some protocols.
- **Overgeneralized:** Complete protected MCM may be milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, and spectator scattering/motional disturbance—not only dephasing—can dominate.
- **Compare matched operations:** Use demonstrated full sequence time, spectator preservation, measurement/reset fidelity, and the actual protected coherence protocol.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Cross-platform reversal remains compelling when evidence-matched.

### “Exotic in 2020, widely supported by 2025” (line 193)

- **Vague historical/current claim:** Define support—research demonstration, cloud instruction, all backends, arbitrary branch logic, low-latency local feedback, or fault-tolerant-scale repeated cycles.
- **Timeline is uneven:** IBM publicly enabled mid-circuit measurement/reset in 2020, while some atomic implementations remained experimental or high-overhead in 2025.
- **The following caveat about nonuniformity is good but does not rescue “widely” without a provider/modality matrix.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Rapid maturation is a good story, presently impressionistic.

### Importance for adaptive algorithms and surface-code readout (line 193)

- **Correct:** These primitives sit on the critical path for teleportation, qubit reuse, iterative phase estimation, syndrome extraction, and measurement-based protocols.
- **Surface-code nuance:** Stabilizer extraction needs repeated ancilla measurement/reset, low data-idle error, leakage management, decoder throughput/backlog, and conditional correction/Pauli-frame updates—not necessarily one gate after every syndrome bit.
- **Measurement-based computation needs basis adaptivity/fanout and may consume batches of outcomes rather than one-bit branches.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Strong relevance statement.

### Vendor nondisclosure does not prove absence (line 193)

- **Excellent epistemic discipline:** Absence of public evidence is not evidence of absence.
- **Product segmentation/documentation explanations are plausible but speculative:** Label them as possibilities, as the text mostly does.
- **Also consider unsupported operation, unstable calibration, endpoint-definition ambiguity, or no service-level guarantee.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Fair-minded skepticism.

### Verify capability before architecture dependence (line 193)

- **Excellent actionable conclusion:** Require an executable acceptance test, not a sales statement.
- **Acceptance-test schema:** Branch types/width, repeated depth, latency distribution, fidelity, spectator preservation, reset/leakage, parallelism, compiler behavior, backend/revision, and service availability.
- **Test under representative load:** A one-qubit demo does not certify repeated many-qubit syndrome extraction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Strong engineering advice.

### Missing §22.11 artifacts and improvement opportunities

- **Pipeline diagram:** Measurement pulse → analog integration → digitization/classification → local/central logic or decoder → fanout → conditioned-pulse start.
- **Probability tree:** Correct and incorrect conditional reset branches, including transitions/leakage, replacing the false product rule.
- **Platform lifecycle table:** Raw detection, protected full MCM, reset, feedforward, spectator error, simultaneous width, exact endpoints.
- **Latency-versus-throughput plot:** Simple branch, parity, decoder, and batched feedback; average/tail/backlog.
- **Pauli-frame example:** Teleportation correction tracked virtually until a later non-Clifford dependency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **10/10 potential.** Decisions literally race decoherence while some qubits fluoresce and others hide—a superb hardware story.

### §22.11 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section separates measurement readiness from later conditional-dispatch latency and treats coherence as a decay scale, not a hard timer.
- **Highest-priority factual repair:** Remove the unsupported shared Willow/Heron 100–500-ns dispatch number and replace it with operation-specific, endpoint-defined primary measurements.
- **Highest-priority mathematical repair:** Replace active-reset fidelity as a product with a conditional probability tree/channel model.
- **Highest-priority timing repair:** Separate raw integration/detection from protected end-to-end MCM; the ion $50$–$500\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ band omits demonstrated millisecond-to-30-ms full-sequence overheads.
- **Highest-priority architectural repair:** Add spectator preservation, simultaneous width, decoder throughput/backlog, leakage, and branch-language capability to the purported “three numbers.”
- **Highest-priority algorithmic repair:** Explain Pauli-frame tracking so teleportation does not falsely appear to require immediate physical corrections.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.9/10 potential, 8.8/10 current.** This could be one of the chapter’s most exciting sections; unsupported flagship latency figures and conflated timing boundaries presently blunt it.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.12 “Calibration Stability and Drift” (lines 195–205)

### Section title: “Calibration Stability and Drift” (line 195)

- **Excellent inclusion:** Most benchmark chapters treat hardware metrics as timeless constants; this section correctly makes time a first-class axis.
- **Related but distinct terms:** Parameter drift, metric variability, calibration validity, uptime, and controller adaptation are not synonyms; define each.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The idea that a machine changes under the reader’s feet creates immediate tension.

### Monday-morning versus Friday-afternoon metric (line 197)

- **Strong, memorable opening:** It instantly communicates nonstationarity without jargon.
- **Time scale may be far shorter:** Superconducting relaxation rates have been observed to switch nearly an order of magnitude over tens of milliseconds, so days are only one scale: https://doi.org/10.1103/gk1b-stl3
- **Time-of-week confounders:** Maintenance, queue/job mix, cooldown state, environmental events, and recalibration policy—not the weekday itself—drive the difference.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Excellent human-scale hook.

### Definition of calibration stability (line 197)

- **Partly correct, but conflates plant and control policy:** Intrinsic parameter stability is how the physical/control parameters vary; “how often recalibration is required” also depends on target tolerance, monitor sensitivity, calibration cost, and feedback strategy.
- **Stability is multidimensional:** Bias, variance, jump rate, drift slope, autocorrelation time, spectral density, worst excursions, recovery time, and spatial correlation all matter.
- **Published-number maintenance is a policy threshold:** A device can drift yet remain within acceptance, or recalibrate frequently despite excellent raw stability to chase tighter performance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Good operational definition, needs separation of physics from policy.

### Example parameters: frequency, pulse amplitude, discriminator threshold (line 197)

- **Good concrete trio:** It spans device physics, coherent control, and classical readout.
- **Expand slightly:** $T_1/T_2$, coupler bias, two-qubit phase/leakage, crosstalk, resonator frequency, amplifier gain/phase, thermal population, timing skew, laser intensity/frequency, motional-mode frequency, and imaging threshold can drift.
- **Parameters and metrics differ:** A pulse amplitude drifts as a control parameter; gate fidelity drifts as an inferred performance metric. The causal map is many-to-many.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Specific knobs make calibration tangible.

### Recalibration cadence varies (line 199)

- **Correct and safely broad:** Cadence depends on modality, component, automation, target error, access model, and detected events.
- **One machine has many cadences:** Readout threshold, qubit frequency, one-qubit amplitude, entangling phase, crosstalk, and full bring-up may update on milliseconds, minutes, hours, days, or event triggers.
- **Event-triggered versus periodic:** Monitoring/control can recalibrate only when a statistic crosses a threshold, so “cadence” may be a distribution rather than a clock.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Sensible setup.

### Quantinuum continuously calibrates in parallel with user circuits (line 199)

- **Unverified vendor attribution:** No primary public source was found in the targeted check that documents this exact Quantinuum policy, endpoint, scope, and concurrency model.
- **“Continuous” and “in parallel” require definition:** Interleaved diagnostic shots, background monitoring, drift estimation, online parameter update, and literally simultaneous operations have different user impact.
- **Potential observer effect:** Calibration traffic may consume capacity or alter crosstalk/context; users need delivered workload performance, not merely the maintenance architecture.
- **Suggested repair:** Cite a Quantinuum systems paper/manual with exact policy or remove the named attribution.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Interesting operational contrast, currently hearsay-like.

### Most superconducting vendors use explicit windows every few hours (line 199)

- **Unsupported and contradicted by at least one official public description:** Google says its QCS devices undergo maintenance calibration every **few days**, while hardware can change significantly in the intervening hours or days: https://quantumai.google/cirq/tutorials/google/identifying_hardware_changes
- **“Most vendors” requires a surveyed cohort and date:** IBM, Google, Rigetti, IQM, OQC, and private/on-prem systems have different policies and may combine scheduled, automatic, and event-triggered routines.
- **Calibration window granularity:** Full-system downtime differs from local calibration, health checks, or per-job characterization.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Clear contrast, unreliable generalization.

### Sawtooth signature (line 199)

- **Good hypothesis:** Gradual degradation followed by recalibration recovery is a useful control-system mental model.
- **Not every calibration improves every metric:** Measurement noise, optimization failure, parameter coupling, overfitting, and changed operating points can produce no jump or a worse result.
- **Delivered fidelity is hard to observe directly:** User outcomes conflate workload, compiler/layout selection, queue timing, mitigation, and shot noise.
- **A figure would help:** Simulated monotone sawtooth, random walk, telegraph jump, periodic fluctuation, and event-triggered correction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10.** “Sawtooth” is the section’s best visual idea.

### Abrupt, nonmonotonic, or scheduler-hidden drift (line 199)

- **Excellent correction to the simple model:** TLS switching, quasiparticles, temperature/control changes, laser jumps, and recalibration interactions can cause abrupt and reversible behavior.
- **Scheduler masking cuts both ways:** The service may route around bad qubits or delay jobs, improving delivered results while reducing availability/latency; benchmark both quality and service behavior.
- **Primary evidence for rapid jumps:** Real-time monitoring found $T_1$ switches over tens of milliseconds: https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/gk1b-stl3
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The machine’s hidden weather is compelling.

### Treat sawtooth as a time-binned-data hypothesis (line 199)

- **Excellent epistemic language:** “Hypothesis to check, not a law” is exactly right.
- **Binning can erase the phenomenon:** Choose bin width from the drift spectrum/correlation time and display raw/event data where possible; a 24-hour bin cannot reveal millisecond jumps.
- **Statistical tests:** Change-point detection, autocorrelation, power spectral density, Allan deviation, and pre/post-calibration paired comparisons are better than visual impression alone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** Turns a metaphor into an investigation.

### Vendors “increasingly publish” time-binned metrics (line 201)

- **Unsupported trend claim:** Name providers, exact dashboards/datasheets, dates, and retained history; current snapshots and rolling medians are not the same as public time series.
- **Publication versus API access:** A value visible only at query time without archive/export is difficult to audit longitudinally.
- **Survivorship/selection:** Metrics may exclude offline qubits, failed calibrations, maintenance, or rejected runs; inclusion rules determine apparent stability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Encouraging trend if substantiated.

### Median over 24 hours (line 201)

- **Potentially useful robust center, arbitrary window:** The right horizon depends on workload length, drift timescale, calibration cadence, and service-level promise.
- **Median hides tails and multimodality:** A device alternating between excellent and poor regimes can share the same median as a stable mediocre device.
- **Needed companions:** Quantiles, worst-duration excursions, availability, sample count, time weighting, excluded intervals, and autocorrelation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Easy to understand; not enough alone.

### “95%-confidence band” (line 201)

- **Statistical category ambiguity:** A confidence interval for the mean/median is not a band containing 95% of future/device observations. If variability is intended, use a 2.5–97.5% empirical quantile/prediction interval.
- **Dependence breaks naive intervals:** Time-series samples are autocorrelated and calibrations create regime changes; bootstrap/block or time-series models may be required.
- **Simultaneous versus pointwise band:** A curve-wide 95% band differs from per-time-bin intervals.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Important but potentially technical; a small visual can clarify.

### Fraction of qubits passing throughout the window (line 201)

- **Useful yield/availability concept:** It captures whether usable width is sustained rather than briefly achieved.
- **Wording ambiguity:** “Passing through the window” could mean passing at every sample, at least once, or a time-weighted fraction; define numerator/denominator.
- **Correlated topology matters:** Twenty passing isolated qubits may not form a connected usable subgraph or support simultaneous gates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Converts drift into usable capacity.

### Time-binned values are “more honest” than instantaneous values (line 201)

- **Value-laden but directionally right:** Aggregates reveal sustained behavior, yet can also conceal short catastrophic periods; honesty depends on inclusion, resolution, and raw access.
- **Instantaneous data still matter:** Compilers and users need the calibration nearest execution time for layout and error modeling.
- **Best practice:** Publish current snapshot plus historical time series/distributions and methodology.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Strong stance, needs balance.

### Variational workloads span calibration cycles (line 201)

- **Plausible and important:** Hybrid optimization may run long enough that objective evaluations see different noise channels.
- **Not unique to variational algorithms:** Tomography, mitigation, benchmark sweeps, training datasets, QEC experiments, and large sampling jobs face the same issue.
- **Optimizer interaction:** Drift can mimic objective change, bias gradients, break line searches, and make convergence/history comparisons invalid.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Makes drift immediately relevant to users.

### Training–inference parameter drift (line 203)

- **Useful analogy, but potentially confusing:** Pulse parameters are calibrated/optimized rather than usually called a trained model; learned classical pre/postprocessors genuinely have training/inference distribution shift.
- **Separate three cases:** Stale pulse calibration, stale noise/readout-mitigation model, and ML model distribution shift.
- **Closed-loop adaptation risk:** Updating parameters during a job changes the effective experiment and can invalidate aggregation unless versions/timestamps are logged.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Familiar ML language helps some readers but blurs categories.

### Precomputed pulse parameters (line 203)

- **Correct concern:** Frequency/amplitude/phase/crosstalk drift makes fixed pulses stale.
- **Compiler abstraction caveat:** Cloud users often submit gates rather than pulses; provider-side recalibration may update implementations transparently, while cached transpilation/layout assumptions remain stale.
- **Robust control tradeoff:** Pulses can be optimized for tolerance to parameter variation, sometimes at duration/power/leakage cost.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Good link between low-level control and application reproducibility.

### Learned classical pre/post-processing (line 203)

- **Strong and underexplored point:** Readout classifiers, mitigation matrices, decoders, noise models, calibration-aware placement, and ML estimators can all face distribution shift.
- **Need validation protocol:** Holdout calibration states, online drift detectors, retraining triggers, versioned artifacts, and uncertainty/calibration tests.
- **Data leakage suspicion:** A model tuned and evaluated on the same calibration epoch can overstate generalization to later runs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Modern and practically valuable.

### Monday-trained model fails Friday; “real problem for VQE” (line 203)

- **Directionally sound, but VQE is only one example:** The severity depends on job duration, parameter reuse, objective sensitivity, mitigation, and recalibration/interleaving strategy.
- **Failure may be subtle:** Drift can bias energy estimates while apparent optimizer convergence remains smooth.
- **Suggested demonstration:** Simulate a drifting readout matrix/gate angle during VQE and show bias, noisy optimization, and mitigation retraining.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A model aging over a week is a relatable story.

### Every metric is conditional (line 205)

- **Excellent governing principle:** Device, subset, protocol, compiler, and timestamp are essential conditioning variables.
- **Add workload/context:** Simultaneous operation, circuit family/depth, native-gate parameters, mitigation, access mode, calibration state, environment, and estimator/confidence method.
- **Avoid “property of the machine” too absolutely:** Metrics are properties of a defined machine-system configuration and procedure; conditional properties remain real and useful.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Strong summary rule.

### Medians versus freshly calibrated best-case records (line 205)

- **Important reporting contrast:** Best demonstrated, typical delivered, worst/availability, and guaranteed/service-level performance answer different questions.
- **“Some/others” needs examples:** Cite exact reports rather than divide vendors into unnamed moral categories.
- **Fresh calibration is itself part of the experimental condition:** A record is legitimate when labeled, but not representative without sustained data.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Helps readers see through leaderboard compression.

### Long jobs can be worse—or better—than snapshots (line 205)

- **Excellent balanced caveat:** Drift is stochastic/nonmonotonic and recalibration can occur during the job.
- **Aggregation problem:** If parameters change mid-job, pooling shots assumes stationarity that may not hold; results should be segmented/versioned by calibration epoch.
- **Selection issue:** Retries or scheduler rerouting can preferentially keep good epochs, altering observed distribution.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Avoids one-directional doom narrative.

### Ask for the sustained distribution, not the headline (line 205)

- **Excellent practical demand, but a marginal distribution alone is insufficient:** Temporal order, correlation, change points, outage periods, calibration interventions, and topology determine job risk.
- **Request package:** Raw/aggregated time series, quantiles, autocorrelation/Allan deviation, calibration/event log, acceptance yield/topology, uptime, job-level delivered metrics, and reproducible schema.
- **Tie horizon to use case:** Sustained over a minute, hour, day, month, or repeated campaign.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** Strong closing maxim.

### Missing §22.12 artifacts and improvement opportunities

- **Drift-gallery plot:** Sawtooth, random walk, periodic noise, telegraph jump, abrupt failure, and event-triggered recovery.
- **Calibration hierarchy:** Fast local retune versus slow full bring-up, dependencies and service impact.
- **Statistical reporting panel:** Snapshot, rolling median, confidence interval, empirical prediction band, tail excursion, and availability—showing they answer different questions.
- **VQE case study:** Objective bias across calibration epochs with stale versus refreshed readout/pulse models.
- **Provider policy table:** Only sourced entries—maintenance cadence, online/interleaved monitoring, historical metric access, exclusions, and revision date.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **10/10 potential.** Quantum hardware as changing weather—complete with storms, forecasts, and interventions—is unusually vivid.

### §22.12 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The Monday/Friday hook, sawtooth-as-hypothesis caveat, and “every metric is conditional” rule correctly challenge timeless spec-sheet thinking.
- **Highest-priority evidence repair:** Remove or source the Quantinuum continuous-parallel calibration claim, the “most superconducting vendors every few hours” generalization, and the alleged common 24-hour reporting formats.
- **Highest-priority statistical repair:** Distinguish confidence intervals from empirical/prediction bands and add autocorrelation/change-point awareness; binning can hide rapid drift.
- **Highest-priority conceptual repair:** Separate physical stability, observed performance variability, recalibration policy, and delivered service behavior.
- **Highest-priority workflow repair:** Split stale pulse calibration, stale readout/noise model, and learned-model distribution shift rather than grouping all as training/inference.
- **Highest-priority reporting repair:** Ask for timestamped current snapshots plus sustained time series, distributions, calibration events, topology/yield, and job-level delivered performance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.9/10 potential, 9.2/10 current.** This is already one of the chapter’s best conceptual sections; sourced operational examples and a drift gallery would make it exceptional.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.13A “Benchmark suites” (lines 207–217)

### Section title and date range (line 207)

- **Scope is useful but internally mixed:** The section combines community suites, individual metrics, a historical QV chronology, and mutable vendor specifications.
- **“2024–2026 vendor cohort” conflicts with line 221’s “as of late 2025”:** Decide whether this is a late-2025 snapshot, a through-2026 survey, or a generated living table.
- **Static-book risk:** A year range in a heading guarantees visible staleness; move mutable cohort data to a generated appendix/data file and keep durable interpretive principles in the body.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** A benchmark league table is compelling, but date ambiguity undermines confidence immediately.

### Community suites give comparisons “more rigorous footing” (line 209)

- **Reasonable motivation, not automatic outcome:** Rigor requires identical versions, instances, compilation/mitigation policy, execution budget, timing boundary, statistical analysis, and raw data.
- **“Community-organized” does not fit every listed item equally:** QED-C and BACQ are consortial; Q-score originated at Atos; mirror circuits are a protocol family rather than one suite.
- **Cross-vendor comparability remains conditional:** Hardware-specific compilation and access constraints are part of full-stack performance but can also make causal comparison difficult.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Promising framing, needs a comparison contract.

### QED-C name and openness (line 211)

- **Name is correct:** Quantum Economic Development Consortium.
- **Open-source/application-oriented characterization is supported:** QED-C announced public availability of its suite and methodology in 2021: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/qed-c-introduces-a-novel-approach-to-measuring-performance-of-quantum-computers-301398063.html
- **Version/repository needed:** “Publishes” should link the canonical code, release/tag/commit, license, and benchmark-specification version rather than only name the organization.
- **Governance matters:** State who adds/changes benchmarks and how backward compatibility/time-series comparison is handled.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The consortium context lends credibility; runnable code would make it concrete.

### QED-C benchmark list (line 211)

- **Broadly plausible but liable to mix releases/extensions:** Bernstein–Vazirani, Grover, QFT, Hamiltonian simulation, amplitude estimation, VQE/chemistry, and optimization appear across QED-C materials, while the exact inclusion/status of Shor and MaxCut should be checked against the named release.
- **Do not flatten algorithms and applications:** QFT is a subroutine; VQE is a hybrid method; small-molecule instances and MaxCut are problem families; amplitude estimation has multiple variants.
- **Instance generators matter more than labels:** Oracle construction, graph ensemble/density, Hamiltonian, ansatz, parameter choice, and success observable can radically change difficulty.
- **Current research description:** The suite sweeps problem sizes/inputs and records result quality, execution time, and gate resources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08985
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Familiar algorithm names help, but a bare inventory becomes catalog-like.

### Per-benchmark metric as size grows (line 211)

- **Correct and important:** Heterogeneous applications need domain-appropriate success measures.
- **Normalization challenge:** Result metrics may have different ranges, baselines, statistical uncertainty, classical reference cost, and practical meaning; plotting them together does not make them commensurate.
- **Resource axis needed:** Size alone omits compiled width/depth/gates, shots, optimizer evaluations, runtime, and classical preprocessing/postprocessing.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Sensible, slightly abstract.

### Compressing heterogeneous results to largest passing size (line 211)

- **Excellent caution:** A scalar discards the benchmark fingerprint and can be controlled by one sparse/failing point.
- **Formal aggregation must be stated:** All benchmarks versus geometric mean versus selected subset, missing points, confidence margin, and interpolation determine the scalar.
- **Prefer a profile:** Performance curves/volumetric plots preserve which structures succeed and fail.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The warning supports the chapter’s core anti-headline theme.

### QED-C-derived suite underpins IonQ AQ (line 211)

- **Substantially correct with wording nuance:** IonQ says AQ draws significant inspiration from QED-C and changes depth/success criteria; it should not be presented as identical to the QED-C suite.
- **Cross-reference consistency:** §22.9 already needs the exact suite/version and formal width/$N^2$-CX box; repeat no looser definition here.
- **“Appears in some vendor documentation” is vague and disposable:** Name examples with dates or remove it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Useful genealogy, weak final clause.

### BACQ identity and consortium (line 213)

- **Core description supported:** BACQ is a French, application-oriented benchmarking project associated with the MetriQs-France program and a consortium including Thales, Eviden/Atos, CEA, CNRS, TERATEC, and LNE: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12205
- **“French/European” is imprecise:** It is a French national-strategy/France-2030 initiative with European relevance/partners; describe governance/funding exactly rather than slash-labeling.
- **“Thales, CEA, and partners” understates the named consortium:** Either list all principal organizations or link the paper.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Useful ecosystem context, currently thin.

### BACQ defines application-level references across architectures (line 213)

- **Intent is supported:** BACQ aims at industry-meaningful reference evaluation criteria across diverse hardware.
- **Maturity/status must be clear:** A project proposing/developing criteria is not necessarily a finalized, versioned, widely executed benchmark suite with cross-vendor public results.
- **Neutral-atom and photonic inclusion needs direct source:** The available abstract stresses platform diversity but the specific modalities should be cited from the suite specification.
- **Give one concrete benchmark/output:** Otherwise BACQ reads as an institutional name without teaching value.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** Worth mentioning, no operational payoff yet.

### Q-score definition (line 215)

- **Broad core is correct:** Atos Q-score uses MaxCut and reports the largest problem-variable count clearing a normalized performance criterion.
- **Algorithm/version nuance:** The original paper defines Q-score around QAOA and an improved approximation ratio; extensions to annealers/classical/hybrid solvers add execution-time/embedding conventions that can yield different scores.
- **Full contract omitted:** Graph distribution, number of instances, optimization budget, QAOA depth, shot count, wall-time boundary, classical optimizer, embedding/compilation, and confidence determine the score.
- **Primary paper:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12973
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** MaxCut supplies an intuitive application target.

### Q-score threshold $\beta^*=0.2$ (line 215)

- **Commonly reported threshold is supported:** Follow-up evaluations explicitly note Atos’s $\beta^*=0.2$ choice.
- **Threshold is conventional/arbitrary, not a usefulness law:** The annealer evaluation notes Atos chose it somewhat arbitrarily and that constraints materially change scores: https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07633
- **Define the normalized score formula:** Saying only “normalized score” leaves readers unable to interpret zero, one, or why 0.2 matters.
- **Notation collision warning is helpful:** Distinguishing this $\beta$ from a QAOA angle prevents a real confusion, but use $\beta^*$ consistently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The threshold invites critical examination.

### Q-score tracks “useful” capability (line 215)

- **Overclaim/value judgment:** MaxCut is application-oriented, but passing a random-graph normalized threshold does not establish economic utility, quantum advantage, or usefulness for other optimization distributions.
- **Classical baseline and time budget are essential:** An application metric should compare solution quality, time, energy/cost, and classical alternatives under matched constraints.
- **Atos’s original press release makes much stronger marketing claims than the evidence warrants; the book should not repeat them as neutral fact:** https://atos.net/en/2020/press-release_2020_12_04/atos-announces-q-score-the-only-universal-metrics-to-assess-quantum-performance-and-superiority
- **Suggested repair:** “One of the few metrics built around an optimization workload rather than an abstract random-circuit capacity test.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Application framing is attractive; “useful” needs discipline.

### Generic mirror benchmark description (line 217)

- **Compute–uncompute core is right:** A circuit followed by its inverse has a known ideal return state and cheap classical verification.
- **Protocol families are being blended:** Simple Loschmidt/echo or mirrored application circuits, randomized mirror circuits, mirror RB, and periodic mirror circuits have different construction and estimators.
- **Random Pauli placement wording is inaccurate:** Formal randomized mirror circuits interleave/dress layers throughout and resample Pauli layers under a prescribed construction, not merely put Pauli layers “in between” $U$ and $U^\dagger$.
- **Primary formal protocol:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09853
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Running a computation backward is inherently memorable.

### Known ideal all-zero answer (line 217)

- **Correct for a $|0^n\rangle$ start and exact compiled inverse under the intended logical construction.**
- **Compilation caveat:** Independently compiling $U^\dagger$ may not produce the exact native inverse of the realized noisy/approximated $U$; formal mirror protocols specify inversion to control this.
- **SPAM remains:** Return probability includes preparation/readout unless decay fitting/normalization separates it.
- **Effective polarization may be preferable to raw all-zero success:** Formal mirror RB can use Hamming-distance-weighted statistics and depth-decay fits.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** A crisp expected answer is satisfying.

### Round-trip noise interpretation (line 217)

- **Correct but not simply twice forward-circuit error:** Forward/inverse gate sets, time ordering, coherent cancellation/reinforcement, drift, and SPAM affect the result.
- **Application prediction is limited:** The inverse half creates an error context absent from the original workload.
- **Layer-error inference requires assumptions and multiple depths/instances, not one return probability.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Useful caution against literal halving.

### Exposing coherent errors that randomized benchmarks average away (line 217)

- **Too broad and internally tense:** Some mirror constructions randomize/twirl coherent errors and aim at average layer infidelity; simple periodic/mirror sequences may amplify certain coherent errors, while exact inverse pairs may cancel others.
- **RB does not merely “average errors away”:** Randomization converts coherent accumulation into interpretable decay under assumptions; it can still reveal an elevated error rate while losing directional diagnosis.
- **Specify which mirror variant diagnoses what:** Randomized mirror RB for scalable average layer error/crosstalk; periodic/repeated sequences for coherent amplification; application mirrors for workload-shaped return tests.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Error cancellation versus amplification is fascinating, but the current sentence oversimplifies.

### Exact inverse cancellation and randomized variants (line 217)

- **Excellent caveat:** A systematic overrotation can partially cancel when followed by the physical inverse, producing an optimistically clean echo.
- **Randomization does more than prevent cancellation:** It shapes/twirls errors, enables ensemble/depth fits, and can make scalable inference possible.
- **Crosstalk evidence:** Randomized mirror circuits have been used to estimate many-qubit layer error and identify substantial crosstalk contribution: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07272
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** The machine undoing both computation and its own mistake is an excellent conceptual twist.

### Missing suite-comparison framework for §22.13A

- **Comparison-contract table:** Owner/governance, version, circuit/application distribution, score, threshold/confidence, resource/time boundary, mitigation, raw data, supported modalities.
- **Suite-versus-metric taxonomy:** QED-C/BACQ suites, Q-score scalar application benchmark, mirror protocol family, QV/AQ/CLOPS/XEB metrics.
- **Instance fingerprint:** Width, logical/native depth/gates, topology, parameters, classical optimizer, shots, runtime, score uncertainty.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10.** A “benchmark chooses its champion” comparison would make metric bias vivid.

### §22.13A local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section broadens the reader beyond vendor headline metrics and correctly warns that scalar summaries compress heterogeneous benchmark behavior.
- **Highest-priority taxonomy repair:** Do not present QED-C, BACQ, Q-score, and mirror circuits as the same kind of “suite.”
- **Highest-priority reproducibility repair:** Add exact versions, repositories, instances, score formulas, thresholds, budgets, compilation/mitigation rules, and raw-data requirements.
- **Highest-priority Q-score repair:** Define $\beta$, label $0.2$ conventional, specify graph/optimizer/time rules, and replace “useful capability” with workload-specific evidence.
- **Highest-priority mirror repair:** Separate compute–uncompute, randomized mirror RB, periodic mirrors, and application mirrors; correct the Pauli-layer construction and diagnostic claims.
- **Highest-priority BACQ repair:** State project maturity and provide one concrete implemented benchmark/result rather than only institutional intent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10 potential, 8.7/10 current.** Reverse circuits and competing benchmark philosophies are highly engaging; organizational catalog prose and taxonomy blur suppress the payoff.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.13B “QV milestone record” (line 219)

### Milestone-list framing

- **A timeline is the right artifact, but one long sentence is too brittle:** It mixes vendors, systems, announcements, demonstrations, launch events, and grouped ranges without consistent dates or sources.
- **Define record criterion:** Highest publicly claimed QV, peer-reviewed result, vendor-released raw data, accessible production system, or independent reproduction can produce different timelines.
- **Use $d^*$ alongside QV:** The exponent is the directly interpretable passing width/depth; the exponential headline obscures incremental scale.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A record chase is inherently compelling.

### IBM Falcon QV 32, January 2020

- **Broadly supported:** IBM announced QV 32 at CES on 8 January 2020, associated with its 28-qubit Raleigh/Falcon-era system: https://brasil.newsroom.ibm.com/2020-01-08-Do-laboratorio-para-a-industria-IBM-anuncia-ultimos-avancos-em-computacao-quantica
- **System naming needs precision:** Identify backend/processor revision and whether “Falcon” is the processor family rather than the public system name.
- **Translate:** QV 32 means $2^5$, a passing size of five—not a 32-qubit benchmark.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Good starting gun.

### Honeywell H0 QV 64 later in 2020

- **Supported with exact date:** Honeywell reported H0 QV 64 on 14 June 2020: https://www.honeywell.com/us/en/insights/articles/the-worlds-highest-performing-quantum-computer-is-here
- **“Later” is needlessly vague:** Give June 2020 and six physical qubits/$d^*=6$.
- **Marketing language should not be inherited:** Honeywell called it “twice as powerful”; the book should say the conventional QV number doubled while passing size rose from five to six.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The cross-vendor handoff is engaging.

### “$128$–$512$ across both vendors through 2021”

- **Chronologically inaccurate/overcompressed:** Honeywell demonstrated QV 128 in September 2020, not merely during 2021: https://www.honeywell.com/us/en/insights/articles/achieving-quantum-volume-128-on-the-honeywell-quantum-computer
- **IBM’s QV 512 belongs to 2022:** IBM’s 2022 annual letter says it improved from 128 to 512 that year: https://research.ibm.com/blog/research-annual-letter-2022
- **Range erases distinct records:** At minimum enumerate Honeywell H1 QV128 (September/October 2020), later Honeywell/Quantinuum H-series values, IBM QV128/256/512 with dates, and avoid suggesting both vendors independently covered every endpoint.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Compression destroys the timeline’s narrative and accuracy.

### Quantinuum H1-2 QV 4096 in 2022

- **Supported by the vendor announcement:** H1-2 passed QV 4096 with a reported HOP of 69.04% and high confidence: https://www.quantinuum.com/blog/quantinuum-announces-quantum-volume-4096-achievement
- **Add exact date, physical qubits, suite/protocol version, and raw-data link.**
- **Distinguish H1-1 and H1-2:** The timeline switches systems; a reader can otherwise infer monotonic upgrades of one machine.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A jump to $d^*=12$ is meaningful when decoded.

### Quantinuum H1-1 $2^{19}$ in 2023

- **Correct and well documented:** Quantinuum announced H1-1 QV $2^{19}=524{,}288$ on 30 June 2023 and linked raw details/data: https://www.quantinuum.com/blog/quantinuum-h-series-quantum-computer-accelerates-through-3-more-performance-records-for-quantum-volume
- **Intermediate context:** The same announcement says H1-1 moved through $2^{17}$, $2^{18}$, and $2^{19}$ and had reported $2^{14}$/$2^{15}$ earlier in 2023.
- **Self-report caveat:** The vendor says runs were interwoven with customer jobs and not special calibration; this is useful methodology but remains a vendor statement unless independently audited.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Rapid sequential passes make a strong engineering story.

### “$2^{21}$ at the H2 56-qubit launch in 2024”

- **Materially false conflation:** H2 launched in **May 2023** with **32 qubits** and QV **$2^{16}=65{,}536$**: https://www.quantinuum.com/blog/quantinuum-launches-the-most-benchmarked-quantum-computer-in-the-world-and-publishes-all-the-data
- **The 56-qubit event was an upgrade, not launch:** Quantinuum’s product-change notice dates the H2-1 $N=56$ upgrade to 29 May 2024: https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/pcns/H2%20Product%20Change%20Notification%202024_05_01%20System%20Model%20H2%20N%3D56%20Upgrade.pdf
- **$2^{21}$ is separately evidenced by March 2025:** Quantinuum described H2 as achieving $2{,}097{,}152=2^{21}$ on 18 March 2025: https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-selected-as-a-founding-collaborator-for-nvidia-accelerated-quantum-research-center
- **Required repair:** Split launch, qubit-count upgrade, and QV milestone into separate dated rows.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Big milestone, currently a composite event that never happened.

### H2 $2^{25}=33{,}554{,}432$ in 2025

- **Correct with a precise month:** Quantinuum reports that its 56-qubit H2 achieved $2^{25}$ in September 2025: https://www.quantinuum.com/glossary-item/quantum-volume
- **Name the exact H2 instance:** H2-1 versus H2-2 and result date/file should be extracted from the public hardware-data index.
- **Again decode:** This certifies $d^*=25$ under the declared protocol, not 33 million qubits or generic operations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Strong climax when interpreted correctly.

### Progression tells a fidelity/high-connectivity story

- **Reasonable inference, not a complete causal result:** QV improvement depends on gate/SPAM error, connectivity/routing, compiler, qubit subset, crosstalk, calibration, and protocol—not fidelity alone.
- **High connectivity reduces compiled overhead, but ion transport/shuttling and scheduling remain physical costs.**
- **“Real story” is rhetorically confident:** Say the sequence is evidence of sustained full-stack improvement on this benchmark.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Good interpretive payoff with multicausal wording.

### Most other vendors no longer report QV

- **Unsubstantiated cohort-wide claim:** Establish which vendors ever reported QV, their last result, current metric portfolio, and formal retirement statements.
- **Some vendors may never have adopted it:** “No longer” falsely implies previous reporting.
- **Absence reasons are not observed:** Verification cost, architectural fit, marketing strategy, access, benchmark preference, or inability to pass higher sizes are hypotheses.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Metric abandonment is interesting, but requires evidence.

### Each architecture chooses favorable metrics

- **Plausible political-economy inference:** Vendors naturally emphasize metrics aligned with their products, but this should be labeled interpretation.
- **Do not equate architectural suitability with fairness:** A benchmark favoring one strength can still expose a genuine application-relevant capability; the question is target workload and full disclosure.
- **Needed visual:** Vendor-by-year matrix of reported/not-reported metrics, with explicit source and “never adopted” versus “retired.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** A benchmark strategy map would be excellent.

### Missing QV timeline artifacts

- **One row per event:** Announcement/result date, vendor/system/revision, physical qubits, $d^*$, QV, HOP/confidence, protocol version, compiler/mitigation, raw-data/reproduction status.
- **Separate event types:** New product launch, qubit-count upgrade, benchmark record, cloud availability, and peer-reviewed publication.
- **Generated source:** Store timeline as structured data and render body/appendix tables to prevent contradictory hand-edited dates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10.** A clean race chart would outperform the dense sentence dramatically.

### §22.13B local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The timeline tries to show sustained full-stack progress and changing vendor incentives rather than merely list current scores.
- **Highest-priority factual repair:** Correct H2: launch May 2023 at 32 qubits/$2^{16}$; upgrade to 56 qubits May 2024; $2^{21}$ documented March 2025; $2^{25}$ September 2025.
- **Highest-priority chronology repair:** Move Honeywell QV128 to September 2020 and IBM QV512 to 2022; eliminate the vague “through 2021” range.
- **Highest-priority interpretive repair:** Decode every QV into $d^*$ and avoid treating doubling QV as doubling generic power.
- **Highest-priority provenance repair:** Define record eligibility and link raw data/protocol/confidence for each event.
- **Highest-priority inference repair:** Treat vendor metric selection and architectural fit as hypotheses supported by a reporting-history matrix, not established motive.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10 potential, 8.3/10 current.** The record race should be thrilling; conflated dates currently turn it into a trust trap.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.13C “2024–2026 vendor cohort” (lines 221–230)

### Cohort label “as of late 2025; subject to revision” (line 221)

- **Internal date mismatch:** A section titled through 2026 cannot rely on a late-2025 snapshot without explicitly saying 2026 entries are planned/announced rather than observed.
- **“Subject to revision” is not a maintenance mechanism:** Give one exact cutoff date, source retrieval dates, and a generated table or remove volatile values from the body.
- **Current review date exposes staleness:** As of 2026-07-23, Heron r3, Quantinuum Helios, IonQ Tempo product information, newer IQM/AWS devices, and other systems make the cohort incomplete.
- **Selection criteria absent:** Explain why these vendors/products are included while Rigetti, D-Wave, AQT, Alice & Bob, Atom Computing, Pasqal, photonic vendors, silicon-spin systems, and others are omitted.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A cohort table is useful, but arbitrary membership and stale dating invite league-table confusion.

### IBM Heron r2 identity and 156 qubits (line 223)

- **Correct historical specification:** IBM documents Heron r2 as a July-2024 156-qubit heavy-hex revision: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/processor-types
- **Not the late-2025 leading revision:** Heron r3 arrived in July 2025, so selecting r2 in a “late 2025” cohort requires a reason or is stale.
- **“Physical qubits” needs active/available distinction:** Fabricated count, enabled count, backend-reported qubits, and the subset used for a metric may differ.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Clear hardware identity, already superseded within the stated cutoff.

### IBM “heavy-hex coupling” (line 223)

- **Correct topology label, but §22.2’s earlier heavy-hex geometry description must be repaired consistently.**
- **Connectivity is more than a noun:** Report degree distribution, disabled couplers, native CZ direction/symmetry, simultaneous-layer constraints, and usable connected subgraphs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Familiar topology reference, no new insight here.

### IBM $F_{2q}\approx0.997$ (line 223)

- **Undefined aggregate:** Mean/median/best/worst, qubit-pair cohort, RB/EPLG/process metric, isolated/simultaneous context, and calibration timestamp are missing.
- **Current IBM reporting emphasizes distributions/layered errors:** IBM reports for a later Heron that 57 of 176 couplings were below $10^{-3}$ error and EPLG 2.15×$10^{-3}$ at 100 qubits, showing why one $0.997$ scalar is inadequate: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/latest-updates
- **Fidelity conversion danger:** Do not convert heterogeneous error metrics to $1-e$ without checking definitions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Compact, not interpretable.

### IBM $T_2^{\rm echo}\sim250\,\mu$s (line 223)

- **Untraceable as a processor scalar:** Coherence varies across qubits and time; source the median/distribution and exact echo protocol/backend/date.
- **Current documentation mentions roughly 350 μs $T_2$ on Pittsburgh, illustrating rapid revision and backend specificity, but does not make all Herons 350 μs:** https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/latest-updates
- **Do not combine best values from different Heron instances into a synthetic device row.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Useful scale only with distribution/protocol.

### IBM CLOPS $\sim200{,}000$ (line 223)

- **Stale under the row’s own late-2025 cutoff:** IBM says 200,000 was the end-of-2024 value and reported 330,000 later in 2025: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/qdc-2025
- **Revision/protocol required:** Current $\mathrm{CLOPS}_h$ uses a hardware-aware 100×100 circuit; do not mix with original QV-tied CLOPS.
- **Backend versus fleet record:** Attribute the exact number to a backend/revision/software stack and date.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Speed headline is attractive, plainly stale.

### IBM sub-microsecond conditional dispatch (line 223)

- **Unsupported:** The targeted official-source check found dynamic-circuit support and qualitative latency constraints, not a public Heron r2/r3 measurement under §22.11’s precise endpoint.
- **Cross-reference compounds an earlier defect:** §22.11’s shared Willow/Heron 100–500-ns claim is itself unsupported.
- **Remove until sourced:** Provide measurement-bit-ready to conditioned-pulse-start latency, branch operation, controller/firmware, average/tail, and date.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Impressive if true, currently rumor-like.

### “IBM no longer reports QV” (line 223)

- **Needs explicit policy source:** IBM shifted emphasis to EPLG/layer fidelity and updated CLOPS, but absence of a new record is not necessarily a formal no-reporting rule.
- **Historical backend metadata may still expose QV:** Distinguish “no longer a headline roadmap metric” from “does not report anywhere.”

### Google Willow 105 physical qubits (line 224)

- **Chip count supported:** Google’s Willow materials describe a 105-qubit processor.
- **Two devices/experiments matter:** Google’s public early-access guidance distinguishes a QEC device and an RCS device with different gates/errors; a single “Willow” row can synthesize incompatible measurements.
- **Active widths differ by experiment:** Report number of active data/measure/leakage-removal qubits for QEC, and active RCS qubits separately.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Recognizable flagship, needs experimental identity.

### Willow “square lattice” (line 224)

- **Too coarse:** The chip is a two-dimensional grid/array, but active QEC patches, coupler layout, boundary/leakage-removal qubits, and RCS device geometry are not captured by “square lattice.”
- **Avoid conflict with §22.2’s connectivity taxonomy:** Give degree/coupling graph and disabled elements rather than a shape adjective.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Familiar picture, underspecified.

### Willow $F_{2q}\approx0.9986$ (line 224)

- **Matches one operation/device context only:** Google’s early-access document reports mean simultaneous two-qubit error 0.14% for an iSWAP-like gate on Device 2, giving 99.86%; Device 1 reports 0.33% for CZ, giving 99.67%: https://quantumai.google/static/site-assets/downloads/willow-early-access-program-instructions.pdf
- **Thus the row cherry-picks or silently selects the RCS-device figure:** Name device, native gate, simultaneous mean, date, and distribution.
- **Do not call $1-$reported error “fidelity” without the metric definition.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Strong number, hidden context.

### Willow distance-7 below-threshold surface-code demonstration (line 224)

- **Broadly supported but grammatically imprecise:** The Willow work compared distance-3/5/7 memories and demonstrated logical-error suppression with increasing distance; distance 7 alone is not what “below threshold” means.
- **Specify experiment:** Logical memory type, rounds/cycles, real-time/offline decoding, postselection/leakage handling, logical error per cycle, and physical-qubit allocation.
- **Primary paper:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y
- **“Supports” could imply product capability:** Say “was used in a research demonstration.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The below-threshold scaling story deserves numbers and a plot.

### Quantinuum H2 56 qubits (line 225)

- **Correct after the May-2024 upgrade:** https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/pcns/H2%20Product%20Change%20Notification%202024_05_01%20System%20Model%20H2%20N%3D56%20Upgrade.pdf
- **Instance/date needed:** H2-1 and H2-2 may have different availability/results; name the system used for each benchmark.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Straightforward.

### H2 all-to-all “via shuttling” (line 225)

- **Directionally correct but compressed:** QCCD transport routes ions into interaction zones; all logical pairs are supported, but gates are not performed arbitrarily everywhere or all simultaneously.
- **Report concurrency and transport:** Zone count, parallel two-qubit operations, movement/cooling/scheduling overhead, and pair dependence matter.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Moving ions through a racetrack is much more vivid than the phrase suggests.

### H2 $F_{2q}\approx0.999$ (line 225)

- **Plausible rounded figure:** Quantinuum described H2 physical two-qubit errors below $10^{-3}$ in later roadmap material.
- **Still undefined:** Gate/angle, RB protocol, mean/median, all-pairs/simultaneous performance, instance, date, and uncertainty are necessary.
- **Do not silently pair H2’s best contemporary fidelity with QV from a possibly different H2 instance/date.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Impressive, insufficiently auditable.

### H2 echo coherence “seconds” (line 225)

- **Too vague to compare:** Seconds could mean 1, 10, or 100; protocol, encoding, DD/echo pulse count, qubit state, and gate compatibility matter.
- **The H2 product row should link an exact data sheet/performance-validation record, not a platform stereotype.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Long coherence sounds impressive but teaches little.

### H2 QV $2^{25}$ (line 225)

- **Correct as a September-2025 vendor result:** https://www.quantinuum.com/glossary-item/quantum-volume
- **Decode and attribute:** $d^*=25$, exact H2 instance/date, HOP/confidence, protocol version, and raw-data file.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Strong anchor.

### H2 logical qubits with multi-second coherent operation (line 225)

- **Too vague and potentially category-blending:** Name code, number of physical/logical qubits, protected operation/memory, duration, logical observable/error rate, decoder, postselection, and break-even baseline.
- **“Coherent operation” could mean memory, logical gates, repeated cycles, or an application experiment; these are not interchangeable.**
- **Appendix reference cannot replace minimum body specifics.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Intriguing claim with no inspectable content.

### Helios “announced for late 2025” (line 225)

- **Stale even at the stated late-2025 cutoff:** Quantinuum commercially launched Helios on 5 November 2025 and said it was available via cloud and on-premise offerings: https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-announces-commercial-launch-of-new-helios-quantum-computer-that-offers-unprecedented-accuracy-to-enable-generative-quantum-ai-genqai
- **Delivered specifications:** 98 physical qubits, vendor-reported 99.921% two-qubit and 99.9975% one-qubit fidelity, with explicit logical demonstrations.
- **Current product documentation adds operational structure:** all-to-all connectivity, four parallel two-qubit zones, seconds-scale $T_2$, dynamic control, and junction transport: https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/data_sheets/Quantinuum%20Helios%20Product%20Data%20Sheet.pdf
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A successor launch should be a major event, not stale roadmap prose.

### IonQ Forte/Forte Enterprise 36 qubits and all-to-all (line 226)

- **Supported by IonQ’s current product comparison:** Both list 36 physical qubits and all-to-all connectivity: https://www.ionq.com/quantum-systems/compare
- **Forte and Enterprise should be separate rows if access/deployment/support differ:** A shared hardware class does not make product availability identical.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Clear comparison point.

### IonQ AQ 36 (line 226)

- **Supported for Forte-class current product claims:** https://www.ionq.com/quantum-systems/forte
- **Formal context still required:** AQ suite/version, width/$N^2$ CX box, $F-\epsilon>1/e$, date, data, and achieved versus product specification.
