### IonQ $F_{2q}\approx0.997$ (line 226)

- **Does not match the current Forte product value:** IonQ lists 99.6% two-qubit gate fidelity / 0.4% error, i.e. approximately 0.996, not 0.997: https://www.ionq.com/quantum-systems/compare
- **Metric source differs:** Forte’s detailed page says the error comes from direct randomized benchmarking; cite protocol and uncertainty.
- **Do not average/round upward without a source.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Small numerical mismatch matters in a benchmark sheet.

### Forte Enterprise as data-center deployment variant (line 226)

- **Broadly supported by vendor positioning:** It is described as rack-mounted/on-premise/data-center-ready.
- **Availability ambiguity:** IonQ’s current comparison labels Forte Enterprise availability separately; give order/delivery/cloud/on-prem status and date rather than only “variant.”
- **Operational metrics missing:** Footprint, uptime, throughput, integration/API, support, power/environment, and service-level performance are more relevant to the deployment distinction than qubit count alone.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Enterprise label without operational detail feels brochure-like.

### IQM “Crystal / Star” as product families (line 227)

- **Taxonomy error:** Crystal and Star are QPU topologies/architectures, while named systems include Garnet, Sirius, Deneb, Radiance, Spark, and others.
- **IQM describes Crystal-20 as nearest-neighbor lattice and Star-24 as resonator-mediated architecture:** https://meetiqm.com/blog/how-iqm-is-tackling-quantum-error-correction/
- **Rewrite as architecture-plus-product rows:** For example, Garnet 20 (Crystal), Sirius 16 (Star), and separately announced/deployed Radiance configurations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Interesting architectures, misleading labels.

### IQM “roughly 20–150 qubits” (line 227)

- **Mixes deployed devices, topology research, products, and roadmap/delivery:** IQM announced 150-qubit Radiance and a 2026 delivery, while cloud-accessible systems have included 16/20/54-qubit devices.
- **The row itself admits status variation, which is a sign the aggregation should be split rather than retained.**
- **Current expansion exceeds the framing:** IQM announced 300-qubit delivery for 2027, outside the snapshot but relevant to generated roadmap data: https://meetiqm.com/press-releases/iqm-to-deliver-world-leading-300-qubit-quantum-computer-to-finland/
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** Range without status is fog.

### IQM two-qubit fidelity around 0.995 (line 227)

- **Supported for one named system, not the whole family:** IQM’s Garnet 20Q white paper reports median 99.5% two-qubit fidelity: https://meetiqm.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/IQM-Garnet-20Q-Whitepaper-2024.pdf
- **Star operations differ:** Qubit–resonator gates, MOVE operations, and effective qubit–qubit compilation need their own metrics; carrying Crystal CZ fidelity across Star is invalid.
- **Use per-product metric distributions and protocols.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** One representative value masquerades as a portfolio spec.

### QuEra Aquila neutral-atom analog mode (line 228)

- **Correct and important category distinction:** AWS describes Aquila as a special-purpose analog Hamiltonian-simulation device, not a universal gate computer: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/11/amazon-braket-neutral-atom-quantum-processor-named-aquila-quera-computing-inc/
- **Use “up to 256 qubits,” not “256 atoms”:** Filling/pre-sequence results can include vacancies; available sites, successfully loaded atoms, and participating qubits differ.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Neutral atoms add welcome architectural variety.

### Aquila Rydberg interactions (line 228)

- **Correct physical mechanism, too terse:** Users program atom geometry plus time-dependent global/local drive/detuning parameters of a Rydberg Hamiltonian.
- **Connectivity is geometry/range dependent rather than a fixed digital coupling graph.**
- **Official program definition:** https://docs.aws.amazon.com/braket/latest/developerguide/braket-quera-submitting-analog-program-aquila.html
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Programmable atoms under a Hamiltonian deserve a visual.

### Analog evolution time versus digital gate count (line 228)

- **Correct warning but insufficient replacement metric set:** Report preparation/filling probability, atom loss, SPAM, Hamiltonian parameter accuracy, coherence/evolution range, geometry constraints, shots/success rate, analog observable accuracy, throughput, and classical reference.
- **Digital gate count is not merely “fraught” but often undefined for the native program.**
- **Aquila can multiplex smaller instances spatially, adding a throughput dimension absent from the row:** https://aws.amazon.com/braket/quantum-computers/quera/
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The category contrast is excellent.

### Vendor-published caveat (line 230)

- **Correct provenance warning:** Self-reported results need protocols, raw data, and independent replication.
- **Not all listed evidence is only a vendor claim:** Some results appear in peer-reviewed papers with public data, while product specifications/roadmaps remain vendor statements. Label evidence tier per cell.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Healthy skepticism.

### “Peak performance on a well-calibrated machine” (line 230)

- **Overgeneralized:** Some rows quote means/medians/typical specs, some best records, some one experiment, and some roadmap targets.
- **Benchmark choice may be standardized rather than arbitrary:** QV, RB, and surface-code protocols have community definitions even if vendors select which to emphasize.
- **Separate best demonstrated, typical specified, fleet median, sustained delivered, and target.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Strong caution, inaccurate uniform characterization.

### Independent reproduction “lags by months” (line 230)

- **Unsupported universal time estimate:** Replication may be impossible due to access/data, immediate on public cloud, performed by collaborators, or never occur.
- **Define reproduction:** Reanalysis of raw data, rerunning circuits on same system, independent hardware implementation, or peer review are different.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Specific duration sounds authoritative without evidence.

### “Silent regressions happen” (line 230)

- **Drift/regression is real; “silent” imputes nondisclosure:** Performance can change because of calibration, hardware/firmware, qubit disablement, metric definition, or service routing.
- **Use observable language:** “Public snapshots may not expose all intervening regressions; preserve time series and acceptance logs.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Punchy but accusatory.

### Vendor numbers as upper bounds, not job performance (line 230)

- **Good practical direction, mathematically wrong label:** A best record is evidence of demonstrated capability under conditions, not a strict upper bound; a later or lucky user run can exceed it, while median/typical values are not upper bounds at all.
- **Better taxonomy:** demonstrated point, specified typical/max error, roadmap target, and delivered distribution.
- **Job prediction needs:** exact backend/time, qubit subset, calibration, compiler/mitigation, circuit family, shots, access mode, queue/runtime, and acceptance tests.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Strong closing lesson after terminology repair.

### Missing cohort-table engineering

- **Structured schema:** Vendor/system/revision; modality; status (research/announced/orderable/cloud/on-prem); physical/active qubits; connectivity/concurrency; native gates; component metric distributions; system benchmark; dynamic capabilities; throughput; as-of date.
- **Evidence tier per cell:** Product spec, vendor experiment, peer-reviewed paper, raw public data, independent reproduction.
- **No synthetic rows:** Never combine fidelity, coherence, QV, CLOPS, and latency from different backends/dates into a fictional “representative machine.”
- **Automated freshness:** Store sources/retrieval dates and render the appendix/body from maintained data; fail lint when “current” rows age beyond a threshold.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10.** A transparent, filterable “benchmark card” would be both useful and fun.

### §22.13C local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The cohort acknowledges that analog and gate-model devices need different metrics and explicitly warns that vendor numbers do not predict a user job.
- **Highest-priority currency repair:** Replace Heron r2/200k, announced Helios, and Forte-only status with a consistent cutoff that includes Heron r3, launched 98-qubit Helios, and achieved/product-status Tempo information—or move all mutable rows to generated data.
- **Highest-priority factual repair:** IonQ Forte’s current quoted two-qubit fidelity is 99.6%, not 99.7%; Willow’s 99.86% belongs to one iSWAP-like RCS device while the QEC device’s CZ error is 0.33%; IQM Crystal/Star are topologies, not one product family.
- **Highest-priority provenance repair:** Remove unsupported IBM conditional latency and define every component metric by method, aggregation, subset, backend, and date.
- **Highest-priority status repair:** Separate achieved research result, vendor specification, cloud availability, commercial launch, on-prem delivery, and roadmap target.
- **Highest-priority comparison repair:** Replace synthetic single rows with per-system evidence-tiered cards and a distinct analog schema for Aquila.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10 potential, 8.1/10 current.** Cross-architecture comparison is inherently fascinating; stale and synthetic rows make the reader spend that attention debugging provenance.

### §22.13 whole-section synthesis

- **Pedagogical strength:** The section recognizes that benchmark choice encodes a workload and that a scalar never eliminates protocol dependence.
- **Structural weakness:** It combines benchmark taxonomies, a historical record race, and a volatile product catalog; these age and fail in different ways and should be three artifacts.
- **Reliability concern:** The H2 launch/$2^{21}$ conflation, Aria/AQ issue inherited from §22.9, stale CLOPS/Helios status, and unsupported latency show that mutable manual tables are already failing.
- **Recommended architecture:** Durable body discussion of benchmark principles; versioned suite cards; generated milestone/vendor appendix from structured sourced data.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.9/10 potential, 8.4/10 current.** Benchmark politics, reverse circuits, record races, ion racetracks, superconducting grids, and analog atom arrays could make a superb comparative chapter centerpiece once provenance is engineered rather than narrated loosely.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 22, §22.14 “How to Read a Benchmark Sheet” (lines 232–260)

### Section title and bridge function (line 232)

- **Excellent closing purpose:** A procedural checklist converts the chapter’s definitions into a reader behavior.
- **“Benchmark sheet” versus “vendor sheet”:** The body alternates terms; a vendor datasheet, live backend calibration page, benchmark paper, and product announcement require different evidence standards.
- **Bridge belongs here:** The move from hardware claims to compilation in Chapter 23 is natural.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Readers like leaving a dense chapter with a usable method.

### Metrics are read together (line 234)

- **Correct governing idea:** No scalar predicts workload performance alone.
- **Interaction effects deserve one phrase:** Connectivity changes compiled gate count; speed changes decoherence exposure; calibration drift changes every input; mitigation changes shot/runtime cost.
- **“Compressed” honestly signals simplification, but the compression must not reintroduce absolutes the chapter just dismantled.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Good synthesis setup.

### First: physical qubit count and coupling graph (line 236)

- **Good first-pass inventory for digital gate-model hardware:** Width and native interaction structure strongly constrain compilation.
- **Not universal across modalities:** Analog Hamiltonian devices, modular/networked machines, photonic time-bin systems, bosonic modes, dynamic ion transport, qubit reuse, and distributed systems do not reduce cleanly to one static coupling graph.
- **Count taxonomy must persist:** Fabricated/installed, active, user-available, algorithmic/logical, and simultaneously controllable qubits differ.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Sensible start, gate-model centric.

### “These cap what is possible” (line 236)

- **Too absolute:** Mid-circuit reset/reuse can realize circuits with more logical wires over time; circuit cutting/distribution changes resource shape; error correction reduces logical width; analog encodings differ.
- **Better wording:** They constrain the immediately available physical width and routing overhead under the stated execution model.
- **Capability also depends on control graph:** Simultaneous operations, direction/native gate, disabled edges, crosstalk, zones, and dynamic connectivity matter beyond adjacency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Strong rule, overstates.

### Ignore “1000 qubits” without a coupling diagram (line 236)

- **Memorable skepticism, overly dismissive:** The absence is a serious documentation gap, but count can still matter for analog simulation, independent sensing, multiplexing, memory, or future calibration even without a digital coupling graph.
- **A diagram is not enough:** Require machine-readable connectivity/native operations, active/disabled elements, simultaneous constraints, and compilation evidence.
- **Use “do not infer usable digital width or routing cost” instead of “ignore.”**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Punchy and practical after nuance.

### Second: two-qubit fidelity and worst-case readout error (line 238)

- **Good high-impact pair for many NISQ gate-model workloads.**
- **Worst-case metric needs cohort:** Worst over all qubits may be irrelevant if compiler avoids one bad site; worst over the selected/required connected subgraph and simultaneous context is more useful.
- **Also request distributions and layer/simultaneous error:** A median plus global worst can hide topology and correlated failure.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Clear triage step.

### “Dominate almost every algorithm” (line 238)

- **Overgeneralized:** One-qubit coherent error, leakage, idling/decoherence, loss, crosstalk, connectivity/routing, measurement latency, state preparation, analog control error, and sampling/statistical error can dominate.
- **Algorithm and observable dependence:** Shallow measurement-heavy circuits, long idle memories, narrow arithmetic, analog simulation, and dynamic circuits stress different components.
- **Suggested repair:** “Often dominate compiled entangling-heavy NISQ circuits.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Useful heuristic, too sweeping.

### No median-fidelity-to-pass formula (line 238)

- **Excellent warning:** Whole-circuit behavior is not determined by a median component metric.
- **Heavy-output success is only one possible whole-circuit statistic:** Do not make it sound like the universal pass criterion; applications use observables, energies, sampling distances, logical error, etc.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Responsibly limits the next heuristic.

### Crude survival $F_{2q}^{N_{2q}}$ (line 238)

- **Useful back-of-envelope under an explicit independent stochastic survival model:** It can expose implausible deep circuits quickly.
- **“Fidelity” is not per-gate success probability:** Average fidelity raised to a gate count does not generally equal circuit survival; coherent errors, gate dependence, SPAM, leakage, idles, routing, and observable sensitivity break the model.
- **Median misuse:** Raising a median pair fidelity to total count ignores which edges/gates the compiled circuit uses.
- **Parallelism does not change the count-product under independent errors, but simultaneous crosstalk and layer error do; distinguish runtime from accumulated error.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** A quick exponential calculation is memorable.

### “Flags a hopeless circuit before any suite metric can dress it up” (line 238)

- **Rhetorically vivid, scientifically too confident:** The crude heuristic can yield false pessimism or optimism and should flag need for better modeling/testing, not pronounce hopelessness.
- **“Dress it up” imputes deceptive intent to system benchmarks:** They measure different circuit distributions and can reveal real compiler/full-stack performance.
- **Mitigation/QEC/postselection caveat:** These can trade samples/resources for improved observables, though not magically restore arbitrary deep circuits.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Punchy reviewer voice, adversarial excess.

### Third: scheduled critical path versus coherence (line 240)

- **Strong improvement over raw gate count:** Compile and schedule a representative circuit, including routing and heterogeneous durations.
- **Global makespan is not each qubit’s exposure:** Inspect per-qubit live intervals, idle/driven windows, resets/measurements, and coherent dependency paths.
- **Use appropriate coherence protocol/noise model:** Echo $T_2$ is not automatically valid during arbitrary idle/gate schedules.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Practical bridge into Chapter 23.

### $T_2^{\rm echo}/t_{2q}$ crude serial ceiling (line 240)

- **Correctly caveated as crude:** Retain the warning that accumulated error often dominates.
- **Not literally a ceiling:** $T_2$ is a decay scale, DD can alter it, error correction can exceed it, and target error determines allowable exposure.
- **Reuse terminology repaired in §22.5:** Call it a coherence-to-gate-duration ratio, not serial gate count.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Useful normalization with repeated caveat.

### Compile representative instance and scale progressively (line 240)

- **Excellent practical method:** Workload-specific compilation is more predictive than headline metrics.
- **One instance is not representative by assertion:** Sample sizes, parameters, seeds, graphs/molecules, compiler randomness, and calibration epochs.
- **Inspect more than schedule:** Native gate histogram/angles, selected qubits/edges, layer error, measurement/reset, dynamic branches, predicted/observed observable error, and runtime/shots.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Actionable and naturally leads forward.

### If one coherence time is spent, switch architecture/algorithm (line 240)

- **Too binary:** First examine target fidelity, decay envelope, DD, scheduling, qubit mapping, circuit optimization, mitigation, reset/teleportation, error detection/correction, and observable locality.
- **A circuit can produce useful observables after a nominal coherence time, or fail much earlier through gate error.**
- **Better rule:** Treat it as a high-risk signal requiring device execution/noise validation and alternatives.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Decisive, excessively so.

### Fourth: MCM/feedforward need (line 242)

- **Excellent early branching question:** If required, unsupported dynamics can disqualify a backend regardless of static gate quality.
- **Capability checklist:** Measurement/reset fidelity/time, spectator disturbance, supported classical logic/control flow, branch fanout/nesting, Pauli frames, repeated depth, simultaneous width, and compiler/service availability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Clear architectural fork.

### Feedforward latency and reset fidelity as gating constraints (line 242)

- **Incomplete pair:** Measurement latency/fidelity/QND/leakage, spectator error, reset time, conditional-gate fidelity, and decoder throughput/tail latency also gate viability.
- **Some algorithms defer or frame corrections:** Required real-time latency depends on the next noncommuting adaptive dependency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Correct focus, too compressed.

### Ask or probe with a small dynamic circuit (line 242)

- **Excellent evidence-seeking advice:** Absence of publication should lead to an acceptance test, not inference.
- **Small demo limitations:** It may not exercise repeated rounds, parallel MCM, spectator preservation, branch complexity, or service-level permissions.
- **Operational safety/cost:** Check access terms, supported backend, compiler transformations, shots, and billing; retain circuit/metadata/raw results.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Empirical and empowering.

### Fifth: QV, CLOPS, AQ, XEB, Q-score as summaries (line 244)

- **Useful shared warning, but taxonomy is uneven:** QV/AQ/Q-score are thresholded scalar summaries; CLOPS is a rate under a protocol; XEB is an estimator/score that must be paired with circuit size and validation method.
- **Never quote XEB alone:** Width, cycles, gate set, sample count, direct/inferred verification, and uncertainty define its meaning.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Good triage list, over-grouped.

### Useful for triage, not go/no-go (line 244)

- **Strong recommendation:** Summary metrics narrow candidates but should not decide application deployment alone.
- **Some can be legitimate hard gates:** If a standardized acceptance requirement explicitly uses a suite/threshold, it can support go/no-go for that distribution; the key is target alignment.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Sensible engineering governance.

### Components diagnose; system benchmarks integrate; workload decides (line 244)

- **Excellent three-level model:** Component → system ensemble → workload is a strong organizing hierarchy.
- **A compiled instance alone does not decide:** Compilation predicts resources; hardware runs, uncertainty, time-to-solution, cost, repeatability, and classical baseline decide.
- **Representative family rather than one instance:** Avoid cherry-picking and compiler/calibration luck.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** One of the closing section’s best formulations.

### Sixth: “mistrust everything new” (line 246)

- **Overly cynical and epistemically asymmetric:** Newness should trigger calibrated scrutiny, not automatic distrust; old results can also be obsolete, irreproducible, or measured under retired definitions.
- **Replace with evidence tiers:** Treat new claims as provisional until method, raw data, uncertainty, access/status, and replication are established.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Memorable, needlessly absolutist.

### Vendor sheets as marketing around real measurements (line 246)

- **Fair genre warning:** Product communications select framing and favorable metrics.
- **Not all sheets are equivalent:** Regulatory/product datasheets, live calibration APIs, peer-reviewed benchmark papers, press releases, investor materials, and blogs have different review/accountability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Healthy media literacy.

### Artifact-to-measurement ratio highest in recent announcements (line 246)

- **Unsupported aphorism:** Recent announcements may have less independent evidence, but can also publish detailed raw data; older claims may retain only marketing residue or outdated methodology.
- **“Artifact” is undefined:** If it means rhetoric/visuals versus reproducible evidence, propose an evidence rubric rather than a ratio.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Clever phrase, more attitude than analysis.

### Wait for independent reproduction before architecture decisions (line 246)

- **Prudent for irreversible/high-cost commitments, too rigid for exploration:** Independent reproduction may be impossible for proprietary hardware or arrive after a decision window.
- **Risk-tier decisions:** Prototype with provisional claims; require stronger evidence for procurement, product dependency, publication, or safety-critical commitments.
- **Alternative evidence:** Raw-data reanalysis, customer acceptance tests, contractual performance criteria, blinded benchmarks, sustained service telemetry, and multiple methods.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Strong governance point after risk calibration.

### Bridge to Chapter 23 (line 248)

- **Natural and clear:** Abstract gate set → compiler/transpiler → pulse/control → device is exactly the next conceptual descent.
- **Minor preview correction:** Chapter 23 should also cover scheduling, routing, dynamic control, calibration-aware compilation, target/backend schemas, and reproducibility—topics this checklist now depends on.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Creates forward momentum.

### Sanity-check heading (line 250)

- **Good active-recall close:** Problems force readers to use rather than recognize metrics.
- **Need answers/solutions and assumptions:** Several questions are deliberately non-unique; the solution should distinguish arithmetic from underdetermined inference.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** Calculations and judgment make a strong ending.

### Exercise 1: QV 64, $F_{2q}=0.99$, 1000 qubits (line 252)

- **Expected crude arithmetic:** Solve $0.99^N=1/e$, giving $N=-1/\ln(0.99)\approx99.5$; about 100 two-qubit gates under the toy independent-survival model.
- **Integer wording:** “Before drops below” requires stating whether 99 or 100/threshold rounding; $0.99^{99}\approx0.370$ and $0.99^{100}\approx0.366$, so the first below $1/e$ is 100.
- **QV decoding:** QV64 is $2^6$, a passing six-by-six random-circuit ensemble on some subset, essentially insensitive to the remaining raw count once enough qubits exist.
- **But “decoupled” is not absolute:** More qubits can offer a better subset/connectivity or enable the next width; QV is simply not proportional to total count.
- **Missing assumptions:** Which two-qubit fidelity/edge distribution, routing, SPAM, one-qubit/idles, correlations, mitigation, and circuit statistic.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Excellent arithmetic-plus-interpretation problem.

### Exercise 2: infer noise from $T_1=200\,\mu$s, $T_2^*=30\,\mu$s (line 253)

- **Fundamentally underdetermined:** Two scalars show dephasing beyond the relaxation limit is substantial, but do not identify the noise spectrum; quasistatic/low-frequency noise is a hypothesis to test, not a deduction.
- **Protocol answer should be exploratory:** Hahn echo first to test refocusable low-frequency noise, then CPMG/XY-family sequences/filter-function spectroscopy depending control errors and target schedule.
- **Largest simple-model bound:** For a two-level Markovian system, $T_2\le2T_1=400\,\mu$s, but DD-extracted decay parameters, non-Markovianity, changing $T_1$, leakage, fitting, and driven/dressed coherence complicate “largest.”
- **Question wording should invite uncertainty:** “What hypotheses and measurements?” rather than “what would you guess?”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Good diagnostic puzzle if underdetermination is the lesson.

### Exercise 3: standard RB versus interleaved RB (line 254)

- **Good noncomparability prompt:** Standard RB usually estimates average Clifford/gate-set decay; interleaved RB estimates a target gate relative to a reference and inherits reference/model bounds.
- **Both labeled $F_{\rm avg}$ is suspicious:** The conversion from decay to average gate fidelity depends on dimension and assumptions; report error per Clifford versus primitive gate.
- **“Which trust more” has no universal answer:** IRB is more gate-specific for CZ but can have wide/bias-prone bounds; standard RB may better reflect average compiled layers but not the target. For algorithms, simultaneous cycle/layer benchmarks and workload circuits may be more predictive than either.
- **Specify identical hardware/date/context:** Otherwise protocol is not the only difference.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Good judgment question, answer must reject a simplistic winner.

### Exercise 4: CLOPS arithmetic (line 255)

- **Toy calculation:** Total nominal layers are $50\times100\times1000\times L=5{,}000{,}000L$. At 5,000 CLOPS, time is $1000L$ seconds; at 200,000 CLOPS, $25L$ seconds.
- **Potential conceptual trap:** A circuit layer repeated over shots/parameters is counted according to the benchmark protocol’s numerator; arbitrary VQE layers cannot simply be divided by published CLOPS, especially across original versus $\mathrm{CLOPS}_h$ definitions.
- **Omitted boundary/resources:** Compilation, queueing, network/client round trips, optimizer/observable aggregation, mitigation, initialization/result return depending protocol, failures/retries, and shot/circuit differences.
- **QV compensation question is correctly open-ended:** Need workload fidelity/observable error, convergence/shot overhead, time-to-solution, cost, access, and representative circuit tests; QV itself does not “compensate” numerically.
- **Update stale comparison carefully:** 200,000 is historical; for a pure exercise label it hypothetical rather than current.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** Strong quantitative systems exercise.

### Exercise 5: sequential feedback-loop arithmetic (line 256)

- **Toy calculation:** Cycle latency $4+0.5=4.5\,\mu$s, so $150/4.5\approx33.3$ and 33 whole cycles fit under the stated hard-window fiction.
- **Correction duration omitted by wording:** “One conditioned correction per cycle” should add the correction gate’s scheduled duration unless feedforward delay is defined through completion rather than start; §22.11 defined it to application/start ambiguously.
- **Excellent self-critique:** Entangling gates/reset add time; Pauli frames remove immediate physical correction; echo $T_2$ is not a deadline.
- **Further real-code corrections:** Parallel ancilla measurement, per-data-qubit exposure, leakage, decoder latency/throughput, syndrome history, spectator error, and QEC extending operation beyond physical $T_2$.
- **Avoid “both directions” as only timing:** The toy can over- or under-constrain for multiple independent reasons, not a clean signed correction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.7/10.** The best exercise because it teaches the failure of its own arithmetic.

### Navigation footer (lines 258–260)

- **Appropriate links:** Previous, table of contents, and next create clear navigation.
- **Link verification deferred to repository-wide/link audit:** Paths look structurally consistent but must be mechanically checked against tracked files and rendered output.
- **Accessibility:** Arrow glyphs are understandable, though link text should remain meaningful without arrows—as it does.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Clean closure.

### Missing §22.14 artifacts and improvement opportunities

- **One-page evidence card/checklist:** Claim, definition/version, device/subset/date, aggregation/uncertainty, workload match, evidence tier, acceptance test.
- **Decision funnel:** Modality/capability → compile representative family → schedule/resources → execute validation → time-to-solution/cost → risk-tier decision.
- **Worked benchmark sheet:** Annotate one real-but-dated sheet, identifying synthetic numbers, missing endpoints, and what can/cannot be concluded.
- **Exercise solutions:** Show arithmetic, assumptions, and “underdetermined” answers rather than only final numbers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.9/10.** A forensic teardown of a spec sheet would be an ideal chapter finale.

### §22.14 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The component → system benchmark → representative workload hierarchy and the dynamic-circuit acceptance-test advice are excellent.
- **Highest-priority tone repair:** Replace “ignore,” “hopeless,” “dress it up,” and “mistrust everything new” with calibrated evidence/risk language; skepticism is strongest when it does not impute motive.
- **Highest-priority modeling repair:** Treat $F^{N}$ and $T_2/t_g$ as screening heuristics that trigger validation, not verdicts or ceilings.
- **Highest-priority scope repair:** Make the checklist explicitly gate-model oriented and add alternate schemas for analog, modular, bosonic/photonic, and dynamically routed systems.
- **Highest-priority decision repair:** A compiled instance predicts resources; representative hardware runs, uncertainty, sustained performance, cost, and classical baselines decide.
- **Highest-priority exercise repair:** Supply solutions—exercise 1 first crosses below $1/e$ at about 100 gates; exercise 4 gives $1000L$ versus $25L$ seconds; exercise 5 gives 33 toy cycles—and explicitly reward recognizing underdetermination in exercises 2 and 3.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.8/10 potential, 9.1/10 current.** The checklist and self-defeating toy models are engaging; adversarial aphorisms occasionally substitute attitude for evidence.

## Chapter 22 whole-file synthesis, exact reconciliation, and checkpoint

- **Coverage reconciled:** Reviewed source lines 1–260, including title/epigraph/opening, §§22.1–22.14, all tables, equations, examples, exercises, bridge text, and navigation footer. The fourteen source headings at lines 13, 27, 41, 69, 91, 107, 119, 141, 153, 165, 183, 195, 207, and 232 each have a corresponding fine-grained ledger entry; §22.13 was deliberately split into A/B/C because its suite taxonomy, QV chronology, and vendor cohort require distinct evidence treatment.
- **Strongest contribution:** The chapter gives readers a useful component-metric → system-benchmark → workload-validation hierarchy. Its recurring insistence that count alone is meaningless, that scheduling matters, and that representative execution outranks a headline number is pedagogically valuable.
- **Most serious systemic defect:** Mutable vendor and milestone facts are embedded manually in durable explanatory prose without a uniform as-of date, source tier, metric version, device configuration, uncertainty field, or regeneration mechanism. The resulting table already contains stale, synthetic, mismatched, and sometimes unsupported comparisons.
- **Definition/version drift:** QV, CLOPS, AQ, XEB, Q-score, RB-derived fidelities, coherence endpoints, and latency endpoints are not merely numbers. Their protocol versions, aggregation rules, participating subsets, compiler/calibration conditions, and confidence claims must travel with every value.
- **Overgeneralized platform ranges:** Several modality-wide speed, coherence, measurement, reset, and calibration claims compress incompatible endpoints and generations into neat ranges. These should become qualified examples or distributions, never taxonomic facts.
- **Synthetic device rows:** Mixing a product-family label, a particular processor generation, an upgrade configuration, and independently sourced best-case metrics can describe a machine that never existed as tested. Every row needs a stable identity and same-configuration rule.
- **Tone:** Skepticism is a strength, but phrases such as “ignore,” “hopeless,” “dress it up,” and “mistrust everything new” occasionally turn evidence discipline into adversarial theater. Replace motive-imputing or absolute language with explicit evidence tiers, acceptance tests, and decision risk.
- **Time and endpoint discipline:** “Latency,” “fidelity,” “coherence,” “calibration interval,” and “qubit count” each need defined start/stop events and inclusion rules. Without those, comparisons can differ by orders of magnitude while appearing commensurate.
- **Recommended architecture:** Keep durable metric principles and failure modes in the chapter body. Move changing records and vendor cohorts into generated, versioned data cards or an appendix with fields for source URL, access/as-of date, protocol/version, device/subset, topology, disabled elements, aggregation, uncertainty, and evidence tier.
- **Recommended reader workflow:** Add a worked forensic benchmark sheet and a compact evidence card: claim → definition/version → device/subset/date → aggregation/uncertainty → workload match → independent evidence → acceptance test → cost/risk decision.
- **Exercises:** The calculations are engaging but require solutions and explicit recognition of underdetermination. Several exercises are most educational precisely when the correct answer is “the supplied metric cannot decide this.”
- **Cross-chapter role:** This chapter should be the book’s measurement-contract chapter: it can define how later hardware claims are dated, sourced, scoped, and compared, rather than merely cataloging contemporary figures.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10 current, 9.6/10 potential.** Races, moving atoms, echoes, schedules, and forensic arithmetic create vivid momentum. Dense catalog tables and repeated metric caveats drag; a recurring benchmark-sheet case study would convert the catalog into a narrative investigation.
- **Checkpoint:** Chapter 22 is complete for this pass. Cumulative tracked-file progress: **26/67 files**; Markdown progress: **26/48 files**; SVG progress: **0/19 files**.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, title, status, navigation, opening, and reading map (lines 1–9)

### Title (line 1)

- **Accurate scope signal:** “Quantum Programming, Compilation, and Tooling” honestly names a broad software-stack chapter rather than pretending it is solely a programming tutorial.
- **Possible expectation mismatch:** “Quantum programming” may make a reader expect executable examples; the opening promises a conceptual tower. Either add a small end-to-end example or qualify the title/subtitle as a systems map.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Clear and professional, but abstract.

### Status metadata (line 3)

- **Internal-production residue:** “prereviewed,” “Phase: 4,” and “Sections drafted: 15 / 15” are useful to maintainers but interrupt a finished-book reader and will age independently of content.
- **Ambiguous state vocabulary:** “prereviewed” does not say whether technical verification, copyediting, code execution, or source verification occurred.
- **Improvement:** Hide build metadata from publication or define its schema in contributor documentation; derive section count mechanically.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **2.5/10.** Administrative rather than narrative.

### Navigation row (line 5)

- **Good continuity:** The links correctly frame Chapter 23 between measurement criteria and classical simulation.
- **Mechanical verification deferred:** Relative targets look plausible; repository-wide rendered-link checking remains necessary.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Efficient orientation.

### Opening stack panorama (line 7)

- **Excellent bridge:** Moving from “what a device is” to how an abstract program becomes control signals is a natural continuation from Chapter 22.
- **Category precision:** A high-level quantum program need not describe a unitary or even a fixed circuit: it may include measurement, reset, stochastic channels, host computation, dynamic allocation, or analog evolution. Replace “a *unitary* or a *circuit*” with a broader semantic object.
- **IR ladder is not universally linear:** Front ends can lower through several IRs, preserve symbolic control, invoke target-specific passes, or stop at analog instructions; pulse generation is not always a final compiler stage visible as a program.
- **QIR characterization is supported:** The QIR Alliance describes QIR as embedded in LLVM IR, using calls over opaque quantum types; distinguishing it from a standalone circuit language is useful. Official reference checked 2026-07-23: https://www.qir-alliance.org/qir-book/concepts/what-is-qir.html
- **Q# and Azure wording needs source and scope:** “used by Q# and Azure” is plausible but vendor/product bindings are volatile; date it and distinguish a language front end from a cloud execution target.
- **Pulse-level endpoint is platform-specific:** Analog neutral-atom, annealing, photonic, and delegated cloud systems do not necessarily expose a gate-to-pulse tower. Say that the description primarily models calibrated gate-based hardware.
- **“Vendor-private” is plausible but too sweeping:** Some pulse/calibration layers are open specifications or locally exposed, while others are inaccessible; “often target- and provider-specific” is more neutral and precise.
- **2026 SDK list is fragile:** The list is neither exhaustive nor governed by inclusion criteria. “Major” should specify adoption measure, region, modality, or pedagogical relevance and carry an as-of date.
- **Taxonomy omission:** CUDA-Q, Classiq, TKET-branded distributions, Strawberry Fields, D-Wave Ocean, and modality-specific stacks illustrate why an unqualified “major SDKs” list invites debate. This is a suspicion about scope, not a demand to enumerate everything.
- **Licensing sentence is valuable:** Mentioning semantics, differentiation, runtime, and licensing prevents a shallow vendor-target comparison; later sections must actually evaluate those axes.
- **Sentence engineering:** At roughly paragraph-length in one sentence sequence, the tower plus parenthetical qualifications overloads working memory. Convert it into a compact diagram or five-step numbered pipeline, followed by exceptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** The notebook-to-pulse image is vivid; the parenthetical density blunts its momentum.

### “How to read this chapter” map (line 9)

- **Strong reader contract:** The four clusters and explicit fast path help both sequential and reference readers.
- **Small taxonomy inconsistency:** The text says §§23.1–23.4 cover “the major IRs,” but §23.2 and §23.3 are specific languages while §23.4 is an SDK survey; QIR is introduced but has no dedicated section.
- **Load-bearing selection deserves rationale:** §23.13 is important for dynamic/hybrid execution, but omitting scheduling and verification from the fast path may leave readers with a misleadingly static pipeline. A one-line reason for each selected section would help.
- **Tone:** “When something does not behave” is approachable, though it subtly frames the detail sections as troubleshooting rather than core conceptual machinery.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Choice and prioritization reduce intimidation.

### Opening evidence and terminology checkpoint

- **QPY must not be called the runtime transport without a runtime-specific source:** IBM documents QPY as cross-platform binary serialization for Qiskit objects and contrasts it with lossy OpenQASM serialization; that does not alone prove every Qiskit Runtime submission serializes over the wire as QPY. Official references checked 2026-07-23: https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/api/qiskit/qpy and https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/guides/save-circuits
- **ISA-circuit distinction is useful but endpoint-dependent:** Preserve the difference between user circuit serialization and the requirement that runtime inputs conform to target instruction/connectivity constraints, with a current Runtime citation later in the section.
- **OpenPulse volatility:** The OpenQASM specification explicitly describes its OpenPulse grammar as actively developing. Present `defcal` as an extension mechanism selecting a calibration grammar, not as a universally fixed pulse language. Official references checked 2026-07-23: https://openqasm.com/versions/3.0/language/openpulse.html and https://openqasm.com/language/pulses.html
- **Braket qualification is supported:** AWS publishes a concrete subset of supported OpenQASM 3 types, statements, pragmas, and OpenPulse features, reinforcing the manuscript’s warning that nominal format support is partial. Official reference checked 2026-07-23: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/braket/latest/developerguide/braket-openqasm-supported-features.html
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The distinctions are intellectually satisfying but need a visual pipeline to become memorable.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, §23.1 “Circuit Description Languages” (lines 11–23)

### Definition and assembly analogy (line 13)

- **Strong semantic emphasis:** Requiring agreement under a semantic version correctly warns that shared syntax is insufficient.
- **Definition too circuit-bound:** In-memory representations can contain unresolved parameters, classical subroutines, noise, timing constraints, calibration annotations, or constructs that cannot yet be “run.” Define the object as precise enough for conforming consumers to interpret or diagnose.
- **“Two implementations … can agree” is aspirational:** Specifications often leave implementation-defined behavior, unsupported features, numerical tolerances, or target-dependent semantics. Conformance profiles and diagnostics matter.
- **Assembly analogy helps, then overreaches:** Classical assembly commonly commits to an ISA and operand model; a portable circuit IR may deliberately avoid physical wiring and native operations. “Like an assembly language” should be labeled a partial analogy.
- **Order nuance:** Circuit languages express dependencies, lexical order, barriers, boxes, or timing constraints, not always one total execution order; independent operations may commute or run concurrently.
- **Classical-control surface list is useful but incomplete:** Add reset, subroutines, memory/storage, I/O, timing, and possibly extern calls; clarify that feature availability differs by language/profile.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** The assembly analogy creates an immediate foothold, though its limits should become a teaching moment.

### Three-category setup (line 15)

- **Useful pedagogical partition, not an ontology:** Embedded DSL, textual IR, and hardware-flavored language overlap. OpenQASM 3 is both textual and able to carry hardware calibration; Quil is textual and has Quil-T extensions.
- **Category-axis mismatch:** “Embedded” describes host-language packaging, “standalone textual” describes serialization/syntax, and “hardware-flavored” describes abstraction level. A two-axis table—representation form × semantic level—would eliminate the overlap.
- **Missing visual:** A small matrix showing Python object/text/bitcode versus algorithm/circuit/gate/pulse levels would make the chapter’s central model much clearer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** The promise of three buckets is satisfying until edge cases blur them.

### Embedded DSLs (line 17)

- **Examples are recognizable:** Qiskit and Cirq syntax quickly ground the abstraction.
- **Cirq syntax may mislead as a statement-level counterpart:** `cirq.H(q0), cirq.CNOT(...)` alone forms a tuple of operations; it does not necessarily build or execute a circuit. Show `cirq.Circuit(...)` if construction is the intended equivalence.
- **“Just the host language’s syntax” understates the DSL:** The library supplies object types, validation, operator overloading, builder semantics, and an internal IR; the host parser is only one layer.
- **Portability is broader than serialization:** A serializer preserves only representable semantics. Portability also requires compatible operation definitions, control flow, parameter types, timing, calibration assumptions, endianness/register conventions, and target capabilities.
- **Add an advantage/tradeoff pair:** Embedded DSLs gain host tooling, abstraction, metaprogramming, and data integration but complicate language-independent exchange and reproducibility.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Concrete code wakes up the page; a minimal complete constructor would make it trustworthy.

### Standalone textual IRs and interchange claims (line 19)

- **QIR distinction is excellent:** Explaining that its textual form is LLVM IR and that bitcode is common prevents the frequent mistake of treating QIR as another gate-list syntax.
- **“First-class languages” is vague:** QIR conventions plus LLVM IR are also formally consumable; say “standalone quantum-language syntaxes” if that is the intended contrast.
- **OpenQASM superlative needs evidence:** “Most common interchange format” and “closest thing” are defensible impressions, not self-proving facts. Add survey/ecosystem evidence or soften to “widely supported.”
- **“Quil is mainly Rigetti-local” is too dismissive and geographically odd:** Prefer “centered on Rigetti’s ecosystem”; note that external parsers/tooling can exist even when hardware execution is provider-centered.
- **QPY transport claim is insufficiently sourced:** Official IBM material checked for this review establishes QPY as a durable Qiskit object serialization format, but not by itself that Qiskit Runtime’s client–cloud transport universally uses QPY. Cite the actual runtime encoder/protocol or restrict the statement to preservation/saving.
- **ISA wording is valuable:** Submission formats and target-conforming circuits are orthogonal. Separate the two claims so readers do not infer that QPY itself makes a circuit hardware-native.
- **Nested punctuation overload:** The parenthesis contains an em-dash qualification containing another em-dash. Split QPY/Runtime behavior into its own paragraph or callout.
- **Loss taxonomy is strong:** Custom operations, control flow, timing, and calibration are exactly the features that make nominal “OpenQASM support” non-binary; add semantic-version and feature-profile fields.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Rich and useful, but qualification nesting feels like reading release notes.

### Hardware-flavored languages (line 21)

- **Concrete vocabulary works:** Waveforms, frames, frequencies, and durations make “lower level” tangible.
- **OpenPulse/`defcal` relation needs precision:** `defcal` is an OpenQASM calibration-definition construct whose body is interpreted by a selected calibration grammar; OpenPulse is one such evolving grammar, not simply a synonymous language layer.
- **Quil-T deserves expansion or deferral:** A reader cannot infer whether it is a language, extension, instruction family, or execution interface from the parenthesis alone.
- **“Most users never touch” needs audience scope:** Calibration researchers, control engineers, and some advanced users do; cloud users often cannot. State that typical algorithm/application users interact through gates or provider APIs.
- **Pipeline anthropomorphism:** “Somewhere to land” is vivid but implies a serialized pulse program always exists. Some providers generate control instructions dynamically or keep this layer inaccessible.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Hardware nouns and the landing metaphor add welcome physicality.

### Typical workflow and handoff (line 23)

- **Good end-to-end recap:** Authoring → serialization/submission → provider lowering gives the reader a usable default path.
- **Do not imply every workflow serializes to text or a file:** Local API objects may be sent through RPC schemas, service models, or provider-specific encodings; “serialize” is fine if used generically and defined.
- **Braket IR needs exact identity:** Specify whether this means the service’s JAQCD JSON schema, OpenQASM program representation, or SDK model; “Braket IR” alone hides multiple representations and evolving device support.
- **Lowering boundary matters:** Some clients transpile into a target ISA before submission; providers may validate, optimize, schedule, or reject rather than performing the entire lowering internally.
- **Modality caveat:** Annealers and analog Hamiltonian-programming devices follow different paths, so label this the typical gate-model workflow.
- **Section transition is clean:** “Top to bottom” reinforces the chapter’s spatial metaphor, though later section order must actually honor it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** A compact journey with a satisfying destination.

### §23.1 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It gives beginners a practical vocabulary for host DSLs, exchange formats, compiler IRs, and calibration-level descriptions while warning that syntax support does not equal semantic portability.
- **Highest-priority conceptual repair:** Replace the three mutually suggestive “categories” with two independent axes: representation/container and abstraction/semantic level.
- **Highest-priority factual repair:** Verify or soften OpenQASM prevalence, Rigetti/Quil scope, and QPY Runtime-transport claims; version every feature-support assertion.
- **Highest-priority example repair:** Use complete, actually constructing Qiskit and Cirq snippets and show one deliberately lossy round trip.
- **Accessibility improvement:** Define IR on first formal use despite the opening expansion, and explain “semantic version,” “bitcode,” “frame,” and “ISA” in plain language or glossary links.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10 current, 9.4/10 potential.** Concrete syntax and the descent toward pulses are engaging; a visual matrix and a lossy-conversion mystery would make the distinctions memorable.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, §23.2 “OpenQASM” (lines 25–46)

### Section title and opening history/feature survey (lines 25–27)

- **Title is correctly direct:** A named-language section needs no clever subtitle.
- **Prevalence superlative remains unsupported:** “The field’s most widely used circuit interchange language” needs a dated survey, repository/package telemetry, or softer “widely used.” QIR and provider APIs make “interchange” itself context-dependent.
- **History is compressed into an unverifiable causal story:** “Became widely adopted because it was good enough and shipped with Qiskit” is plausible and lively, but “good enough” is subjective and Qiskit distribution is not proved as the cause. Attribute or recast as an interpretation.
- **OpenQASM 2 description omits classical conditionals and declarations:** Calling it a minimal sequence of gates, measurements, and includes is directionally useful but too narrow to serve as a definition.
- **OpenQASM 3 chronology needs an exact release object:** Distinguish the 2021 paper/specification milestone, version 3.0 publication, later live specification, and subsequent revisions. “First published” is ambiguous.
- **Feature list is strong:** Typed classical data, structured control, timing, and calibration constructs communicate that version 3 is not merely syntax modernization.
- **Real-time caveat:** A language’s ability to express arithmetic on measurement results does not imply a target can execute it within a hardware feedback deadline. Separate language semantics from backend support.
- **`defcal` wording:** `defcal` attaches calibration definitions interpreted under a selected calibration grammar; it is not by itself the pulse-level extension. The official OpenQASM pages explicitly mark OpenPulse as evolving.
- **“Reference tooling” may overstate authority:** The `openqasm3` Python package supplies parser/AST tooling, but identify its governance and whether it is normative or merely maintained alongside the specification.
- **Named SDK support requires direction/version fields:** “Provide importers/exporters” hides asymmetric support. Current Qiskit documentation calls parts of import exploratory; Cirq documents limited OpenQASM 2/3 importing and exporting; tket documentation advertises OpenQASM import, but the exact OpenQASM 3 export/profile needs a direct versioned citation.
- **Conversion-loss warning is excellent:** It should become a feature matrix with rows for custom definitions, control flow, timing, calibrations, aliases, modifiers, annotations, and externs, and columns for import/export/hardware execution.
- **Official evidence checked 2026-07-23:** Qiskit OpenQASM 3 guide/API: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/interoperate-qiskit-qasm3 and https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit/qasm3 ; Cirq interoperability: https://quantumai.google/cirq/build/interop ; OpenQASM specification: https://openqasm.com/versions/3.0/index.html

### Example introduction (line 29)

- **Good restraint:** A minimal Bell-state circuit is the right first syntax example.
- **Opportunity:** State the intended semantics before the code and invite readers to predict the measurement correlation; otherwise it is only a syntax specimen.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Clear anticipation, limited drama.

- **Assignment form is idiomatic OpenQASM 3:** It nicely contrasts with the older arrow syntax readers may encounter.

The prose currently makes a fading interface pattern sound central.
- **Official evidence checked 2026-07-23:** IBM feature matrix: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/qasm-feature-table ; AWS subset: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/braket/latest/developerguide/braket-openqasm-supported-features.html ; Quantinuum QIR transition notice surfaced at https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/pcns/Quantum%20System%20Product%20Change%20Notification%202024_12_02%20%28QIR%20Addendum%29.pdf
- **Interoperation-path claim needs a reproducible test:** “Common leg in Qiskit–Cirq–tket interoperation” may be practically true for simple circuits, but should cite actual converters and document semantic losses. Native adapters may be preferable.
- **`u3` versus `U` explanation is technically muddled:** OpenQASM 2’s base-language universal gate is `U`; lowercase `u3` is a `qelib1.inc` library convention. OpenQASM 3’s `stdgates.inc` includes `U` under its conventions. This is not simply a version-2-to-version-3 rename.
- **Vendor `defcal` claim is suspicious:** A provider requiring native physical-qubit instructions or provider pragmas is not the same as requiring users to write a `defcal`; verify with a named interface.
- **Dynamic-circuit provider claim is volatile:** IBM’s feature table demonstrates per-feature SDK/runtime distinctions. For Quantinuum, cite its current language/QIR profile and hardware classical-compute capabilities rather than relying on an advertisement category.
- **“Query capabilities everywhere” is sound advice with an awkward absolute:** Say “for every target and service version used,” and show the API or capability document readers should query.
- **Sentence overload:** One paragraph carries universality, vendor interfaces, SDK bridges, gate naming, calibration, dynamic circuits, and operational advice. Split into “portable core,” “known losses,” and “target capability checks.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10 concept, 7.8/10 execution.** The gotchas are inherently engaging, but the sentence becomes a thicket.

### §23.2 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section makes the crucial distinction between a rich language specification and the much smaller feature intersection that tools and hardware actually share.
- **Highest-priority factual correction:** Repair the false `u3`/`U` version contrast and remove or substantiate the claim that vendors require user-supplied `defcal` blocks for native gates.
- **Highest-priority evidence correction:** Replace “every major SDK,” “several vendors,” and “common leg” with a dated, executable compatibility matrix and round-trip tests.
- **Highest-priority pedagogical improvement:** Show the ideal Bell-state output, then add one rich OpenQASM 3 feature that deliberately fails or degrades across a named tool boundary.
- **Maintenance improvement:** Generate support tables from pinned package versions and tiny conformance fixtures; prose cannot safely track fast-moving import/export profiles.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10 current, 9.5/10 potential.** A portability trial—same program, three tools, one semantic loss—could turn a language catalog into a memorable experiment.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, §23.3 “Quil” (lines 47–62)

### Language identity and gate-level feature survey (lines 47–49)

- **Core identity is supported:** Quil is Rigetti-centered and remains the language in which QCS calibration/native-gate information is exposed.
- **“Native input format” needs an interface diagram:** Users submit through pyQuil/QCS services, compilation and translation intervene, and executable control-system binaries are lower still. “Native program language for Rigetti QCS” is safer than implying raw Quil directly enters hardware.
- **Chronology is vague:** “Predates OpenQASM 3 by several years” is true-looking but should name Quil’s publication/introduction year and the OpenQASM 3 comparison milestone.
- **“Reads more simply” is subjective:** It is useful reviewer voice if illustrated, but it should not pose as an intrinsic language property. Say its gate-list syntax is visually terse in the example.
- **Gate-level summary is good:** Named gates, memory, branching, pragmas, reset, `DEFGATE`, and `DEFCIRCUIT` convey more expressive breadth than the earlier “Rigetti-local” shorthand.
- **Classical-memory phrasing:** Measurements may target memory, but gate parameters can also reference memory; spell out memory regions/types and shot-time parameter use if this distinction matters later.
- **`DEFGATE` parenthetical is incomplete:** The current specification also describes other definition forms, including permutation and Pauli-sum forms; “matrix-defined” sounds exhaustive.
- **Specification maturity deserves disclosure:** The public Quil specification currently identifies language version 2021.1 as **DRAFT**, despite later documented changes. A book treating it as stable should cite the exact supported QCS profile, not only the general spec.
- **Official evidence checked 2026-07-23:** Quil specification: https://quil-lang.github.io/ ; QCS language-support profile: https://docs.rigetti.com/qcs/guides/quil/language-support
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Terse syntax and named constructs are approachable; historical specificity would add character.

### pyQuil introduction (line 51)

- **Terminology correction:** pyQuil is better called a Python library/SDK than “the Python binding”; binding implies a relatively direct wrapper around a single native library.
- **Name relationship is memorable:** This is an opportunity to say that Python objects construct Quil programs and QCS APIs compile/execute them.
- **Versioning:** Cite/test against the current documented pyQuil version; the checked official documentation reports 4.17.0.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Brief and functional.

### Bell-program code fence and declaration (lines 53–54)

- **Fence should use a Quil lexer if available:** `text` prevents incorrect highlighting but also forfeits useful syntax color; verify renderer support for `quil`.
- **Declaration is clear:** `ro` conventionally suggests readout storage, but that name is conventional rather than reserved; say so.
- **Memory semantics omitted:** Explain that `BIT[2]` declares a classical region and that returned shot data are associated with it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** The compact declaration invites comparison with OpenQASM.

### Gate instructions (lines 55–56)

- **Excellent side-by-side comparison:** Uppercase `H`/`CNOT` and integer qubit addresses make Quil’s terseness visible.
- **Same semantic narration is needed:** State that these prepare an ideal Bell state; do not make readers reverse-engineer why the identical example reappears.
- **Physical-address ambiguity:** Integer qubits can look inherently physical. Explain whether these are logical placeholders before compilation or target addresses in this program/profile.
- **Native-gate caveat:** `H` and `CNOT` need not be current native calibrated operations on every Rigetti target; compilation can rewrite them according to the calibration program.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Minimal notation makes the comparison satisfying.

### Measurement instructions (lines 57–58)

- **Clear destination syntax:** These lines visibly bind qubit outcomes to specific classical addresses.
- **Bit-order/result note again needed:** State the ideal correlated outcomes and how pyQuil returns the `ro` columns.
- **Scheduling inference warning:** Text order does not by itself explain whether acquisitions overlap on a target.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Clean and readable.

### Quil-T significance and constructs (line 61)

- **Historical-influence claim is unsupported:** “Shaped a lot of subsequent thinking in the field” and “influential well beyond it” need citations to later specifications/design discussions or softer attribution.
- **Core Quil-T description is accurate:** Official documentation calls it an extension providing explicit RF-waveform control and a notion of time; the spec defines frames, waveforms, pulse/capture operations, calibration matching, and synchronization.
- **`DEFCAL` matching nuance:** Calibrations match gate name, parameters, qubits, and modifiers; they are not merely bindings to “specific qubits,” since formal-qubit patterns can apply more broadly.
- **Construct relation is slightly reversed:** `DEFFRAME` and `DEFWAVEFORM` are top-level definitions used by calibration/pulse instructions, not merely “companion constructs” declared through a block.
- **Freedom is constrained more than “safety limits”:** The current QCS language-support table lists supported/unsupported instructions and authorized raw-control paths; frame attributes, sample rates, translation rules, and available hardware channels constrain programs. Replace the vague safety phrase with capability/profile validation.
- **Important tooling caveat omitted:** Official pyQuil documentation says Quil-T instructions are not supported by `quilc` or the QVM. Readers need this immediately because it breaks the intuitive “compile/test locally, then run” workflow.
- **Provider calibration precedence:** Current Rigetti docs say native calibrations are used by default and user-specified calibrations take precedence when supported. This is a more precise and practical explanation than “user-defined gates can be assembled.”
- **OpenQASM analogy needs boundaries:** Both use calibration definitions, frames, and waveforms, but syntax, matching, timing semantics, grammar extensibility, tool support, and target exposure differ. “Similar role” is correct if followed by these differences.
- **2026 usage-frequency claim has no evidence:** “Rarely used” requires corpus/download/survey data. “Primarily documented and deployed in Rigetti’s ecosystem” is observable and avoids pretending to know all private use.
- **Official evidence checked 2026-07-23:** Quil-T guide: https://pyquil-docs.rigetti.com/en/stable/quilt.html ; calibration guide: https://pyquil-docs.rigetti.com/en/latest/quilt_getting_started.html ; QCS FAQ: https://docs.rigetti.com/qcs/faq
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The sudden descent from `H 0` to RF frames and waveforms is vivid; a tiny calibration example would capitalize on it.

### Missing comparison artifact

- **Add one three-column semantic comparison:** OpenQASM 3, Quil, and Quil-T for declaration, Bell preparation, measurement, control flow, timing, calibration, serialization, and target execution.
- **Add one compilation trace:** Show `H 0` before compilation, the matching calibration/native rewrite, and a pulse-level excerpt, clearly labeling which layers users normally see.
- **Add one compatibility warning box:** General Quil spec ≠ QCS-supported subset ≠ QVM/`quilc` support ≠ authorized QPU pulse features.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** Revealing what lies beneath one terse gate would be a strong narrative payoff.

### §23.3 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The repeated Bell example makes Quil’s gate-level economy immediately comparable with OpenQASM, and Quil-T provides a concrete bridge to control engineering.
- **Highest-priority factual qualification:** Disclose the public spec’s draft/version status and the documented limitation that `quilc` and QVM do not support Quil-T instructions.
- **Highest-priority scope repair:** Replace unsupported claims about rarity/influence with dated, observable ecosystem facts and sources.
- **Highest-priority pedagogy repair:** Explain the roles of pyQuil, compilation, translation, calibration retrieval, and executable binary as distinct boundaries.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10 current, 9.6/10 potential.** It is compact and physical; a gate-to-pulse reveal would make it one of the chapter’s most memorable sections.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, §23.4 “SDK Landscape” (lines 63–84)

### Landscape framing (lines 63–65)

- **Necessary orientation, hazardous permanence:** A landscape section is useful, but every row needs an as-of date, pinned version, scope, license identifier, and source because provider rosters and integration packages change within months.
- **“Consolidated” is an empirical claim without evidence:** Package downloads, contributor activity, education surveys, or job/task volume would be needed. New modality-specific and compiler stacks make consolidation debatable.
- **Categories overlap:** Braket is multi-provider but service-centric; PennyLane is multi-device and differentiation-centric; tket is compiler-centric but also constructs and executes circuits. Use axes rather than exclusive labels.
- **Good disclaimer, insufficient protection:** Calling the sketch a simplification does not excuse factual mismatches inside individual rows. A matrix can orient without pretending each tool has one identity.
- **Missing evaluation criteria:** Add primary abstraction, supported modalities, execution model, dynamic-circuit support, differentiation, IR/serialization, compiler role, provider coupling, license, governance, and maintenance status.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Readers like maps; prose lists are less inviting than a carefully designed matrix.

### Qiskit row (line 67)

- **Community/depth superlatives need measures:** “Very large,” “deepest,” and “among the most common” may be true but require dated evidence or neutral phrasing.
- **Version claim is broadly current but imprecise:** Qiskit 2.0 release notes support the 2.x line and substantial API removals, but the row should state the exact reviewed version rather than only a major series.
- **Release date should be directly sourced:** Retain March 2025 only with the official release announcement/tag date, not inferred from a version line.

- **Runtime/SDK boundary is useful:** Explain that Runtime is a remote service/client package, while `SamplerV2`/`EstimatorV2` are interface families with local and service implementations; avoid implying all primitives live only cloud-side.
- **Aer wording:** Aer is a separate high-performance simulator package/provider rather than “the” singular local backend. Qiskit also includes reference statevector/operator tooling and can connect to other simulators.
- **Pulse irony:** The surrounding chapter discusses pulse-level programming, but Qiskit 2.0 removed `qiskit.pulse`; this must be reconciled explicitly in §23.5.

## Second-pass review — Chapter 23, §23.5 “Pulse-Level Programming” (lines 85–98)

### Gate-to-control opening (lines 85–87)

- **Strong physical descent:** The contrast between an abstract gate and an analog envelope is one of the chapter’s clearest layer transitions.
- **“Gate is an abstract unitary” is too narrow:** Reset, measurement, delay, channels/noise, conditional operations, and nonunitary primitives inhabit gate/assembly IRs; even calibrated gates can implement channels rather than ideal unitaries.
- **Envelope model needs its carrier convention:** A complex baseband envelope is typically mixed/upconverted relative to a frame/carrier; saying it is simply “played … at the transition frequency” hides detuning, sidebands, virtual phase, multiple channels, and rotating-frame conventions.
- **Control-line mapping is not one-to-one:** Cross-drive/control channels, flux lines, readout resonators, shared resources, and crosstalk complicate “a control line.”
- **Other modalities are compressed:** Laser/RF fields cover ions and atoms only partially; photonics, spin qubits, annealers, and analog neutral-atom programs need distinct control descriptions.
- **Definition overpromises directness:** Pulse-level programming may specify symbolic waveforms, frames, calibrations, or allowed templates rather than raw DAC samples. “Write that control directly” should become “express lower-level control within an exposed target profile.”
- **Override is not essential:** Users can inspect, compose, parameterize, or invoke provider calibrations without overriding them; some systems forbid overrides entirely.
- **Validation sentence is good:** Expand it into the actual contracts—syntax/type checks, supported frames/instructions, sample rate, amplitude/bandwidth, timing alignment, resource conflicts, authorization, and device-specific safety policies.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The abstract-to-analog reveal is vivid; a small envelope diagram would make it exceptional.

### Calibration/tune-up use case (line 89, first unit)

- **Rabi and DRAG are not parallel categories:** Rabi experiments estimate/control response; DRAG is a pulse-shaping technique usually tuned through experiments; error amplification is a broader calibration strategy.
- **Sweep dimensions are useful:** Amplitude, phase, and duration make the work tangible; add frequency/detuning and waveform parameters.
- **RB contrast needs qualification:** Standard RB can be performed at circuit/gate level without user pulse access, but its circuits execute calibrated pulses underneath; pulse access may still be used in closed-loop calibration workflows.
- **GST contrast likewise:** Gate-set tomography consumes circuit experiments but can guide pulse optimization; “need no pulse access” should mean the characterization protocol’s user-facing input, not the surrounding calibration loop.
- **Missing measurement calibration:** Readout amplitude/frequency/integration/kernel/classifier calibration is a major pulse-level use case and deserves mention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Laboratory verbs and sweeps create motion.

### Custom-gate use case (line 89, second unit)

- **Good motivation, overly specific implementation:** A useful unitary might be realized with an optimized waveform or native fractional interaction, but “a single shaped pulse on the cross-resonance drive” is superconducting/architecture-specific and may require echoes, simultaneous drives, frame updates, cancellation tones, or multiple segments.
- **Efficiency objective is incomplete:** Fewer source gates does not necessarily mean shorter duration, lower error, less leakage, or better robustness. Compare scheduled duration and experimentally characterized process/application performance.
- **Compiler could already support fractional/native gates:** IBM explicitly replaced common custom-pulse rotations with fractional ISA gates; the section should show that gate-set enrichment can remove the need for pulse access.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The idea of collapsing a long decomposition into tailored control is compelling.

### Optimal-control use case (line 89, third unit)

- **GRAPE/CRAB name-dropping needs expansion:** Spell out the acronyms or link to the control chapter/glossary; explain gradient-based versus basis/randomized optimization at a high level.
- **“Target unitary” again narrows the objective:** Real workflows optimize robust gates, state transfer, leakage suppression, ensemble performance, bandwidth, duration, power, or noise-sensitive costs.
- **Model-to-hardware gap missing:** Numerically optimal pulses can fail under Hamiltonian/model error, transfer-function distortion, drift, quantization, and unmodeled crosstalk; closed-loop validation is essential.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Control optimization has strong puzzle appeal; one before/after pulse would help.

### Interface-list setup (line 91)

- **Plural promise is good:** The subsequent bullets actually mix language constructs, an ecosystem, and a non-interface market observation. Rename to “Access paths and availability.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Functional transition.

### OpenQASM `defcal`, Qiskit removal, and IBM withdrawal (line 93)

- **Most important fact is buried:** IBM removed pulse-level control from all processors on **2025-02-03**, and Qiskit 2.0 removed pulse APIs, circuit/DAG calibration data, pulse-related transpiler passes, scheduler APIs, backend channel/calibration accessors, and pulse QPY support. This is a major software-stack case study, not a parenthetical.
- **Deprecation chronology is supported:** Qiskit Pulse was deprecated in 1.3 and removed in 2.0. Cite official changelog/migration pages directly.
- **“Language-level home” is too universal:** `defcal` is a calibration-definition construct interpreted under a chosen calibration grammar. Whether a provider accepts, preserves, compiles, or executes it is profile-specific.
- **Reject-or-ignore distinction matters:** Silently ignoring a calibration would be semantically dangerous; state actual provider behavior per interface rather than speculating. A conforming tool may reject unsupported constructs or strip non-executing metadata under documented rules.
- **Cloud-endpoint wording:** IBM’s official current statement is stronger and cleaner: pulse-level control was removed from all IBM Quantum processors. Use that rather than “notably” or “withdrawn endpoints.”
- **Replacement path omitted:** IBM directs many former use cases to fractional gates in the target ISA. Include this because it teaches how abstraction boundaries evolve.
- **Offline/research tooling nuance:** Removal from Qiskit 2.x/IBM hardware does not erase pulse simulation, legacy Qiskit 1.x artifacts, Qiskit Dynamics, or non-IBM pulse front ends; distinguish unsupported production paths from historical/local research.
- **Official evidence checked 2026-07-23:** IBM changelog: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/latest-updates ; Qiskit 2.0 migration: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/guides/qiskit-2.0 ; fractional-gate migration: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/guides/pulse
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10 potential, 8.3/10 current.** The rise and removal of an abstraction is a fascinating story, but parentheses smother it.

### Quil-T bullet (line 94)

- **“Original” is historically risky:** Earlier pulse-control languages and vendor systems existed; if “original pulse-level IR” means first prominent open quantum circuit extension of this form, state and source that narrower claim.
- **“Structurally similar” teaches little:** Compare frame identity, waveform generators, calibration matching, timing, capture, modifiers, and tooling constraints with OpenQASM/OpenPulse.
- **Current access caveats required:** Quil-T is documented by Rigetti, but QCS supports a target-specific subset; `quilc` and QVM do not support Quil-T instructions, and authorization/capabilities vary.
