- **Measurement wording:** Sampling from \(|\alpha_x|^2\) correctly describes computational-basis projective measurement of the whole register. Partial measurement, arbitrary bases, sequential/mid-circuit measurement, reset, and classical control require collapse/branch semantics not described here.
- **Expectation values:** \(\langle\psi|O|\psi\rangle\) is exact with respect to sampling only; it remains subject to floating-point error and the cost depends heavily on \(O\)’s representation. A dense \(O\) is itself exponential-square, whereas Pauli sums, sparse operators, and local observables admit structured evaluation.
- **“Exact” terminology:** “Exact up to floating-point round-off” is standard but internally tensioned. Prefer “deterministic full-state numerical simulation” or “exact within the chosen floating-point arithmetic/model,” and later distinguish numerical, truncation, Monte Carlo, and model error.
- **Gate universality overclaim:** “Supports every gate the user can write down” excludes malformed/nonunitary maps, unsupported dynamic operations, arbitrary channels, very large opaque matrices, analog/time-dependent evolution, and backend-specific instructions. Say “arbitrary supported unitary gates in principle.”
- **Schrödinger equation sentence:** A circuit statevector simulator applies discrete gate unitaries; it does not necessarily numerically integrate the differential Schrödinger equation. “Schrödinger-picture simulation” contrasts evolving states with Heisenberg-picture observables and path sums more accurately than “integrated as repeated unitary multiplication.”
- **Stride pairing:** The pairing \(x\) with \(x\oplus2^q\) for indices with bit \(q=0\) is correct under the stated implicit little-endian integer indexing. Define \(x\), the index range, and convention in prose immediately beside the formula.
- **Matrix-entry presentation:** “Rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\)” removes ambiguity. Consider using \(u_{00},u_{01},u_{10},u_{11}\) to reduce collision with later use of \(d\) for circuit depth.
- **Operation count:** Four complex multiplications and two complex additions per generic pair is the naïve dense formula. Specialized matrices, fused kernels, fused multiply-adds, and real/zero entries change actual instruction counts. Label it an unfused arithmetic count.
- **Two-qubit extension:** “Same trick on quadruples” is intuitive but deserves the explicit four index offsets and \(2^{n-2}\) quadruples; readers could then derive the generic \(k\)-qubit cost themselves.
- **Diagonal gates:** The full-sweep qualification is good. A controlled phase’s affected set requires all relevant controls/targets to meet the phase condition, not merely “control bits are set” for every possible controlled-phase definition. Also distinguish physically updating amplitudes from accumulating a symbolic diagonal frame.
- **Permutation gates:** They require no floating-point arithmetic only if represented as exact index permutations; swapping complex payloads is still memory work, and an \(X\) may be fused with later operations. The sentence appropriately notes this but could quantify the traffic contrast.
- **Locality sentence:** Low-numbered qubits are contiguous only under a particular indexing/layout and loop strategy. For a pair update, the least-significant active bit creates short pair separation, but vectorization, cache-line use, threading, and fused-block layouts can favor different orderings. Present it as one conventional layout, not a universal optimum.
- **Reordering semantics:** Reordering commuting gates can improve locality; transposing logical-to-array qubit positions requires maintaining the observable/measurement mapping. Mention that semantic bookkeeping, because it is precisely where simulator-only endianness bugs occur.
- **Hardware-transpiler contrast:** Useful connection to Chapter 23. “Opposing objective” is plausible—hardware mapping may introduce a memory-unfriendly simulated layout—but a simulator executing a transpiled circuit may still independently remap its internal bit positions without changing logical semantics.
- **Mutable implementation roster:** Qiskit Aer, qsim, cuStateVec, and Intel-QS need exact official product names, links, versions/access dates, supported precisions/platforms, and evidence for each listed optimization. In particular, verify the current branding and maintenance status of Intel Quantum Simulator rather than freezing a potentially stale name.
- **SIMD expansion:** Expanding SIMD and naming AVX/NEON helps experts but burdens beginners. A glossary or “vector instructions process several amplitudes at once” gloss would improve accessibility.
- **Performance claim:** “Approach memory-bandwidth peak” needs benchmark scope and a cited roofline-style measurement. Some fused or multi-qubit kernels become compute-bound; communication dominates distributed runs; GPU utilization varies with state size.
- **Practical ceiling:** \(33\)–\(35\) qubits on a high-memory single node is a reasonable complex128 payload heuristic, but precision, headroom, GPUs versus host RAM, number of devices, and operation type determine the ceiling. Treat the range as an as-of-date example rather than an enduring boundary.
- **Supercomputer ceiling:** “Mid-40s for the largest supercomputers” is representation- and date-sensitive and may conflict with the immediately cited approximately 48-qubit compressed run. Separate dense complex128, dense lower precision, compressed full-state, and task-specific records.
- **JUQCS claim:** The approximately 48-qubit, adaptive two-byte encoding, and approximately 0.5-PiB figures require a primary citation and exact experiment/date. Arithmetic sanity check: \(2^{48}\times2\) bytes is \(2^{49}\) bytes = 512 TiB = 0.5 PiB, so the payload statement is internally consistent.
- **Record-list skepticism:** “Any … quoted from memory should be distrusted” is refreshingly candid but sounds like an editorial note rather than finished book prose. Move the dated record table to Appendix F as proposed, cite it here, and replace the admonition with a reproducibility checklist: representation, precision, amplitudes versus samples, circuit depth/gates, hardware, runtime, and verification.
- **One-qubit-per-doubling insight:** Excellent, compact, and memorable. It would benefit from a visual staircase that shows how precision reduction buys an additive number of qubits, never an asymptotic escape.
- **“Cannot simulate noise” defect:** A basic pure-state unitary statevector cannot directly represent a general mixed state, but statevector-based Monte Carlo trajectories, stochastic channels, purification with ancillas, and explicit environment models can simulate noise under different costs. Replace the absolute with the precise representational limitation.
- **“Cannot exploit structure” defect:** The dense representation stores all amplitudes even for a product state, but implementations exploit gate sparsity, diagonality, symmetry, zero amplitudes, fusion, and sometimes compression. Say it does not *intrinsically compress state entanglement/product structure*.
- **“Gold standard”:** Useful colloquially for small noiseless circuit validation, but undefined and potentially misleading where high-precision tensor-network or analytic results are the reference. Specify the validation domain and what is being benchmarked.
- **Example lead-in:** Access to amplitudes and exact probabilities is the right demonstration. A symmetric GHZ state is easy to recognize but poor at exposing qubit ordering; supplement it with one asymmetric amplitude pattern.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** The stride mechanics, memory traffic, and one-qubit-per-doubling wall turn abstraction into machinery. The record paragraph is exciting but crowded with caveats; a sourced “record card” would preserve wonder while improving trust.

## §24.3 statevector code example and output, lines 65–89

- **Coverage:** Reviewed every import, circuit-construction line, statevector construction, dictionary conversion, formatting/rounding operation, and displayed output.
- **Snippet scope:** The example cleanly demonstrates exact amplitude and probability access with minimal setup. It should state the tested Qiskit and Python versions, installation command/environment lock, expected filename invocation, and whether the repository’s linked example is mechanically synchronized with the embedded snippet.
- **Imports:** `QuantumCircuit` and `qiskit.quantum_info.Statevector` are appropriate public interfaces. Current compatibility should be checked in the repository’s pinned environment rather than inferred from an unversioned global installation.
- **Circuit construction:** \(H(0)\), CNOT \(0\to1\), then CNOT \(1\to2\) correctly prepares \((|000\rangle+|111\rangle)/\sqrt2\) from \(|000\rangle\).
- **Comment placement:** The comment on only the final CNOT says it “prepares” the GHZ state, though the whole three-gate sequence does. Place the explanation above the block or say “completes.”
- **Statevector constructor:** `Statevector(qc)` is compact, but `Statevector.from_instruction(qc)` may communicate intent more explicitly and has historically been the pedagogical spelling. Use whichever the pinned current API documents, and test it.
- **Global phase:** The output represents one valid GHZ phase convention. Add a note that global phase is physically irrelevant while the relative plus sign is meaningful.
- **Dictionary key semantics:** Qiskit’s displayed basis strings can conceal little-endian qubit-index conventions. Here `000` and `111` are invariant under reversal, so the example teaches no ordering intuition and cannot catch an ordering bug. Add an asymmetric state such as \(|001\rangle\) prepared by \(X(0)\), then explain how the string maps to qubits.
- **Sorting:** Lexicographic sorting is deterministic for fixed-width bitstrings and makes output reproducible. If registers introduce spaces or heterogeneous labels, state the expected representation or keep this example explicitly single-register.
- **Amplitude formatting:** Printing real and imaginary components with explicit signs is readable. Negative-zero artifacts can appear for tiny floating-point values; threshold values before display or use a library-aware formatter if exact snapshot output is tested.
- **Probability conversion:** `probabilities_dict()` already produces numeric probabilities. Converting keys with `str(k)` appears redundant for ordinary bitstring keys; document why it is needed or remove it.
- **Rounding semantics:** `round(v, 3)` followed by `float` is display formatting, not an exact probability computation. The prose says “exact probabilities,” yet the code immediately rounds them. Preserve unrounded values for assertions and format only at print time.
- **Normalization check:** Add `assert np.isclose(sum(probs_raw.values()), 1)` and amplitude assertions to turn the demonstration into an executable test rather than a visual transcript.
- **Output accuracy:** \(1/\sqrt2\approx0.70710678\), so `+0.707+0.000j` and probabilities \(0.5,0.5\) match the circuit and formatting.
- **No-sampling claim:** Correct: neither amplitude nor probability output here is estimated from finite shots. Explicitly contrast this with `measure_all()` plus a shot-based backend in a two-column example.
- **Missing complexity connection:** The snippet does not expose memory or runtime, despite following the exponential-barrier discussion. Print `sv.data.nbytes` and compare it with \(16\,2^3\); readers can then scale the same expression to 30+ qubits.
- **Failure-mode opportunity:** Show one deliberate basis-order assertion failure or a nonnormalized hand-constructed vector error. That would connect the “internals” advantage to real debugging rather than only producing a familiar state.
- **Accessibility:** Explain `amp`, `sv`, and the `:+.3f` format for readers new to Python. The output’s `j` denotes the imaginary unit, while the prose uses mathematical \(i\); mention the language convention.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** It is satisfying to see the two surviving amplitudes, but GHZ is the most predictable possible reveal. An asymmetric “guess the printed bitstring” challenge would add useful surprise.
- **Section close:** There is no explicit takeaway, sanity check, or exercise after the output. Add a one-sentence rule: dense statevectors give privileged exact numerical access on tractable instances, at an exponential payload cost and under an explicit bit-order convention.

## §24.4 “Density-Matrix Simulation,” lines 90–99

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the mixed-state motivation, density-matrix definition and memory ladder, unitary/Kraus evolution, measurement rule, trajectory alternative, Pauli-mixture/stabilizer special case, and transition boundary.
- **Mixed-state motivation:** Coupling to an unobserved environment, classical uncertainty, and nonunitary noise motivate density operators. “The pure-state description fails” is too strong for a larger closed system: system plus environment can remain pure, while the reduced system is mixed after tracing out the environment. State that distinction.
- **Definition:** Positive semidefinite with unit trace is correct for a finite-dimensional quantum state; Hermiticity follows from positive semidefiniteness under the standard definition. Adding \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) explicitly would help readers encountering numerical implementations, where Hermiticity is checked separately.
- **Payload equation:** \(16\,4^n\) bytes is correct for a dense complex128 \(2^n\times2^n\) matrix. As in §24.2, call it a payload minimum; channel application often needs work buffers or vectorized superoperators that can demand substantially more.
- **Threshold arithmetic:** The listed payloads are correct: \(n=15\) is 16 GiB, 17 is 256 GiB, 20 is 16 TiB, and 25 is 16 PiB. “Feasible width roughly halves” means the qubit count at a fixed memory budget halves relative to complex128 statevectors; spell this out because the phrase could be mistaken for halving dimension.
- **Machine labels:** “Workstation,” “large server,” “top-cluster territory,” and “any current machine” are mutable and ignore overhead/distribution. Date and source machine capacities or keep only the durable payload values. The 25-qubit “any current machine” assertion is especially brittle and should not appear without an as-of date and definition of usable aggregate memory.
- **Unitary evolution:** \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) and the Heisenberg-picture contrast are correct. For an open subsystem, note that a unitary on the total system followed by a partial trace induces the channel.
- **Kraus condition:** \(\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k=I\) characterizes trace-preserving channels; trace-nonincreasing operations/conditioned measurement branches use \(\le I\). The current paragraph later discusses measurement, so one sentence would clarify why measurement outcomes use separate nonnormalized branches.
- **Channel scope:** Kraus form covers finite-dimensional completely positive trace-preserving maps, not every temporally correlated, non-Markovian, state-preparation-and-measurement, leakage, or continuous-time device error through a simple independent per-gate channel. “Arbitrary noise” later overclaims the model.
- **“Direct to apply”:** Algebraically direct does not mean computationally cheap. Cost scales with matrix size, number/rank/locality of Kraus operators, and implementation strategy; applying a channel through a full superoperator is worse than exploiting locality.
- **Measurement statement:** \(p_k=\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_k\rho)\) is correct for projective measurement. General POVMs use effects \(E_k\); post-measurement state additionally requires instruments/Kraus operators. “Full distribution” may itself contain exponentially many outcomes and therefore cannot always be enumerated cheaply.
- **“Exactness against arbitrary noise” defect:** Dense density-matrix evolution is deterministic and sampling-free for represented Markovian channels, but still has floating-point/model/discretization error and cannot encode an unknown real environment merely by being dense. Replace “exactness” with “explicit mixed-state evolution for the specified channel model.”
- **Trajectory terminology:** Quantum-jump/Monte Carlo wavefunction evolution with an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is appropriate for Lindblad dynamics. For discrete Kraus sampling, probabilities depend on \(\langle\psi|K_k^\dagger K_k|\psi\rangle\), followed by normalization; printing that formula would make the analogy rigorous.
- **Unraveling nuance:** A channel or Lindblad master equation may admit multiple trajectory unravelings with different variance and computational behavior. The average density operator converges to the modeled evolution, while a finite trajectory estimate has statistical uncertainty.
- **What is averaged:** “Per-trajectory measurement statistics” is slightly vague. One can average trajectory expectation values or sampled outcomes; total error combines trajectory count and any within-trajectory shot sampling.
- **Trajectory count:** “Often hundreds to thousands” is an unsupported rule of thumb and can be dramatically wrong for rare events, long-time dynamics, high precision, or variance-reduced observables. Give a \(1/\sqrt{N}\) Monte Carlo scaling statement with variance/confidence and label any count as a worked example.
- **Parallelism:** Independent trajectories are embarrassingly parallel absent shared adaptation, but initialization, aggregation, memory, RNG reproducibility, load imbalance from jumps, and accelerator batching still matter. “Right tool” should become “one strong option.”
- **Alternatives omitted:** Matrix-product density operators, locally purified tensor networks, low-rank methods, stochastic Pauli/noise propagation, Heisenberg-picture observable evolution, process-tensor methods, and problem-specific solvers may beat both dense matrices and simple trajectories. A decision table should include them or explicitly delimit scope.
- **Pauli-mixture special case:** Sampling Pauli errors while preserving stabilizer states is efficient for Clifford circuits and compatible stabilizer inputs/measurements. This is an important structural connection and deserves a miniature example.
- **Channel examples:** Depolarizing and dephasing can be written as Pauli mixtures under common definitions; “biased Pauli noise” is tautologically in the class. Amplitude damping is notably not a Pauli mixture and provides a useful counterexample.
- **Million-qubit claim:** Polynomial representation permits enormous widths, but “circuits with millions of qubits” still depends on gate/measurement count, connectivity, shots, decoder coupling, correlations, and requested output. Cite an actual fault-tolerance simulation and distinguish simulating the stabilizer/noise model from simulating general logical quantum data with non-Clifford magic.
- **Fault-tolerant phrasing:** Fault-tolerant computation is not simply “Clifford operations with Pauli noise”; universal fault tolerance includes non-Clifford state injection/distillation and realistic error models can include leakage/correlations. Say that large stabilizer subproblems central to QEC are tractable.
- **Missing visual:** A side-by-side diagram should show (1) density matrix propagated once, (2) many stochastic pure-state paths, and (3) their ensemble average, with memory and sampling-error annotations.
- **Pedagogy:** Add a one-qubit amplitude-damping calculation performed both by two Kraus operators and by sampled trajectories. Readers could observe convergence and separate model error from Monte Carlo error.
- **Accessibility:** Define PSD, CPTP, POVM, and “non-Hermitian drift” if introduced; the current section moves from Chapter 11 recall to advanced open-system numerics in four paragraphs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The quadrupling ladder and swarm-of-trajectories alternative create strong images. The ending’s million-qubit leap is exciting but risks sounding magical unless a concrete stabilizer-noise experiment grounds it.
- **Section-level takeaway:** The durable rule should be: choose density matrices for tractable explicit mixed states; choose an unraveling when its statistical cost is cheaper than \(4^n\); choose structured representations when the state, channel, observable, or circuit admits them.

## §24.5 “Stabilizer Simulation,” lines 100–109

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the Gottesman–Knill statement, generator encoding, destabilizer tableau and complexity claims, Aaronson–Gottesman/CHP attribution, later-representation list, Stim performance claims, QEC application, and non-Clifford boundary.
- **Theorem scope:** Computational-basis stabilizer input, Clifford gates, and computational-basis measurement are a valid restricted formulation. The efficiently simulable class can be stated more generally using stabilizer states, Clifford operations, Pauli measurements, and adaptive Clifford control; saying this is a “foundational result” is fair.
- **Gate set:** \(H,S,\mathrm{CNOT}\) generates the Clifford group up to phase, but Pauli gates and CZ are common direct instructions. Readers may mistake the parenthetical for an exhaustive operational set rather than generators; label it.
- **Simulation task ambiguity:** “Simulated classically” can mean sampling outputs, updating a state description, computing certain probabilities, or strongly simulating the full distribution. Gottesman–Knill variants differ in allowed inputs/measurements and strong-versus-weak outputs. Define the task promised here.
- **Generator description:** A pure stabilizer state is specified by \(n\) independent commuting Pauli generators not containing \(-I\). “A list of \(n\)” should include independence and phase consistency.
- **Bit encoding:** A Pauli string uses \(2n\) binary symplectic bits plus phase information. Calling the last bit merely “a sign” works for Hermitian stabilizer generators but tableau phase conventions differ; \(Y\) and update phases deserve care. Also, “two bits per qubit for the \(\{I,X,Y,Z\}\) choice” should explain the \(X/Z\) bit mapping.
- **Representation transition:** The first paragraph says the state uses \(n(2n+1)\) bits; the next introduces an Aaronson–Gottesman-style \(2n\times(2n+1)\) tableau with destabilizers. Distinguish the minimal stabilizer-generator description from the doubled algorithmic tableau so readers do not see a contradiction.
- **Destabilizers wording:** Destabilizers are not additional stabilizers of the state; they form a canonical symplectic partner basis that accelerates operations such as measurement. Quotation marks do not fully explain this.
- **Storage complexity:** \(O(n^2)\) is correct for this dense binary tableau. Bit packing changes constants; sparse/graph-state forms can behave differently.
- **Gate-update complexity:** Updating all \(2n\) tableau rows for one Clifford gate costs \(O(n)\) in the straightforward Aaronson–Gottesman representation. In a bit-packed implementation, instruction batches and representation choice alter practical/asymptotic word-operation costs.
- **Hadamard update:** Swapping \(X/Z\) columns is incomplete without the phase flip for rows having \(Y\) on that qubit. The following CNOT phrase mentions phase rules, but the Hadamard example could teach an incorrect update if read literally.
- **Measurement determinism:** Whether \(Z_q\) commutes with all stabilizers and belongs appropriately to the stabilizer determines deterministic outcomes; if it anticommutes with a generator the result is random. The current “measured Pauli’s membership” shorthand needs the \(\pm\) eigenvalue and sign.
- **Runtime formula:** \(O(ng+n^2m)\) matches the stated naïve per-gate and row-reduction measurement bounds, but deterministic versus random measurements, improved/inverse tableaus, word packing, and circuit structure change it. Label the algorithm rather than presenting a universal stabilizer-simulation complexity.
- **Primary-source attribution:** The manuscript should cite Scott Aaronson and Daniel Gottesman, “Improved Simulation of Stabilizer Circuits,” *Physical Review A* 70, 052328 (2004), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevA.70.052328. The paper explicitly describes CHP and the factor-two storage tradeoff used to remove Gaussian elimination: [APS article](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.70.052328).
- **“CHP” expansion:** CNOT–Hadamard–Phase, not merely “after the simulator,” should be expanded; the source abstract provides the expansion.
- **Later-method catalogue:** Graph-state and symplectic tableau representations are not simply a chronological ladder where each dominates the prior one. Performance depends on circuit topology, measurement pattern, output task, and sparsity. Cite specific algorithms rather than naming broad representation families.
- **Stim architecture:** The text attributes its advantage vaguely to “constants.” Stim’s 2021 paper emphasizes an inverse tableau for faster deterministic measurement, cache-friendly 256-bit SIMD layout, and compile-once/reference-sample plus batched Pauli-frame sampling. These are pedagogically richer and more precise than the current superlative: [Stim paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02202).
- **Stim scale mismatch:** The primary paper’s headline benchmark is a distance-100 surface-code circuit with about 20,000 qubits, 8 million gates, and 1 million measurements analyzed in 15 seconds, followed by full-shot sampling at about 1 kHz. That does **not** directly substantiate the manuscript’s “\(10^6\) qubits” and “\(10^8\) gate operations per second on a laptop” sentence.
- **Required repair to performance claim:** Either cite an exact current benchmark that defines the million-qubit circuit, instruction mix, hardware, thread count, preprocessing, samples, and throughput denominator, or replace the claim with the published 2021 workload. Do not combine maxima from different workloads into one apparent benchmark.
- **Current project source:** Link the maintained [Stim repository](https://github.com/quantumlib/Stim) with an access date and pinned release/commit; “Stim simulator” alone gives no reproducible interface or benchmark baseline.
- **“Orders of magnitude” claim:** Requires a named comparator, version, hardware, circuit suite, and output task. Stim’s speedups can arise from reference sampling and detector-error-model workflows that are not apples-to-apples with constructing arbitrary tableau states or returning full state descriptions.
- **QEC bottleneck:** Decoder-versus-simulator dominance is workload-dependent. Detector error model generation, circuit sampling, I/O, matching/decoding, correlated-error handling, and statistics can each dominate. Cite one end-to-end profiling study or soften to “often.”
- **“Millions of stabilizer measurements per shot”:** The sourced Stim example has one million measurements in a distance-100 circuit, but the manuscript generalizes to surface-code benchmarking. Give code distance, rounds, observable, shots, and whether repeated detectors or raw measurements are counted.
- **Non-Clifford boundary:** \(T\) is the canonical Clifford+T boundary and maps generic stabilizer states outside the stabilizer set. However, a \(T\) acting on \(|0\rangle\), or canceling/commuting into a Clifford-equivalent action, need not create magic; the manuscript’s “generic” and later structure caveat correctly anticipate this.
- **Tableau update wording:** There is no exact update *within a single stabilizer tableau* for a generic magic-producing \(T\), but exact simulation can use sums/mixtures/quasiprobabilities of stabilizer objects or enlarged representations. Make the representational boundary explicit.
- **Magic cost:** Worst-case exponential dependence is not characterized by raw \(T\)-count alone. Relevant quantities include stabilizer rank/extent, \(T\)-depth, interaction/cancellation, magic-state structure, measurement/adaptivity, desired additive/multiplicative error, and output task. The transition to §24.6 should preview those parameters.
- **Missing example:** Evolve \(|00\rangle\) through \(H\), CNOT, then show its two stabilizer generators and their tableau updates. Apply \(T\) to a qubit where it actually creates magic and demonstrate why \(X\) conjugates outside the Pauli group.
- **Accessibility:** Define Clifford group, Pauli generator, symplectic, tableau, destabilizer, SIMD, and detector error model locally or through a glossary. This mandatory-looking chapter route otherwise jumps abruptly into specialist implementation language.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The dramatic change from exponential amplitudes to bit-packed algebra is inherently delightful, and the \(T\)-gate cliff creates suspense. A worked tableau and a defensible Stim benchmark card would make the performance feel earned rather than legendary.
- **Section-level rule:** Efficient stabilizer simulation is a promise about a restricted state/operation/measurement/output class; every scale or speed claim must name all four plus the implementation and machine.

## §24.6 “Near-Clifford and Magic-State Simulation,” lines 110–125

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the \(k\)-non-Clifford cost slogan, stabilizer-rank definition and exponent claims, magic-state injection description, runtime equation, two historical demonstrations, quasiprobability method, resource-theory synthesis, and claimed \(T\)-count implication.
- **Opening cost slogan:** “Exponential in \(k\), polynomial in everything else” describes important known upper bounds for particular Clifford+\(T\) simulation tasks; it is not the universally “right” cost model. Gate placement, cancellation, \(T\)-depth, diagonal structure, measurements, desired output, approximation error, stabilizer extent/rank, and alternative algorithms can dominate.
- **Parameter definition:** Define \(k\) as raw non-Clifford gates, injected magic states, or optimized resource count after Clifford simplification. These are not interchangeable, and “inserted” suggests a syntactic count before compilation.
- **Stabilizer decomposition:** Any finite-dimensional pure qubit state can be expanded in the stabilizer-state span because computational-basis states are stabilizer states. This existence fact is correct but trivial; the computational value comes from a *low-rank* or low-extent expansion plus efficient overlap/update algorithms.
- **Rank definition:** Stabilizer rank is the minimum number of stabilizer states in an exact linear combination. Coefficients can be complex and terms need not be orthogonal. Approximate stabilizer rank additionally requires a specified norm/error; introduce it explicitly before quoting approximate bounds.
- **Single-state rank:** \(\chi(|T\rangle)=2\) is correct because \(|T\rangle\) is non-stabilizer but lies in a two-dimensional space spanned by stabilizer basis states. The manuscript should define its phase convention, e.g. \((|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
- **Exponent wording:** “\(2^{\alpha k}\) with \(\alpha\approx0.4\) for the exact rank” is an upper-bound construction, not an established asymptotic equality or unique exponent. Write \(\chi(T^{\otimes k})\le O(2^{0.3963k})\) with all finite-size/polynomial factors and the cited theorem’s precise state convention.
- **Exact versus approximate splice:** The parenthetical combines an exact-rank upper bound with the 2016 approximate sampling runtime \(2^{0.23t}t^3w^3\). They solve different tasks under different error/output assumptions and should not share one \(\alpha\) in the displayed runtime.
- **2016 primary result:** Bravyi–Gosset report two tasks: fixed-output probability in \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m)+2^{0.5t}t^3\), and output sampling in \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m)+2^{0.23t}t^3w^3\), with additional approximation/error semantics described in the paper. Cite and state the task rather than calling \(0.23\) generic “approximate-rank scaling”: [Bravyi–Gosset preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.07601).
- **Magic-state reduction:** Replacing \(T\) gates with injected \(|T\rangle\) resources and Clifford gadgets is a standard reduction, but “every simulator therefore preprocesses every \(T\)” is false. Direct diagonal-gate handling, phase-polynomial simplification, path-integral methods, decision diagrams, and hybrid representations need not use that pipeline.
- **Adaptivity/postselection:** A teleportation-style injection introduces measurements and classically conditioned Clifford corrections; the simulator must account for outcome probabilities/branches or algebraically absorb them. The current description hides this mechanism.
- **Displayed runtime:** \(\operatorname{poly}(n)2^{\alpha k}\) suppresses the number of Clifford gates \(m\), measured outputs \(w\), target error/confidence, decomposition construction, memory, and whether the task is amplitude, probability, expectation, or sampling. It is acceptable only as a labeled schematic upper bound.
- **“Underlying Clifford circuit on each term”:** This is conceptually helpful but can imply completely independent repeated tableaux. Algorithms reuse structure, batch inner products, sample decompositions, and exploit correlated terms; note that the literal implementation can be more sophisticated.
- **2016 demonstration:** The primary abstract supports a 40-qubit hidden-shift circuit with a few hundred Clifford gates and nearly 50 \(T\) gates. “In hours on a workstation” needs the exact table/instance, machine, task, error, and wall time; it is not established by the abstract and should not be repeated uncited.
- **2019 demonstration:** The 2019 paper reports 40–50-qubit algorithms with over 60 non-Clifford gates without HPC, including hidden-shift instances up to 64 \(T\) or 16 CCZ gates. Cite the exact instance/output mode rather than merging maxima: [Bravyi et al., *Quantum* 3, 181](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2019-09-02-181/).
- **Dense comparison:** “Would have cost roughly \(2^{50}\)-plus amplitudes” is an awkward unit. A 50-qubit complex128 vector has \(2^{50}\) amplitudes and a 16-PiB payload; state that exact comparison while noting that a dense simulation is not necessarily the best competing method.
- **Quasiprobability scope:** Pashayan–Wallman–Bartlett estimate selected outcome probabilities using quasiprobability representations. The algorithm’s convergence depends on a 1-norm negativity measure; it is not simply a general trajectory simulator returning arbitrary full outputs: [PRL article](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.070501).
- **Frame claim:** A representation in which all stabilizer states, Clifford transformations, and relevant measurements are simultaneously nonnegative is obstructed in important qubit settings by contextuality. The manuscript acknowledges this but still says the frame is “chosen so that the free sector” is nonnegative. Specify the dimensional/frame restrictions and exactly which preparations/operations/effects remain nonnegative.
- **Signed sampling language:** “Importance-samples trajectories carrying signed weights” is intuitive. Quasiprobabilities may also be negative or complex depending on representation; define the estimator, normalization/1-norm overhead, variance, and error/confidence scaling in a one-gate example.
- **Negativity normalization:** Saying magic is “constant for Clifford circuits” is vague; in a suitable nonnegative representation the relevant channel/state 1-norm overhead is ideally 1, while composition can multiply overheads. Contextual frames and representation optimization complicate the statement.
- **Magic measures are plural:** Stabilizer rank, approximate rank, stabilizer extent, robustness/mana, channel negativity, and \(T\)-count are related but not identical or monotonically interchangeable in every setting. The “two viewpoints” paragraph should explicitly resist collapsing them into one scalar magic.
- **No-lower-bound caveat:** Excellent and crucial. Known exponential upper bounds do not prove an unavoidable exponential cost for every classical algorithm or every circuit family. Elevate this qualification into a displayed warning.
- **“The T-count is the magic resource” defect:** \(T\)-count is a compilation/resource metric for Clifford+\(T\) fault-tolerant circuits, not the unique magic resource. CCZ states, arbitrary rotations, qudits, catalysis, measurements, synthesis accuracy, \(T\)-depth, factory throughput, and space-time cost all matter. Use “a central resource count.”
- **Advantage-cap wording:** Few \(T\) gates can make these particular simulations tractable when the polynomial factors and requested task are manageable; it does not automatically cap all notions of advantage, especially if input/output size or Clifford scaffold is itself enormous. The manuscript’s “against these particular methods” is the right caveat but needs to govern the whole sentence.
- **High-\(T\) asymmetry:** The closing statement that high \(T\)-count proves nothing about all classical algorithms is exemplary. Add the symmetric warning that low raw \(T\)-count is not sufficient for cheap simulation until preprocessing, precision, and output task are specified.
- **Missing worked comparison:** For one \(T\) injection, show (1) a two-term stabilizer sum and (2) a signed quasiprobability estimator, then tabulate rank/1-norm and how two copies compose. This would turn an acronym-heavy research survey into a learnable mechanism.
- **Citation hygiene:** Give full titles/DOIs once, distinguish publication year from preprint year, and attach each number to a theorem/table/benchmark. “Bravyi et al. 2019” is too weak for a section whose argument rests on exact exponents.
- **Accessibility:** Define magic state, teleportation/injection, stabilizer rank, approximate rank, quasiprobability, negativity, importance sampling, contextuality, and CCZ. This is likely the chapter’s steepest conceptual jump so far.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** Charging only for the “magic” is a wonderful organizing idea, and the \(T\)-gate as a simulation tollbooth is memorable. The exponent thicket currently blunts the insight; a one-\(T\) worked example and a task-specific benchmark table would restore momentum.
- **Section-level rule:** Never quote a near-Clifford exponent without naming the resource measure, exact/approximate criterion, simulation output, error metric, polynomial factors, and circuit family.

## §24.7 “Tensor-Network Simulation,” lines 126–137

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the limited-entanglement premise, tensor/bond representation, storage formula, MPS contract/truncate cycle, entropy/Schmidt-rank logic, MPS/PEPS topology and software claims, volume-law failure mode, GHZ counterexample, and favorable-regime examples.
- **“Leading method”:** Plausible in important low-entanglement many-body and structured-circuit regimes, but “leading” needs a task/field/metric. Tensor networks coexist with quantum Monte Carlo, exact diagonalization, Krylov methods, dynamical mean-field methods, coupled cluster, neural quantum states, and problem-specific techniques.
- **Scope drift:** The section title and opening discuss tensor networks generally, but “one tensor per site,” one bond dimension \(\chi\), \(O(n\chi^2)\) storage, and balanced-cut \(2^{n/2}\) bounds describe an open-boundary MPS most directly. General PEPS/circuit networks have degree-dependent storage and multiple bond indices.
- **Tensor definition:** Explain that a tensor is a multidimensional array, physical indices encode local basis states, and contracted auxiliary indices are summed. “Small tensors” is relative: their entries can still scale exponentially with vertex degree or bond dimension.
- **Bond dimension:** Networks can have a different dimension \(\chi_e\) on every edge. A single \(\chi\) usually denotes the maximum/uniform cap. State this before using \(\chi\) as the global expressive-control knob.
- **Product-state claim:** An MPS with every bond dimension 1 represents product states. A more general network with all auxiliary bonds dimension 1 also factors over sites, assuming no multi-site physical tensor; the stated architecture should be explicit.
- **Arbitrary-state bound:** Any \(n\)-qubit pure state admits an MPS whose maximum bond dimension is at most \(2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\), with cut-dependent dimensions \(2^{\min(j,n-j)}\). “Bond dimension \(2^{n/2}\) represents an arbitrary state” should be labeled as the MPS worst-case upper bound, not a claim about one arbitrary tensor-network edge.
- **Rank language:** In numerical computing, the full coefficient array is an order-\(n\) tensor, not necessarily a “rank-\(n\)” tensor—rank has several conflicting meanings (CP rank, matrix rank, tensor rank). Use “order \(n\)” to avoid collision with Schmidt rank.
- **Per-site storage:** A bulk MPS tensor for qubits has \(2\chi_{j-1}\chi_j\) entries; endpoints and nonuniform bonds differ. PEPS tensors scale like physical dimension times a product of several bond dimensions, e.g. \(O(d\chi^4)\) on a square lattice. Restrict \(O(n\chi^2)\) explicitly to MPS.
- **“Lazily on demand”:** Some networks are contracted partially, optimized, sliced, cached, or updated locally; others are maintained in canonical form. “Lazy” is an implementation strategy, not the definition. The core point is that the full \(2^n\) coefficient tensor need not be materialized.
- **Compression qualification:** Tensor networks may be exact factorizations with exponential bonds or approximate compressed representations after truncation. Call them “potentially compressed” and make the discarded-weight/error criterion visible.
- **MPS update:** Applying a local two-site gate, reshaping, SVD, and truncating is a TEBD-style update. One-site gates need no bond SVD; long-range gates require swaps or alternative contractions; time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution introduces Trotter or other integrator error.
- **SVD cost omitted:** Typical two-site MPS update cost depends polynomially (often cubically) on \(\chi\), local dimension, symmetry, and implementation. The section gives storage but no compute formula, leaving readers unable to compare methods.
- **Truncation contract:** State whether \(\chi\) is a hard cap or selected from a discarded singular-value weight/tolerance. Record cumulative truncation error, normalization drift, time-step error, and observable convergence—not just the chosen bond dimension.
- **Entropy bound:** For a cut with Schmidt rank \(r\), \(S\le\log_2 r\); an MPS bond across that cut must have \(\chi\ge r\) for exact representation. The text currently says the Schmidt decomposition has at most \(\chi\) nonzero values before clearly restricting to a state represented by that network.
- **Circular notation:** “If rank stays \(\le2^S\), \(\chi=2^S\)” uses \(S\) as though it were simultaneously entropy and a log-rank bound. Entropy \(S\) does not determine rank. Introduce \(r_{\max}\), then separately relate \(S\le\log_2 r_{\max}\).
- **Low-entropy approximation:** Low von Neumann entropy can bound how much Schmidt probability lies in a tail only with a quantitative error/rank relationship; “modest \(\chi\)” depends on target norm/observable error and system size. Give the actual inequality or say it is heuristic without further spectral assumptions.
- **Area-law tractability:** One-dimensional gapped ground states have powerful MPS approximation results under stated assumptions. An area law alone, especially in higher dimensions, does not automatically make PEPS contraction or state preparation efficient. The sentence should not generalize MPS experience to all tensor networks.
- **Entropy is not the only load-bearing quantity:** For a chosen MPS ordering, all cut spectra matter. For arbitrary circuit networks, contraction treewidth, graph topology, gate tensors, output set, slicing, and cancellation can dominate even without interpreting an evolving state’s entropy.
- **Topology terminology:** MPS is a chain tensor-network ansatz; PEPS generalizes it to higher-dimensional graphs. DMRG is an optimization algorithm and TEBD an evolution algorithm, so keep those categories distinct from topology.
- **Software ecosystem:** ITensor, TeNPy, Quimb, and cuTensorNet are heterogeneous: libraries/frameworks differ in language, algorithms, GPU/distributed support, licensing, and whether they target many-body states or general circuit contraction. Add official URLs, versions/access dates, and a capability matrix; avoid implying interchangeability.
- **“For decades”:** Accurate for DMRG/MPS history in broad terms, but PEPS emerged later and production maturity differs. The existing parenthetical recognizes this; replace the rhetorical duration with dated citations to foundational/review literature.
- **Baseline attribution:** Name the benchmark, circuit geometry, contraction strategy, approximation, hardware, and metric for each “strongest” classical baseline. Cross-reference §24.14 only after ensuring it supplies those details.
- **Volume-law statement:** For an MPS exact representation across a balanced cut, entropy \(S=\Theta(n)\) requires \(\chi\ge2^S\), hence exponential bond dimension. “Toward \(2^{n/2}\)” applies to near-maximal balanced-cut entropy, not every volume-law state with an arbitrary coefficient.
- **Deep-random qualifier:** Random circuits often generate near-volume-law entanglement after sufficient geometry-dependent depth, but a deep Clifford circuit remains stabilizer-easy and a circuit may have exploitable contraction structure. Entanglement defeats MPS compression, not necessarily every simulator.
- **GHZ contrast:** Excellent example. “Maximally nonlocal” is rhetorically suggestive but not a standard scalar classification; GHZ has long-range multipartite correlations and only one ebit across any bipartition. Say that precisely.
- **Low-depth claim:** Constant-depth local circuits may admit favorable causal-cone or contraction algorithms in some geometries/tasks, but two-dimensional network contraction can remain difficult and “local entanglement” alone is insufficient. Give dimension, depth scaling, observable/output, and approximation criterion.
- **Variational warning:** Valuable skepticism. Some ansätze are intentionally entangling; others preserve symmetry, locality, shallow depth, or low effective bond dimension. Avoid treating “substantial entanglement” as synonymous with classical hardness.
- **Missing contraction-complexity concept:** Introduce graph treewidth/contraction width alongside bond entanglement. This is necessary before §24.11 and prevents readers from believing \(\chi\) is the universal tensor-network cost coordinate.
- **Missing error example:** Use a six-site chain, list Schmidt values at one cut, truncate from rank 4 to 2, and compute discarded weight/fidelity/observable error. Then contrast exact GHZ \(\chi=2\) with a random state’s bond growth.
- **Accessibility:** Expand MPS, PEPS, SVD, TEBD, and DMRG on first local appearance or link the promised definitions immediately. Draw tensor-network diagrams with shape/labels, not color alone, and give alt text explaining physical versus bond legs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.5/10.** “Entanglement structure, not entanglement per se” and GHZ’s cheapness provide a genuinely surprising payoff. A visual sequence of bonds swelling and being truncated would be both beautiful and clarifying.
- **Section-level rule:** Every tensor-network performance claim must name network topology, ordering/contraction tree, maximum bond dimensions, exact versus truncated status, error metric, requested output, and hardware.

## §24.8 “Matrix Product States and TEBD,” lines 138–153

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the MPS equation and boundaries, bond/storage statement, one- and two-site updates, nonlocal-gate routing claim, TEBD definition/Trotter pattern/cost, variant list, area-law and quench regimes, and quantum-circuit/software conclusion.
- **Equation clarity:** Specify \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) and open boundary conditions. The product of the boundary-compatible matrices is a \(1\times1\) scalar coefficient; without that explanation the expression looks like a matrix multiplying a ket.
- **Tensor notation:** Each site is more naturally a rank-3 tensor \(A^{[i]\,x_i}_{\alpha_{i-1},\alpha_i}\), with a physical index \(x_i\) selecting a matrix. Giving both notations would bridge tensor diagrams and the displayed algebra.
- **Normalization/gauge freedom:** MPS representations are nonunique under inserting \(G G^{-1}\) on a bond. Left-, right-, and mixed-canonical forms make norms, Schmidt values, truncation, and local expectation values stable and efficient. Their absence leaves the SVD algorithm conceptually incomplete.
- **Bond control:** \(\chi_i\) upper-bounds Schmidt rank across cut \(i|i+1\); equality holds in an exact canonical minimal form. “Controls entanglement” should distinguish rank capacity from the actual singular-value spectrum/entropy.
- **Storage formula:** For local dimension \(d=2\), storage is \(\sum_i d\chi_{i-1}\chi_i\), bounded by \(O(nd\chi^2)\). The stated \(O(n\chi^2)\) is correct with fixed qubit dimension but hides nonuniform savings and complex-number precision.
- **Single-site update:** A local gate contracts with the physical index of \(A^{(i)}\) and does not increase adjacent Schmidt ranks. It may disturb canonical form and require re-canonicalization depending on the workflow.
- **Two-site update:** The standard sequence should name: contract two tensors, apply the \(d^2\times d^2\) gate, reshape, SVD, retain singular values according to rank/tolerance, and redistribute factors. “Past \(\chi\)” omits adaptive tolerance and normalization.
- **Truncation error:** Record discarded squared singular values at every update and explain how local discarded weight relates imperfectly to global state/observable error. A hard \(\chi\) alone is not a reproducibility or accuracy guarantee.
- **Long-range gates:** Adjacent SWAP routing is one approach; swap networks, dynamic site reordering, direct MPO gates, TDVP-like updates, and general contraction can be preferable. Do not present routing there-and-back as mandatory.
- **SWAP/entanglement nuance:** A physical SWAP is non-entangling as a two-qubit unitary on the swapped pair in isolation but moving already correlated logical degrees of freedom through an MPS ordering can raise intermediate cut ranks. The sentence’s “entanglement the SWAPs spread” is intuitive but technically imprecise; describe ordering-induced Schmidt-rank growth.
- **Overhead formula:** One gate at separation \(\ell\) requires \(O(\ell)\) adjacent swaps/updates, but total overhead is \(O(\sum_g \ell_g)\), at worst \(O(gn)\) for \(g\) long-range gates. Calling it “up to quadratic” assumes a gate-count scaling that is not stated.
- **TEBD scope:** TEBD applies local time-evolution gates to an MPS, commonly after a Suzuki–Trotter decomposition. It also covers imaginary-time variants; distinguish real-time unitary evolution from ground-state projection.
- **Hamiltonian assumptions:** \(H=\sum_i h_{i,i+1}\) should note finite-range nearest-neighbor terms and whether even/odd terms internally commute. Boundary conditions, time dependence, and longer-range interactions alter the decomposition.
- **Trotter structure:** The even/odd brick wall is exact only as the chosen product formula, not for the full exponential; give first- versus second-order ordering and global/local error dependence on timestep, commutators, time, and system size.
- **Cost formula:** \(O(n\chi^3)\) per sweep/timestep is a useful fixed-\(d\), roughly uniform-\(\chi\), dense-SVD estimate. Include \(d\), retained rank, symmetry/block sparsity, truncation algorithm, and number/order of substeps; wall time may be dominated by memory or parallelization.
- **Variant classification:** Higher-order Suzuki formulas reduce discretization error at extra gates and sometimes negative time steps; TDVP projects dynamics onto the MPS manifold and has one-site/two-site variants with different conservation and bond-growth behavior. It does not simply “control truncation error” in one generic way.
- **Area-law theorem:** Hastings’ one-dimensional gapped-ground-state area law supports efficient MPS approximation results under formal assumptions, but \(S=O(1)\) alone does not imply that a fixed small \(\chi\) achieves arbitrary global accuracy independent of \(n\), target error, gap, and observable.
- **Method mismatch:** Ground-state simulation is primarily the subject of §24.9’s DMRG or imaginary-time algorithms, not a direct example of ordinary real-time TEBD “winning.” Use the area law to motivate MPS representation, then reserve algorithmic ground-state claims for the next section.
- **Empirical \(\chi\) range:** “Tens to a few hundred” is model-, coupling-, boundary-, symmetry-, precision-, observable-, and algorithm-dependent. Present as dated examples with convergence plots, not a generic sufficiency range.
- **Chemical-accuracy warning:** Excellent category correction. If the term appears only to disclaim it, consider omitting it here or define its conventional energy threshold and explain why spin-chain observables need their own tolerances.
- **Quench generalization:** Linear entanglement growth is common after global quenches in many clean one-dimensional systems, but local quenches, integrability, many-body localization, conservation laws, confinement, disorder, and constrained dynamics change it. The current caveat is good; “commonly” still needs a specified family.
- **Entropy-to-bond consequence:** If entropy grows \(S(t)\propto t\), an exact or uniformly accurate MPS often needs exponential \(\chi\), but the quantitative relation depends on the Schmidt-spectrum tail and error criterion. State that entropy supplies a lower bound \(\chi\ge2^S\) for exact representation.
- **Failure boundary:** “Rapidly, if not at one sharp instant” is honest and useful. Give operational stop criteria: maximum \(\chi\), discarded weight, norm/energy drift, observable nonconvergence, or memory/time budget.
- **Circuit examples:** Low depth alone does not guarantee low MPS bond dimension; geometry and one-dimensional site ordering matter. “Adiabatic preparations near the gap” is unclear—small gaps generally demand slow evolution and can increase difficulty; perhaps the intended favorable case is a path that remains gapped and weakly entangled.
- **Mutable software claim:** Verify current official products and interfaces. NVIDIA cuQuantum is a suite, while tensor-network and MPS functionality is associated with cuTensorNet APIs; Quimb supports tensor-network circuit simulation through particular modules. Name versions, backend modes, GPU requirements, exact/truncated settings, and tested examples.
- **“Hundreds of qubits”:** Width without depth, geometry, \(\chi\), precision, output, and error is almost meaningless for MPS. Replace the scale boast with a reproducible benchmark matrix.
- **Missing comparison:** Simulate the same 1D quench at \(\chi=16,32,64,\dots\); plot entropy, discarded weight, energy drift, local observable, memory, and time. The breakdown should be visible rather than asserted.
- **Accessibility:** Expand TEBD, SVD, TDVP, MPS, and “quench”; draw the even/odd brick wall and label the SVD cut. Ensure singular-value plots remain interpretable without color.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The matrix chain and brick-wall evolution are visually intuitive, while the sudden exponential entanglement growth supplies tension. Software boasting is less engaging than watching a convergence plot visibly fail.
- **Section-level rule:** An MPS result is incomplete without site ordering, boundary conditions, \(\chi_i\)/cap, truncation tolerance and discarded weights, canonicalization/update method, timestep/product formula, precision, and observable convergence.

## §24.9 “DMRG and Ground-State Methods,” lines 154–163

- **Coverage:** Reviewed DMRG history and MPS interpretation, target/MPO scope, two-site sweep mechanics, convergence and benchmark claims, model list, two-dimensional cylinder mapping, complementary methods, and quantum-computing baseline argument.
- **Historical statement:** Steven R. White introduced DMRG in 1992; provide the foundational paper citation and distinguish infinite-system and finite-system algorithms. “Modern MPS reformulation” should cite the conceptual bridge rather than imply the original method was merely renamed.
- **Optimization description:** Modern finite DMRG variationally optimizes an MPS, usually at fixed/adaptive bond constraints, by solving local effective eigenproblems. The global MPS energy landscape is nonconvex under practical constraints, so local variational updates do not guarantee the global ground state.
- **Target geometry:** One-dimensional and quasi-one-dimensional systems are the natural strength, but DMRG also treats impurity mappings, momentum-space/orbital chains, cylinders, finite-temperature purifications, and excited states with varying difficulty. The current scope is a fair core route.
- **MPO expansion:** Define matrix product operator and explain that long-range terms may raise MPO bond dimension; “MPO handles” is not a free computational promise. Quantum-chemistry Hamiltonians have dense two-electron couplings and orbital ordering/localization strongly affect cost.
- **Sweep mechanics:** The two-site description is correct at a useful level. Clarify construction/application of the left and right environments, iterative eigensolver tolerance, canonical center movement, and why two-site updates can adapt bond dimension.
- **Lanczos/Davidson:** These solvers do not normally materialize the full effective Hamiltonian; they require efficient matrix-vector products. Their convergence depends on spectral gaps, conditioning, preconditioners, and target/root selection.
- **SVD truncation:** Preserve the discarded weight and show how the two-site tensor is split/gauged. One-site DMRG can be cheaper and conserve bond dimension but may need subspace expansion/noise to escape local minima.
- **Convergence-rate overclaim:** “Often geometrically in sweep count” needs a defined error measure and benchmark evidence. Energy can appear smooth while variance/correlations/state identity remain unconverged; no general geometric convergence rate should be suggested.
- **“Well-conditioned”:** Define it operationally—finite gap, favorable entanglement, nondegenerate target, good initialization, stable symmetry sector, and effective eigenproblem conditioning—or avoid the vague adjective.
- **Metastability warning:** Excellent. Expand it to include local minima, wrong topological/symmetry sector, nearly degenerate states, broken-symmetry bias, poor orbital/site ordering, and finite-\(\chi\) hysteresis.
- **Dominance claim:** “The dominant method” is plausible for many 1D strongly correlated ground-state problems but is a superlative requiring scope and evidence. Bethe ansatz, QMC for sign-free cases, exact diagonalization, free-fermion methods, coupled cluster, and specialized solvers can dominate particular tasks.
- **Precision benchmark:** Relative energy precision around \(10^{-10}\), \(\chi\le1000\), hundreds of sites, and a workstation combine maxima/conditions without a source. Give one reproducible Hamiltonian, parameters, boundary conditions, symmetry use, datatype, convergence tolerances, hardware, runtime, and reference energy.
- **Relative-error problem:** Relative ground-state energy error can be ill-defined or misleading under arbitrary energy shifts and extensive scaling. Prefer energy per site, absolute error, variance \(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\), discarded-weight extrapolation, and observable convergence.
- **Energy caveat:** The warning that tiny energy error does not guarantee accurate correlations is excellent. Also distinguish short-range observables, long-distance correlators, entanglement spectra, gaps, and topological quantities.
- **Model catalogue:** Heisenberg, \(t\)-\(J\), Hubbard, and Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) models are reasonable examples; expand SSH and state dimensions/fillings/regimes. “Mapped extensively” is vague and risks implying completed phase diagrams.
- **“Hard regimes”:** Name them: critical systems, long-range interactions, large local dimension, frustration, high entanglement, near degeneracy, two dimensions, dynamics, finite temperature, and difficult fermionic/orbital orderings.
- **2D snake mapping:** Mapping a cylinder to a one-dimensional ordering introduces long-range couplings and cuts crossing \(O(w)\) physical bonds. Under area-law entanglement this often induces \(\chi\sim e^{cw}\), with model/state-dependent coefficient; the qualitative statement is sound.
- **Width direction:** “Narrower spatial direction” assumes a cylinder/strip and a sensible snake orientation. State circumference \(w\), length \(L\), boundary conditions, local dimension, and whether fermionic mapping strings affect the MPO.
- **Reachable-width claim:** \(w\approx8\)–12 is highly model-, symmetry-, \(\chi\)-, hardware-, accuracy-, and date-dependent. Width alone is not a benchmark; cite representative studies or replace with a scaling discussion and examples.
- **Controlled extrapolation:** Extrapolating cylinders toward 2D requires multiple widths/lengths, finite-entanglement and truncation analysis, boundary/geometry comparisons, and phase-sensitive observables. “For some” is properly cautious but should name a case.
- **Complement list:** PEPS, variational Monte Carlo, and sign-free QMC are not universally interchangeable. Include neural quantum states, exact diagonalization, series methods, coupled cluster, and embedding methods only if a selection table can explain their assumptions; otherwise state the list is illustrative.
- **Baseline scope:** DMRG is especially strong for active-space quantum chemistry with favorable orbital entanglement and for 1D/quasi-1D lattice problems. It is not one uniform baseline for all chemistry/simulation algorithms; comparison must match basis, Hamiltonian, symmetry, target error, observable, and total classical preprocessing.
- **Acronym accumulation:** Expand selected configuration interaction (CI), dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the other methods locally or point to a glossary.
- **Hubbard counting:** A spinful 50-site single-orbital Hubbard model has 100 fermionic spin orbitals/modes and maps naïvely to 100 qubits under Jordan–Wigner or Bravyi–Kitaev-style occupation encodings before tapering/symmetry reduction. The correction is valuable; qualify spinful/single-band/common encoding.
- **Fair VQE comparison:** Compare total resources, not only ansatz execution: state preparation, measurements/shots, optimization, mitigation, basis/active-space choice, error, hardware queue, and classical tensor-network convergence. Ensure both solve the same finite Hamiltonian and target state.
- **“Interesting regimes” rhetoric:** Scientifically interesting regimes are not only those where DMRG fails. Quantum value may involve dynamics, thermal states, sampling, response functions, scaling, or energy/accuracy economics; classical difficulty must be demonstrated against all suitable baselines.
- **Excited states:** Orthogonality constraints and root tracking add cost, but correction-vector, tangent-space, MPS quasiparticle, DMRG-X, shift-invert, time evolution, and spectral methods have different regimes. Avoid presenting excited-state spectroscopy as generically beyond DMRG.
- **Missing reproducibility checklist:** Hamiltonian and convention, lattice/orbital ordering, boundary conditions, conserved symmetries, MPO compression, initial state, one-/two-site mode, \(\chi\) schedule, truncation/eigensolver tolerances, sweeps, energy variance, discarded weight, multi-start agreement, and observables.
- **Missing visual:** Plot energy, variance, discarded weight, and a long-range correlator versus sweep and \(1/\chi\) for both an easy gapped chain and a deceptive metastable case.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The back-and-forth sweep has an appealing “polishing a chain” image, and the width wall creates a strong transition to PEPS. Dense benchmark lists would be more engaging as a convergence detective story.
- **Section-level rule:** A low DMRG energy is evidence, not certification; credible ground-state claims require convergence across bond dimension, sweeps, initialization/sector, variance/discarded weight, size/boundary conditions, and target observables.

## §24.10 “PEPS and Variational Tensor Methods,” lines 164–173

- **Coverage:** Reviewed PEPS geometry and entropy capacity, two-dimensional contraction hardness, approximate contraction families and dual bond dimensions, scientific application/state-of-art claims, quantum-advantage bridge, and neural quantum states.
- **PEPS definition:** PEPS generalizes MPS to higher-dimensional/graph geometries, with a physical index plus virtual indices on incident edges. The four/three/two bond count is correct for an open square lattice; periodic boundaries, other lattices, irregular graphs, and fermionic PEPS differ.
- **Projected construction missing:** Explain the name: one may picture maximally entangled virtual pairs on edges projected by a local map into each site’s physical Hilbert space. This gives readers a mechanism rather than merely a high-rank tensor.
- **Bond dimensions:** As with MPS, each edge can have its own dimension; \(\chi\) is normally a maximum/uniform choice. Physical dimension \(d\), lattice coordination, symmetries, and tensor precision also set storage and compute.
- **Cut-bound logic:** Entanglement entropy is bounded by the logarithm of Schmidt rank, and cutting \(b\) PEPS bonds of dimension at most \(\chi\) gives \(S\le b\log_2\chi\). This general formula should precede the square-lattice example.
- **“Arbitrary cut” defect:** An arbitrary jagged partition of an \(L\times L\) lattice can cross far more than \(O(L)\) edges. A straight/minimal boundary separating macroscopic regions crosses \(O(L)\). The sentence begins with “arbitrary” and then silently narrows to “straight”; repair it.
- **Area-law capacity:** Excellent use of “capacity” and explicit warning that the state need not saturate it. Also note that PEPS can represent some critical and topologically ordered states; matching an area-law scaling does not establish accurate or efficiently discoverable representation.
- **Approximability caveat:** The statement that efficient PEPS approximability of all gapped 2D ground states is not proved is appropriately cautious. Add the separate distinction among existence of a compact PEPS, ability to find/optimize it, and ability to contract it.
- **Hardness statement:** Exact contraction of general two-dimensional tensor networks/PEPS is #P-hard in the worst case under specified encodings. Give the foundational citation and define #P at least intuitively; worst-case hardness does not mean every physical PEPS instance is intractable.
- **Partition-function analogy:** A classical partition function can be represented as a tensor-network contraction, which establishes the connection; not every PEPS contraction is literally one ordinary positive Boltzmann partition function. “Can encode” is safer than “is.”
- **Approximation hardness:** Approximate contraction can also be difficult under particular error promises, while physical heuristics often work. The section should distinguish exact value, norm, local observable, environment approximation, and desired relative/additive error.
- **Algorithm taxonomy:** Boundary MPS, corner transfer-matrix renormalization group/environment methods, tensor renormalization group, tensor network renormalization, and belief-propagation-like methods have distinct assumptions and artifacts. Expand names and avoid presenting three labels as exhaustive peers.
- **Auxiliary bond notation:** \(\chi_b\) is not universally named or defined across boundary-MPS and corner methods; environment dimension is often denoted \(\chi\) while PEPS bond dimension is \(D\). Choose notation that avoids colliding with source conventions and define algorithm-specific truncation.
- **Two-parameter convergence:** Excellent warning. In practice convergence also depends on system size/unit cell, boundary conditions, Trotter step for imaginary/finite-temperature evolution, optimization tolerance, environment update, initialization, symmetry, sampling, and contraction scheme.
- **Optimization versus contraction bias:** Important distinction. Add “simple update” versus “full update” or automatic-differentiation/variational optimization, because an apparently converged contraction can still support a biased optimization path.
- **“Far more expensive”:** Broadly true for comparable dense bond dimensions, but quantify representative asymptotic powers only with algorithm/lattice assumptions. Some MPS long-range/cylinder problems and specialized PEPS contractions complicate the comparison.
- **Application superlative:** “Leading contender” and “state-of-the-art” require dated citations, exact Hamiltonian/parameter/observable, lattice size or thermodynamic-limit method, bond/environment dimensions, compute budget, and comparison protocol.
- **Finite-temperature wording:** Purification represents a mixed state as a pure state on enlarged physical+ancilla space; PEPO means projected entangled-pair operator. Expand PEPO and distinguish thermal-state preparation from contraction.
- **Fermionic handling:** Fermionic PEPS require parity-aware tensors, swap signs/orderings, or Grassmann formulations. “Hubbard model” alone hides this important implementation difficulty.
- **Contested-territory sentence:** Excellent epistemic framing. It should become a concrete reproducibility rule: agreement across PEPS, cylinders, QMC/VMC, finite-size scaling, symmetry sectors, and observables is stronger than one lowest variational energy.
- **High-\(T_c\) notation:** Expand high-temperature superconductivity and define whether \(T_c\) refers to a transition temperature; claims about pairing structure are especially sensitive to model parameters and extrapolation.
- **Quantum-advantage bridge:** Correct that classical baselines move, but a quantum simulator must be compared on the same observable, system size, Hamiltonian fidelity, temperature/time, accuracy, confidence, and total resource cost—not against the word “PEPS.”
- **NQS definition:** Parameterizing complex amplitudes \(\langle x|\psi\rangle\) with a neural network and optimizing variational energy through Monte Carlo is a useful core description. Specify normalized versus unnormalized ansätze and how sampling is performed.
- **Historical attribution:** Carleo and Troyer’s 2017 work was influential/popularizing, not necessarily the origin of all neural-network wavefunction ideas. Give the exact *Science* citation and avoid a priority claim beyond “popularized.”
- **Architecture diversity:** Restricted Boltzmann machines, autoregressive models, convolutional nets, transformers, graph networks, and complex-valued/equivariant architectures have radically different sampling, sign/phase, symmetry, and scaling behavior. “A neural network” is too singular for performance claims.
- **Optimization detail:** Stochastic reconfiguration is closely related to natural-gradient optimization but involves covariance/Fisher-like systems, regularization, Monte Carlo noise, and solver choices. Expand both terms and describe stability costs.
- **Benchmark claim:** “Matched—and exceeded” requires exact dated papers and comparable compute, parameter count, symmetries, boundary conditions, sampling error, optimization effort, and observables. Lowest reported variational energy alone can reward unequal tuning.
- **Error-bar nuance:** Variational energies provide an upper bound when evaluated accurately for the exact Hamiltonian and normalized ansatz; Monte Carlo statistical uncertainty can be estimated. What is usually uncertified is ansatz/optimization bias and proximity to the true ground state. Replace the blanket “lack certified error bars” with this decomposition.
- **“Heavier compute”:** Heavier than what, at matched accuracy and hardware? NQS can have cheap autoregressive sampling or expensive Markov-chain mixing; PEPS contraction can be enormous. Remove the unqualified comparison.
- **Bias taxonomy:** “Architecture and sampling bias” is useful but add optimization/local-minimum, finite-sample/autocorrelation, symmetry, sign-structure, and estimator bias. “No formal area-law guarantee” is not inherently a disadvantage when the target violates or does not require such a law.
- **Missing neural-state caution:** Sampling can fail to mix across modes/sectors; effective sample size and autocorrelation must be reported. Autoregressive exact sampling changes this but imposes architectural ordering.
- **Missing visual:** Show the same \(4\times4\) lattice as a PEPS, snake-MPS cylinder, and NQS factor graph; annotate which edges/cuts create cost and which error controls each method exposes.
- **Accessibility:** Expand PEPS, PEPO, NQS, VMC, CTMRG/TRG if used, #P-hard, purification, frustration, sign problem, and stochastic reconfiguration. The current ten-line section carries a graduate-review density.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The paradox—compact 2D state, hard contraction—is excellent, and the contested scientific frontier adds real stakes. The catalog of fields and algorithms needs one concrete disputed case to become narrative rather than résumé.
- **Section-level rule:** Separate representational capacity, contraction accuracy, optimization success, and physical extrapolation; none proves the others.

## §24.11 “Schrödinger–Feynman and Hybrid Path-Sum Methods,” lines 174–187

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the inserted-basis path-sum equation, naïve term count and locality argument, blockwise Schrödinger–Feynman method, operator-Schmidt cut cost, tensor-network reformulation/contraction hardness, Sycamore historical claim, and advantage-statistic conclusion.
- **Path-sum setup:** Inserting computational-basis resolutions of identity between operators gives the displayed amplitude formula. State whether each \(U_t\) is one elementary gate or a full layer; the later branching argument changes interpretation depending on that choice.
- **Index range:** Explicitly write \(z_t\in\{0,1\}^n\). If \(d=1\), the empty intermediate sum should reduce cleanly to \(\langle y|U_1|x\rangle\).
- **Time-order convention:** \(U=U_d\cdots U_1\) correctly applies \(U_1\) first. A small two-gate expansion would prevent readers from reversing the order.
- **Naïve count:** There are \(2^{n(d-1)}\) intermediate assignments when each inserted \(z_t\) ranges independently over all basis strings. This counts summands, not necessarily nonzero paths or arithmetic after exploiting sparsity/reuse.
- **“Feynman path integral”:** This is a discrete sum-over-computational-paths analogy, not necessarily a continuum action/path integral. Say “discrete Feynman-style path sum” to avoid claiming a stronger formal identity.
- **Locality argument:** A \(k\)-qubit gate has matrix elements diagonal in untouched bits, so nonzero transitions preserve those bits. For a generic dense local gate, each incoming local basis assignment can branch to up to \(2^k\) outputs; diagonal/permutation gates branch less.
- **Layer caveat:** Helpful and necessary. If \(U_t\) is a full parallel layer, the layer may factor into local gate tensors rather than require one monolithic \(2^n\)-branch operator. Align this with the initial notation.
- **Interference:** The path count alone is not runtime; cancellation, Clifford/phase structure, repeated subexpressions, decision diagrams, dynamic programming, and tensor contraction can sum many paths jointly. State this before moving to hybrid methods.
- **Name/attribution:** “Markov, Boixo, Smelyanskiy, and others, 2017–2020” is too vague to audit and may combine several algorithms/papers. Give full citations, distinguish original Schrödinger–Feynman partitioning from later slicing/contraction implementations, and attach each complexity claim to one algorithm.
- **Block sizing:** For \(B\) equal blocks, each statevector has \(2^{n/B}\) amplitudes only when \(n\) divides evenly and all block widths are equal. Runtime/memory are governed by the largest block, number of blocks, replicas, and path/slice schedule.
- **Cut decomposition:** A two-qubit operator has operator-Schmidt rank at most 4 across a one-qubit/one-qubit partition; CZ/CNOT-like gates can have rank 2 and product gates rank 1. Decomposing crossing gates into sums of product operators is the mechanism that creates path indices—show one example.
- **Cost multiplication:** Naïvely, ranks of crossing-gate decompositions multiply, giving a factor like \(\prod_j r_j\); algebraic compression, reuse, slicing, balanced partitions, batched amplitudes, and parallelism change actual work/memory. “Set by” is too deterministic.
- **Partition quality:** Few crossing gates is not enough; their operator ranks and arrangement in time, block widths, target amplitudes/samples, and cache/reuse determine cost. Finding the partition itself is an optimization problem.
- **“Low depth”:** Depth is geometry- and gate-layout-dependent. A shallow layer with many cut-crossing gates can still be expensive; a deeper circuit aligned within blocks may be favorable. Use cut width/treewidth rather than depth as the direct predictor.
- **Tensor-network unification:** Excellent conceptual bridge. A circuit amplitude becomes a tensor-network contraction after fixing input/output legs; a probability, marginal, expectation, or batch has a different doubled/open network and cost.
- **World-line wording:** Qubit wires are indices connecting gate tensors; calling them “bonds” is intuitive. Measurement/output legs may be fixed, summed, or left open depending on the task, and this choice can dominate complexity.
- **Contraction-order hardness:** Finding an optimal contraction order under a specified cost model is related to treewidth and is NP-hard in general. Treewidth is a graph parameter, not the name of the optimization problem itself; hypergraphs, tensor dimensions, slicing, memory caps, and FLOP versus peak-size objectives complicate the correspondence.
- **Heuristics claim:** “Very effective” needs benchmark evidence and failure cases. Greedy, hypergraph-partitioning, tree-decomposition, simulated-annealing, cotengra-style, and learned optimizers trade planning time against contraction cost; optimization overhead should be counted.
- **Sycamore primary facts:** Pan, Chen, and Zhang’s *Physical Review Letters* paper reports one million uncorrelated bitstrings for the 53-qubit, 20-cycle Sycamore circuit, sampled from an approximate state with fidelity \(F\approx0.0037\), in about 15 hours on a 512-GPU cluster: [APS full text](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.090502).
- **Comparison repair:** Google’s original 2019 paper reported about 200 seconds for one million samples and an estimated 10,000 years for a then-modeled classical task, with predicted circuit fidelity around 0.2%: [Nature paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1666-5). A fair historical table must align circuit instance, samples, target/XEB fidelity, correlation, verification, hardware, precision, energy, and whether time is measured or extrapolated.
