- **Ion speed ratio:** One to four orders of magnitude slower depends on comparing native gate to native gate, parallelism, transport, measurement/reset, and total circuit latency. Give actual distributions or remove the broad ratio.
- **Ion connectivity:** “All-to-all” describes effective pairwise addressing within some chains, but mode crowding, laser addressing, chain length, crosstalk, and shuttling impose constraints. It is not zero-cost complete connectivity.
- **Mid-circuit maturity:** “Mature” across IonQ, Quantinuum, and Oxford Ionics is a product/capability claim requiring exact supported APIs, reset/feed-forward latencies, fidelity, and availability. Platform potential is not synonymous with customer access.
- **Neutral-atom count:** Distinguish assembled atoms, logical/encoded atoms, coherently controlled atoms, gate zone size, simultaneous gates, survival, and end-to-end circuit. A thousand trapped atoms is not automatically a thousand-qubit digital computation.
- **Neutral-atom fidelity:** “Reaching 99.5% on best devices” is explicitly record-like, which is better, but still needs primary citation, SPAM correction, gate type, atom pair/array size, and parallel-operation result.
- **Reconfiguration claim:** Atom movement can improve connectivity but incurs transport latency, loss, heating, reloading, calibration, collision constraints, and schedule complexity. The manuscript includes most of this caveat well; add whether computation pauses and how many moves were demonstrated.
- **Photonic category:** PsiQuantum and Xanadu pursue different architectures (fault-tolerant photonic plans versus continuous-variable/measurement-based systems). Grouping them only to say comparison is hard is not informative; name sources, demonstrated hardware, modes, photons, loss, squeezing, feed-forward, and logical resource metrics.
- **Stationary-qubit contrast:** Photonic encodings can define qubits as well as modes; “natural unit is the photon mode” is architecture-dependent. Time bins, spatial modes, frequency modes, squeezed modes, photons, and logical qubits should not be collapsed.
- **Omitted platforms:** Semiconductor spin qubits, silicon/donor, NV/defect centers, cat/bosonic qubits, annealers, and analog simulators need either rows or an explicit scope statement explaining why four categories suffice.
- **Parallel-degradation claim:** Simultaneous gates can suffer crosstalk and frequency/collision constraints, but degradation is not universal or one-directional under all calibrations. Cite simultaneous RB/cycle benchmarking or say it must be measured.
- **Quantum Volume:** Quantum Volume incorporates random square circuits, compilation, connectivity, and whole-circuit success under its protocol; it does not uniquely decompose parallel contextual degradation. The current “folds some in” is cautious but needs metric-specific detail.
- **CLOPS:** Correctly described primarily as throughput, but it is tied to a particular circuit-execution workflow and should not be treated as raw gate speed. Use Chapter 22’s exact definition and ensure no circular inconsistency.
- **Missing uncertainty:** Every numerical row should include variation over qubits/time, confidence/error bars, calibration timestamp, sample size, and whether numbers were independently reproduced.
- **Pedagogy:** Keep the toy model, then ask readers to populate \(G_2\) from a sparse circuit and compare predicted global fidelity with one local observable under depolarizing versus coherent overrotation noise.
- **Accessibility:** Define transmon, optical tweezer, RB, SPAM, crosstalk, heavy-hex, coherence, mid-circuit measurement, Quantum Volume, and CLOPS. Use a table with footnotes rather than four dense prose bullets.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.3/10.** The “four global layers versus 200 worldline gates” calculation is arresting. The vendor taxonomy reads like a market slide; live calibration distributions and a toy-model failure demonstration would be more engaging.
- **Subsection rule:** Never feed a cross-platform “fidelity” number into a circuit survival formula until the metric, channel model, simultaneous context, gate count/causal cone, calibration date, and target observable are defined.

## §25.2 connectivity, control, and takeaway, lines 41–48

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the two vendor-announcement cautions, two-dimensional/one-dimensional SWAP scaling, platform routing-cost comparison, shot-count/time/VQE example, and wide-but-shallow conclusion.
- **Ranking overclaim:** “Connectivity matters more than qubit count” is not universally true. Connectivity, active high-quality width, gate fidelity, parallelism, native gate set, compiler quality, coherence, measurement/reset, and workload graph jointly determine performance.
- **Graph assumptions:** A square nearest-neighbor grid has diameter \(O(\sqrt n)\), so routing one worst-separated pair together can require \(O(\sqrt n)\) adjacent moves; a length-\(n\) chain has \(O(n)\) diameter. State rectangular geometry and occupied/full grid assumptions.
- **Gate-versus-layer routing:** Worst-case distance per nonlocal gate does not directly equal whole-circuit SWAP count or depth. Parallel token swapping, initial placement, interaction reuse, logical relabeling, teleportation, routing algorithms, and congestion determine aggregate overhead.
- **All-to-all workload:** An all-to-all interaction graph may contain \(O(n^2)\) interactions, but structure, commutation, edge coloring, parameter sharing, and native global/multiqubit operations can reduce schedules. Define the hypothetical algorithm rather than attaching one distance bound.
- **SWAP cost:** A logical SWAP is often decomposed into three CNOT-like gates but some hardware has native exchange/iSWAP/fSim interactions or can absorb permutations into mapping. Translate routing into native two-qubit count/error/duration, not abstract SWAPs alone.
- **1,000-qubit rhetoric:** The raw scale adds drama but no mathematics; the asymptotic statement holds for general \(n\). If retained, compute actual grid dimensions, path length, native gates, added depth, and fidelity under a named device.
- **Platform currencies:** The acknowledgement that every connectivity model pays elsewhere is excellent. Add ion transport/shuttling and segmented traps, calibration/laser addressing, neutral-atom gate-zone capacity/reloading, and superconducting tunable-coupler/crosstalk constraints.
- **“Superconducting devices pay in SWAPs”:** Some superconducting layouts use native interactions, tunable couplers, teleportation/dynamic circuits, modular links, or compiler relabeling; “often pay through additional routing operations” is safer.
- **Control-bandwidth title mismatch:** Shot rate is bounded by gate sequence duration, measurement/reset, controller trigger/data path, batching, feedback, host/network transfer, scheduling, and service policy. Classical control bandwidth is one contributor, not the umbrella for all.
- **Shot definition:** A shot is one repetition/sample of a circuit/program under a defined execution mode; a user submission/job typically contains many shots and possibly many circuits/parameter values. “Each circuit execution is a shot” can confuse API and physical levels.
- **Shot-count range:** \(10^3\)–\(10^6\) depends on observable variance, coefficient weights/grouping, precision/confidence, allocation, mitigation/randomization overhead, gradients, number of terms, and adaptive stopping. Give \(N\sim\sigma^2/\delta^2\) as the basic estimator rule.
- **Expectation-values plural:** Hamiltonian estimation can require multiple measurement bases and circuits; total shots are distributed across terms/groups/settings. One “expectation value” and one full VQE energy/gradient have different budgets.
- **Per-shot timing:** Tens of microseconds may describe repeated fast QPU execution under batching, while milliseconds may include measurement/reset; queueing is not a per-shot physical duration. Separate circuit duration, repetition/reset cadence, batch latency, job queue, result transfer, and optimizer wall time.
- **Platform timing evidence:** Provide named services/devices, dates, circuit depths, shot counts, execution modes, and measured timestamps. Backend/API scheduling can change faster than the book.
- **VQE multiplication:** Total evaluations equal optimizer iterations times parameter points/gradient shifts times observable groups times mitigation/randomization variants times shots, subject to batching. Print this expansion—the hidden multiplier is more educational than “hours.”
- **“Hours” claim:** VQE can take seconds in simulation, hours/days on services, or be infeasible; queue and cost vary. Give a traced pinned experiment with QPU time, queue time, classical optimization, data transfer, billed usage, and confidence.
- **Data movement claim:** End-to-end orchestration can dominate, but on-device circuit/measurement/reset or shot volume can also dominate. Profile rather than generalize.
- **Omitted constraints:** Calibration drift/staleness, qubit selection, compilation/routing, native instruction support, parameter binding latency, dynamic-circuit feedback, readout, leakage, job limits, quotas/pricing, reproducibility, availability, and data governance deserve explicit treatment.
- **Wide-but-shallow slogan:** Memorable but increasingly incomplete as logical/error-detected operations coexist with unencoded workloads and platforms have different width/depth tradeoffs. Define effective circuit volume for a task.
- **Algorithm prescription:** NISQ algorithms benefit from shallow circuits, but shallow construction alone is insufficient; they need measurement efficiency, noise robustness, trainability, connectivity awareness, classical competitiveness, verification, and favorable end-to-end economics.
- **Absolute “have to”:** Sampling advantage experiments may use nontrivial cycles; analog simulations do not map neatly to gate depth; error mitigation can deliberately execute deeper/folded circuits. Use “must respect a measured task-specific error budget.”
- **Missing worked compiler example:** Map the same 20-node interaction graph onto a chain, square grid, heavy-hex-like graph, and all-to-all device; report native entangling count/depth, simulated fidelity, and routing time.
- **Missing wall-time ledger:** For one VQE iteration, show circuit generation/transpilation, parameter upload, queue, QPU gates, reset/readout, shots, mitigation expansion, result transfer, expectation aggregation, and optimizer step.
- **Accessibility:** Define interaction graph, graph diameter, routing, native gate, shot, batching, expectation precision, queue versus QPU time, and orchestration.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** “Different currencies” is a strong metaphor and the hidden VQE wall-clock multiplier has real-world bite. The section would be more fun and convincing as an invoice/timeline that reveals where each minute went.
- **Section-level rule:** Report a NISQ workload in native gate volume/depth, connectivity/routing, simultaneous error, shots and estimator precision, batch/QPU/queue/host times, cost, calibration timestamp, and useful output—not raw width or a single fidelity.

## §25.3 “Variational Algorithms in Practice,” lines 49–71

- **Coverage:** Reviewed historical framing, VQE/QAOA loop and variational argument, all three obstacles, shot arithmetic, four mitigation methods and parenthetical toolbox, bias–variance/cloud-cost synthesis, and claimed 2026 demonstration/no-advantage frontier.
- **Historical “field’s bet”:** Variational algorithms were a major NISQ research program, not the whole field’s singular bet. Analog simulation, sampling, error correction, annealing, sensing, and hardware benchmarking followed different theses.
- **Outcome framing:** “Has not paid off as cleanly as hoped” is fair in tone but undefined. Separate publication volume, hardware feasibility, accuracy, classical competitiveness, useful advantage, and production adoption; otherwise success can be rhetorically moved.
- **“How anything runs” overclaim:** Variational techniques are not part of every noisy-hardware execution. Compilation, calibration, characterization, randomized compiling, dynamic circuits, analog protocols, and nonvariational benchmarks operate independently.
- **Loop description:** The expectation-minimization structure captures VQE and some QAOA formulations, but QAOA typically optimizes a classical cost Hamiltonian and returns sampled candidate bitstrings/approximation quality, not necessarily a physical ground-state energy. State the output distinction.
- **Hamiltonian expansion:** \(H\) must be decomposed into measurable terms/groups; basis rotations, coefficient weights, shot allocation, and estimator covariance are the practical center of the loop. Introduce them before optimizer cost.
- **Ansatz state:** On noisy hardware the prepared object is generally \(\rho(\theta)\), not pure \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle\). This matters for the variational bound and mitigation discussion.
- **Variational bound:** For any normalized physical state/density operator and exact expectation of the exact Hermitian target \(H\), \(\operatorname{Tr}(H\rho)\ge E_0\). Finite shots, mitigation/quasiprobabilities, Hamiltonian truncation, calibration, readout correction, and optimizer noise can yield an estimate below \(E_0\); clarify what remains robust.
- **Ground versus combinatorial target:** A low expected QAOA cost does not guarantee sampling the optimum with useful probability. Report approximation ratio, success probability, sample complexity, and classical postprocessing.
- **Expressibility:** More expressibility can worsen trainability/barren plateaus and increase depth/noise; the original “hope” was never simply that both independently suffice. Include inductive bias/problem structure.
- **Barren-plateau theorem scope:** The exponential gradient-variance statement is appropriate for specified random/expressive ansatz ensembles, global costs, initialization, and concentration assumptions. Give a primary citation and write the relevant \(O(b^{-n})\) result rather than a universal equality \(\sim2^{-n}\).
- **Noise-induced plateaus:** Noise can itself exponentially suppress gradients with depth/system size under particular models. Add this separate mechanism instead of treating noise only as a biased objective.
- **Workaround language:** Local costs, shallow structured ansätze, symmetries, layerwise/problem-informed initialization, parameter correlation, and geometry can help under conditions; none is a generic cure. The current caveats are strong.
- **Classical-initialization inference:** Starting near a classical solution may reduce marginal quantum value, but it can also seed a refinement task where the quantum ansatz captures missing correlations. “Undercut” is a question to measure, not a foregone conclusion.
- **Gradient-rule scope:** Two shifts per parameter applies to simple generators with two eigenvalues and one occurrence/independent parameter under the standard parameter-shift rule. General spectra, shared parameters, stochastic rules, linear combinations, finite differences, SPSA, adjoint simulation, and analytic hardware support change evaluation counts.
- **Shot-unit defect:** If \(S\) is “per expectation value,” the stated \(2pGS\) multiplies by \(G\) again. Define \(S\) as shots **per measurement group** for \(2pGS\), or define total shots per energy evaluation \(S_{\rm tot}=\sum_g S_g\) and use \(2pS_{\rm tot}\).
- **Expectation versus circuit:** Each group can require one or multiple circuits after basis rotations, symmetry checks, mitigation variants, randomized compilations, and covariance strategies. Parameter batching may amortize submissions but not QPU samples.
- **Numerical example:** With \(p=100\), \(S=10^4\) per group, and \(G=5\), \(2pGS=10^7\) shots **per gradient step**, not merely an unspecified multi-million count. A hundred steps gives \(10^9\) shots.
- **Shot-rate arithmetic:** At 1 kHz uninterrupted sampling, \(10^8\) shots is about 27.8 hours and \(10^9\) about 11.6 days. “A day to weeks” is numerically plausible before queue/setup, but gate depth/reset and batching determine rate; print the arithmetic and distinguish QPU from wall time.
- **Optimizer comparison:** Gradient-free does not automatically reduce queries; it may require many noisy objective evaluations. SPSA uses two evaluations per iteration independent of \(p\) but has variance/convergence tradeoffs. Adaptive shot allocation needs stopping/confidence rules.
- **Missing observable coefficients:** Shot complexity can depend on \((\sum_j|h_j|)^2/\delta^2\), grouping covariance, and estimator choice, not just group count. Chemistry Hamiltonians may have many terms even after grouping.
- **Noise “moving target”:** A fixed noise channel defines a fixed but biased/noise-flattened objective; stochastic shots make estimates noisy, while calibration drift makes the target move over wall time. Separate bias, variance, and nonstationarity.
- **Optimizer behavior:** Noise can create spurious minima, wash out gradients, change parameter periodicity, and interact with mitigation; optimizers may also exploit the noisy objective rather than approximate the ideal one.
- **Mitigation “dominant”:** Dominant by publication, deployments, providers, or successful experiments? Error mitigation is a major toolkit, but application-specific calibration, circuit design, postselection, suppression, and better hardware can matter more.
- **Correction contrast:** Fault-tolerant correction does not necessarily “decode at runtime” in one simple loop; Pauli-frame tracking/decoding can be asynchronous/streaming. Mitigation does not guarantee less bias and may alter the target.
- **Taxonomy mixing:** Readout mitigation, symmetry verification/postselection, randomized compiling/suppression, ZNE, PEC, CDR, and virtual distillation have different goals: characterize/correct measurement, reshape noise, reject outcomes, extrapolate, invert channels, learn a correction, or spectrally transform a state. Do not place all under one estimator sentence without axes.
- **Chapter overlap:** §25.3 substantially duplicates Chapter 18’s mitigation material. Keep only a cost-oriented summary and cross-reference the full derivations to avoid inconsistent updates.
- **ZNE scale parameter:** Real hardware rarely offers a known scalar \(\lambda\) that can be multiplied uniformly. Gate folding and pulse stretching can change noise composition, duration, leakage, drift, and crosstalk rather than simply \(2\lambda,3\lambda\).
- **Pulse-stretching staleness:** Chapter 23 already notes removal of Qiskit Pulse/IBM pulse-level access. Do not imply general customer availability; name the platform/API/date where stretching is supported.
- **ZNE fitting:** Richardson extrapolation uses chosen scale factors/order under smoothness assumptions; polynomial/exponential fits trade bias, variance, conditioning, and model mismatch. Include coefficient norm and confidence bands, not just fitted zero intercept.
- **PEC mechanism:** The inverse of a noisy channel is generally non-CPTP and represented as a signed quasiprobability combination of implementable operations. Exact model/invertibility/basis and stable decomposition assumptions are essential.
- **PEC overhead:** Squared 1-norm overhead for estimator variance/sample complexity is the key point. Show how per-gate norms multiply and how model drift creates residual bias despite “unbiased in principle.”
- **Characterization cost:** Excellent inclusion. Add gauge/context dependence, correlated noise, calibration timestamp, and whether characterization circuits themselves dominate the budget.
- **CDR naming:** Expand Clifford data regression and cite the primary paper. Training circuits must be close enough to target yet classically tractable; generation, ideal simulation, hardware execution, model selection, and held-out validation can be expensive.
- **CDR “cheap”:** Unsupported and often false relative to one unmitigated run. Say “can be less model-intensive” and account for training-set size and classical simulation.
- **CDR generalization:** The manuscript correctly flags it as the core assumption. Require out-of-distribution checks, uncertainty, nonlinear versus linear mapping, circuit-feature matching, and data leakage avoidance.
- **Virtual-distillation target:** \(\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho^M)/\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^M)\) suppresses subdominant eigencomponents relative to the dominant eigenvector; it does not recover a noiseless state if the dominant eigenvector is wrong. The current coherent-error caveat is excellent.
- **Copies/measurements:** Simultaneous copies require \(M\) state registers plus permutation/collective measurement and connectivity; sequential/memory variants have different assumptions. State preparation must be sufficiently identical/independent.
- **Attribution:** “Huggins et al.” needs full title/year/DOI and parallel attribution to related purification/virtual-cooling work if priority is shared.
- **Universal bias–variance statement:** ZNE/PEC often increase estimator variance; CDR adds learned-model bias/variance; symmetry verification changes acceptance/effective samples; virtual distillation changes the target state. None is guaranteed to reduce bias on a finite, misspecified experiment.
- **Shot-cost mantra:** Good and important, but mitigation also costs additional circuits, depth, qubits, calibration, compilation, queue, classical fitting, and model maintenance—not merely shots.
- **Cloud pricing:** Provider billing modes/plans are volatile. Move them to a dated generated service matrix and include free tiers/reservations/minimums/queue, or keep the durable instruction to estimate billed QPU time/tasks.
- **“Research grant” line:** Concrete and human. Add an example budget with uncertainty to make economics teachable rather than rhetorical.
- **End-to-end definition:** Does it include active-space/orbital selection, ansatz construction, optimizer, all measurements/mitigation, convergence, and independent validation—or only one energy evaluation? Define it before listing scale.
- **50-spin-orbital claim:** No exact primary citation is attached, and a targeted search did not establish a generic hardware VQE milestone at this scale. Contextual/active-space methods can begin with a larger chemistry problem while reducing the actual quantum register drastically; report original and hardware-active modes separately.
- **Active-space wording:** Correctly defines the basic idea but must give electrons/orbitals, frozen/core/external treatment, symmetry/tapering, effective Hamiltonian generation, and classical cost. “Roughly one qubit each” applies to common occupation encodings before tapering/compact encodings.
- **Chemistry comparison:** Hardware energy should be compared with FCI in the same active space, DMRG/selected CI/coupled cluster and other methods at matched basis/error, plus total active-space preparation cost.
- **Time-evolution claim:** “Few tens of sites” needs exact Hamiltonian, dimension, time/depth, Trotter order, observable, error, qubits, hardware, mitigation, and classical baseline. A short-time local observable is not the same task as full-state dynamics.
- **100-vertex QAOA claim:** An ORNL 2025 summary reports graph decomposition followed by single-layer QAOA on reduced problems for ten 100-vertex graphs, 500 samples each on Quantinuum H1-1: [ORNL summary](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/graph-decomposition-techniques-solving-combinatorial-optimization-problems-variational). This must not read as direct 100-qubit encoding of the full graph.
- **“Classical heuristics in seconds”:** Needs named hardware/algorithm/instances and whether exact optimum or good solution is obtained. It may be true for small benchmark graphs but cannot be attached generically to all 100-vertex problems.
- **No-clean-win conclusion:** Broadly defensible only after a systematic dated benchmark survey with precise useful-task/advantage criteria. State “this review found no independently validated end-to-end advantage as of [date]” and document search protocol.
- **Classical-reproduction placeholder:** “Specifics belong in Appendix F” is not enough. Name the demonstrations/classical responses here or link a verified table; otherwise the section asserts a trend without auditable evidence.
- **Matched-task requirement:** Excellent phrase. Enforce same Hamiltonian/circuit/input, observable/output, error/confidence, preprocessing, hardware resource, and total time/cost; many alleged reproductions match only a subset.
- **Missing success evidence:** Balance the negative conclusion with what variational experiments have taught—control, measurement reduction, ansatz/optimizer behavior, noise diagnostics—without inflating this into computational advantage.
- **Missing practical stop rule:** Before hardware, run exact/tensor-network/classical baselines; set target error and budget; estimate full execution expansion; define a kill criterion; validate on classically tractable instances; report negative results.
- **Accessibility:** Expand VQE, QAOA, UCC, ZNE, PEC, CDR, VMC if mentioned, ansatz, parameter-shift, measurement grouping, quasiprobability norm, active space, spin orbital, and bias/variance.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** The escalating shot bill and mitigation “interest payments” create strong real-world tension. Four dense mini-reviews interrupt the story; a single VQE iteration traced from 100 parameters to invoice and uncertain energy would be irresistible.
- **Section-level rule:** A variational hardware result is incomplete without the original and reduced problem sizes, ansatz/native depth, optimizer/evaluation count, term grouping/allocation, complete mitigation expansion, QPU/queue/cost, uncertainty, convergence history, and matched strongest classical baselines.

## §25.4 “Quantum Supremacy and Quantum Advantage Experiments,” lines 72–85

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the claimed 2019–2025 sequence, Sycamore/IBM response, Jiuzhang/classical response, IBM Eagle utility experiment/reproductions, repeated-arc synthesis, and computational-versus-practical advantage distinction.
- **Scope/date defect:** A section promising 2019–2025 history stops substantively at the 2023 IBM experiment and omits 2025 D-Wave and Google Quantum Echoes publications, as well as Zuchongzhi and later Jiuzhang-family milestones.
- **Duplication:** This repeats §24.14 almost immediately, creating two independent timelines that already disagree in details (Pan GPU count/depth phrasing) and will drift. Maintain one generated frontier ledger; use this section to analyze communication/era implications.
- **Cautionary-tale framing:** Strong and worthwhile, but it risks a predetermined arc. State selection criteria and include claims whose classical gap persisted, changed, or remains unresolved, not only those fitting “headline softened.”
- **Sycamore cycle correction:** The 2019 hardest benchmark used 53 active qubits and 20 cycles; “depth-20 random circuit” is not equivalent to 20 elementary layers. Use original circuit/gate-count terminology.
- **Sycamore output:** It sampled an ensemble of random quantum circuits and was evaluated with linear cross-entropy benchmarking. “Sampled from the output distribution” should not imply exact noiseless sampling; report experimental fidelity/acceptance metric and sample count.
- **Timing/accounting:** Approximately 200 seconds and 10,000 years come from the original paper’s quantum run and then-current classical estimate under specified assumptions. Label measured versus estimated and include hardware, fidelity, samples, energy, and processor/end-to-end time.
- **IBM-response verb:** IBM’s October 2019 argument proposed that secondary storage could enable simulation in about 2.5 days on Summit; “published a strategy that brought the estimate down” can sound like a completed measured run. Say proposed/estimated unless execution evidence exists.
- **“Within weeks”:** Give exact publication/blog/preprint dates. The speed of the response is part of the story and therefore must be auditable.
- **Matched-follow-up warning:** The manuscript’s samples/fidelity/hardware caveat is excellent. Add correlated versus independent samples, exact versus approximate state, precision, contraction planning, and verification.
- **“Classical-simulability frontier” defect:** There was no proved frontier defined by an XEB score. Google compared with known classical methods and complexity assumptions; later score-spoofing work shows why XEB alone is not a general classical-intractability certificate.
- **“Experiment was real”:** This sounds defensive and sets up a fake-versus-real straw man. The important audit is whether the hardware data, benchmark score, classical estimate, and interpretation each support their stated claim.
- **As-of-time defense:** Saying advantage held “as classical simulation stood at the time” depends on what counts as demonstrated versus proposed and whether the original task definitions match. Use a dated table rather than a retrospective verdict.
- **Jiuzhang task:** Report Gaussian boson sampling architecture, input states, modes, detected photon events/clicks, sample count, loss/postselection, validation, and classical baseline. “Up to 76 detected photons” alone is insufficient.
- **\(10^{14}\) factor:** Identify whether this was a runtime extrapolation, what classical algorithm/machine it used, target sample count, and accuracy. A fourteen-order headline should never appear without its denominator/assumptions.
- **Classical-narrowing claim:** Name the exact algorithms/papers and quantify the revised matched task. “Exploiting structure” and “approximate sampling” are too vague to verify and may refer to different validation/task notions.
- **Trust rhetoric:** “Not merely whose benchmarks one trusts” implies a social dispute where the issue is technical task alignment. Replace with a reproducibility ledger and uncertainty ranges.
- **IBM date heading:** The quantum experiment/paper is 2023; “2023–2024 utility-scale experiments” appears to include later classical responses under IBM’s heading. Rename “IBM Eagle experiment (2023) and classical responses (2023–2024).”
- **IBM primary claim:** The paper reports accurate expectation values on a noisy 127-qubit Eagle processor at circuit volumes beyond brute-force classical computation and argues this is evidence of utility before fault tolerance: [Nature paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06096-3).
- **Hamiltonian/task specificity:** Name the kicked transverse-field Ising dynamics, heavy-hex geometry, Trotter layers, observables, initial states, noise amplification/ZNE, device, and exact circuit depths instead of “an Ising-model time evolution.”
- **“Beyond statevector” triviality:** Any generic 127-qubit dense statevector exceeds ordinary memory; the scientific issue is whether structured classical methods can compute the selected observables. Avoid making brute-force impossibility sound like advantage.
- **Utility semantics:** Quote/paraphrase the authors’ stated criterion precisely and separately label the book’s gloss. “Consistency-plus-validation” may be a useful interpretation but should not overwrite the paper.
- **Classical response evidence:** At least two named primary routes exist: tensor-network simulation of the Eagle kicked-Ising experiment ([Tindall et al. preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14887)) and sparse-Pauli dynamics ([Begusić–Gray–Chan preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16372)). Add publication versions, exact matched observables/depths, error, compute, and limits.
- **Method-list precision:** MPS, isometric tensor-network states, graph PEPS, belief-propagation-like methods, sparse Pauli dynamics, and neural quantum states should not be merged unless each actually reproduced the same published data. Cite individually.
- **Commodity-GPU claim:** Verify hardware for every reproduction. Some used GPUs, CPU clusters, laptops, or different scaling; “commodity GPUs” cannot describe all named methods without evidence.
- **Temporal claim:** “Within months” is plausible from June 2023 preprints but needs exact dates. Fast response is meaningful only if the matched instances/results were public and reproduced.
- **“Narrowed, not refuted”:** Thoughtful and fair. Also distinguish showing one classical method works for the published observables from invalidating every possible definition of utility; avoid adjudicating beyond evidence.
- **Pattern overgeneralization:** “Each claim” is false for a selected list and prematurely characterizes recent unresolved claims. Use “several prominent claims.”
- **No-commercial-stake aside:** Academic affiliation does not prove absence of commercial, reputational, funding, or intellectual stakes and is irrelevant to correctness. Remove it; assess code/data/method instead.
- **“Defensible benchmark”:** A benchmark can be carefully executed yet weakly connected to the claimed inference. State exact experimental validity, hardness assumptions, and acceptance criteria rather than granting “defensible” globally.
- **Headline-softening arc:** Compelling communication analysis. Add original headline/claim text, paper claim, company press language, later paper, and what specifically changed. Do not treat media shorthand as the scientific claim.
- **“Largest ever” ambiguity:** Require metric—physical qubits, active qubits, circuit volume, entangling operations, logical operations, samples, fidelity, time, or Hilbert-space estimate. The parenthetical acknowledges this and should become a table field.
- **Only-quantum standard:** No finite empirical comparison proves no classical algorithm can run a task. The defensible claim is advantage over the best documented baselines under defined resources/error as of a date, plus complexity evidence.
- **Computational-advantage definition:** It requires correct task completion at matched error/success probability and resource accounting, not merely any fast output. “Even a useless one” correctly separates utility but should not erase verification.
- **Preferred terminology:** “Literature’s preferred neutral term” needs usage evidence or softer phrasing. Computational advantage, supremacy, utility, and practical advantage are used inconsistently across communities.
- **Practical-advantage definition:** Add total end-to-end cost, classical preprocessing/postprocessing, energy, availability, validation, reproducibility, and a user/scientific value threshold—not only “useful task.”
- **2026 current-status omission:** D-Wave’s *Science* paper “Beyond-classical computation in quantum simulation” (2025) claims scientific relevance/advantage and has active classical challenges: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ado6285). Google’s 2025 Quantum Echoes *Nature* paper claims verifiable advantage on OTOCs: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09526-6). Both must appear before asserting no widely accepted useful production demonstration.
- **“Widely accepted”:** Define a review protocol—independent replication, classical-baseline search, task utility, peer review, data/code, and cutoff date. Otherwise absence of consensus becomes untestable.
- **“Production workload”:** This is stricter than “practical useful advantage” and excludes scientific experiments by definition. Decide whether the criterion is scientific utility, commercial production, or both, and report separately.
- **Missing entries:** At minimum include Zuchongzhi series, Jiuzhang updates, Willow RCS if discussed, D-Wave 2025, Quantum Echoes 2025, and any 2026 classical responses up to cutoff—or explicitly narrow to three case studies.
- **Missing visual:** A claim-evolution table with columns for original scientific claim, press framing, exact task/metric, classical baseline then, later response, what remained, and open dispute would deliver the chapter’s communication lesson.
- **Accessibility:** Define GBS, XEB, kicked Ising, MPS/isoTNS/PEPS, brute force, commodity GPU, utility, matched accuracy, and “production workload.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.6/10.** The moving-frontier cases are gripping and naturally skeptical without dismissing the experiments. Repetition and missing 2025 climax blunt the narrative; one evidence-normalized timeline would make it superb.
- **Section-level rule:** Separate experiment, benchmark score, classical comparison, complexity assumption, scientific interpretation, company/media framing, and later response; a change in one does not retroactively falsify all the others.

## §25.5 “Benchmarking Progress Over Time,” lines 86–97

- **Coverage:** Reviewed the complementary-metrics premise, physical count, QV definition/record/adoption claim, AQ definition/standardization, CLOPS throughput, logical metrics, qualitative trends, and \(10^4\)-qubit/decade scenario.
- **“Settled into common use”:** Overstates consensus. Physical count is ubiquitous; QV, AQ, CLOPS/layer fidelity, XEB, randomized/cycle benchmarking, application benchmarks, logical metrics, and vendor roadmaps have different ownership/adoption and sometimes competing definitions.
- **Benchmark governance:** For each metric record owner/specification version, implementation/code, compiler freedom, mitigation allowance, circuit ensemble, sampling/statistical pass rule, hardware access, audit/replication, and last update.
- **Physical-count example:** Correctly shows why qubit number alone is weak. The example still assumes 98% versus 99.5% are comparable simultaneous two-qubit fidelities; specify metric/connectivity/gate speed and task before implying the 100-qubit device is superior.
- **Capability vector:** Count, usable yield, connectivity, native gates, simultaneous error, circuit depth/volume, measurement/reset, throughput, logical behavior, output accuracy, and availability should be reported together.
- **QV notation:** Standard Quantum Volume is \(2^m\), where \(m\) is the largest tested square-circuit size (width \(m\), depth \(m\)) satisfying the heavy-output-generation success criterion with statistical confidence. Use \(m\) consistently and state trials/shots/confidence/threshold.
- **QV “combined width/depth”:** It also incorporates compilation, connectivity, gate/readout error, and control for the chosen subset/implementation. It does not decompose failure sources or predict every structured workload.
- **QV verification cost:** Ideal heavy-output sets require classical simulation of random circuits and scale exponentially; statistical/device execution also costs resources. Name exactly which verification component motivates declining use.
- **QV record:** The \(2^{25}\) Quantinuum 2025 claim requires a primary official/technical report, device, date, circuit count/shots, compiler, qubit selection, confidence, raw data, and independent audit. A search surfaced secondary references but not a clearly indexed primary record; do not publish it unsourced.
- **Record freshness:** As of 23 July 2026, verify whether \(2^{25}\) remains the record and whether postselection/error detection/mitigation or special compilation was allowed. “Milestone record runs to” is awkward; say “largest documented claim located by cutoff.”
- **Vendor-reporting claim:** “Most other vendors have stopped reporting QV” and the reasons given are empirical/intent claims requiring a reporting survey and vendor statements. Metrics may be absent because of architecture, marketing, low score, verification cost, or strategy; do not infer motives.
- **“Saturated”:** No definition is given. A metric can become classically expensive to verify, cease to discriminate a vendor roadmap, or hit device-width constraints; these are distinct.
- **AQ ownership:** Correctly identifies Algorithmic Qubits/#AQ as IonQ’s metric inspired by QED-C application-oriented benchmarks, not an independent cross-vendor standard.
- **AQ formal definition omitted:** IonQ’s current explanation defines #AQ \(=N\) through the largest width-\(N\), depth-\(N^2\) box for which every selected structured benchmark meets success criteria, with IonQ-specific depth/success modifications: [IonQ definition](https://www.ionq.com/resources/algorithmic-qubits-a-better-single-number-metric).
- **AQ mutability:** IonQ explicitly says the algorithm set can evolve as applications change. Scores across specification versions are therefore not automatically a time series; pin benchmark suite, commit/version, circuits, postprocessing, success rule, and mitigation.
- **“Application-anchored”:** Structured benchmark circuits resemble algorithmic kernels but do not establish real-world utility or classical advantage. “More application-anchored than QV” is fair only as design intent.
- **AQ mitigation:** Official material discusses results after error-mitigation/debiasing steps. Raw and mitigated scores, classical postprocessing, shot cost, and failure cases must be reported separately.
- **CLOPS mutability:** CLOPS was proposed through a specific parameter-update/Quantum-Volume-derived workflow, and IBM later introduced hardware-efficient CLOPS variants. Cite specification/version rather than defining it generically: [IBM metric update](https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/quantum-metric-layer-fidelity).
- **CLOPS interpretation:** It measures end-to-end throughput for a benchmark workflow, not universal “how fast the device executes layers.” Circuit depth/width, shots, parameter updates, compilation caching, communication, batching, and API stack define the number.
- **Variational relevance:** High CLOPS can reduce iteration time, but total VQE time also depends on observable groups, shots, mitigation, optimizer, queue and fidelity. A speed metric without accuracy can reward fast wrong answers.
- **Logical metrics strength:** The shift from physical to logical error per round/gate/algorithm is exactly right, and the warning not to interchange them is excellent.
- **Logical denominator:** Define memory round/cycle duration, logical gate/opportunity, circuit location, decoder latency, erasure/postselection, acceptance, state-preparation/measurement, and confidence/rare-event estimation.
- **Suppression formula:** Below threshold, logical error can scale approximately like \(A(p/p_{\rm th})^{(d+1)/2}\) for phenomenological families under assumptions, but coherent/correlated/leakage errors, boundaries, decoder, finite size, and circuit-level operations change it. “Roughly exponentially” is appropriately cautious.
- **Trend-data contradiction:** The text says the book maintains no curated dataset, then asserts count-growth percentages and error improvements. Without data, those trend numbers are impressions and should not appear as measured trends.
- **Cross-vendor aggregation warning:** Excellent and should precede all trend claims, not merely disclaim them afterward.
- **“Tens of percent per year”:** Define geometric/CAGR interval, platform, physical-versus-active count, released/announced systems, starting/ending sources, and survivorship. One percentage across modalities is meaningless.
- **“Severalfold error decline”:** Average infidelity, best pair, median, simultaneous, cycle error, and platform differ. A factor change also depends on benchmarking protocol; provide a curated dataset or omit.
- **QV-reporting trend:** A count of public reports by vendor/year could establish this; motives still require sources.
- **Scenario inputs:** \(10^4\) physical qubits and \(10^{-3}\) two-qubit error do not alone determine code performance. Need topology, code, syndrome/reset/measurement errors, leakage/correlations, cycle time, decoder, logical target, routing/factories, and usable yield.
- **Direct factual contradiction:** The claim that this future regime is “where small distance-\(d\) codes outperform their physical constituents” is already outdated. Google’s 2025 distance-7 logical memory exceeded its best physical qubit lifetime by \(2.4\pm0.3\) on Willow: [Nature QEC paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y).
- **Correct future milestone:** Possible decade-scale milestones are many simultaneously operating below-threshold logical qubits, fault-tolerant logical entangling/non-Clifford gates, long algorithmic logical circuits, real-time decoding, and application-relevant logical volume—not first break-even small codes.
- **Date forecast:** “Around the turn of the decade” is a vendor-roadmap scenario, not derivable from the supplied trend. The manuscript correctly says not to bank on it but should attach named assumptions/probabilities or remove the date.
- **PQC implication:** No hardware trend extrapolation in this section should set cryptographic migration deadlines. Standards/compliance and data lifetime dominate action timing.
- **Missing benchmark families:** Layer fidelity/error per layered gate, mirror/randomized/cycle benchmarking, XEB, application-oriented QED-C suites, volumetric benchmarks, Q-score/algorithmic benchmarks, logical randomized benchmarking, logical circuit volume, throughput-at-fidelity, energy, and total time-to-solution deserve a selection map.
- **Metric gaming:** Benchmark-specific compilation, qubit subset selection, postselection, mitigation, excluded failures, changing suite versions, and unpublished raw data can optimize a score without general capability. Require preregistered rules/independent runs where possible.
- **Missing longitudinal artifact:** Maintain a machine-readable, sourced dataset with raw metric, spec version, confidence, raw/mitigated, system availability, date, and independent/first-party status; generate plots rather than hand-writing trends.
- **Accessibility:** Expand QV, AQ, QED-C, CLOPS, heavy-output generation, logical error, threshold, decoder, and syndrome round. Explain why logarithmic \(2^m\) branding can visually exaggerate one increment.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The “headline numbers are contested” hook is strong, but a list of vendor metrics feels bureaucratic. A benchmark decathlon where one machine wins width, another accuracy, another throughput, and none wins the workload would be illuminating and fun.
- **Section-level rule:** A benchmark score is interpretable only with its specification version, raw circuits/data, compiler/mitigation/postselection rules, statistical confidence, hardware/calibration, independent reproducibility, and correlation with a named target workload.

## §25.6 “Transition to Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing,” definition, demonstrations, overhead, magic, and scenarios, lines 98–120

- **Coverage:** Reviewed early-FT definition, threshold scaling equation, Google/Quantinuum chronology, rotated-surface-code overhead arithmetic, algorithm conversion factor, magic-state mechanism/demonstrations/resource claim, and 2030/2035–2040 projections plus caveat.
- **Fuzzy-boundary opening:** Correct and important. Early fault tolerance should be described as a capability vector, not a universal era: below-threshold memory, repeated correction, logical operations, entanglement, non-Clifford resource, decoder feedback, logical volume, and application output can mature separately.
- **“Awkward middle” repetition:** The phrase was already used to define NISQ; using it again blurs the two. Give early FT a distinct identity: protected but scarce logical resources with error budgets that constrain algorithms.
- **Logical-versus-physical comparison:** “Logical error rates better than underlying physical rates” is meaningless unless denominators/tasks align—per syndrome round versus physical memory cycle, per logical gate versus best physical gate, encoded circuit versus unencoded circuit with equal function, and postselection/acceptance.
- **\(10^{-15}\) target:** A logical-location error of \(10^{-15}\) is one scenario for a very large circuit, not a universal “fully fault-tolerant assumption.” Total failure budget, number/type of logical locations, correlations, verification/restarts, and algorithm tolerance determine the target.
- **Threshold theorem wording:** The theorem does not belong uniquely to “the surface code”; threshold theorems cover fault-tolerant schemes under assumptions. The surface code has a code/noise/decoder-specific threshold and suppression curve.
- **Suppression equation:** \(p_L\sim A(p/p_{\rm th})^{(d+1)/2}\) is a common phenomenological fit for odd-distance surface-code memory/logical failures under particular stochastic circuit-level noise and decoder assumptions. Define \(p_L\)’s denominator and \(A\).
- **Approximation limits:** Finite distances, measurement errors, boundaries, circuit operations, leakage/correlations, coherent errors, decoder mismatch, and rare events can violate a simple one-parameter fit. Do not present it as a theorem’s exact prediction.
- **Experimental below-threshold criterion:** Decreasing \(p_L\) with increasing \(d\) under matched hardware/noise/task is core evidence, but multiple distances alone do not establish arbitrary scalable suppression. Require confidence, comparable cycles, leakage treatment, decoder, and finite-size fit.
- **Google chronology:** Google’s distance-3/distance-5 scaling paper was published in *Nature* in 2023. The distance-7 Willow work appeared as a 2024 preprint/announcement and a 2025 *Nature* publication; state both dates to avoid calling it simply a “2024 result.”
- **Google result strength:** The Willow paper reports distance-5 and distance-7 below-threshold memories, real-time decoding for one experiment, and distance-7 lifetime \(2.4\pm0.3\) times its best physical qubit. Include exact metric/cycles and remaining rare correlated-error limitations: [Nature](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y).
- **“First claims”:** Priority language needs a systematic cross-platform search and precise below-threshold definition. Use “Google reported…” unless the book can defend firstness.
- **Quantinuum vagueness:** “Different code family” is not enough. Name code(s), encoded task, physical/logical baseline, syndrome rounds, postselection, acceptance, error metric, device, date, and peer-reviewed technical paper.
- **Platform-count claim:** “More than one platform” must list every qualifying primary demonstration under one consistent criterion. Microsoft/Quantinuum reports 11×–800× improvements over corresponding physical-circuit baselines and repeated-QEC metrics, but these are not automatically the same surface-code distance-scaling test.
- **Fact-check placeholder:** “Which the factcheck layer must carry” is editorial debt, not publishable prose. The chapter is itself the layer that must attach sources/definitions before claiming cross-platform status.
- **Plans-versus-demonstrations warning:** Excellent. Apply it equally to announced qubits, roadmaps, target fidelities, commercial availability, and future logical operations.
- **Rotated-patch formula:** \(2d^2-1\) correctly counts \(d^2\) data plus \(d^2-1\) syndrome ancillas for a standard rotated planar surface-code memory patch. It excludes boundaries/routing/factories/control/readout/spares and architecture-specific leakage ancillas.
- **Arithmetic:** \(d=7\Rightarrow97\) physical qubits (about 100); \(d=21\Rightarrow881\) (about 900); \(d=29\Rightarrow1681\) (about 1,700). These checks are correct for the stated patch model.
- **\(d=29\) inference:** It depends on assumed \(A,p,p_{\rm th}\), denominator, and \(10^{-15}\) target. Referencing a later sanity check before showing assumptions makes the main text look more certain than the exercise.
- **Memory-versus-computation:** One isolated patch count is not cost per algorithmic logical qubit. Lattice surgery, logical gates, routing, factories, measurement, parallelism, code deformation, interconnect, and storage/active layouts alter space-time cost.
- **Conversion-factor range:** \(10^2\)–\(10^3+\) physical per usable logical qubit is a scenario range, not a conversion constant. Modern qLDPC, color, erasure, biased-noise/bosonic, LDPC-concatenated, and modular architectures can change overhead and requirements.
- **Dead-qubit inclusion:** Yield/spares matter, but quantify a fabrication/operation yield model rather than casually adding “dead qubits” to every architecture.
- **Cryptographic-distance warning:** Excellent. Shor’s required logical error is set by complete compiled circuit, error allocation, architecture, runtime, verification/retry, and threat scenario.
- **Clifford statement:** Surface-code schemes often implement/track Clifford operations more cheaply than non-Clifford \(T\), but “most logical operations on a surface code are Clifford” confuses available primitive set with an algorithm’s operation distribution.
- **Magic-state mechanism:** Injection/teleportation consumes a suitable encoded magic state to implement a non-Clifford operation, often \(T\). Distillation consumes multiple noisy encoded states plus logical Clifford operations/measurements to improve fidelity. Show one protocol’s input/output/error scaling.
- **Alternative universality:** Code switching, gauge fixing, transversal gates in other codes, pieceable FT, direct rotations, catalysis, magic-state cultivation, and other schemes alter the non-Clifford path. “Standard scheme” helps but a alternatives note is needed.
- **Distillation chronology correction:** The 2025 logical magic-state distillation demonstration used a **neutral-atom** processor with distance-3 and distance-5 color codes: [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15165), later published in *Nature* 645, 620–625 (2025).
- **Quantinuum distinction:** A 2025 trapped-ion experiment demonstrated high-fidelity logical magic states via **code switching**, not the same logical distillation protocol: [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14169). Do not cite “Quantinuum and others” generically as distillation.
- **“First” and publication status:** State submission/publication dates, peer-review status at cutoff, device, codes/distances, input/output logical fidelities, acceptance/postselection, qubit/circuit resources, and whether the improvement exceeds a distillation threshold.
- **Critical-path claim:** Magic-state supply is critical for common surface-code Clifford+\(T\) architectures, but a few-\(T\) application still needs injection fidelity and total error; “more than a few” has no universal threshold.
- **\(10^9T\) claim:** Name algorithms/instances/resource estimates. Demanding workloads span many orders, and Toffoli/CCZ/rotation counts are not raw \(T\)-counts until a synthesis/factory model is fixed.
- **One-state-per-\(T\):** Common injection consumes one appropriate magic state per \(T\), but catalysis, multi-output factories, CCZ resources, rotation synthesis, measurement-based schemes, and compilation can change accounting. Use the standard-model qualifier.
- **Factory fraction:** Factories can dominate or form a sizable budget depending on runtime target, parallelism, data-block layout, physical error, code distances, protocol, and algorithm \(T\)-rate. “Any future machine” is an overclaim.
- **Projection derivation absent:** “Combining current trend lines” is untenable because §25.5 explicitly maintains no dataset. Name a scenario model/vendor roadmap or do not imply quantitative combination.
- **2030 scenario:** Tens of logical qubits at modest distance may already be claimed under some error-detection/postselection definitions in 2024–2025. Define continuously corrected logical qubits, allowed operations, error, runtime, and availability so the forecast is not overtaken semantically.
- **“Beyond NISQ reach”:** A few logical qubits can execute deeper protected circuits but may remain classically simulable. Specify the demonstration class and value.
- **Chemistry caveat:** Good: useful chemistry needs state preparation, QPE/other algorithm, precision, strong classical comparisons, and total resources. Add Hamiltonian/basis/active space and observable.
- **2035–2040 scenario:** Thousands of logical qubits and \(10^9+\) logical operations do not alone establish RSA-2048 factoring. Need logical non-Clifford count/depth, code cycles, factories, physical qubits, decoder, runtime, success probability, and chosen factoring circuit.
- **Threat wording:** “Plausible under common assumptions” must identify the resource-estimation paper and exact architecture. For security decisions, possibility/time distributions and harvest-now-decrypt-later matter more than a central year.
- **Wide-error-bar caveat:** Necessary but insufficient; provide scenario names, parameter tables, distributions/sensitivity, and provenance. Otherwise precise years invite anchoring despite the disclaimer.
- **Missing milestones:** Add logical two-qubit gates, logical teleportation, repeated correction, real-time decoding, logical non-Clifford preparation/injection/distillation, multi-logical-qubit algorithms, logical-volume benchmarks, and independently accessible operation.
- **Missing visual:** A milestone ladder should show demonstrated as of cutoff, peer-reviewed/preprint/announced, and what each proves/does not prove. Never place projections on the same visual footing as measurements.
- **Accessibility:** Define code distance, threshold, syndrome ancilla/round, patch, lattice surgery, magic state, injection, distillation, Clifford+\(T\), factory, QPE, logical location, and error budget.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.4/10.** The overhead ladder and magic-state factory turn “logical qubit” into visible machinery. Mixing demonstrations and forecasts weakens suspense; a verified milestone ladder followed by scenario sliders would be gripping.
- **Subsection rule:** Every early-FT milestone must name encoded task, code/distance, physical resources, rounds/operations, raw/postselected metric, physical baseline, decoder/control, confidence, publication status, and which next capability remains missing.

## §25.6 projection critique, industry guidance, sanity checks, and footer, lines 121–142

- **Coverage:** Reviewed forecast-retrospective paragraph, “honest industry view,” all four capability-building arguments, recommended adoption pattern, all five sanity checks, separator, and bottom navigation.
- **Forecast-history claim:** “Early-2010s forecasts generally…” and “several 2020-era timelines slipped” need a collected forecast dataset with prediction date, target capability/date, revisions, and outcome. The paragraph itself acknowledges selection bias; without the dataset, delete the directional verdict.
- **Missed “both directions”:** If claiming misses in both directions, provide examples of unexpectedly fast and unexpectedly slow progress under fixed milestone definitions. Otherwise the phrase functions as balance without evidence.
- **“2025-vintage projections”:** There is no single current best guess. Vendor roadmaps, expert elicitation, markets, national plans, and resource-estimation scenarios differ and have incentives. Name sources and cutoff; by July 2026, 2025 projections are not automatically current.
- **Best-guess language:** A scenario is not a forecast distribution. Provide assumptions/sensitivities and avoid ranking it “best” without calibration.
- **“Honest industry view” framing:** No single industry view exists. Label this as the authors’ evidence-based recommendation and document consultation/search methodology; “honest” delegitimizes disagreement.
- **Production-advantage conclusion:** It may be reasonable that no broadly accepted public production-workload advantage exists at the cutoff, but this requires definitions and a systematic review, especially after 2025 D-Wave and Quantum Echoes claims.
- **Unavailable-answer epistemology:** One cannot prove an answer is unavailable from every laptop/HPC/tensor network. Say that no documented classical method under the matched resource/error budget was found. Include all classical methods, not only tensor networks.
- **Hardware-result value:** “Getting an answer” is not enough; require correctness/uncertainty, reproducibility, task utility, total cost/time/energy, and a matched classical baseline.
- **Proprietary claims:** Correctly identified as hard to assess. Treat missing circuit/data/code/cost as unverified, not as evidence for or against advantage.
- **Five-year counterfactual:** “Might not be able to get classically in five years” is speculative and may reverse direction as classical methods improve. Build capability because of strategic learning/options under explicit scenarios, not an unverifiable future classical gap.
- **Business-case structure:** Separate option value, research learning, workforce development, supplier evaluation, cryptographic compliance, and expected computational value; each has a different owner, budget, horizon, and success metric.
- **Tooling lead-time claim:** Multi-year team-building depends on starting expertise, scope, hiring/partners, and whether work is experimental or production. Cite organizational evidence or state a planning scenario.
- **VQE-centric skill risk:** Training primarily for “VQE-style code” may overfit a declining NISQ paradigm. Durable skills include quantum information, Hamiltonian/problem structure, resource estimation, compilers, error correction, benchmarking, classical HPC/tensor methods, uncertainty, and crypto agility.
- **Problem formulation:** Not every relevant task should be forced into a Hamiltonian. Include circuits, channels, sampling, linear algebra, chemistry encodings, and classical reformulation; a failed mapping can manufacture an artificial quantum project.
- **Start-late aphorism:** Catchy but ignores opportunity cost and vendor/tool churn. Recommend staged reversible investments with review gates rather than universal early hiring.
- **Algorithm-R&D claim:** “Many algorithms have not been written yet” is unfalsifiable. Better: current known algorithms/resource estimates leave gaps in state preparation, I/O, fault-tolerant primitives, constants, verification, and application mapping.
- **Real-device relevance:** NISQ behavior can teach control, compilation, measurement, workflow, and benchmarking, but early-FT logical interfaces/noise/cost may differ radically. Identify transferable versus perishable knowledge.
- **PQC duration:** A blanket 10–15-year exercise is organization-specific and, from 2026, may extend beyond official 2035 targets. Replace it with jurisdiction/sector guidance and asset-specific plans.
- **Current NIST guidance:** NIST’s PQC page says organizations should begin migrating and describes deprecation/removal of quantum-vulnerable standards by 2035, with high-risk systems earlier: [NIST PQC project](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/Post-Quantum-Cryptography).
- **Current UK guidance:** NCSC targets initial estate-wide planning by 2028, highest-priority migration by 2031, and completion by 2035: [NCSC timeline](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/pqc-migration-timelines).
- **Migration rationale:** The asymmetry/harvest-now-decrypt-later reasoning is strong. Also include standards maturity, protocol/product dependencies, long-lived roots of trust, asset secrecy lifetime, signing/update chains, interoperability, inventory, crypto agility, and rollback.
- **Action separation:** PQC migration is justified by finalized standards, government guidance, data lifetime, and migration lead time; it must not wait for the chapter’s speculative hardware schedule.
- **Workforce claim:** Scarcity, cost, and future hiring-price direction require labor-market data. “Hire now because later costs more” is an investment prediction; alternatives include training, partnerships, consultants, shared centers, and vendor services.
- **Workforce target:** “Quantum-aware” is too vague. Specify roles and competencies, and avoid building a team whose only success criterion depends on hardware advantage arriving.
- **Typical-team recommendation:** Simulators-first and small controlled hardware pilots are sensible low-regret steps. Require a classical-baseline-first policy, narrow hypotheses, reproducibility, budget caps, security/IP assessment, and explicit stop/continue gates.
- **Chapter 26 cross-reference:** Chapter 26 should provide the actual pilot template and current service access; otherwise this remains strategy prose without execution.
- **Capital-investment ambiguity:** Distinguish purchasing hardware/equity, cloud credits, research hiring, partnerships, migration, and production integration. “Defer serious capital” is not one actionable rule and could conflict with approved PQC spending.
- **Advantage gate:** Waiting for an algorithm with demonstrated advantage on the exact team problem may be too late for supply/integration, while investing before technical validation may waste capital. Use real-options/staged milestones instead of a binary deferral.
- **Quarter/long-arc aphorism:** Memorable and appropriately cautious. Pair it with quarterly deliverables—inventory, benchmark, trained staff, baseline, reproducible pilot—so the long arc has accountability.
- **Sanity check 1 arithmetic:** Solving \(nd\epsilon/2=1\) with \(n=100,\epsilon=0.005\) gives \(d=4\). The per-worldline \(1/\epsilon=200\). The discrepancy is 50 entangling-gate locations per full layer versus one per worldline; global \(1/e\) fidelity does not determine local observable utility.
- **Check 1 precision:** Reiterate that \(\epsilon\) must be a toy stochastic failure probability, not silently a benchmarked average infidelity.
- **Sanity check 2 arithmetic:** \((0.1)^{(d+1)/2}\le10^{-15}\) requires \((d+1)/2\ge15\); the smallest odd \(d\) is 29. Patch count \(2(29)^2-1=1681\). The supplied boundary hint is correct.
- **Check 2 realism:** \(A=1,p/p_{\rm th}=0.1\) is hypothetical; the result is a memory-patch payload, not a full logical qubit/factory/computer. Ask sensitivity for \(A\), ratio, and total operation count.
- **Sanity check 3 arithmetic:** \(2pSK=2(200)(10^4)(300)=1.2\times10^9\) shots. At \(1\) ms/shot serially, \(1.2\times10^6\) seconds = 333.3 hours = **13.89 days**, before queue/overhead.
- **Check 3 bottleneck:** Under the toy assumptions, serial shot acquisition dominates. Measurement groups increase circuits/shots; adaptive allocation can reduce or redistribute them; batching reduces submission/control overhead but does not eliminate physical repetitions.
- **Check 3 wording:** It defines \(S\) per expectation and one group, avoiding §25.3’s ambiguity. Add optimizer objective evaluations if a baseline/line search is also required.
- **Sanity check 4 logical inconsistency:** §25.4 defines computational advantage broadly enough to include useless synthetic tasks and says such advantage was plausibly demonstrated. Asking for reasons Sycamore/Jiuzhang “do not directly establish quantum advantage in the §25.4 sense” contradicts that framing.
- **Check 4 repair:** Ask separately whether each establishes (a) matched, dated computational advantage and (b) practical useful advantage; then discuss classical-estimate uncertainty, verification/metric, utility, and later baselines.
- **IBM comparison:** IBM’s experiment targeted physical observables/“utility,” not a sampling-supremacy benchmark. Later classical reproduction bears on comparative advantage, while measurement accuracy/scale and scientific-method contribution can remain. The answer key must preserve this distinction.
- **Sanity check 5 count:** With 1,000 physical qubits and one isolated rotated patch, \(2d^2-1\le1000\) gives \(d\le22.37\); largest conventional odd distance is \(d=21\), consuming 881 qubits, so only one such maximum-distance patch fits before all other overhead.
- **Check 5 ambiguity:** “Number of logical qubits simultaneously” depends on chosen \(d\): at \(d=21\), one; smaller distances permit more. No target logical error/algorithm is supplied, so there is no optimal distance/count.
- **Check 5 underdetermined verdict:** A 99.5% “fidelity” alone cannot identify \(p/p_{\rm th}\), code-cycle error, measurement/reset/leakage/correlations, decoder, or required \(p_L\). Therefore one cannot determine whether count or fidelity is dominant. Make recognizing insufficiency the explicit intended answer.
- **Missing sanity check:** Add a PQC planning exercise based on data lifetime + migration time > uncertain threat time, using current NIST/NCSC milestones rather than asking readers to predict Q-day.
- **Missing chapter bridge:** There is no prose bridge to Chapter 26 after the exercises; add what readers will actually do next and which claims they will test on a simulator/hardware service.
- **Footer:** Previous/TOC/next links are appropriate and match the top navigation; exact rendered-link verification remains for the global audit.
- **Accessibility:** Split multi-part checks into labeled subparts, state assumptions/units, provide answer keys, and define HPC, PQC, VQE, QPE, FT, code patch, threshold, and production workload.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** The strategy section speaks directly to real decisions, and the sanity checks expose headline arithmetic. Unsupported workforce/forecast claims feel like consultancy prose; official migration milestones and a staged pilot decision case would add credibility and tension.
- **Chapter-close rule:** Invest according to independently valuable milestones and reversible learning; migrate cryptography on standards/risk timelines; never make security or capital plans depend on a single quantum-hardware forecast.

## Chapter 25 whole-file synthesis, exact reconciliation, and checkpoint

- **Coverage reconciled:** Reviewed source lines 1–142, including title/status/navigation/opening/reading map, §§25.1–25.6, all platform/constraint/mitigation/benchmark/scenario/industry bullets, two equations, five sanity checks, separator, and footer. All six source headings at lines 11, 23, 49, 72, 86, and 98 have corresponding fine-grained ledger entries; longer §§25.2 and 25.6 were intentionally split without gaps or overlaps.
- **Strongest conceptual contribution:** The chapter tries to convert hype into operational quantities: global versus local error budget, connectivity overhead, shots and wall time, mitigation variance, classical-baseline movement, logical-code overhead, and organizational lead time. Its repeated refusal to equate a hardware milestone with useful advantage is valuable.
- **Strongest rhetorical contribution:** “Reality check,” “different currencies,” “the system you are not yet able to compute with,” and “do not bet the quarter on the short arc” make abstract limitations vivid. The skeptical tone is most credible when paired with arithmetic.
- **Primary structural weakness:** NISQ, advantage history, benchmarking, error mitigation, early-FT resource estimates, industry strategy, and PQC migration are too many jobs for 142 lines. Sections compress research reviews into confident sentences, while §25.4 duplicates Chapter 24 and §25.3 duplicates Chapter 18.
- **Primary currency weakness:** A chapter explicitly set in 2026 stops its advantage narrative before major 2025 D-Wave and Quantum Echoes publications, calls 2025 forecasts the current best guess without sources, uses mutable vendor metrics/specs, and leaves “factcheck layer” placeholders in prose.
- **Highest-priority factual repairs:** Replace Sycamore “depth 20” with 20 cycles; describe IBM’s 2.5-day result as a proposed estimate, not a completed matched run; correct Pan’s GPU count via the Chapter 24 ledger; distinguish Google’s 2024 preprint/2025 publication for Willow; acknowledge below-threshold distance-7 memory already beat a physical-qubit lifetime; distinguish 2025 neutral-atom logical magic-state distillation from Quantinuum code switching; add D-Wave 2025 and Quantum Echoes 2025 before making current advantage claims.
- **Highest-priority quantitative repair:** The \(2pGS\) optimizer formula requires \(S\) per measurement group, not per full expectation. Explain RB/process infidelity versus stochastic failure probability before multiplying \((1-\epsilon)\). Treat \(O(\sqrt n)\) as one routing-distance bound, not total overhead. Do not use physical fidelity alone to decide a surface-code distance.
- **Highest-priority security repair:** Replace “PQC migration is a 10–15-year exercise” with current jurisdiction/sector guidance. NIST calls for migration now and targets removal/deprecation of vulnerable standards by 2035 with high-risk systems earlier; NCSC targets planning by 2028, priority migration by 2031, and completion by 2035. Cryptographic action must be independent of speculative quantum timelines.
- **Era-model repair:** Replace a linear pre-NISQ → NISQ → post-NISQ calendar with overlapping capability axes: active physical scale, task circuit volume, error detection, below-threshold memory, logical operations, multi-logical entanglement, non-Clifford resources, real-time decoding, logical volume, and application output.
- **Benchmark discipline:** QV, AQ, CLOPS, layer fidelity, logical error, and application benchmarks require specification versions, raw/mitigated status, circuit suite, compiler freedom, postselection, success thresholds, confidence, hardware/calibration, and independent replication. Do not hand-write trend percentages without a dataset.
- **Advantage discipline:** Separate physical experiment, acceptance score, matched output/error, classical algorithm/hardware, measured versus projected resource, complexity assumption, scientific utility, company/media framing, and later response. “No known public production advantage” must be a dated systematic-review conclusion, not an industry slogan.
- **Variational discipline:** Expand total execution as optimizer points × gradient shifts × measurement groups × mitigation/randomization variants × shots; report original and active-space problem sizes separately; include all classical preprocessing and matched baselines. Mitigation is a family of different bias/variance/model transformations, not a generic correction knob.
- **Fault-tolerance discipline:** Compare logical and physical errors with aligned denominators/tasks; distinguish memory from gates/algorithms; attach code/distance/rounds/decoder/postselection/confidence to every milestone; distinguish demonstrations, peer-reviewed results, preprints, and roadmaps.
- **Recommended architecture:** Use a dated capability dashboard, one worked 100-qubit workload/invoice, one claim-evolution case study linked to Chapter 24, a versioned benchmark table, a verified early-FT milestone ladder, and explicit scenario sliders. Move full mitigation theory to Chapter 18, classical frontier history to Chapter 24, hands-on service details to Chapter 26, and binding crypto guidance to Chapter 27.
- **Reproducibility contract:** For current hardware/advantage claims archive source/cutoff, device and calibration, active qubits/connectivity, native gate/error metric and simultaneous context, circuit/task/output, compiler/mitigation/shots, raw data/confidence, queue/QPU/host/energy/cost, strongest matched classical baseline, and later revisions.
- **Pedagogy:** The toy global-fidelity calculation and all five exercises are strong foundations. Fix exercise 4’s contradiction about Sycamore/Jiuzhang “not establishing” the chapter’s own broad definition; make exercise 5’s underdetermination explicit; provide answer keys including \(d=4\), \(d=29/1681\), \(1.2\times10^9\) shots/13.89 days, and \(d=21/881\) patch arithmetic.
- **Accessibility:** Acronyms and expert terms accumulate quickly: NISQ, QEC, RB, QV, AQ, QED-C, CLOPS, VQE/QAOA/UCC, ZNE/PEC/CDR, QPE, PQC, OTOC/XEB/GBS, code distance/patch/factory. Expand locally or link a glossary, and visually separate evidence, scenario, and recommendation.
- **Best new artifacts:** 2026 evidence dashboard; stochastic-versus-coherent toy-model lab; cross-platform calibration distributions; routing compiler comparison; VQE execution invoice; mitigation bias–variance map; normalized advantage claim timeline; benchmark-governance matrix; early-FT milestone ladder; logical resource calculator; PQC official-deadline checklist; staged industry pilot scorecard.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10 current, 9.8/10 potential.** The chapter has unusually high stakes and a lively skeptical voice. Its weakest passages read like unsourced market analysis; letting readers audit named 2025 claims, calculate hidden costs, and choose staged decisions would turn it into an excellent evidence-driven narrative.
- **Checkpoint:** Chapter 25 is complete for this pass. Cumulative tracked-file progress: **29/67 files**; Markdown progress: **29/48 files**; SVG progress: **0/19 files**.

# Chapter 26 — Practical Access and Hands-On Work

## Chapter 26 opening matter, lines 1–10

- **Coverage:** Reviewed title, status banner, navigation, keyboard-bridge opening, and linear reading instruction.
- **Title:** Clear and appealing, but “hands-on work” promises executable labs, commands, expected output, troubleshooting, and current access instructions. The chapter must deliver more than a service/SDK catalogue.
- **Status banner:** “prereviewed,” “Phase 5,” and “8 / 8” are editorial workflow metadata; decide whether public readers need them and define the status if retained.
- **Navigation:** Previous Chapter 25, TOC, and next Chapter 27 are structurally appropriate. Exact link verification remains deferred.
- **Bridge hook:** “Between book and keyboard” is concise and effective. It creates a strong expectation that readers will do something within minutes.
- **Scope list:** Simulator/device choice, access, SDK, experiment design, device-time efficiency, and literature reading are all valuable, but literature reading is a different skill from executing hardware. A compact chapter can support both if it offers actual checklists/templates.
- **“First few weeks”:** Assumes a novice/practitioner audience and a specific ramp. Add learning outcomes and prerequisites: Python/environment management, linear algebra/circuits, cloud accounts, payment/terms, and basic Git/data handling.
- **Linear instruction:** Unusually direct and useful. If every section depends on preceding choices, make the dependency explicit; the source headings suggest experiment design/reproducibility should arguably precede mutable SDK/hardware shopping.
- **Two-section recommendation:** SDK choice and reproducibility are plausible high-value picks, but skipping simulator/hardware and experiment-design sections can cause exactly the wasted device time the chapter promises to prevent.
- **Author-experience claim:** “In the author’s experience” is anecdotal, undefined, and shifts voice from the book’s collective/objective style. Either identify the experience/scope or say these are common failure modes supported by examples.
- **Missing success criteria:** By the end, readers should have a pinned environment, one simulator baseline, one small hardware run, cost/time/error ledger, archived raw results, and a reproducible report. State this upfront.
- **Missing safety/ethics:** Cloud credentials, billing caps, data/IP terms, export/access restrictions, institutional approval, and unpublished research data can matter. A practical-access chapter should at least flag them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** “Book to keyboard” promises welcome relief from theory. The reading note is efficient but not yet playful; a concrete mission—reproduce a Bell experiment locally and on hardware with a fixed budget—would supply narrative momentum.
- **Opening artifact:** Provide a one-page lab brief with goal, budget, time, required accounts, expected artifacts, and stop conditions; every later section should fill one field.
