### Opening-unit assessment

- **Central strength:** The chapter has a highly useful mission: detach “quantum computation” from a single circuit notation while retaining a rigorous equivalence and hardware map.
- **Central defect:** Model, encoding, resource set, hardware platform, algorithm family, and complexity class are repeatedly treated as interchangeable categories.
- **Strong universality correction:** Universal AQC/MBQC, anyon-model-dependent TQC, and non-Gaussian-resource-dependent CV computation need separate conditions. Quantum annealing and boson sampling must not inherit universal circuit equivalence.
- **Strong absolute correction:** Replace “every SDK/textbook/architecture paper” with evidenced majority/centrality claims.
- **Strong maturity correction:** Commercial annealers, MBQC demonstrations, universal AQC theory, topological aspirations, and photonic samplers occupy different evidence levels.
- **Strong causal correction:** Circuit dominance also comes from compositionality, digital abstraction, universality, complexity theory, compilation, and fault tolerance—not merely classical control/current hardware.
- **Recommended master table:** For every section list state space, initial resource, allowed operation, adaptivity, output, universality, efficient simulation relation, hidden precision/energy assumptions, native platforms, and maturity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The promise of multiple alien-looking but sometimes equivalent ways to compute is excellent. Conditional universality is the source of intrigue, not a caveat to bury.

## §32.1 — Adiabatic Quantum Computation

### Line 13 — section heading

- The heading correctly names the formal universal model rather than the more heuristic/physical quantum-annealing regime treated next.
- The section should explicitly preserve that distinction throughout: closed-system AQC theorem/equivalence versus open-system thermal annealing practice.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.7/10.** Energy-landscape computation is naturally inviting.

### Line 15, sentence 1, clause 1 — computation as Hamiltonian evolution

- The high-level description is accurate: encode the computation in a path of Hamiltonians rather than a sequence of gates.
- “Slow” is relative to the changing Hamiltonian, gap, matrix elements, desired error, and schedule; it is not an absolute speed.
- State that the system is ideally isolated and evolves under the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. Open-system thermalization belongs to quantum annealing.
- AQC can encode more general history-state constructions than “optimization answer in final ground state”; avoid reducing universality to classical minimization.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** Replacing instructions with a continuously reshaped energy landscape is an excellent conceptual shift.

### Line 15, sentence 1, clause 2 — easy initial ground state

- Efficient preparation of the initial ground state is a necessary algorithmic requirement.
- “Easy” should mean preparable with polynomial resources under the chosen model.
- The initial state should have sufficient overlap with the desired adiabatic branch; degeneracy and symmetry sectors can complicate the story.
- The energy scale/norm of \(H_0\) belongs in resource accounting.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.5/10.** Beginning in a simple valley is intuitive and sets up the journey.

### Line 15, sentence 1, clause 3 — final ground state encodes answer

- A final Hamiltonian can encode an answer in its ground state or ground subspace, commonly via a problem Hamiltonian.
- “Encodes” must specify readout: computational-basis measurement, local observables, energy estimation, or postprocessing.
- A degenerate solution set may occupy a ground space; the first “excited-state gap” definition below then needs treatment relative to that subspace.
- Constructing a local, bounded-norm \(H_1\) efficiently from the input is part of the algorithm and cannot be assumed free.
- The final gap may be small even if the classical solution is easy to describe.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The answer as the bottom of an engineered landscape is memorable; readout completes the picture.

### Lines 15–19 — linear interpolation

- The displayed path \(H(s)=(1-s)H_0+sH_1\) is the canonical introductory interpolation.
- It is only one path. Catalyst Hamiltonians, nonlinear schedules, inhomogeneous drivers, counterdiabatic terms, and alternate paths can change the minimum gap and runtime.
- The source contains likely malformed doubled spacing commands in `(1 - s)\\, H_0` and `s\\, H_1`.
- \(s=t/T\) enforces a linear schedule. Later discussion should distinguish changing the Hamiltonian path from changing the schedule \(s(t)\).
- Specify that \(H_0,H_1\) act on \(n\) qubits, are efficiently implementable/local, and have bounded norms/precision. Otherwise an arbitrary Hamiltonian can hide exponential resources in coefficients or interactions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** The interpolation is visually simple; an avoided-crossing energy diagram would make it vivid.

### Line 21, clause 1 — preparation under \(H_0=-\sum_iX_i\)

- With the usual Pauli convention, each \(|+\rangle\) is the \(+1\) eigenstate of \(X\), so \(-\sum_iX_i\) has unique product ground state \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\). This is correct.
- The ground energy is \(-n\) and the first excitation gap is \(2\); showing that makes “easy” concrete.
- State preparation by Hadamards is a circuit-model description useful for the equivalence theme, though native transverse-field initialization may be more physical.
- “Typically” is fair for Ising-style constructions, not universal across all AQC encodings.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** A delocalized uniform state as the starting valley is a good bridge from circuits.

### Line 21, clause 2 — evolution time

- Total runtime \(T\) is the central resource, but control precision, Hamiltonian strength, locality, temperature, and final measurement also count.
- A rescaling \(H\mapsto cH\) changes the gap and time, so gap-based claims need a bounded energy/norm convention.
- The schedule may pause or slow near the minimum gap rather than use \(s=t/T\).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.3/10.** The race between evolution speed and spectral response creates useful tension.

### Line 21, sentence 2, clause 1 — adiabatic theorem guarantee

- The adiabatic theorem broadly supports staying close to an instantaneous eigenspace when the Hamiltonian changes sufficiently slowly and an appropriate gap remains open.
- “Guarantees” needs a named theorem/version, differentiability conditions, spectral isolation, initial eigenstate, and desired error.
- Runtime depends not only on inverse gap but also on matrix elements/norms of derivatives such as \(\|\partial_sH\|\), boundary terms, schedule, and theorem formulation.
- “Relative to the inverse of the minimum spectral gap” is incomplete and may imply \(1/\Delta\) when common elementary sufficient conditions scale like a derivative matrix element over \(\Delta^2\).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** A theorem protecting the path is satisfying; the narrowing gap supplies the obstacle.

### Line 21, sentence 2, clause 2 — “stays throughout”

- **Strong exactness overstatement:** At finite \(T\), the evolved state generally remains **close** to the instantaneous eigenstate/subspace within an error bound; it does not stay exactly in it.
- The state also accumulates dynamical and possibly geometric phase, usually irrelevant for final computational-basis readout but conceptually important.
- Near degeneracy requires degenerate adiabatic theory; level crossings can invalidate the simple nondegenerate statement.
- In open hardware, decoherence and thermal transitions mean the closed-system theorem is not a complete performance guarantee.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Imperfect following around an avoided crossing is more physically interesting than exact gliding.

### Line 21, sentence 2, clause 3 — final solution state

- With sufficient runtime and conditions, the final state has high overlap with the target ground state/subspace.
- “Ends in” should be “ends close to” with success probability/fidelity.
- If the interpolation stops abruptly, endpoint smoothness and final measurement timing can affect error.
- Even a correct ground state may encode a solution that is hard to decode or validate; define output.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** Reaching the correct valley is a satisfying endpoint, especially if success probability is explicit.

### Lines 13–21 — AQC definition/theorem unit synthesis

- **Central strength:** The model is introduced through one clean path, one easy product ground state, and one final answer Hamiltonian.
- **Strong theorem correction:** Add closed-system, smoothness, gap, derivative/norm, schedule, and error conditions. Replace exact “stays/ends” with closeness to the instantaneous eigenspace.
- **Strong resource correction:** Bound Hamiltonian norm, locality, coefficient precision, control, and state/readout cost; otherwise gap/runtime can be rescaled or hidden.
- **Strong model correction:** Linear interpolation and \(s=t/T\) are examples, not the definition of AQC.
- **Pedagogical opportunity:** Plot \(E_0(s),E_1(s)\), mark \(\Delta_{\min}\), and animate fast diabatic leakage versus slow following.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** The landscape narrative is strong; an avoided-crossing figure would make this one of the chapter’s clearest model shifts.

### Line 23, sentence 1 — “runtime is gap-limited”

- The minimum spectral gap is often the dominant asymptotic bottleneck in closed-system adiabatic analysis.
- Runtime is not determined by the gap alone: path derivatives/matrix elements, schedule, error tolerance, Hamiltonian norm/energy scale, locality, preparation, and readout matter.
- “Gap-limited” is a good mnemonic if immediately expanded to “gap-and-path limited.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The narrowing gap gives the model a clear antagonist.

### Line 23, sentence 2 — minimum-gap definition

- For a nondegenerate ground state, \(\Delta_{\min}=\min_s[E_1(s)-E_0(s)]\) is the standard definition.
- If the computational solution is a degenerate ground space, the relevant gap is between the target ground subspace and the first state outside it; \(E_1-E_0\) may be zero inside the degeneracy.
- Require a positive gap along the finite-size path for the simple theorem.
- Energy ordering can change at crossings; symmetries may permit exact crossings between uncoupled sectors that do not cause transitions. The matrix element as well as raw gap matters.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.7/10.** A single smallest separation is a clear diagnostic, though degeneracy adds useful nuance.

### Lines 23–27 — displayed cubic sufficient condition

- Bounds containing terms of order \(\|\partial_sH\|^2/\Delta^3\) do occur in rigorous adiabatic theorems, so the expression can represent one contribution to one sufficient condition.
- **Strong incompleteness:** A rigorous bound commonly also contains \(\|\partial_s^2H\|/\Delta^2\), endpoint and/or path-integral terms, and explicit target error \(\varepsilon\). Displaying only one term as “the standard sufficient condition” is misleading.
- Other elementary formulations use a transition matrix element divided by \(\Delta^2\), while local schedules yield integrated gap dependence. The text’s following caveat helps but arrives after an authoritative equation.
- Specify \(\hbar=1\); otherwise the units of \(T\) need \(\hbar\).
- State whether norms and derivatives are maxima over \(s\), evaluated near the gap, or integrated. As written, \(\|\partial_sH\|\) has no \(s\) argument or supremum.
- The source contains suspicious escaped norm delimiters `\\|...\\|`, likely rendering as line breaks rather than \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\).
- “\(\gg\)” is not a quantitative theorem. Use an error-bound inequality \(T\ge C(\cdots)/\varepsilon\) tied to a citation.
- A Hamiltonian rescaling changes numerator and gap; a bounded norm/energy scale is necessary.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** The cubic gap penalty is dramatic, but an incomplete pseudo-theorem is worse than a clear scaling sketch.

### Line 29, clause 1 — cubic versus quadratic bounds

- It is good to state that there is no unique adiabatic theorem and that gap exponents depend on hypotheses/formulation.
- “Reduced to quadratic under tighter hypotheses” is too vague. Name assumptions such as boundary cancellation, analyticity, local schedule, relevant transition matrix element, or a specific theorem.
- Some improvements change error dependence or use path-integrated local gaps rather than merely replacing a power globally.
- Do not imply quadratic inverse-gap scaling is always tight or necessary.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** Competing bounds reveal real subtlety; one named comparison would help.

### Line 29, clause 2 — one-directional implication

- This is excellent epistemic hygiene. A sufficient-condition failure does not prove the algorithm or all schedules fail.
- “Closing gap” should distinguish exponentially small but nonzero finite-size gap, exact crossing, and gap closing only in the thermodynamic limit.
- A diabatic protocol, alternate path, catalyst, symmetry restriction, or problem-specific transition can succeed despite failure of a generic adiabatic bound.
- Preserve this sentence; it models the claim discipline encouraged elsewhere in the book.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The theorem not being a converse is a satisfying and important twist.

### Line 29, clause 3 — inverse-polynomial gap and polynomial runtime

- With bounded polynomial derivatives, bounded energy scale, inverse-polynomial target error as appropriate, and efficiently implementable evolution, an inverse-polynomial gap supports polynomial adiabatic runtime.
- “Bounded” should be “polynomially bounded” in system/input size.
- State the schedule and uniformity/precision assumptions; specifying Hamiltonian coefficients to exponential precision can hide complexity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** The complexity connection is clear and useful.

### Line 29, clause 4 — gap estimation hardness

- Determining minimum gaps can indeed be computationally difficult, and exact/approximate local-Hamiltonian spectral questions connect to QMA-hardness and subtler spectral-gap problems.
- “As hard as the original problem” is informal and task-dependent. Give a precise result or say “can itself be computationally intractable.”
- One need not always know the exact gap to run a heuristic schedule, but a performance guarantee may require a lower bound.
- Numerical finite-size gaps can mislead extrapolation to larger systems.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** The certificate of speed being hard to obtain is a compelling meta-computational obstacle.

### Line 31, sentence 1 — attribution and date

- Aharonov, van Dam, Kempe, Landau, Lloyd, and Regev are the correct authors of the landmark equivalence work.
- The result appeared as a 2004 preprint/conference-era work and later journal publication; use a precise bibliographic year matching the reference entry.
- The title “Adiabatic Quantum Computation is Equivalent to Standard Quantum Computation” should be cited directly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.2/10.** Historical anchoring is useful, especially for a foundational equivalence.

### Line 31, sentence 1, forward simulation — circuit to AQC

- A polynomial-size quantum circuit can be encoded into a polynomial-duration adiabatic computation using a local history-state Hamiltonian under the theorem’s construction.
- “Polynomial-norm Hamiltonian” is insufficient by itself. The Hamiltonian must have an efficient uniform classical description, polynomial locality/sparsity, controlled coefficient precision, and an inverse-polynomial gap.
- Specify the locality achieved by the cited construction and any geometry assumptions.
- Output extraction often uses clock padding so a measurement of the history state yields the final circuit output with adequate probability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Turning a time-ordered circuit into one static history encoded in a ground state is a beautiful result.

### Line 31, sentence 1, reverse simulation — AQC to circuits

- Efficiently specified local time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution of polynomial norm/time can be simulated by the circuit model with polynomial overhead and target accuracy.
- State dependence on locality/sparsity, smoothness, evolution time, norm, and approximation error. An arbitrary dense black-box Hamiltonian is not covered merely by polynomial norm.
- This direction is closely related to Hamiltonian-simulation algorithms and discretization, not an automatic “vice versa.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** The mutual simulation completes the equivalence; asymmetric assumptions deserve visibility.

### Line 31, sentence 2 — history-state construction

- Feynman’s clock/history-state idea and Kitaev’s local-Hamiltonian construction are the right conceptual lineage.
- The ground state encodes a coherent superposition over computational time steps, not simply the final state.
- Introduce the clock register:
  \[
  |\Psi_{\mathrm{hist}}\rangle\propto
  \sum_t |t\rangle_{\mathrm{clock}}|\psi_t\rangle.
  \]
- Explain propagation/check terms at a high level and why locality/clock encoding matters.
- “Sharpened by Kitaev” is informal but directionally fair; give exact references.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** A computation becoming a spatial ground-state history is one of the chapter’s most rewarding perspective shifts.

### Line 31, sentence 3 — universality conclusion

- Under the defined AQC model and theorem assumptions, calling AQC computationally universal is correct.
- “Not a weaker heuristic” is an effective contrast with quantum annealing but could imply every adiabatic hardware implementation realizes the universal construction.
- Say “the formal AQC model is universal; restricted annealers may not be.”
- Universality is not evidence of practical speedup or efficient implementation for a chosen problem.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The theoretical parity is a strong climax to the section.

### Line 33, sentence 1 — practical caveat transition

- “The practical caveats are heavy” is concise and appropriately shifts from theorem to engineering.
- Replace general weight with a structured resource audit: locality, coupling graph, energy scale, gap, control precision, temperature, coherence, calibration, and readout.

### §32.1 synthesis

- **Central achievement:** The section gives a clean linear path, an easy transverse-field ground state, the minimum-gap bottleneck, and the history-state equivalence theorem, then turns honestly to locality overhead.
- **Strong theorem correction:** Replace the incomplete \(\|\partial_sH\|^2/\Delta^3\) pseudo-condition with a cited error bound including derivative/integral terms, norm convention, \(\varepsilon\), and \(\hbar=1\), or present it explicitly as one scaling contribution.
- **Strong exactness correction:** Finite-time evolution ends close to the target eigenspace; it does not exactly remain in/finish in the ground state.
- **Strong degeneracy correction:** Define the gap above a target ground subspace when solutions are degenerate.
- **Strong equivalence correction:** Polynomial norm/duration alone are insufficient. Add locality/sparsity, efficient uniform description, coefficient precision, gap, approximation, and output extraction.
- **Strong universality correction:** Formal AQC is universal; restricted 2-local stoquastic/open annealers do not inherit that conclusion automatically.
- **Strong hardware correction:** Define \(k\)-locality, quantify gadget costs, and remove unsupported “most implementations.”
- **Strong transition correction:** Annealing is not merely AQC with its guarantee dropped; open-system thermal/diabatic dynamics can be intrinsic.
- **Recommended visual:** Avoided-crossing spectrum plus history-state clock diagram and locality-reduction inset.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** The history-state mapping and gap drama are excellent. A rigorous theorem box would make the section both exciting and dependable.
- **Readiness assessment for §32.1:** Not publication-ready until the adiabatic condition, finite-error wording, equivalence assumptions, locality/universality scope, and annealing transition are corrected.

## §32.2 — Quantum Annealing

### Line 35 — section heading

- The heading correctly separates annealing from formal AQC.
- The section should distinguish the algorithmic paradigm, ideal closed-system quantum annealing, open-system finite-temperature hardware, and products marketed as annealers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Annealing is accessible because energy-landscape intuition carries over directly.

### Line 37, sentence 1 — “noisier, heuristic cousin”

- The phrase is lively and conveys practical distance from ideal AQC.
- It is also reductive. Quantum annealing is a family of optimization/sampling protocols using quantum fluctuations and time-dependent Hamiltonians; it is not defined solely as failed/noisy AQC.
- Formal AQC can also be noisy, and ideal quantum annealing can be analyzed in closed-system adiabatic or deliberately diabatic regimes.
- “Cousin” is a good metaphor if followed by a comparison table rather than treated as a definition.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Memorable and conversational, but it prejudges the model before defining it.

### Line 37, sentence 2, clause 1 — shared physical picture

- A transverse-field driver annealed toward a classical Ising problem Hamiltonian is the standard commercial quantum-annealing architecture.
- It is not the only possible driver/path. Nonstoquastic drivers, reverse annealing, pauses, offsets, catalysts, and alternate encodings broaden the model.
- “Same physical picture” should not imply the universal AQC history-state construction; optimization annealing typically targets a classical cost landscape.
- Define a full schedule \(H(s)=A(s)H_D+B(s)H_P\), temperature, and readout basis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** Tunneling/fluctuations across a changing landscape are intuitively appealing.

### Line 37, sentence 2, clause 2 — not insisting on adiabaticity

- Many practical anneals are too short, open, or thermal to satisfy a simple closed-system adiabatic theorem.
- **Strong scope correction:** Quantum annealing does not categorically reject adiabatic operation. Some protocols aim to remain near equilibrium/ground state, some exploit diabatic transitions, and commercial schedules can contain approximately adiabatic segments.
- “Cannot guarantee” should attach to a particular device/problem/run and performance theorem. Ideal AQC also lacks an efficient guarantee when gaps close.
- The useful distinction is objective and operating regime, not guarantee versus no guarantee in absolute terms.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The ambiguity over whether transitions help or hurt is a strong practical theme.

### Line 37, sentence 3, item 1 — schedule too fast

- A fast schedule can induce diabatic transitions away from the instantaneous ground state.
- Diabatic transitions are not always purely harmful; carefully designed schedules can exploit them and later return amplitude to useful states.
- “Too fast” is relative to gaps, matrix elements, schedule, and target success metric.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Overshooting and recovering through excited states gives annealing more character than a failed slow evolution.

### Line 37, sentence 3, item 2 — environment too warm

- Thermal excitations matter when \(k_BT\) is not small relative to relevant instantaneous gaps.
- The environment can also relax excited populations toward lower energy, so open-system coupling can help or hurt depending on timing/rates.
- State physical temperature, effective energy scale, freeze-out, decoherence basis, and control noise; “warm” alone is not informative.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** A thermal bath acting as both enemy and possible relaxation aid is an engaging complication.

### Line 37, sentence 3, item 3 — 2-locality

- **Logical category error:** Being 2-local does not imply nonadiabaticity or absence of an adiabatic guarantee. It constrains expressivity/embedding and the available Hamiltonian family.
- Universal 2-local AQC exists with suitable interactions/encodings, as the previous paragraph itself states.
- Commercial transverse-field Ising restrictions—coupler graph, coefficient range/precision, stoquastic driver—matter more specifically than “2-local only.”
- Move locality into a hardware/encoding-cost sentence, not a list of reasons adiabaticity fails.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.1/10.** Important engineering constraint, currently placed in the wrong causal chain.

### Line 37, sentence 4, clause 1 — sampled output

- Repeated anneals do return classical bit-string samples after measurement, rather than a mathematical guarantee of the ground state.
- One run yields one readout (subject to readout/error processing); many runs define an empirical distribution.
- The device’s distribution is generally not a simple Gibbs distribution of final \(H_1\). Freeze-out, open-system dynamics, control errors, embedding, schedule, and readout transform it.
- For sampling applications, diversity and distribution quality may matter independently of best-found energy.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Treating the machine as a sampler rather than an oracle is an important mental shift.

### Line 37, sentence 4, clause 2 — “biased toward low energy”

- **Guarantee overstatement:** A well-functioning annealing protocol is designed to concentrate probability on low-energy states, but arbitrary schedules/devices need not produce a reliably low-energy-biased distribution.
- Define performance empirically: time to solution at target confidence, residual energy, approximation ratio, success probability, time to target, or sampling divergence.
- Calibration error means the implemented \(H_1\) may differ from the programmed one; a low energy under hardware can differ from low intended logical energy.
- Ground-state success can be exponentially small even when typical samples improve over random.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The probabilistic treasure hunt is engaging once success is measured rather than promised.

### Lines 35–37 — annealing-definition unit synthesis

- **Central strength:** The paragraph rapidly communicates that practical annealers are finite-time samplers rather than guaranteed ground-state oracles.
- **Strong definition repair:** Define quantum annealing positively as an optimization/sampling paradigm using a time-dependent quantum driver, not only as noisy AQC.
- **Strong causal repair:** Separate diabatic schedule, thermal/open-system dynamics, and Hamiltonian locality; 2-locality does not cause nonadiabaticity.
- **Strong output repair:** Describe the empirical device distribution and metrics; do not guarantee it is low-energy biased or final-Hamiltonian Gibbs.
- **Pedagogical opportunity:** A regime diagram with axes \(T_{\mathrm{anneal}}\Delta\), \(k_BT/\Delta\), and system–bath coupling would distinguish coherent adiabatic, diabatic, thermal-relaxation, and frozen regimes.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The practical landscape is rich and approachable; treating dynamics as more than “failed adiabaticity” will make it more interesting.

### Lines 39–43 — final Ising problem Hamiltonian

- The displayed form
  \[
  H_1=\sum_i h_iZ_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j
  \]
  correctly represents a diagonal 2-local Ising problem Hamiltonian under a common convention.
- The physical annealing Hamiltonian also includes a time-dependent transverse driver and schedule functions, typically schematically
  \(H(s)=A(s)H_D+B(s)H_P\). Saying the machines “implement an Ising model” and showing only \(H_1\) hides the actual anneal.
- Sign, scale, and factor conventions differ between documentation and theoretical Hamiltonians; define which spin value corresponds to a \(Z\) eigenstate.
- Hardware biases/couplings have bounded programmable ranges, finite precision, calibration error, and working-graph defects. Those limits are computational resources.
- Constant energy offsets do not affect argmin but matter when deriving QUBO conversion.
- The source again contains likely malformed doubled spacing commands after \(h_i\) and \(J_{ij}\).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** A compact energy function is accessible; overlaying the fading transverse driver would make it truly an annealer.

### Line 45, clause 1 — restricted coupling graph

- Connectivity alone does not determine embeddability/performance; coefficient ranges, chain strength, yield, and calibration matter.

- Current commercial figures are volatile and should come from dated filings or audited disclosures, with vendor framing labeled.
- Suggested wording: “This broad formulation has supported an ecosystem of research, pilot, and commercial engagements, although public evidence rarely isolates end-to-end QPU advantage.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** Real adoption matters, but case-study evidence is more interesting than customer-count implication.

### Line 49, sentence 4, clause 4 — no complexity guarantee

- It is correct that commercial use does not require a complexity-theoretic speedup theorem; heuristics can create value through quality, workflow, or convenience.
- Conversely, customer use is not evidence of computational advantage. The sentence should keep both directions.
- Define business success metrics separately from quantum-advantage metrics.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** The theory-versus-value distinction is mature and useful when supported with outcomes.

### §32.2 synthesis

- **Central achievement:** The section gives a coherent practical arc from time-dependent Ising dynamics through QUBO submission, sparse connectivity, embedding, samples, benchmarks, and customer-facing applications.
- **Strong definition correction:** Quantum annealing is not just noisy AQC; adiabatic, diabatic, thermal, and open-system regimes coexist. Two-locality is not a cause of nonadiabaticity.
- **Strong hardware correction:** Show the full \(A(s)H_D+B(s)H_P\), hardware ranges/precision, and Chimera → Pegasus → Zephyr/Advantage2 chronology.
- **Strong workflow correction:** Algebraic QUBO mapping is only the first step. Include constraint penalties, quadratization, embedding, chain tuning, coefficient scaling, gauges, unembedding, and postprocessing.
- **Strong runtime correction:** Separate anneal microseconds from programming, thermalization, readout, embedding, cloud latency, hybrid processing, and time to target/solution.
- **Strong equivalence correction:** The restricted D-Wave model is not known circuit-equivalent; broad enough annealing/AQC models can be universal.
- **Strong evidence correction:** Present the 2025 D-Wave *Science* beyond-classical simulation claim, classical challenges, and July-2026 contested status. Do not map it to generic industrial QUBO advantage.
- **Strong tunneling correction:** Quantum dynamics/tunneling can be physically real without causing a best-classical computational speedup.
- **Strong embedding correction:** Embedding is conditional on graph mismatch; chain strength has a two-sided tradeoff, and decoder/postprocessing choices alter outputs.
- **Strong industrial correction:** QUBO encodability and customer engagements do not prove QPU usefulness or advantage. Require logical-size overhead, independent outcome, and isolated QPU contribution.
- **Recommended visual:** End-to-end funnel showing business model → QUBO → logical Ising → minor embedding → scaled hardware coefficients → anneal/readout → chain decoding → classical validation, with variable/qubit counts and wall time at each step.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** The hardware pipeline, tunnel-versus-hop metaphor, and live supremacy dispute are excellent. This can become a standout evidence-literacy section.
- **Readiness assessment for §32.2:** Not publication-ready until model regimes, 2-local causality, current hardware chronology, end-to-end timing, 2025–2026 evidence, tunneling inference, embedding tradeoffs, and commercial causality are corrected.

## §32.3 — Measurement-Based Quantum Computation

### Line 51 — section heading

- The heading clearly names the model and follows the expected progression from continuous Hamiltonian evolution to measurement-driven computation.
- The section should distinguish the original qubit cluster-state model, general graph-state MBQC, fusion-based computation, and continuous-variable MBQC.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Computing by destroying a prepared entangled state is naturally counterintuitive.

### Line 53, sentence 1, clause 1 — acronym and one-way terminology

- Expanding MBQC and naming the one-way model is correct and useful.
- Raussendorf and Briegel proposed the model in 2000/2001; the detailed Raussendorf–Browne–Briegel treatment appeared in 2003. Align dates/authors with exact references.
- “One-way model” originally refers specifically to cluster-state computation; MBQC now includes broader resource states and formalisms.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** The “one-way” name creates curiosity that the consumption explanation later rewards.

### Line 53, sentence 1, clause 2 — “inverts the gate-model picture”

- The contrast is effective: gates distribute coherent processing through time, whereas MBQC front-loads entanglement and uses measurements/classical control.
- MBQC resource preparation itself ordinarily uses entangling operations or fusion, so unitary/gate-like work has not vanished.
- Gate teleportation already connects the two pictures; “repackages” may be more precise than “inverts.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** The apparent reversal is an excellent section hook.

### Line 53, sentence 2, clause 1 — simple circuit input versus resource state

- Standard circuits often begin with a simple product input and apply gates, while MBQC begins with an entangled resource plus any injected input.
- Some circuits begin with nontrivial entangled/magic resources, and MBQC must still encode or inject an arbitrary input. Avoid an absolute dichotomy.
- “Large, fixed” should mean a fixed graph-state family for a compiled computation; resource size and shape depend on the algorithm.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Front-loading a giant entanglement fabric is visually compelling.

### Line 53, sentence 2, clause 2 — “highly entangled”

- Cluster states possess multipartite entanglement that enables universality, but “amount of entanglement” alone does not determine resource quality.
- Some highly entangled states are not universal MBQC resources, and too much generic entanglement can even correlate with classical simulability/poor structure in certain senses.
- The relevant properties include graph structure, localizable entanglement, measurement flow, and correctability.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The distinction between entanglement quantity and useful structure is a rewarding nuance.

### Line 53, sentence 2, clause 3 — 2D square-lattice cluster

- A two-dimensional cluster state is the canonical universal resource and a good default example.
- One-dimensional cluster states support only limited/single-qubit processing and are not universal for arbitrary quantum computation, which explains why 2D matters.
- Other universal graph/resource states and topological 3D cluster constructions exist.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** A quantum “fabric” with a spatial computation direction is easy to visualize.

### Line 53, sentence 2, clause 4 — adaptive single-qubit measurements

- Adaptive local single-qubit measurements with classical feed-forward are the defining runtime operations in one-way MBQC.
- Some measurements (notably Clifford portions) can be parallelized or made nonadaptive with Pauli-frame tracking; non-Clifford dependencies drive measurement depth.
- Measurement bases, order/partial order, outcome processing, and output qubits should be explicit.
- “Sequence” may imply total seriality; use dependency layers.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** Random measurements collectively enacting deterministic logic is the model’s central fascination.

### Line 55, sentence 1 — cluster-state construction

- Initializing \(|+\rangle\) on graph vertices and applying controlled-\(Z\) on every edge is the standard graph/cluster-state construction.
- Neighboring CZ gates commute, and on a square lattice can be scheduled in a constant number of edge-color layers under ideal parallel control.
- In photonics, deterministic CZ is precisely the hard operation, motivating probabilistic fusion/resource factories; do not let the simple definition imply simple preparation.
- A graph-state notation \(|G\rangle=\prod_{(u,v)\in E}CZ_{uv}|+\rangle^{\otimes |V|}\) would help.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** One repeated entangling rule generating the entire resource is elegantly simple.

### Line 55, sentence 2, clause 1 — stabilizer property

- A cluster state is a stabilizer state, with generators \(K_v=X_v\prod_{u\in N(v)}Z_u\).
- Giving this formula would connect directly to earlier stabilizer/error-correction chapters and make verification methods concrete.
- Being a stabilizer state means the unmeasured resource is efficiently classically describable; quantum computational power arises with the measurement pattern/adaptivity and non-Clifford bases.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.3/10.** The apparently classically tractable starting state becoming universal through measurements is a productive surprise.

### Line 55, sentence 2, clause 2 — universal measurement patterns

- A sufficiently large 2D cluster state with suitable adaptive single-qubit measurements is universal and can implement arbitrary circuits approximately.
- “Any logical quantum circuit” needs a gate set, approximation tolerance, input/output mapping, and resource overhead.
- Universality is a property of the resource family plus allowed measurements/feed-forward, not of one fixed finite cluster.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** One universal substrate serving every circuit is a strong concept.

### Line 55, sentence 2, clause 3 — logical rows/columns

- Mapping logical wires to rows and computational time to columns is a useful introductory picture for rectangular cluster compilations.
- It is not universal notation: measurement patterns can route, delete, merge, teleport, and use irregular graph states; orientation can be exchanged.
- Nonlocal gates may require routing/crossings/extra width unless the circuit is already nearest-neighbor.
- State “in a simple rectangular compilation.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** Space becoming computational time is an excellent visual shift.

### Line 55, sentence 2, clause 4 — measurement teleportation/gates

- Measuring intermediate qubits teleports logical information through the graph while applying basis-dependent rotations and Pauli byproducts; this is correct.
- Give the one-bit teleportation identity for a short chain. It would explain the model much better than prose alone.
- An angle \(\theta_k\) does not specify the plane/sign convention; commonly measurements use \(M(\alpha)=\{|\pm_\alpha\rangle\}\) in the equatorial plane.
- Two-qubit logical gates rely on graph connectivity and measurements, not merely independent row teleportation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Teleportation doing useful gates as a side effect is one of the chapter’s best moments.

### Line 55, sentence 3, clause 1 — random outcomes

- Individual measurement outcomes are intrinsically random, even though the intended logical computation can be made deterministic up to known byproducts.
- Outcome distributions may also contain algorithmic output randomness; distinguish byproduct randomness from desired sampling.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Deterministic computation assembled from random local events is an excellent paradox.

### Line 55, sentence 3, clause 2 — adaptive corrections

- Later basis angles can depend on previous outcomes so unwanted Pauli byproducts propagate in a controlled Pauli frame.
- Not every byproduct requires a physical correction; classical tracking can defer many corrections to output interpretation.
- Measurement dependencies are characterized by flow/gflow in graph-state MBQC; mentioning this would turn “known correction rule” into a precise structural condition.
- Classical latency and detector/switch timing can limit photonic clock rates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.8/10.** Feed-forward taming randomness is the model’s key algorithmic trick.

### Line 55, sentence 3, clause 3 — one-way consumption

- Measurements irreversibly consume measured resource qubits/entanglement, motivating the “one-way” terminology.
- The computation can still include logical reversible/unitary evolution; “one-way” refers to resource consumption, not irreversibility of the logical algorithm.
- Failed preparation/fusion may permit rerouting around defects in sufficiently redundant resource states.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.7/10.** A quantum fabric burning behind the computation is a memorable image.

### Line 57, sentence 1 — universality theorem attribution

- Raussendorf, Browne, and Briegel’s 2003 detailed work proves universality of one-way computation on cluster states; the original Raussendorf–Briegel proposal dates to 2000/2001.
- Cite exact paper/year rather than call it only “the key theorem.”
- “Arbitrary single-qubit measurements” should include adaptive choice and classical processing; universality does not mean any arbitrary set of measurements succeeds.
- Output qubits may remain unmeasured or be measured for classical output.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.4/10.** The theorem is a satisfying formal payoff to the teleportation picture.

### Line 57, sentence 1, clause 2 — polynomial equivalence

- Universal MBQC and circuit computation can simulate one another with polynomial overhead under standard uniformity/precision assumptions.
- The reverse direction is straightforward because cluster preparation/measurements can be represented by circuits; the forward compilation requires resource-state creation and adaptive measurements.
- Equivalence in computational power does not equal fault-tolerant, photonic, or constant-factor equivalence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Another alien-looking model returning to BQP reinforces the chapter’s thesis.

### Line 57, sentence 2 — \(O(wd)\) cluster overhead

- **Qualification required:** A circuit with \(S\) local gates can generally be compiled to a graph/cluster measurement pattern with polynomial and often constant-per-gate overhead, but a blanket \(O(wd)\) rectangular claim assumes a suitable gate set, nearest-neighbor layout/routing, and depth definition.
- Width times depth upper-bounds circuit slots only when each layer has \(O(w)\) local gates; arbitrary nonlocal interactions may require routing and extra spatial area/depth.
- Measurement pattern size includes wires, gate gadgets, input/output, error correction, and possible padding.
- Fault-tolerant topological cluster-state overhead scales with code distance and magic-state resources far beyond bare \(wd\).
- Use circuit size \(S\) for the clean equivalence claim, then give \(O(wd)\) only for a specified local rectangular compilation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.9/10.** Space–time area is a powerful intuition; assumptions determine whether it is trustworthy.

### Line 57, sentence 3 — classical feed-forward

- Feed-forward is intrinsic rather than an auxiliary correction layer, which is an important architectural observation.
- A section reference to §9.9 should later be checked for exact notation/content.
- “Cost built into the model” does not mean cost-free. Classical processing, signal fanout, detector latency, switching speed, synchronization, and memory determine measurement depth and hardware clock.
- Clifford byproducts can often be tracked cheaply; non-Clifford adaptive choices impose causal latency.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.2/10.** Quantum speed being gated by classical reaction time is a useful systems insight.

### Line 59, sentence 1 — photonic fit

- MBQC/fusion-based architectures are highly relevant to photonics because destructive measurement is natural and deterministic photon–photon entangling gates are difficult.
- Photonics is not the only natural MBQC platform; trapped ions, neutral atoms, superconducting qubits, and solid-state emitters can generate graph states.
- “Naturally” should be tied to loss tolerance, flying qubits, multiplexing, and measurement rather than treated as self-evident.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The model solving a substrate-specific interaction problem gives theory a clear engineering purpose.

### Line 59, sentence 2, clause 1 — photon preparation

- **Overstatement:** High-quality indistinguishable single photons on demand are not simply easy to prepare. Source brightness, purity, indistinguishability, collection efficiency, multiplexing, spectral matching, and deterministic timing are major challenges.
- Parametric sources are probabilistic and can generate multiphoton noise; quantum-dot/emitters require fabrication/coupling/control.
- Some photonic architectures use squeezed/GKP/encoded states rather than bare single photons.
- Suggested wording: “Photons propagate and are measured naturally, but deterministic indistinguishable source generation and photon–photon interaction are difficult.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** The source challenge is an important part of the photonic engineering drama.

### Line 59, sentence 2, clause 2 — photon measurement

- **Overstatement:** Single-photon detection is mature relative to deterministic optical interaction, but high-efficiency, low-dark-count, low-jitter, fast-reset, photon-number-resolving detectors with scalable cryogenic/readout integration are not “easy.”
- Detection is destructive, which fits MBQC but makes loss indistinguishable from some logical outcomes unless encoded/flagged.
- Include detector efficiency and loss threshold as architecture resources.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Destructive measurement being a feature rather than a bug is compelling.

### Line 59, sentence 2, clause 3 — interaction difficulty

- Deterministic high-fidelity two-photon gates are difficult because photons interact weakly in ordinary media; this is a sound motivation.
- Measurement-induced nonlinearities, ancilla photons, matter interfaces, and fusion operations trade determinism for resources and loss tolerance.
- “Each other” could be replaced by “deterministically at the single-photon level.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** Noninteracting light forcing architectural ingenuity is a strong constraint story.

### Line 59, sentence 3 — offline resource-state generation

- Moving entangling/fusion work into resource-state factories is the central architectural shift.
- “Offline” does not always mean a whole cluster is prepared in advance. Fusion-based schemes can build resource states just in time with multiplexing, switching, and percolation/error correction.
- Storage/delay lines are needed to synchronize probabilistic successes, introducing loss.
- The manuscript commendably says the interaction problem is relocated, not eliminated; preserve that claim.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Relocation rather than magical removal is an excellent engineering lesson.

### Line 59, parenthetical — fusion/multiplexing/switching/loss

- The listed costs are exactly the right photonic bottlenecks.
- Add source quality, detector performance, mode matching/indistinguishability, delays/memory, feed-forward latency, and fault-tolerance overhead.
- “Probabilistic and expensive” varies by fusion protocol and encoding; give success probabilities and loss thresholds for a cited architecture.
- Resource count should include photons per successful logical operation/resource state.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** The factory logistics are complex but visually engaging and concrete.

### Line 59, sentence 3, runtime clause

- Once a valid resource state exists, computation proceeds primarily through local measurements and classical feed-forward.
- Resource generation may be interleaved with runtime, so separating “offline” and “runtime” can be architecturally false.
- Photon propagation, delay, switching, detector reset/readout, decoding, and adaptive basis choice set clock speed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.1/10.** A measurement pipeline consuming a streamed cluster is a strong systems picture.

### Line 59, phrase “high-efficiency but short of deterministic”

- The grammar is unclear: measurements are deterministic operations conditioned on photon arrival, while detection efficiency is below unity and fusion succeeds probabilistically.
- “High-efficiency” requires a number, detector type, system efficiency, and date.
- Detector loss and fusion failure are distinct erasure/probabilistic events with different architectural handling.
- Rewrite as: “detectors can be highly efficient but still lose photons; fusion operations are intrinsically probabilistic in common linear-optical schemes.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.6/10.** Precise failure modes are more informative than a compressed qualifier.

### Line 59, company clause — PsiQuantum

- PsiQuantum publicly identifies fusion-based quantum computing as the basis of its photonic architecture, so inclusion is supportable.
- Vendor architecture, roadmap, fault-tolerance thresholds, manufacturing claims, and timelines should be dated and linked to technical papers rather than executive pages alone.
- “Target” signals roadmap rather than deployment, which is appropriately cautious.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **7.8/10.** Named architecture programs make the theory current, provided marketing is labeled.

### Line 59, company clause — Xanadu

- Xanadu is unquestionably a major photonic/CV quantum-computing company and has public GKP-state work relevant to fault-tolerant photonics.
- **Architecture-specific evidence needed:** The available official result emphasizes on-chip GKP photonic qubits and loss reduction. The manuscript should cite the exact paper showing how the current target architecture belongs to the same MBQC/fusion/cluster family.
- Xanadu’s historical CV cluster-state and Gaussian boson-sampling work should not be conflated automatically with its current fault-tolerant roadmap.
- State whether the intended reference is temporal-mode CV cluster computation, GKP-encoded MBQC, or another architecture.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** Contrasting fusion-based and GKP/CV routes could enrich the section substantially.

### Line 59, final sentence — CV cluster bridge

- Continuous-variable cluster states are a direct and appropriate bridge to §32.5.
- Finite squeezing introduces noise at each teleportation step; Gaussian cluster states alone need non-Gaussian resources for universal quantum computation.
- Previewing those two constraints would make readers eager for the later section.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The qubit-to-oscillator extension is a natural cliffhanger.

### §32.3 synthesis

- **Central achievement:** The section explains the one-way model through a clean prepare-entanglement → measure → teleport/gate → adapt → consume sequence and connects it credibly to photonic architecture.
- **Strong attribution correction:** Separate the 2000/2001 Raussendorf–Briegel proposal from the 2003 Raussendorf–Browne–Briegel detailed universality treatment.
- **Strong mechanism correction:** Add graph-state stabilizers and one-bit teleportation; these two equations would make the model click.
- **Strong overhead correction:** \(O(wd)\) requires local compiled circuits and ignores routing/fault tolerance. Use circuit size \(S\) for the general polynomial claim.
- **Strong classical-cost correction:** Feed-forward is native but not free; measurement dependency depth, latency, switching, and decoding matter.
- **Strong photonics correction:** Photon preparation and measurement are not simply easy. Separate source, detector, fusion, interaction, delay, and loss challenges.
- **Strong architecture correction:** “Offline” can be just-in-time/streamed; measurements, detection loss, and fusion failure are different.
- **Strong vendor correction:** PsiQuantum fusion-based status is supported; identify the exact Xanadu CV/GKP/cluster architecture rather than group by company name.
- **Recommended visual:** A five-qubit linear cluster one-bit-teleportation derivation, followed by a rectangular cluster with measurement dependency arrows and a streamed photonic resource factory.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.2/10.** Random outcomes, teleportation gates, classical corrections, and a consumed entanglement fabric make this one of the chapter’s most engaging sections.
- **Readiness assessment for §32.3:** Not publication-ready until theorem chronology, \(O(wd)\) assumptions, measurement identities, feed-forward costs, photon-source/detector difficulty, and vendor architecture specificity are corrected.
